text:
FLORA

OF THE PHILIPPINES,

ACCORDING TO THE SEXUAL SYSTEM OF LINNAEUS:

By Father Fr. Manuel Blanco,
CALCED AUGUSTINIAN.

SECOND PRINTING, CORRECTED AND ENLARGED

BY THE SAME AUTHOR.

MANILA:
Press of D. Miguel Sanchez.
1845.

MISSOURI
BOTANICAL
GARDEN.

PROLOGUE.

It was never my intention to compose a treatise on plants worthy of public attention. A simple curiosity moved me to write down what I found interesting; but some distinguished persons who learned of this useful pastime urged me repeatedly to publish it. Our August Sovereign, the former Governor, also had the inexplicable kindness to direct that I be exhorted to do so; and although this was for me a source of great confusion, it overcame my reluctance in the end, and I brought to light for the first time the work entitled Flora de Filipinas.
Fortunately my work has merited (so it appears) the acceptance of the learned, and received applause when I least expected it — applause that can only be owed to my patience. Compelled a second time by the repeated requests of persons of learning and standing, and equally desirous of being useful with my limited knowledge, the said work is now reprinted, after correcting many faults caused by the haste and carelessness with which it was written the first time, and enlarged as my advanced age and habitual ailments have permitted; for although in the judgment of the learned it will fall far short of a perfect work, it will serve at least to give some notice, however slight, of the immense riches of this pleasant land, and at the same time will encourage and spur others to continue the same labor.

1

II
The history of the plants of the Philippines is, therefore, a worthy undertaking for a professional Botanist who enjoys the confidence of the learned, and whose work might appear without embarrassment before the enlightened public of our times. Yet I had no teachers, no herbaria, and scarcely any books at all when I began to understand this subject. My only guide at the time was Linnaeus's Systema Vegetabilium. I later acquired some works by the same author, and the immortal work of Jussieu, along with other books.
In these Islands there have always been individuals passionate about this field of study, who, if they have made less progress, it has certainly not been through laziness, but rather through the extreme scarcity of books on the subject, the poor quality of the paper and printing, and the incorrigible incompetence of the native copyists. Had we been aided by more favorable circumstances, we would have no reason to envy other nations their most famous naturalists. It is incredible how much has been written in these Islands on all subjects; yet almost all of it remains unpublished for the same reasons.
But confining myself to the natural sciences, the Fathers Clain, Delgado, Mercado, and Santa-María will always deserve eternal gratitude: the first two belonging to the Society of Jesus, the third an Augustinian, and the fourth a Dominican. I have drawn upon all of them for this work. Father Clain, in addition to other pious books, published a work on practical medicine which, with some modifications, would still be very useful even for our Spain.
Father Delgado, a man of singular talents, wrote an immense work on the natural riches of this country, which has not been published for the same reason.
Father Mercado explained with great acclaim the properties of many plants, accompanying his explanations with beautiful hand-drawn illustrations; but this most valuable work, which was kept in the infirmary of the convent of St. Augustine in Manila, has disappeared, as Father Agustín María, another celebrated writer of the same convent, had predicted. Some loose fragments of the work of this diligent Friar do survive, however, and they make the loss of the rest all the more keenly felt.

III
Father Santa-María, tireless in uncovering the secrets of plants, published a curious little work that is quite well regarded.
If these men and others whom I omit had enjoyed better circumstances, we would today find ourselves abundantly informed regarding the inestimable riches of the Philippine plant kingdom. They did not manage to produce masterful and select works that could have served as guides, and in these times only the occasional one reaches us by chance, despite the islands being abundantly supplied with every whim and trifle that novelty-seeking Europe produces each day.
Our benevolent monarchs have not been remiss in ordering that the natural productions of this land be carefully investigated, and at the beginning of this century the learned botanist Don Antonio Pineda, sent by our Kings for this very purpose, died in these Islands.
As for the work I offer to students of the subject, I must note that I have taken every possible care to determine the names that the native peoples give to plants, since they possess precious secrets concerning their virtues, though some of these are not very well founded. Nevertheless, one should not expect to find in this complete certainty, for it is intolerable how easily they confuse and mix up names. For this reason I have often noted the place where a plant is found and the name given to it there, even though unfortunately many of these are not widely known. For those that are known, it will not be difficult to identify them through one of the names listed in their entries. On this point the indolence of the natives is astonishing, and anyone wishing to devote himself to this kind of investigation must be prepared to endure great hardships and constant frustrations, sometimes merely to obtain the flower or fruit of a tree, or to determine its name with certainty. Very few individuals value this type of occupation, and many look upon it with disdain. I myself have been discouraged by this very thing a thousand times, and entire years have passed without my setting a single stroke of the pen in my notes.
At the beginning of this work I have given a brief idea of botanical philosophy, along with a short nomenclature of

IV
the most precise terms of this science, since books dealing with this subject are very rare in these Islands. In this I claim no merit other than having compiled it from other authors.
I find it convenient to note that when I say a plant is found in a certain town, and that it flowers in a certain month, I mean only to indicate the place and time when I personally saw it in flower.
Finally: anyone who does not wish to tire himself reading the description of each plant, but whose desire is to learn about its history and properties, may pass directly to the two dashes that follow, after which I set down everything I have been able to gather that is most reliable and curious about them. I have done it this way for two reasons: first, because many people consider this the most interesting and agreeable part, and second, to foster an appreciation and esteem for a science so unjustly looked down upon. For this same reason I have indicated the uses that plants may have with regard to medicine and industry; for while in other countries this might be considered unnecessary, in this one it is useful, and even essential.

INTRODUCTION.

1. Botany is a branch of natural science whose object is the study of plants.
2. Plants comprise seven families, which are Fungi, Algae, Mosses, Ferns, Grains, Palms, and Plants. By grains are understood the gramineous plants, e.g. wheat, barley, oats, etc.
3. The foundation of Botany consists of Classification and Nomenclature. Classification encompasses the division or grouping of plants. The classification of plants by joining or separating them from one another based on the characteristics of their fructification is an invention of the moderns. This arrangement or coordination of plants by means of a system or method began to be practiced principally in the eighteenth century. Botany is chaos without the guidance of a system. Suppose a plant from a distant land is presented. One wishes to know what plant it is, and to find out one must search through all the descriptions, figures, and indexes. Only by chance might one come to know it. But one who is guided by a system easily identifies it and places it in its proper position.
4. It is true that by means of a system we wish to imagine a certain order of things that perhaps does not exist in nature: that of the systems invented for identifying plants, some are clearly unsuitable for the purpose, and others can easily lead us astray, grouping together in monstrous fashion genera that ought to be kept apart, and vice versa. To this the response is: since a natural method is as yet unknown — one that would join or separate plants from one another in the hidden manner that God has ordained, or since the natural classes that truly unite those plants which should be united, and separate those which by natural right should be separated, are not well known; and since it is on our part indispensable to know plants — not in just any manner, but with exact precision, for they supply us with food, drink, medicine, clothing, and a host of other articles necessary or useful for life — it is essential that we devise some means of knowing them, whatever it may be. It only remains to choose the one that is least at odds with what is observed in nature.
5. The systems invented by the moderns for identifying plants are therefore not natural but artificial; their purpose is to discover the characteristics that distinguish some plants from others, and those they have in common, and in this way to unite those that resemble one another, to distribute them into classes, orders, and genera, and to separate those that are unlike. The best known and most widely followed systems

VI
Until recently, the systems used by scholars were two: that of Tournefort, and that of the cavalier Carlos Linnaeus.
6. The first is founded on the shape of the corolla. The second on the number, proportion, and position of the stamens, which are the male parts of plants. From these Linnaeus formed his classes, taking the orders from the female organs, which are the pistils. He published his system in 1734.
These two artificial methods, like others yet to be invented, will be all the more valuable the closer they approach that hidden order and natural chain that exists among plants. This conformity, or natural chain, has been the object of study for many celebrated Botanists, including Linnaeus himself, who found the fragments he proposed in his works. The famous Antonio Lorenzo de Jussieu also presented to the public his immortal work General Plantarum, based on careful examination and observation of the constant conformity that plants share among themselves. This method, according to which one must carefully observe the insertion of the stamens and corolla, is undoubtedly far superior to the others and should be preferred, because it is not founded, as they are, on a single character — for example that of the stamens, which is sometimes very unreliable — but rather on the conformity or resemblance among all their organs, some of which are of greater value than others. Following this method, many genera that strictly require being united are not left so widely separated and disordered, since they share many common points of contact, as happens with the others, where proceeding by those methods there is always some risk of error. It is true that until the links of the natural chain of plants are fully uncovered, this method will be no more than artificial; but among these it is undoubtedly the best. On this subject, read the authors who deal with this matter.
7. The system for identifying plants proceeds by dividing them into classes, orders, genera, species, and varieties. Just as to identify a particular person within a kingdom we would divide it into provinces, these into towns, these into households, and finally the households into individuals. Varieties are nothing more than species or individuals disguised or modified by some accident.
8. Thus a class is a collection of many genera that agree in the parts of fructification, according to the principles of nature and art. Orders contain the same genera of a class, divided into groups: or they are a subdivision of classes so that, with the genera distributed into many sections, it is easier to find the one being sought — for it will be found more quickly among ten than among a hundred.
9. If certain specific species share certain common characters of fructification, we say they are similar, and this similarity is what is called a genus.

VII
10. Genera, then, being a subdivision of orders, are at the same time a collection of the specific modes of fruiting that are common to all the species falling under each one. There are as many genera as there are different fructifications, or as many close and shared attributes as are found among different natural species. A genus may be very aptly compared to a family or kindred, whose members share a common surname, even though each individual has a particular name by which we distinguish him. But when is a difference in fruiting sufficient to warrant forming a new genus? This is precisely where botanists disagree: some insisting that the difference must be very marked, others being satisfied with a small one — which is why some are very rigid and reluctant to form new genera, while others multiply them with ease. In my view, the latter fault is the more harmful of the two.
11. Species are a subdivision of genera; they agree with one another in all that is essential to fructification, while differing in the other parts that make up a plant. To include a species within a genus, some botanists require that it agree with the other species in all generic characters; but others only require agreement in the greater part, even if it differs in some other respect — for otherwise there would be as many genera as there are species, since among the latter some difference is always to be noted.
12. Varieties are the different plants that arise accidentally from the seed of one and the same species, or are the same species altered in various ways. These alterations reduce to flavor, color, texture, and size. Hence these accidents produced by cultivation constitute varieties of one and the same species, but do not form a distinct species. Habit, Appearance, or Exterior aspect in plants refers to a certain conformity observed among vegetables that are related to one another. It is noted, for example, that many plants resemble one another most in the manner of Rooting, in Branching, in their Glands, Buds, Stipules, Milky juice, etc.
13. Classes may be natural; (6) but until these are perfectly understood, they are replaced by the artificial classes of the systems, and the orders, which are merely a subdivision of the classes. (8) Genera (says Linnaeus, though others deny it) are natural, and so likewise are species. The resemblance found among the species in the greater part of the characters that agree with one another, as was said above, is what constitutes the natural generic character, by means of which we arrive at knowledge of the genus.
14. It should be noted that the generic character may be Artificial, or Factitious, Essential, or Natural.
15. The Artificial character, better called by others Differential, is formed by assigning to a genus a single note by which it must be distinguished from the others that fall under the same section or

VIII
order, and not from the others found in distinct orders. This generic character called Artificial would be the easiest, if all genera were already discovered; but since they are not, it follows that this character is deceptive; beyond which, once a new genus is discovered, all the nearest characters become false, as do all those derived from the division or branch to which they are united.
16. The Essential character, which is not arbitrary, and which would be the best of all, consists of a singular note common to all the species belonging to the same genus, as is manifested in the nectaries of Parnasia, Nigella, and Ranunculus. But it is difficult to find this Essential character in all genera; although Linnaeus has discovered it in some others, and has placed it among the singular or outstanding notes of his Systema naturae. Moreover, the character presently held as essential may one day cease to be so: as if a plant of the natural genus Ranunculus were found that lacked the nectariferous pore, which today is considered essential to that genus, for then that character would be false, since it would not be common to all the species.
17. Having set forth the disadvantages of the Factitious and Essential characters for the better knowledge of plants, there remains only the Natural Generic Character, which sets out all the possible characteristic notes of fructification, and it was for this reason that Linnaeus decided upon it. This character encompasses the other two, and consists, as has been said, in the resemblance that species bear to one another, not in one but in all parts of their fructification. The notes that stand out most among all those constituting the natural generic character, and which should not be called essential except in a few cases, but rather singular or outstanding, are those which I set forth in this treatise under the Description of the genus. It is true that they do not always furnish a sufficiently clear idea of the genus; but in such cases one may consult the works of other authors, where the natural generic character is found in full detail.
18. For the formation of genera, no other characteristic notes should be taken than those founded on the Number, Figure, Site, and Proportion of all parts of fructification. These parts of fructification, namely the Calyx, Corolla, Stamens, Pistil, Pericarp, Seed, and Receptacle, with the various forms each one may have, combined with the number, figure, site, and proportion of those same parts, are more than sufficient for the description of thousands of genera that may exist. The proportion of the same parts of fructification, however, must still be set aside, as it is not constant.
19. The character of the genus is thus formed so that the genus may be known. So it is that the character flows from the genus, and not the genus from the character. The character does not constitute the genus, but rather the genus constitutes the character. It should be understood, however, that other authors maintain the contrary. The figure of the flower is more reliable than that of the fruit; but the Proportion of its parts is very diverse and not always constant. The Number in the parts of fructifica-

IX
tion is more slippery than the Figure. The site of the parts of the
fructification is entirely constant.
20. Every plant without exception is endowed with flower and fruit,
which is what constitutes fructification. The flower and fruit comprise
seven things, namely: Calyx, Corolla, Stamens, Pistil,
Pericarp, Seed, and Receptacle.
21. The calyx, which is what surrounds the corolla from the outside, and covers it, or what others call rosette, exists in seven forms, according
to the different shapes it takes. Namely: 1st Perianth, which is
the one observed in the greater part of plants. 2nd Involucre.
3rd Ament or Trama, or Beard. 4th Spathe or Garrancha. 5th
Glume. 6th Calyptra or Cover. 7th Volva or Sac. The Peri-
anth is distinguished from the Bract in that the former withers at the
ripening of the fruit and the bracts do not. See these words in the
nomenclature. Sometimes the calyx is monophyllous, or of one piece, and is
split at the edge in various parts, which are called Laciniae. In
this treatise, whenever I speak of the calyx, without adding anything else,
I understand it as the perianth calyx. The calyx is diphyllous, triphyllous, tetra-
phyllous etc., when it is of two, three, four, or more pieces or leaflets.
Today botanists call the calyx of one piece monosepалous; and disepalous, trisepalous, tetrasepalous, and polysepalous, those of two,
three, four, or more pieces.
22. The Corolla is that part of the fructification that draws everyone's
attention for the beauty and arrangement of its parts. Some
Spanish botanists very aptly call it Rosette.
The piece or pieces that form it are called Petals, whose number
must be counted from the base of the corolla. It may consist of
one petal or of many. If of one, it is called monopetalous, and di-
petalous, tripetalous, tetrapetalous, pentapetalous, hexapetalous etc., if it
is composed of 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 etc., pieces or laminae, which is
well known when the flower dries. Sometimes the corolla is mono-
petalous; but the limb is split in various parts, which are called
Laciniae, and the number of these is taken from the middle of the limb.
If the corolla is polypetalous and its laminae are split in parts,
then the number of these Laciniae is taken from the middle
of the laminae.
23. The corolla has various parts which are the Limb, Claw, La-
mina or Piece. See these words in the nomenclature. It should be
noted carefully that regularly each stamen corresponds
to the incisions of the corolla: or it alternates (in position)
with the stamens, and in this it differs from the calyx (when one or
the other is absent) because the calyx is opposed to the stamens, or its
parts stand opposite the stamens. I said above regularly,
because occasionally one sees that the corolla does not alternate with the
stamens. Sometimes there is in the corolla a part called
Nectary, which is a deposit that contains honey; but this term
has been much criticized by botanists for the vagueness of
its meaning.
24. The authors who pride themselves on following the method they call
2

X
natural man, they scrupulously observe the insertion of the corolla
with respect to the germ, which is of three kinds, namely: epigynous,
hypogynous, and perigynous. Epigynous is the term used when it rests upon
the germ, as in the composites, for example in the Thistles,
Chamomiles, in the Umbellifers, Rubiaceae and others. Hypogynous is
when the germ rests upon it, as in thyme and radish.
Perigynous is when it is inserted around the germ, or upon the
calyx as in the Amaranth family and Rosaceae. (Lathyrus, Rosa.)
25. The stamens are the masculine parts of the flower, and are com-
posed of Filaments, Anthers, and the Pollen that these shed
for the act of reproduction. See Nomenclature. The stamens may
be united, either by the anthers as in the class Syngenesia,
or by the filaments, forming one body, and from this results the
class monadelphia. If they are united in two bodies, the result is the class
called diadelphia: and if in three or more, the class polyadelphia.
26. In the same way as we said regarding the corolla (24), one should ob-
serve the insertion of the stamens with respect to the germ: the
stamens will thus be Epigynous when they or the monopetalous
staminiferous corolla are inserted upon the germ as in the Umbellifers,
or Aparasoladas. They will be Hypogynous if they are inserted below
the germ, as in the Labiates and Cruciforms. Perigynous, if
they are inserted in the calyx, as in the Rosaceae. Sometimes the in-
sertion of the corolla, if the stamens arise from it, indicates the in-
sertion of these: and so in the sunflower (Helianthus) the stamens are in-
serted in the corolla, and the corolla upon the germ: consequently the
insertion of the stamens is epigynous.
27. The Pistil is the female part of the flower, and consists of the Germ,
Style, and Stigma. See Nomenclature.
28. The Pericarp is like the Uterus, or the Ovary in animals,
and it is what contains and covers the fruit. By the various forms
it takes, it may be a Cagilla, Berry, Silique, Legume, Folli-
cle, or Husk, Drupe, Pome, Citino, Samara, Glande, and
Cone. See Nomenclature. It may also be an Achene, Dia-
chenium, Triachenium etc., as in the umbellifers, parsley etc., and
Caryopsis like the grains of wheat, oats, etc.
29. The seed is the fruit that is to give rise to the new plant.
By its various shapes it is called Seed, Nut, and Propagule. See No-
menclature. The seed has its own teguments, which break open
at the expansion of the cotyledons in the plants that have them:
for there are some that lack them, others have only one, and
others have two, such as beans, broad beans, and kidney beans, in which
two thick little lobes are clearly visible at germination, which are the
so-called cotyledons or seed leaves. Also notable in the
seed is the scar called by Linnaeus the hilum and by others the um-
bilicus, through which the umbilical cord enters, which joins the seed to
the placenta. Finally, botanists carefully observe in the
seed the perisperm, which Jussieu names it, and which today others call
endosperm, which is like the white of an egg and serves as
nourishment for the expansion of the embryo.

XI
30. The Receptacle, also called the thalamus, is the base or ground upon which the parts of the fructification are placed, and by its various forms it is called the Proper Receptacle, Common Receptacle, Umbel, or Parasol, Cyme, and Spadix. (Spadix.) See Nomenclature.
31. The parts of the flower, then, are: the Calyx, Corolla, Stamens, and Pistil. The parts of the fruit are: the Pericarp, Seed, and Receptacle. The fructification, therefore, is composed of the flower and the fruit.
32. The structure or form of the fructification can be of three kinds: Most Natural (which may also be called Regular), Different, and Singular; and this according to the four criteria of Number, Figure, Proportion, and Site.
33. The most natural structure of the fructification is taken from what is most generally observed in plants, and it is as follows. The Calyx tends to be thicker and shorter than the corolla; the corolla is generally more delicate than the calyx. The Pistil occupies the center of the flower within the stamens. The Anthers occupy the tip of the stamens. The Stigmas are found at the upper end of the Style. The natural Structure is recognized by experience.
34. The most natural Number consists in the segments of the calyx being as many as those of the corolla, with an equal number of stamens, and each of these with its own anther. The parts of the pistil tend to correspond in number with the cells of the pericarp.
35. The most natural Figure is: that the calyx, rising nearly upright, supports the corolla, which widens more than it, along with the stamens and pistil, erect and tapering toward the tips; and when all these parts perish, except the calyx, it thickens and extends into the pericarp, which contains the seeds. The corolla most often approximates more or less the shape of a funnel.
36. The most natural Proportion is: that the calyx be smaller than the corolla; that the stamens and pistils be equal in length when the flower is upright; if it is inclined downward, the pistil is longer. If the flower rises forming an arch, the stamens and pistils are hidden beneath the upper side.
37. The most natural Site is: that the calyx in plants (21) envelops the Receptacle; above it grows the corolla farther inward; then follow the filaments, at whose tips the Anthers are found. The center of the Receptacle is occupied by the germen, above which rises the style, and at the tip of the style the Stigma. When these parts fall away, the germen grows (and is called the Pericarp), supported by the calyx, and encloses the seeds.
38. The Different Structure is taken from those parts of the fructification that differ greatly among various plants. This is the basis for genera and their character.
39. The Singular Structure is taken from some rare mode of fructification observed in a few genera, such as the articulated filaments in sage (salvia).
40. The Receptacle is found at the base of the germen in the greater part of plants. It is also found at the apex of the germen

XII
in many. And it is found finally encircling the germ in several, and in others it surrounds it on all sides. This observation is of importance, since the Icosandrias and others of the natural order that Linnaeus brings under numbers 45, 46, 47, and 48, have a monopetalous calyx, on the inside of which runs a line to which the petals and stamens are attached. In the Cucurbitaceae, the calyx surrounds the Receptacle on all sides, and to it the corolla is as if glued.
41. The Filaments of the stamens are fixed in the monopetalous corollas (except those that have bicornate Anthers;) but in the polypetalous corollas the filaments are not fixed within them, except rarely or in very few plants.
42. Flowers are either Complete or Incomplete. Complete flowers are those that have both a calyx and a corolla. Incomplete flowers lack one of the two. If they lack a Corolla, they are called Apetalous; if they lack a Calyx, Naked: though this name is more properly given to those lacking both. Jussieu always calls calyx whichever of the two things is present when there is only one; but Linnaeus calls it calyx if it is not colored, and corolla if it is. Mr. Cavanilles always calls corolla the tegument that immediately covers the germ and stamens, whatever color it may be.
43. Flowers are also either Simple or Aggregate. A Simple flower is one whose parts of fructification have nothing in common with other flowers, but is rather an isolated flower with no relation to others.
44. An Aggregate flower is one in which many partial flowers or florets are united in such a way that if one is removed, the form of the whole is destroyed; or they share some part of the fructification in common, namely the Receptacle or the Calyx. The Aggregate flower is of seven kinds: Compound, Umbellate, or Parasol-like, Cymose, properly Aggregate, Amentaceous, Barbate, Glumose, and Garranchose, or Spataceous.
45. A Compound flower is an aggregate of many sessile florets, contained within a common calyx and a whole Receptacle common to all; each one has a one-piece corolla and is epigynous, with the anthers united in a cylinder and a single seed, as in the Syngenesiae, which are the only ones that should properly be called compound. The compound flower is Ligulate, Tubular, or Radiate. Compound ligulate florets (which Tournefort calls Semiflosculose) are those whose corollas are all flat and spread out toward the outer side, like ribbons. Compound Tubular florets (which Tournefort calls flosculose) are those whose corollas are all tubular, or equal, and not ribbon-like. Compound radiate florets are so called when the corollas of the Disk (the center of the flower) are tubular, and those of the Margin (or circumference) are irregular, whether ligulate or virtually naked.
46. An Umbellate or Parasol flower is an aggregate of many flowers whose common receptacle is divided into Peduncles radiating from a single center. The properties of Umbellate flowers are

XIII
1st the ovary below the corolla: 2nd five deciduous and distinct stamens: 3rd the bifid pistil: 4th two seeds joined at the end. The anise. Furthermore, in Umbellate flowers there is an involucre; Umbel and Radius (See Nomenclature.)
47. The Cymose flower, or Cup inflorescence, according to Cavanilles, is an aggregate of many flowers whose common receptacle divides into peduncles that emerge from a single center; but the partial peduncles are scattered irregularly, and not with equal spacing; nor are they bare as in the umbel, but rather have other shorter little stalks.
48. The properly Aggregate flower or Head is one that has a flattened receptacle, on which the florets sit as if sessile, forming a head as in the composites (45), and also the Knautia, the Cephalanthus, and the Globularia, etc.: but these are distinguished from those by their anthers and in other respects.
49. The Amentaceous flower, or catkin, barb, or weft, is one whose receptacle for the florets is filiform, or of equal thickness, distinct with scales. The Pine, the Cypress, the Parietaria, the Willow.
50. The Glumose flower is one that has a filiform receptacle called a rachis, rib, or chaff, which contains many small sessile florets or ones with a small stalk, separated from each other by small scales called glumes. Wheat, Barley, etc. This inflorescence is called a spike, and it is simple when the spike does not divide into others, as in those cited: if it subdivides into other spikes, it is called a compound spike.
51. The Spatheceous or Garranchosa flower is one whose florets are fixed on a common receptacle called a Spadix or Tamara, and this is found inside a bag or membranous covering that bears the name Spathe or Garrancha. The spadix or universal stalk of the flowers is branched when it subdivides into other smaller ones as in the palms, or simple as in the arums.
52. Besides what has been said, flowers also occur in Racemes, in Panicles, in Spikes, in Clusters, in Stars or Whorls, etc. See Nomenclature.
53. It is necessary to note that Monstrous or Luxuriant flowers occur, and this happens when the calyx and the corolla multiply in such a way that the other principal parts of the flower are destroyed. These monsters in flowers occur in various ways: Multiplied, Full, Proliferous, and Mutilated flowers are given.
54. A Mutilated flower is one that lacks a corolla, even though it should have one.
55. A Multiplied flower is said to occur when the corolla (with some stamens spared) doubles or triples. The Calyx and the Involucre rarely contribute to a multiplied flower: and the stamens almost never do. Monopetalous flowers multiply frequently. Polypetalous flowers also multiply sometimes.
56. A Full flower is when the corolla multiplies to such a degree that all the stamens are excluded. This occurs when the stamens turn into petals, and filling the flower, they smother the pistil, principally when the stamens are completely excluded. Polypetalous flowers very often become full, like the Rose, the Carnation, the Tulip, and the Gumamela. Monopetalous flowers

XV

68. Aggregate (Flowers) See introduction 44.
69. Thread-like (Filaments, tube of the corolla, etc.) In my opinion, this word may be substituted in place of filiform.
70. Wing (Of a seed.) It is a membrane attached around it. Dioscorea
71. Wing (Of the stem of a plant.) It is a leaf-like membrane that runs along the length of the stem. Some Syngenesiae. The same is said of the Wing of the petiole.
72. Wings (of the Butterfly flower.) These are the two petals that are on either side of the Keel or Quilla.
73. Halberd (Leaves shaped like.) See up to lance-shaped. Folia hastata.
74. Winged (Leaves) or Pinnate. Those that have a common simple petiole, which has many leaflets on its sides. The leaflets may be alternate (79) winged, and opposite (337) winged. They may also have an Odd one at the tip, which refers to a leaflet that is in the middle of the last two at the end of the petiole. They may be winged without an Odd one, when they lack such a leaflet at the tip of the petiole. The Cassia. Beyond this: they may be two, three or four times winged, when the primary petiole subdivides two, three or four times. See twice winged. (201) They will also be called interruptedly winged when between the large leaflets there are other small ones, as in the country tomatoes. They will also be called jointed-winged, when there are joints between the leaflets. Finally they will be called scurringly pinnate, when the common petiole is winged. The Quassia of the islands.
75. Right wing or Left wing. This is said commonly of climbing plants, that curl or twist toward the right of someone imagined standing in the center facing south, or toward their left (471.) Dextrorsum Sinistrorsum volvulis caulis.
76. Awl-shaped (Stipules, Leaves, Petals, Pistil, etc.) All these things are called such, when being linear (307) at the base, they taper imperceptibly toward the tip. Folia subulata.
77. Scimitar. It is the fruit in some plants, and of that shape. Legumen acinaciforme.
78. Smooth (Trunk or stem.) When it has no roughness or prominences. Caulis laevigatuus.
79. Alternate (Leaves.) When those on one side of the trunk follow one another and as if by degrees, with respect to those on the opposite side.
80. Butterfly-shaped or papilionaceous (Flower) Flos papilonaceus. This is said when the corolla is irregular, namely: the inferior petal, shaped like a little boat and called the Keel: the two lateral petals, the Wings: and the upper petal called the Standard or Vexillum. All these parts, as they together vaguely resemble a butterfly, take their name from it. The diadelpias, and other plants.
81. Catkin, beard or weft. It is one of the species of the calyx

XVI
(21) which contains many flowers clustered on a thread-like receptacle furnished with many scales. Hence the flowers are called Amentaceous, or flowers of trama, or candelilla. (446.)
82. Heaped (Leaves.) The same as imbricated or packed, but not pressed together, rather separated from one another. Folia conferta.
83. Angiospermia. One of the two orders of Didynamia, comprising all those genera in which the fruit is covered or enclosed within a pericarp. By this the fruit is distinguished from one that has no pericarp, or is naked, and which in that case belongs to the other order called Gymnospermia.
84. Angular (leaves): those that have many prominent angles along their edges.
85. Anthers. One of the parts of the stamen, found regularly at the tip of the filament. The shape of the anthers is usually like a small tassel, though they also occur in various other forms. They constitute the male genital part, releasing the pollen enclosed within them so that the germ may be fertilized. The anthers are sometimes fused together, and from this arises the class Syngenesia of Linnaeus. Sometimes they also do not emerge from the tube of the corolla, and are then called included or enclosed: if they protrude outward, they are called exserted, exsertas, or exterior. The same may be said of the filaments.
86. Anthodium: the calyx of the Syngenesiae.
87. Ovate (Leaves): those whose outlines resemble the shape of a hen's egg, so that the most pointed part is the apex of the leaf. If the most pointed part is the base of the leaf, they are called reversed ovate, or obovate.
88. Ovate-lanceolate (Leaves): those that are ovate at the base and then become lanceolate, approaching an oblong shape.
89. Ovate-oblong (Leaves): those that are ovate at the base and then become lanceolate, approaching an oblong shape.
90. Paired (Leaves): See Twinned.
91. Appendaged (Petiole with): said of one that has at its base some scales like small pieces of leaves.
92. Apetalous (Flower): one that lacks petals. (42.)
93. Apex (of the leaf): the name given to its extremity opposite the base, where there is sometimes a notch or indentation, in which case it is called Apex emarginatus. See Notched.
94. Packed (leaves, seeds): the same as imbricated, or what Mr. Cavanilles calls slate-tiled (empizarradas).
95. Locules (of the pericarp): the cells or compartments into which it is divided. Accordingly it is called uni-, bi-, tri-, quadrilocular, etc. When it has one, two, three, or four, etc. cells or locules.
96. Keeled (Leaves): those whose lower surface is not flat but raised lengthwise along the middle, forming a shape like a small keel. The same is said of petals, glumes, etc.
97. Shrub: the name given to any plant whose trunk is perennial but which grows without having buds.

XVIII
117. Biflora. (Glume.) One that contains two flowers.
118. Bilabiate. These are some flowers that have two lips on the corolla, an upper and a lower. The Didynamias. They are also called open-mouthed. Corolla bilabiata. Corolla ringens.
119. Bilobed, Trilobed, etc. (Leaves.) Those that have two, three, etc. lobes (309.)
120. Bohordo. (Plant with) This term is used for a plant that has no stem, but whose leaves emerge directly from the ground.
121. Open-mouthed (Ringens Corolla.) One that has no closed throat, nor a palate, which is what distinguishes it from the Personata. It is the same as bilabiate.
122. Fuzzy. (Leaves) See Tomentose.
123. Bracts or Laminae. These are spurious leaves, situated close to the flower, distinguished from the other floral leaves by their color and shape, and which do not wither like the perianth at the ripening of the fruit. If many bracts are gathered around the flowers, they are then called coronary bracts. Bracteae comosae.
124. Arms. (Trunk with) One that has opposite branches, such that when the trunk is cut diagonally, the two opposite angles are acute and the other two are obtuse. See Aspado.
125. Bulbous. (Root.) One that has a kind of bulb; or scaly like that of the Lily, consisting of tightly packed layers; or solid and compact with no tunics, like the tulip; or finally tunicate, if it consists of many tunics like the common onion. It must not be confused with the tuberous root.

C

126. Cabezuela. See Capitulum.
127. Nodding. (Flowers) When they are inclined or bent downward. Flores nutantes.
128. Capsule. The Pericarp, when it is membranous, hollow, and breaks open at certain determined points: it is composed of valves or ventallas, of Partitions, of Cells, and of Seeds. The ventallas are the segments or pieces that make up the covering of the Pericarp; hence, capsule uni-bi-tri-quadrivalve, etc., according to the number of said segments. The Partitions are those that divide the capsule into compartments called Cells or locules.
129. Calyptra. This is the calyx of Mosses, shaped like a hood, and which covers the Anther. It is called Calyptra, hood, or cowl. Authors vary greatly in designating the functions of the organs of mosses. Nevertheless, many believe that the seeds are found inside small capsules, or as within a somewhat solid, juicy pulp.
130. Calyx. See Introd. When it has one, two, three, etc. pieces, it is called monophyllous, diphyllous, triphyllous, etc., and today monosepalous, disepalous, trisepalous, etc. It is sometimes doubtful whether what certain flowers have is a calyx or a corolla: to resolve the doubt, bear in mind that the corolla alternates with the stamens, while the calyx is opposed to them. (23.) The calyx must always be observed with great care. (42.)

XIX

131. Calceate. (Calyx) is the same as enlarged.
132. Campanulate, or bell-shaped. (Corolla) One that is swollen; and from the base it widens without having a tube all the way to the end or limb.
133. Capillary. (Pappus.) One that has its rays or hairs entire, and not divided.
134. Capitulum or head. A cluster of flowers gathered almost into a globe. Flores Capitati.
135. Fleshy. (Leaves) Those that are thick, and are filled like a juicy and somewhat solid pulp. Folia Carnosa.
136. Cartilaginous. (Leaves.) Those whose margins are bordered by a cartilage-like membrane that is distinct from the rest of the leaf. Fol. Cartilaginea.
137. Castrated. (Stamens) Those that lack anthers (85.)
138. Scar of the seed called hilum by Linnaeus. V. Introd. (29.)
139. Cyme. V. Introd. (47.)
140. Ligule. V. Ligula.
141. Circumcised. (Cagilla) One that has a covering, which separates by splitting circularly and horizontally. It might perhaps be more brief and accurate to call it truncated cagilla. The purslane.
142. Cirrus. A thread in the form of a spiral, which some plants use to coil around another body. Also called Tendril. The grapevine.
143. Cytinus. It resembles a legume; but it never opens, and has two coverings: the outer one, leathery or woody; and the inner one, pulpy or fleshy. The tamarind, the cassia fistula. Scytinum.
144. Club-shaped. (In the shape of) Said of the Peduncle, the Stigma, or another part of the plant, which being slender at the base, thickens toward the tip. Also called Mace-shaped.
145. Connate. (Leaves) When they are opposite: and are fused, joined, or united at the base. Folia connata, seu coadunata. If they are only slightly united, they are called subconnata.
146. Colored. (Calyx, Leaves, and all parts of the plant, except the corolla.) They are called such when they have a color other than green, which is their usual color. It might perhaps be better to call them Colorful or tinted.
147. Little column. V. Ege.
148. Complete. (Flowers) When they have both calyx and corolla.
149. Compressed. (Fruit, seed, etc.) When it is flattened; not from above, but from the sides.
150. Compound. (Flowers and Leaves.) V. Int. Leaves are compound when more than one leaflet is joined on a single petiole. (271.) They will be doubly compound or recompound if from the second petiole yet more leaflets emerge. The same is said of flowers.
151. Compound. (Pappus) One whose rays or hairs are not simple or entire, but are branched.
152. Compound. (Raceme) Said when it is branched, or divided into many parts.

XXII
195. Dioecious. (Plant) One that bears male flowers on one individual and female flowers on another distinct one. This is the class Dioecia. The common Papaya.
196. Disk. A slightly concave rounded plate, but not much so, like a dish, found at the base of some flowers. Rhamnus.
197. Disk. (Of the radiate composite flower.) See Int. (45.) It is the entire surface of the receptacle, except for the rim or margin where the ray florets are found in the radiate flower.
198. Discoid. (Flowers.) Those that are regular in the corolla, whether hermaphrodite or female. Also called flosculose.
199. Dissepiment or Diaphragm. It is like a partition or wall that keeps the cells or compartments divided from one another. When it runs toward the middle of the valves or walls of the pericarp, it is called a Dissepiment or Diaphragm, contrary or opposite; but if it runs parallel to the valves, it is called parallel, ending then at the junction of the two valves. It also happens that these (the valves) have the diaphragms attached to themselves, and in this case they are called valvae medio septiferae. In the legume one finds false dissepiments, which divide it into many small cells, as in the cassias.
200. Distichous. (Leaves) Those that face the two opposite sides of the branch, even if they are inserted all around it. The same is said of spikes, flowers, or other parts of the plant.
201. Folds. See Plicas.
202. Twice-winged or pinnate. (Leaves) When the primary petiole has on each side other partial petioles, in which winged leaves are also inserted. Folia bipinnata. Leaves occur three and more times winged. Care must be taken with the number of partial petioles, as this distinguishes one species from another, as in the Mimosas.
203. Drupe. The pericarp when it is fleshy without valves, and contains a stone inside. If the outer covering of the pericarp has no juice, it is called a dry Drupe; if it does, it is called a juicy Drupe. Other Spanish botanists call it pruna. A mango is a Drupe.

E

204. Incumbent. (Anthers.) See Incomventes.
205. Eге. A small central column, found sometimes inside the fruit, where the seeds are fixed. Called Columella. The Ates.
206. Elevations. (Of the pericarp.) Said when it has certain calluses, prominences, convexities, or places higher than others on the surface, as in some tomatoes. Pericarpium torosum. The same is said of leaves; but if the elevations are hollow underneath, like blisters or bladders, the leaves are called Folia bullata.
207. Emarginate. (Leaves.) When they have a notch or indentation at the apex. Could they not be called Puntiescotadas? See that word.

XXIII

208. Funnel-shaped [Embudada]. (Corolla.) See Funnel.
209. Funnel. (Corolla in the shape of) See Infundibuliform. Also called funnel-shaped corolla.
210. Entire. (Leaves.) Those that lack any sinus on their margins. Hence the term very-entire leaves.
211. Epigynous. (Stamens. Corolla.) See Introd. 24, 26.
212. Erect. (Stem) Raised or perpendicular to the ground. May be called straight. Caulis erectus. If, while being erect, it bends irregularly toward its tip, it will be called reclining. If the stem, peduncle, or legume are very straight, they will be Caulis strictus. Pedunc. etc.
213. Bristly [Erizado]. (Stem, Pericarp, etc.) When they are set with spines or prickles. Pericarpium echinatum.
214. Rough [Escabroso]. (Stem. Leaf.) When they have points or somewhat rigid prominences on the surface. Folium asperum, scabrum. If they have soft little hairs, they are called velvety. Folium pubisecus, villosum. If the hairs are somewhat stiff, hairy or shaggy. Folium pilosum, hirsutum. If the stiff hairs are rough to the touch, they are called bristle-haired. Folium hirtum, hispidum. See Fuzzy and Silky.
215. Scape. A type of peduncle that rises directly from the root, appearing like a stem without leaves, and supports the flowers. Also called Hastil.
216. Scarious [Escariosas]. (Leaves) Those that are of a dry, arid substance and of a different color from that ordinarily seen in other plants.
217. Notched [Escotadas]. (Leaves) Those whose margins have incisions that face neither toward the base nor toward the apex. If the margins are composed of small circular segments joined one to another, they are called obtusely notched. If the segments rise toward the middle at an angle, they are called acutely notched. Thus, notching is the same as Incision. Some call recortadas the leaves just described, others call them afestonadas. Folia crenata. But note: that folia, Filamenta etc. emarginata, are such when they have a sinus or notch at the apex; but Folia etc. marginata means that they are enlarged at the margin with wings or some other feature.
218. Decurrent [Escurridas]. (Leaves) Those that run or slide down the petiole. Folia decurrentia.
219. Spadix [Espadice]. It is a common receptacle for many flowers, found inside a membranous sheath called the spathe. (51.) The spadix can be simple, as in Arums, or branched as in Coconut palms. Also called tamara.
220. Scattered [Esparcidas]. (Leaves) Those that are neither opposite nor alternate, and follow no order in their insertion.
221. Spathe or garrancha. It is a sheath that contains the spadix (51.)
222. Spike [Espiga]. It is composed of many alternate, sessile flowers, or with stalks shorter than themselves, fixed upon a common peduncle or simple rib. The spike can be simple without forming new spikes, and the flowers will then be called simply spicate:

XXIV
but if the main spike is composed of other spikelets, they are called in this case compound spikes. The rib of the spike is called raspa, according to Cavanilles, in Latin rachis.
223. Spine. A stiff point that emerges from the wood and not from the bark of the tree, and which disappears many times with cultivation.
224. Spur is like a little horn, which in some flowers serves as a Nectary: and hence: Corolla calcarata.
225. Stamens are the masculine parts of the flower, and are composed of Filaments, Anthers, and Pollen.
226. Standard (of the Papilionaceous flower or butterfly-shaped flower.) It is the superior petal, and is also called Vexillum.
227. Sterile. (Flower.) See Infecunda.
228. Stigma. The tip of the Pistil, which is regularly moistened, to receive the fertilizing pollen of the stamens, and is equivalent to the vulva in animals. See Introd.
229. Stylet. It is a small point that some leaves have at their tip.
230. Style. It is the part of the pistil that lies between the ovary and the stigma, and on whose tip the stigma is placed. See Introd.
231. Stipe. (of the Frond) A kind of trunk that transitions into a leaf. In general it means Little piece, and hence: Pericarp, seed, pappus etc., with a little piece.
232. Stipules. They are like small scales, which grow at the base of the Petioles of the leaves. They are considered a kind of Fulcrum. The Malvaceous Plants.
233. Stolons. (To propagate by) Said of some plants, called creeping, which spread along the ground, and which, sending out roots at the nodes, give rise there to new plants. The new plants, then, that emerge from the nodes, are called Stolons.
234. Star, or Whorl. (Flowers or leaves in) those that surround the trunk in great numbers. The Didynamia. (See the sexual key.)
235. Stria. The same as canal: hence: striated trunk, or channeled.
236. Strobilus, or Pine cone. It is an imbricated Pericarp, formed by a compact Catkin (81), with hard scales. The pine. The Ates.
237. Extended. (Leaves, Petals etc.) It is the same as Patent. Mr. Cavanilles calls them open. (59) Folium Patens.

F

238. Scalloped, or Festooned. (Leaves) Those that have blunt or rounded teeth on the margin. Folia crenata. Cavanilles: see Notched.
239. Filaments. (Of the stamens) They are the threads of these, on whose tip the anther is placed. (85.)
240. Filiform. Thread-shaped, or in the manner of a thread, that is: the peduncle, the tube of the corolla, or the Pistil etc., when they are of equal thickness from beginning to end. Could one not call it ahilado?

XXV
241. Fistulous. (Trunk) One that is hollow inside. The Cangcong.
242. Flexuous. (Stem) See: Wavy.
243. Floral. (Leaves) Those that are close to the flower and are distinguished from the rest of the leaves by their number and shape.
244. Flosculous. (Flowers) The same as Discoid, as distinguished from Radiate.
245. Follicle or Husk. It is a species of membranous Pericarp with a single valve, which splits lengthwise on one side, and which holds the seeds fixed on a proper Receptacle. Folliculus. The Asclepiad.
246. Frond. These are the leaves in which the stipe of ferns is resolved, and which carry the fruiting bodies underneath.
247. Fulcra. These are like supports for Plants and their members. Seven species are counted: 1. Stipules. 2. Bracts. 3. Hairs, wool, down, etc. 4. Glands. 5. Spines. 6. Prickles. 7. Tendrils.
248. Fusiform. (Root) Shaped like a cone or spindle. The radish.

G

249. Hooks. These are the curved points or prickles seen on the trunk of some plants. Aculei. See: Prickles.
250. Throat (of the corolla). It is the opening found at the end of the tube of the corolla between the incisions of the limb.
251. Garrancha. The same as Spathe.
252. Glaucous. (Color) Leaves, etc. When their color is between green and white. Folia glauca.
253. Genitals. (Organs or Parts) In Plants these are the Stamens (225) and Pistils (370).
254. Germen. It is the rudiment, principle, or embryo of the fruit. The Germen is either Superior or Inferior. See those entries.
255. Gymnospermia. One of the orders of Didynamia, when the fruit is uncovered and not hidden beneath a Pericarp. (360.)
256. Glans. It is a pericarp containing a single seed of firm flesh, covered and barely joined to a fibrous rind, like the Areca, the Thoa, and the Acorn of the Oak. Glans.
257. Glands: these are excrescences noted in Plants. Sometimes they are sessile and sometimes they have a small stalk. The mallow plants. The Ricinus. The Cassia. Sometimes they are also hollow inside, with an opening at the tip, and resemble small jars.
258. Glume. It is the calyx of Gramineous Plants, and it has valves.

H

259. Fascicle. (Flowers in a fascicle or Fastigiate.) A cluster of flowers joined in a head, whose peduncles are erect, parallel, and of equal height. Flores fasciculati.
260. Harp. (Leaves shaped like) When they are triangular and se-
4

XXVI
resembling that musical instrument. The pugahan palm. Folia lirata.
261. Lance-shaped. (Leaves of this figure) They are like arrow-shaped leaves (103) but the angles of the base also have a sinus at the side of the leaf, and are as if perpendicular to the petiole: whereas in arrow-shaped leaves there are no sinuses at the sides of the leaf. They are also called Halberd-shaped, or Spear-shaped. Folia hastata.
262. Hastil. See Escapo.
263. Female. (Flowers) Those that have only Pistils, and lack stamens.
264. Cleft. (Leaves) those that are divided with linear sinuses, whose margins are straight, and do not form an angle with each other. If these sinuses form a row on each side, the leaves are called pinnatifid. (366) Folia incisa.
265. Hermaphrodite. (Flower) One that has a Pistil, Stigma, and Anthers; and thus a hermaphrodite Plant is one that produces such flowers.
266. Hermaphroditic. (Flowers) They are called such when they lack a stigma, as occurs in some Syngenesias.
267. Paired, or twin. (Leaves) When the common petiole supports only one pair of opposite leaflets. Folia binnata, or geminata. Sometimes the petiole divides in two and each side supports a pair of leaflets. In this case the leaves are twice-paired or twice-appearing: or they are paired-pinnate. The Camonchile. Folia conjugata or bigeminata.
268. Hybrid. (Plant) is the same as mestiza, or one that arises from the combination of two distinct species.
269. Hypogynous. (Corolla, Stamens) See Introd. 24 and 26.
270. Floral Leaves. See Bracts.
271. Leaflets. These are the partial leaves of the compound leaf. (150.)
272. Hollejo. See Follicle.
273. Spindle-shaped. (of this figure) See Fusiform.
274. Imbricate. (Leaves, seeds) Those that are laid one over another, like the tiles of a roof. They are also called overlapping, or slated.
275. Odd. (With and without) See Winged.
276. Inclined. (Stem) One that grows obliquely and then bends toward the ground. It seems to be the same as Reclinatus.
277. Incomplete. (Flowers) When they lack a corolla or calyx. When only one of the two things is present, botanists divide them, some calling it calyx and others corolla. Mr. Cavanilles always calls corolla the tegument that immediately surrounds the germen and stamens, whatever its color and shape may be.
278. Incumbent. (Anther) One that lies upon the filament making right angles with it; but without turning around as the versatile one does.
279. Indefinite. (Stamens) Some Authors thus call the

XXVII
stamens, when their number exceeds ten. They are also called
indeterminate.
280. Indeterminate. (Stamens) The same as Indefinite.
281. Infecund. (Flower) The same as sterile, and this occurs
either on the part of the males, when the anthers are not perfect
or perish before releasing the pollen, or on the part of the fe-
males, when they lack a stigma.
282. Inferior. (Flower or calyx) When the germen is found on
the receptacle, or when the pistil turns into fruit according to
Tournefort. In this case the germen is superior, and the calyx or flower
is inferior. This is the free calyx and free germen according to the botanist
Ventenat, whom Cavanilles follows. See Adherent.
283. Inferior (Germen) When it is found below the receptacle
and is equivalent to the same as a superior Flower or Calyx. This is the
adherent calyx and adherent germen of Ventenat. See Adherent.
284. Inflorescence. The act of a plant producing its flowers.
Also called Anthesis.
285. Infundibuliform. (Corolla) When the limb is conical and is
placed upon a tube, so that it resembles a Funnel. Also called
funnel-shaped.
286. Involucre. It is the calyx of the umbel, and of verticillate
flowers: in the umbel it stands apart from the flowers. The involucre is
monophyllous, diphyllous, triphyllous, etc., or null.
287. Ismos. (between the seeds) Partitions that are seen in
many legumes, and which are sometimes like simple thin membranes, sometimes
thicker in spongy or fungous consistency, or yet of other
forms, and which divide the seeds from one another.

J

288. Jarrito (Small Jar shape) (Corolla) One that is cylindrical and
barely widens at the tip. (Cyathiformis) It amounts to the same
as the shape of a Jar, but this one has no neck and does not
widen.

L

289. Lips (of the corolla) Bilabiate corollas are called such
because they have two lips: one superior, called the Galea or Mor-
rion, and another inferior, called the Barba. In Orchid plants
found in the class Gynandria, the small lip is the name given
to what Linnaeus calls the nectary, which is the lower part of the
three inner ones, which together with the other three outer ones make up a calyx
(according to some) of six divisions, and according to Linnaeus a corolla
of five petals and a nectary.
290. Lacerated. (Corolla) whose limb is cleft with many small
incisions. Leaves can also be lacerated.
291. Laciniate. (Leaves, Calyx, and Corolla) They are called such when
they are variously and immediately cleft: the leaves at the edges;
the monophyllous calyx at its border; the polyphyllous at its segments; the co-

XXVIII
rola monopetala, on the limb; and the polipetala on its blades. In the calyx and corolla of one piece, the laciniae must be counted from the middle of the edge, in the calyx; and from the middle of the limb, in the corolla: and if this, or the calyx, are of many pieces, the laciniae are taken from the middle of these. If the divisions both in the calyx and in the corolla are very deep, they are no longer called laciniae, but parts.
292. Lactescence. By this name is understood a certain liquid that flows from some wounded plants. This liquid is white, yellow, or red.
293. One-sided. (Spikes, Panicles, Flowers) When all the peduncles and flowers face the same direction. Spica, Penicula, Secunda. If they face two opposite sides, they are called Distichous.
294. Glabrous. (Leaves) Those whose surfaces are entirely clean, without down, hair, wool, etc., even if they have prominences. (Folia glabra).
295. Lanceolate. (Leaves) Those that have the shape of a lance head, or that narrow at both ends and widen in the middle. Folia lanceolata.
296. Lanceolate-ovate. (Leaves) Those that are lanceolate at the base and ovate at the tip.
297. Lateral. (Peduncles) Those that arise from one side of the base of the leaves. The solanum.
298. Legume. The Pericarp is called this when it is membranous, of two valves, of one compartment or more, formed by false septa, and which holds the seeds fixed only at one of the two sutures. The Diadelpiae. If the seeds are fixed at both sutures, it is called a Silique. Sometimes the legume is composed of fused segments, and then it is called articulate; and lomentaceous, when it is a citino. (143).
299. Tongue-shaped. (Leaves of this shape) Those that are linear, fleshy and obtuse, and somewhat rounded on the underside.
300. Free. (Calyx, Ovary) Cavanilles uses this term for the inferior calyx, and for the superior ovary of Linnaeus. See Adherent.
301. Ligula is a thin membrane found at the base of the leaflets of gramineous plants, and is truncated, or lanceolate, or bifid, etc.
302. Ligulate. (Corolla) That which is simple, with a short tube, and a flat limb resembling a small ribbon, directed outward, whose apex is truncated, or has three or more small teeth. These flowers are what Tournefort calls Semiflosculose. Corolla ligulata.
303. Ligulate. (Leaves) This is the same as Linguiform, or tongue-shaped: that is, linear (307), fleshy, and convex on the underside.
304. Ligulate. (Flowers) These are the composite flowers (45) that have all the corollas of their florets flat, clustered together and spread outward.
305. Limb. (of the monopetalous corolla) This is the upper part of the corolla, which regularly widens more than the rest.

XXIX

306. Lined. (Leaves) Those that are furrowed or hollowed out, with sunken veins.
307. Linear. (Leaves) Those whose two lateral edges are parallel: they regularly narrow at both ends.
308. Smooth. (Leaves) Those that have no prominences or roughness. (Laevia) The Calophyllum.
309. Lobed. (Leaves) Those that are divided up to their midpoint into a certain number of parts called lobes, which are separated from one another. Hence leaves may be bilobed, trilobed, etc., according to the number of lobes. The Ricinus.
310. Lobes in the Calyx, Ovary, Stigma, etc., are broad, not very deep elevations or angles that are sometimes seen in these parts.
311. Lunulate. (Leaves) When they are rounded at the top and hollowed at the base, with two sinuses that form a half-moon shape.
312. Lyrate, or lyre-shaped. (Leaves) Those that are divided crosswise into parts, such that the upper ones are larger and more widely spaced.

M

313. Cluster. (Inflorescence in) See Carimbosas.
314. Male. (Plants) Those that produce only male flowers.
315. Male. (Flowers) Those that have only stamens without Pistils: and if they do have pistils, these lack a stigma; in this case they are sterile hermaphrodite flowers on the part of the females.
316. Apple. A type of fleshy Pericarp, without valves, containing a core inside. Others call it Poma or Pomo.
317. Marginate. (Leaves, etc.) When the edges are enlarged by a wing or some other structure. See Escotadas.
318. Mask-like. (Corolla) See Personata.
319. Masculine. (Parts) In flowers these are the Anthers, within which the pollen is deposited, for reproduction.
320. Melon. The pericarp is fleshy like the Pomo, but the cells are distant from the axis of the fruit and not immediately adjacent to it. The melon can be solid as in the Cucurbita, and hollow as in the Passiflora.
321. Twin. (Cells or Anthers) See Didyma. Leaves are called twin when they are paired.
322. Membranaceous or Membranous. (Leaves) The same as aviteladas: that is, those that are thin and resemble parchment.
323. Truncate, Lopped. (Seeds or other parts of the flower) When they lack small horns, awns, hairs, or similar structures that other species of the same genus usually have. Semina mutica.
324. Monophyllous. (Calyx) It is called this when it is of a single piece.
325. Monogyny, Digyny, Trigyny, Tetragyny, Pentagyny, Hexagyny, Polygyny. These are the subdivisions of many classes, and which

XXX
they are called Orders, and are founded on the number of Pistils; that is: Monogyny, when there is one pistil. Digyny, when there are two Pistils, etc. The number of Pistils must be taken from the base of the style (230) and if there is no style, as occurs in some flowers, it is taken from the number of stigmas. (228)
326. Monoecious. (Plant) One that has male flowers (315) separate from the female flowers (263) on the same plant. Also called Androgynous. Maize. The Castor plant, and many other plants. From this the class called Monoecia is taken.
327. Monopetalous. (Corolla) One that is of a single piece. (22)
328. Monospermous, Dispermous, Trispermous, etc. (Cagilla) One that contains within it one, two, three, etc., seeds.
329. Bitten. (Leaves) Those which, being very blunt, are also terminated with unequal incisions. Folia præmorsa.

N

330. Nectary. Some Botanists have criticized Linnaeus for having introduced this term, because they say it causes confusion, being very vague. The Nectary that Linnaeus names is sometimes inserted in the Petals, sometimes it is a part distinct from them: it sometimes has the shape of a spur or little horn, giving rise to the Spurred Corolla: or they may be scales, glands, or borders found in the flower. In Orchid plants the nectary is called the small lip, which is the lower and inner division of the calyx.
331. Veins. (Leaves with) When these run from the base to the tip without dividing: hence Tri-Quinque-Septenerved, when the leaf has three, five, or seven veins. But Triplinerved means that the three veins meet before reaching the base.
332. Nucleus. It is the epidermis or bony cortex that covers the seed of the drupe. Sometimes the epidermis is not bony, but leathery. Most authors do not speak of the word nucleus as it is not necessary: they simply say that the nut of the drupe is more or less hard.
333. Nut. When the seed is found covered with a bony epidermis, it is called a nut: it may have one or more chambers. The nut may also be found entirely bare, or clothed with a dry and adherent tunic. In this second case it is called a tunicate nut, and in the first a bare nut. Some consider the Nut to be a drupe with very little flesh: and if it has much, as in the mango, others call it a covered nut or berry nut. Accepting the word nut with these distinctions, the word drupe could be omitted.

334. Oblong. (Leaves) Those that are several times longer than wide.

XXXI
335. Undulate. (Leaves) Those whose surface (not the edge) has highs and lows resembling the waves seen in water. Also called Unduladas.
336. Undulate. (Stem) When at each node it changes direction, forming inward and outward angles. Cauliflexuosus.
337. Opposite. (Leaves) When they are placed facing one another, and the two that follow form a cross with the previous pair.
338. Orbicular. (Leaves) Those that are as long as they are wide.
339. Eared. (Leaves with) When they have two appendages like small ears at the base, or near the petiole. Folia aurita. The citrus aurantium.
340. Oval. (Leaves) Those that from orbicular (338) become oblong (334) and whose ends are equal and rounded. Also called elliptical and ovate.

P

341. Pages. The upper or lower surfaces of the leaves.
342. Chaff. Small scales that grow from the receptacle, separating the florets and seeds from one another in composite flowers. Receptáculum paleaceum.
343. Palmate. (Leaves) Those that are divided beyond the middle into nearly equal lobes, which are joined to one another at the base. Some call them Palmeadas. Folia palmata.
344. Palate. A prominence or hump found in the throat of the Corolla in some flowers, which for this reason are called personate, or masked. The Snapdragon (Antirrino).
345. Panicle. (Flowers in) Those that are scattered on variously divided and subdivided peduncles: if the small florets form spikelet clusters on the peduncles, it will be called a spiked Panicle.
346. Papilionaceous. (Flower) The same as Butterfly-shaped (80.)
347. Parasitic. (Plant) One that does not grow in the ground but on the trunk of another plant.
348. Umbel. The receptacle that originates from a single point, elongating and dividing into peduncles arranged with proportion or regularity.
349. Parts. See Divided.
350. Divided. (Leaves) Those that are cleft almost to the base. The same is said of the Calyx and Corolla: thus a part is distinct from a piece, since in the Calyx or Corolla these are leaflets or petals. For brevity, instead of saying: Corolla cleft into four or five parts, (for example) I will say: Corolla in four or five parts. If the divisions are not deep in the calyx and corolla but only reach halfway up their height, they are then called laciniate and not parted.
351. Patent. (Leaves) Those that form an acute angle with the stem: that is, they are neither erect nor horizontal. The same

XXXII
is said of other parts of plants; others call them extended, and Mr. Cavanilles calls them open.
352. Petiole. It is the small stalk or little piece found at the base of the leaves, connecting them to the trunk. There are common, partial, and proper petioles. The common one supports all the leaves when they are compound (150). The partial one supports only part of them; the proper one supports just one.
353. Petiolate. (Leaves) Those that are not sessile, but rather have a petiole.
354. Peduncle. It is the small stalk or little piece that supports, or upon which flowers are placed. There are common, partial, and proper peduncles. The common one supports all the flowers. The partial one supports part of them; and the proper one supports just one.
355. Fused. (Anthers) When they are not only placed close together but actually joined, so that they cannot be separated without some effort. Anteræ coalitæ. This is the same as soldered.
356. Scaly. (Leaves, Trunk) See 214.
357. Plume. This is also the name given to the pappus (vilano).
358. Perianth. It is properly the calyx that is adjacent to the fruit, and which is observed in the greater part of Plants. Some Botanists call it simply calyx; so that without adding another word, it is understood that the calyx is the perianth, and not the spathe, follicle, glume, etc., and the same is to be understood throughout this Treatise.
359. Perfoliate. (Leaves) Those that entirely surround the stem at their base, without forming a sheath or tube. They are also called pierced. Folia perfoliata.
360. Pericarp. The ovary or uterus of Plants, which covers the seeds. In its various forms it is called: Cagilla, Silique, Legume, Citino, Follicle or Husk, Drupe or Plum, Berry, Strobile, Pome, Melon, and Samara; Achene, and Careopis.
361. Perigynous. (Corolla, Stamens) See Introd. 24, 26.
362. Persistent. (Calyx or Corolla) That which does not perish before the fruit ripens.
363. Personate or Masked. (Corolla) That which, being bilabiate, is closed or has a palate (344) between the lips, as distinct from the open-mouthed type, which is not closed and has no palate. Corolla personata.
364. Ciliate. (Leaves) Those that are bordered on their edges by stiff, parallel hairs like eyelashes. Folium ciliatum.
365. Petals. These are the pieces of which the corolla is composed. If it is of one piece, it is called monopetalous; if of many, polypetalous, and others call it roseaceous. (22)
366. Pinnatifid. (Leaves) When they are cut into horizontal oblong lobes. If they are cut twice, they are called doubly pinnatifid or bipinnatifid.
367. Prickles. (Stem with) These are the spines (381) when they are straight. Caulis aculeatus.
368. Pine cone. See Strobile.

XXXIII

369. Spots. (Leaves, Stem, or Fruit, etc., with) When they are marked with dots or colored blotches (Folia picta).
370. Pistil. It is the female genital organ in flowers. It consists of the germ (254), the style, which is the thread that arises from the germ (230), and the stigma (228). The number of pistils is counted from the base of the style; and if there is no style, from the number of stigmas.
371. Placenta. It is that organ of the plant to which the seeds are attached.
372. Folds or Creases. These are the marks that remain in places where something has been folded, which can sometimes be seen on leaves.
373. Feathery. (Pappus) The one that has winged hairs. Pappus plumosus.
374. Pollen. See Polvillo.
375. Polygamy. (Plant) It is one that produces precisely hermaphrodite flowers, and in addition to these, male flowers or female flowers, or both. If in one tree, for example, there are hermaphrodite flowers and also male or female flowers on the same tree, it is called Poligamia monoecia. If the said tree has only hermaphrodite flowers, and a different tree has male or female flowers, it is called Poligamia dioecia, as occurs in Diospyros. Finally, if one tree has hermaphrodite flowers, another has male flowers, and a third has female flowers, this is called Poligamia trioecia. It can also happen in this last case that one tree has hermaphrodite flowers and male flowers, and a second tree has female flowers. On the above is founded the class called Polygamia. Polygamous plants are not hybrids (268).
376. Pollen or Polen. It is a substance regularly visible in the manner of a powder or flour, enclosed within the anther, and which, when this breaks open, emerges so that the pistil may be fertilized.
377. Pome or Poma. It is a pericarp more or less fleshy, without valves, and with the cells situated near the axis of the fruit.
378. Proliferous. (Flower or Umbel) See Introd. 58.
379. Prominences. (Legume or Pericarp with) See Elevaciones.
380. Propago. It is the seed of Mosses that lacks a covering, cotyledons, and bark.
381. Spines. (Stem with) The one that has stiff pricks or points that emerge straight or curved from the bark. If they are straight, they are called puas or pinchos; if curved, ganchos (249) caulis aculeatus.
382. Soft spines. (Stem with) When the pricks or spines are not stiff but soft. Caulis muricatus.
383. Notched tips. Thus I believe one might call leaves that are notched at the apex. See Emarginadas.
384. Dots. (Leaves with) Those that are marked with small pits: if the dots protrude above the surface of the leaves, they are called raised dots, projecting dots, or tubercles. The same is said of other parts of plants.

5

XXXIV

Q

385. Keel. (Of the papilionaceous corolla) It is the part that encloses the stamens and pistil; it is composed of two united petals. Carina.

R

386. Raceme. Consists of a common peduncle, on which many individual lateral peduncles are fixed. Flores racemosi.
387. Radiate. (Flowers) When the small flowers of the disk are tubular, and those of the circumference have strap-shaped petals and are not tubular. See Introd. (45) Flores radiati.
388. Radiate. (Umbel) One whose marginal flowers have petals larger than those of the remaining flowers.
389. Radicant. (Stem) One that clings to other plants by means of lateral roots it puts out. The pepper plant. Therefore the radicant plant is a climber. Caulis radicans.
390. Ray. (Of the composite flower) It is the circumference where the ligulate corollas are found. (45.)
391. Ray. (Of the Umbel and Pappus) This name is also given in the former to the Peduncles, and in the Pappus to the stiffest hairs.
392. Corymb. Some say that ramillete and corimbo are synonyms, and that ramillete is distinct from the fascicle. (259.)
393. Ramous. (Leaves) When the common petiole divides into two parts, and the leaflets are attached only on the inner side. Folia pedata. The Cissus.
394. Creeping. (Plant) One that crawls or spreads along the ground putting out roots. Caulis repens. If in addition it sends out stems where they touch the roots, it is called stoloniferous or spreading. If it spreads without putting out roots, it is called prostrate. Caulis procumbes.
395. Receptacle. It is the base upon which the parts of the fructification are seated, and is either common or proper. It is also called Thalamus. See Introd.
396. Reclinate. When the upright trunk. (212) has its branches disordered at the top. Caulis reclinatus. Ficus.
397. Recompound. (Leaves, Umbel, Flower) Cavanilles properly applies this name to what others call Decompound or overcompound. See this word. Folia decomposita.
398. Cut. (Leaves) See Notched.
399. Resupinate. (Corolla) When the lip that should face upward faces downward. The same is said of leaves. Corola resupinata.
400. Twisted. (Corolla or other parts of plants) Corola contorta. See this word.
401. Retuse or blunt. (Leaves) Those that end in a very obtuse notch. The same is said of the fruit. Folia retussa.
402. Bordered. The edges of petals or other parts are so called

XXXV

parts of the flower, when they are very finely waved, crisped, bristled, or as if they had fringes: petala fimbriata.
The Banaba.
403. Rima. The same as a cleft, crack, or slit.
404. Kidney. (Leaves of this shape) When they are wider than long, and are hollowed out at the base. Folium reniforme.
405. Curled. (Petals or other parts of the flower) The same as bordered.
406. Gnawed. (Leaves) Those that have small, blunt sinuses and unequal lobes. Folia erosa.
407. Rhombus. (Leaves of this shape) The rhombus is a figure whose sides are all equal; but the opposite angles are not right angles, but obtuse and acute: and from this, leaves that approach this figure are called as I said above. If only the opposite sides are equal, and the angles are not right angles either, they are called rhomboidal leaves.
408. Rosaceous. (Corolla) It is the corolla of many petals.
409. Rosette. This name is aptly given by some learned Spaniards to the corolla.
410. Wheel. (Corolla of this shape) One that is monopetalous, whose limb is flat, and placed upon a very short tube. Corola rotata.
411. Runcinate. (Leaves) When they are pinnatifid and have deep sinuses and projecting angles, whose strips or lobes are sharp and curved downward. Folia runcinata.

S

412. Exserted. (Stamens) They are called this when they extend beyond the corolla. Stamina exerta.
413. Samara. It is a pericarp without valves or holes, of one or more cells, leathery, membranous, extended almost always like a wing around its margin or apex. It may have one, three, or four wings. Aylanthus.
414. Silky. (Leaves) When they are covered with soft, matted, spreading, and shiny hairs. Folia sericea.
415. Semiflosculose. (Flowers) See Ligulate.
416. Seed. It is the fruit that is to give origin to the new plant. Its number is sometimes prodigious. A single maize plant has been known to produce two thousand seeds.
