A poppy, thirty-two thousand; and a tobacco plant, up to three hundred and sixty thousand. In seeds, botanists observe the navel (hilum), the albumen that often surrounds the embryo, like the flour of a grain of wheat, called by Jussieu perisperm and by some modern authors endosperm, and the Cotyledons. (See Introd. 29.)
417. Sinuses. (of leaves) These are excavations formed at an angle along the margins, base, or apex. If the points or strips formed by the sinuses are convex on top, the leaves are called runcinate. Folia Runcinata.

XXXVI
418. Sepals. The pieces of the calyx are thus called today. Introd. 21.
419. Wavy (Leaves). Those that are undulate (335) not on the surface, but on the edges. Folia repanda. Others call them festooned or scalloped.
420. Sessile. (Leaves, Pappus, Flower) When they are found without a petiole, stalk, or peduncle.
421. Silicula. It is a small Pod or Silique (423), nearly round, oblong, heart-shaped in reverse, which has a Style. Both the small pod and the pod have various shapes, such as rounded, compressed, swollen, quadrangular, lanceolate, notched, solitary, unilocular, and locular, bilocular, and others.
422. Siliculose. (Tetradynamia) When the style is regularly as long as the silicula. It is an Order of the class Tetradynamia. (See the Sexual Key.)
423. Silique. A membranous Pod or Pericarp, with two valves, which has the seeds fixed along both sutures, and in this it differs from the legume, which has them fixed along only one Suture.
424. Siliquose. (Tetradynamia) Consists of a very long pericarp whose style is very short and hardly noticeable. It is an Order of Tetradynamia.
425. Simple. (Calyx) In composite flowers, it is so called when it has only a single series of scales that encircle the florets.
426. Without an odd one. (Winged leaves) (74.)
427. Superdecompound. (Leaves, Racemes) It is the same as recompound. (397)
428. Over Compound or over recompound. (Leaves, Racemes, etc.) When the petiole divides several times and gathers many leaflets. Folium supra decompositum.
429. Connate. (Anthers) It is the same as fused. Anteræ coalitæ.
430. Superior. (Flower, or Calyx.) When the ovary is situated below the receptacle, or when the calyx becomes the fruit according to Tournefort. Thus when the flower or calyx is superior, the ovary is inferior. According to Ventenat, in this case the calyx is adherent, and the ovary likewise is. See Adherent.
431. Superior. (Ovary) That which is enclosed within the corolla or sits above the receptacle. In this case the flower or the calyx is inferior. According to Ventenat, in this case the ovary is free, and the calyx likewise is. See Adherent.
432. Groove. It is the same as channel.
433. Suture. It is the same as seam. In some species of Pericarp there appear structures like nerves, where the seeds are fixed along the inner part. Legumes (298) have two sutures; but the seeds are fixed along only one.

T

434. Septum. It is the same as dissepiment, membrane, or diaphragm, which causes the fruit to be divided into compartments. Sometimes the septa

XXXVII
are parallel to the valves, sometimes contrary, and sometimes also attached to the same valves. Septa valvis parallela . . . contraria; valvæ medio septifera.
435. Stem. It is the part of the plant that begins above the root and supports the leaves, flowers, and fruits. Caulis. There are plants without a stem, and they are called Acaulis. See Bohordo. The other plants have either herbaceous or woody stems: that is, they have either a stalk or a trunk: the stalk belongs to herbs, and the trunk to woody plants. It can be of various forms. Round, cylindrical or circular in cross-section. Caulis teres: triangular, trigonous or of three angles or sides; triangularis, trigonus, triqueter. Tetragonal or quadrangular; tetragonus, cuadrangularis. Pentagonal, Hexagonal, etc. Pentagonus, Hexagonus, etc.
436. Tamara. (Inflorescence in) It is the same as Spadix. (219.)
437. Tarro. (Corolla or Calyx in the shape of) It is of cylindrical shape, without any neck, and not widening at the tip like the Jarrito or Cubilete. It must not be confused with the taza or cuenco.
438. Taza. (Corolla or Calyx) in the shape of a cup. See Cuenco.
439. Prostrate. (Stem) When it lies flat on the ground. Caulis procumbens.
440. Terminal. (Flowers) Those found at the ends of the branches and are not axillary.
441. Ternate. (Leaves) See three by three.
442. Ternillosas. (Leaves) See Cartilaginous.
443. Thyrse. (Inflorescence in) When the partial peduncles arise from various points and do not all reach the same height as in the corymb. Also called Infloresc. en toba.
444. Tomentose. (Leaves) Those covered with soft, interlaced hairs, without the individual threads being distinguishable. Also called borrosas and afelpadas. Folia tomentosa.
445. Tortuous. (Trunk) When it twists and turns in various directions. Spondias.
446. Trama. It is the same as Amento, or Candelilla.
447. Climbing. It is so called when it ascends trees or neighboring objects, using either tendrils, or small rootlets, or little hand-like structures like Betel. Caulis Scandens. If it spreads along the ground, putting out roots, it is called a creeper, or one that serpea. Caulis repens. And if in addition to creeping it puts out roots and shoots, it will be stoloniferous or cundidora. If it climbs by coiling or twining around things, it is called Voluble. Some call this last scandens. It would be very good to fix the meaning of all these words precisely.
448. Three by three. (Leaves of) Those that are digitate. (194) and are placed on a common petiole. If they have their own petiole they are called petiolate; if they do not have one, they are called Sessile. They may be called three on a branch, and are also called Ternate by Linnaeus, Jussieu, and other Authors. But lately in the Spanish translation of Richard, I have seen Verticillate leaves of three by three, or of three in a star, called ternate.
449. Triangular. (Leaves) Those that have three angles, like a bayonet, and are fleshy.

XXXIII
450. Tricoccous. (Capsule) One that is humped, with three knobs or projecting angles, and contains three compartments, being in reality three capsules joined together. Would it not be better to call it a capsule of three in one? Capsula tricoca. Jatropha.
451. Trilobed. (Leaves) Those that have three lobes (309). Folia triloba.
452. Triple-nerved. (Leaves) (331) When the veins of the leaf do not meet at the base, but a little higher up. Folium triplinerve.
453. Trunk. See Stem.
454. Top-shaped. (Capsule, seed in the form of) When they have the shape of an inverted cone. Capsula turbinata.
455. Tubers. Certain solid, fleshy parts at the root that appear to hang from a thread. Hence the term tuberous root. Solanum tuberosum, Amomum, Yuca. Not to be confused with the bulbous root. (125) The name tubercles is also given to the raised points that are sometimes found on leaves, etc.
456. Tuberous. (Root) See Tubers.
457. Tubulate. (Corolla) One that is monopetalous, with a cylindrical tube and a limb shaped like a bell, split into several parts.
458. Tubulous. (Flower) It is the composite (45) that has all its florets tubulate and more or less uniform.

V

459. Valves. The same as ventallas: they are coverings or small doors that, joined and closed together, form the type of pericarp called Cagilla. But this is said to have two, three, or more valves.
460. Veined. (Leaves) When the vessels running across the blade are very branched. When the leaf has no veins, it is called Folium avenium.
461. Ventallas. The same as valves. (459.)
462. Versatile. (Anther) One that surrounds or turns upon the filament.
463. Whorled, or stellate. (Leaves, Branches, Flowers) Those that, being more than two, encircle the stem.
464. Vexillum. See Standard.
465. Pappus. A kind of crown that certain seeds have at their upper end, consisting of hairs that are either simple, branched, or feathery, or of other shapes. The pappus serves to carry the seed through the air and to spread the plants easily. Some call it milano. The Asclepiad and many plants of the same family. Pappus.
466. Urceolate. (Corolla of the shape of) One that is wide at the bottom and then narrows past the middle. Urceolata Corolla. One that is shaped like a jug, is cylindrical, and neither narrows nor widens at the tip.
467. Violin-shaped. (Leaves of the shape of) Those that are oblong (334), wider at the bottom than at the top, and also pinched in on the sides.

XXXIX
like a Violin, or a Pilgrim's Gourd. Follum panduraeforme.
468. Umbel. It is the same as parasol (348.)
469. Uncinate. (of shape) When the stigma, or another part of the plant, is curved in the shape of a hook or crook: and from this, stigma etc. uncinado.
470. Clawlets. (Of the polypetalous corolla) These are the lower extremities of the petals that narrow at that part, and by which they are fixed to the receptacle.
471. Twining. (Stem) One that climbs by twisting in a spiral and coiling around another body. It is also called revuelto. If it twists toward the right (75) it is called twining against the movement of the Sun. If to the left, according to the movement of the Sun. It must not be confused with plants that climb straight up, for these should only be called scandent. See Syst. Veget. edit. Gmel. p. XI.
472. Urn. (In mosses) In the opinion of many botanists, what is called an urn or capsule (theca) in mosses is nothing more than the place that contains the seeds. It has a covering or calyptra at the tip, which breaks open in a circular manner, and then the orifice or peristome appears, which is sometimes simple and bare, and other times fringed or toothed. Some believe that the urn contains a hermaphrodite flower, and others find in it, as they see it, males and females in the plant.

Z

Tendril. It is the same as cirrus.

XXXIX

Pome like a Pear, or a Gourd with a pericarp. They form pandanas primmy, gymnolantagous, ser. amaranth, &c. ft. ramaceous, &c. pelines. Umbel. This is the same as pariesol (314). From another part of the

XLI

EXPLANATION

OF THE KEY TO THE SEXUAL SYSTEM OF LINNAEUS.

1. MONANDRIA: A single stamen in the hermaphrodite flower.
2. DIANDRIA: Two stamens in the hermaphrodite flower.
3. TRIANDRIA: Three stamens in the hermaphrodite flower.
4. TETRANDRIA: Four stamens in the hermaphrodite flower.
5. PENTANDRIA: Five stamens in the hermaphrodite flower.
6. HEXAGINIA: Six stamens in the hermaphrodite flower.
7. HEPTANDRIA: Seven stamens in the hermaphrodite flower.
8. OCTANDRIA: Eight stamens in the hermaphrodite flower.
9. ENNEANDRIA: Nine stamens in the hermaphrodite flower.
10. DECANDRIA: Ten stamens in the hermaphrodite flower.
11. DODECANDRIA: Stamens from eleven to nineteen inclusive in the hermaphrodite flower.
12. ICOSANDRIA: Stamens from twenty to one hundred or more, attached to the calyx or corolla, not to the receptacle, in the hermaphrodite flower.
13. POLIANDRIA: Stamens from twenty to one hundred or more, attached to the receptacle in the hermaphrodite flower.
14. DIDINAMIA: Four stamens: two longer than the remaining two.
15. TETRA-DINAMIA: Six stamens: four longer than the remaining two.

ORDERS OF THE CLASSES.

In the Classes Monandria, Diandria, Triandria, &c., through Polyandria inclusive, which are the first thirteen, the orders or subdivisions of the Classes are taken from the number of Pistils. These are counted at the base of the style. If there is no style, the number of stigmas is counted. Thus Monoginia, Diginia, Triginia, Tetragenia, Pentaginia, Hexaginia, &c. Polyginia means there is one, two, three, four, five, six, &c. or many Pistils.

In the class Didynamia, the orders are taken from the absence or presence of the Pericarp. Consequently there are two orders. Gymnospermia, that is: when there is a Pericarp, and the seeds are enclosed within it.

In the class Tetradynamia there are two orders, Siliculosa, and Sili-

XLIII
quosa. The siliculose or small-pod type is when the style is as long as the silicula. The Siliculosa or pod type consists of a very elongated pericarp whose style is very short (See Siliqua and Silicula in the Nomenclature.)
In Monadelphia, Diadelphia, and Polyadelphia, the orders are taken from the number of stamens, and are therefore Pentandria, Hexandria, etc.
In Syngenesia the orders are taken from the different forms of the florets. Poligamia Igual (Equal Polygamy) or Poligamia Espuria (Spurious Polygamy) may occur. The latter is subdivided into Superflua, Frustanea, and Necessaria; or there may also be Poligamia segregada and Poligamia monogamia. These are to be understood in the following way.
Poligamia igual. When the florets are hermaphrodite or have both stamens and pistils.
Poligamia supérflua. When the florets of the Disc are hermaphrodite and have stigmas and bear fruit, and the florets of the ray or circumference are female and bear fruit fertilized by the male flowers of the Disc. Example: the Hagonoy.
Poligamia frustanea. When the florets of the Disc are hermaphrodite and have stigmas and bear fruit, but the female florets of the ray lack a stigma and do not produce perfect seeds.
Poligamia necesaria. When the florets of the Disc are hermaphrodite but, lacking stigmas on their pistils, cannot produce perfect seeds; whereas the female florets of the ray, having a stigma, produce perfect fruit.
Poligamia segregada. When many florets, in addition to sharing a common calyx, each also have their own individual calyx.
Poligamia monoginia. In this order there is no more than a single flower inside each calyx: that is, the flowers are simple. Example: Impatiens.
In the class Gynandria the orders are taken from the number of stamens, as in the first thirteen classes.
In the classes Monoecia and Dioecia the orders are taken either from the number of stamens, as in the first thirteen classes, or from the manner in which they are arranged. Thus the orders are Monandria, Diandria, etc., Polyandria, Adelphia when they form or are united in bodies, Syngenesia when the anthers are united among themselves, and Gynandria when the stamens are attached to the pistils.
In the class Polygamia there are three orders: Monoecia, Dioecia, and Trioecia. The first, when hermaphrodite flowers and male or female flowers are found on the same plant. The second, when they are found on two different plants. The third, when all of the above are found on three plants or feet.
In the class Cryptogamia the orders are the Ferns, the Mosses, the Algae, and the Fungi.

NOTE. At the end of the description of each plant, the names will be given in the languages of the Islands — Tagalog, Camarines, Visaya, Pampango, and Ilocano — under the initials T. C. V. P. I. Be advised that the h in these languages has the sound of j; that the d at the end of a word is a sound midway between d and r; that the ñ is pronounced nasally; and finally that the u as in ualisin is to be pronounced by striking the u toward the a; but sometimes I have written it in a way that approximates what the pronunciation ought to be, even though in reality it is not quite so: as molauin, though it should be molavin, and Hauili, though it should be Havili. At the same time, and for brevity, certain words will be abbreviated as follows: Cal. Calyx. = Cor. Corolla. = Estam. Stamens. = Pist. Pistils. = Gén. Genus. = Ant. Anthers. = Nect. Nectary. The calyx is to be understood as monopetalous and the corolla as monopetalous when it is said that they are cleft into laciniae or divided into a certain number of parts.

MONANDRIA.

MONOGYNY.

RENEALMIA. Description of the genus. Corolla cleft into three laciniae. Nectary oblong. Calyx of one piece. Anther sessile, opposite the nectary. Berry fleshy. Palau. Part. práct. t. 2. 1.

RENEALMIA EXALTATA. RENEALMIA EXALTADA. Stem cylindrical. Leaves lanceolate, with folds running from one end to the other, and smooth. Petioles sheathe the stem. Flowers terminal, in a spike. Cal. monopetalous, splitting longitudinally, and with three sharp little teeth. Cor. very deeply cleft into three parts: one larger than the others. Nect. fixed to the corolla, composed of two parts: one shaped like a small boat, with two little ears toward the base, and divided at the tip into three lobes, the middle one bifid. The other supports the anther, more than half an inch long. Style as long as the stamen, surrounded at the base by a body composed of

2
many small fleshy leaflets. Stigma funnel-shaped, compressed. Lower capsule oval, fleshy before ripening, crowned with all the parts of the flower, with three valves and as many chambers, each containing many seeds. = This plant, whose thickness will be no more than two inches, rises to the height of eight feet, and I have seen it in Malinta reach more than eight yards. The fruit is bittersweet and is eaten. Its root is fragrant. The Indians make some use of it in medicine. The water of the tagbac is the best of all for macerating the tinder taken from the Pugahan. * T., Tagbac. P., V., Catcatan, Catotang, Tagbac, Salbac, Bagombon. Palau. ibid. 16.
AMOMUM. Cor. (Cal. according to Jussieu) divided into three to six parts: the first upper section open. Capsule resembling a berry, inferior, with three or more chambers. Lin. Sist. veg. 5.
Amomum zingiber. Amomo agengibre. Root irregular, fleshy, with lateral branches. Leaves half-lanceolate, broad, with a whitish and thin membrane following the edges, entire and smooth. Petioles sheath the stem. = This plant, known throughout all the Islands, is cultivated intentionally, because its aroma makes it very widely used and beneficial in cooking. The Indians use it a great deal and with good reason, and are in this more sensible than some timid Europeans, who fear it as a heating spice: some physicians use it to give energy to purgatives, and to relieve nausea. * T., Luya. C. Laya. Lin. ibid.
Amomum zerumbet? Amomo zerumbet? Root irregularly tuberous, with short and thick branches. Leaves lanceolate, sheathing the stem. Flowers placed on a cylindrical and blunt receptacle, composed of many overlapping, egg-shaped scales; on each scale one flower, and at the base of each fruit a narrow, concave small leaflet, and another very thin small leaflet over the same fruit. Flower scape short and simple. Calyx double. (Jus.) the outer one very long, somewhat two-lipped: the upper lip entire, lanceolate, and the lower one larger, divided into two lanceolate parts. The inner one, also somewhat two-lipped, attached to the outer calyx. The upper lip very narrow, lanceolate and arched. The lower one much larger, divided into three parts: the middle one very wide. Stamen one. Filament none. Anther long, attached to the upper lip of the inner calyx, and which can be split in two. At the lower part of the tube, two long, awl-shaped little bodies are visible, which resemble another sterile anther divided in two. Ovary egg-shaped, beneath the flower. Style a very long thread, which passes through the middle of the anther. Stigma funnel-shaped, hairy. Capsule? with three chambers, each containing many seeds. = This plant, known to the Indians, rises to the height of three or four feet. Its root has a very strong and pleasant smell. The natives use it in

3
medicine. An Indian assured me that, when transplanted to gardens, it turns into true ginger. Flowers in September. * T., Luyang osiu, Lampuyan! — I doubt whether this is the same species. Lin. ibid.
Amomum echinatum. Spiny Amomum. The capsule is shaped like a half-cylindrical berry, with a navel at the apex where the flower once was, covered with short spines, with three chambers and many seeds. = I have seen nothing of this plant but the fruit, which consists of a compact terminal cluster. The berries are an inch or more in length, and the flesh is a beautiful crimson. It was sent to me from Angat, and it is without doubt the Costus echinatus of Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 3. and the Amomum echinatum of Willd. espec. pl. L. 1. p. 3. It is also the plant that Rumphius describes under the name Globba uviformis, 6. p. 134. t. 61. f. 1.
COSTUS. Inner corolla or nectary swollen, open-mouthed, and the lower lip divided into three parts. Lin. ibid. 7.
Costus nigricans. Blackening Costus. Root large, with short, thick branches and fibers from which hang many globose tubers. Leaves lanceolate, with a whitish, transparent membrane following the margins, entire, smooth, and with a blackish stripe toward the middle. The petioles sheathe the stem. Flowers in an oblong receptacle composed of ovate, imbricate scales, placed on a scape or stalk somewhat compressed and short. Each scale contains more than five small flowers. Calyx monopetalous, conical, breaking irregularly at the time the flower expands. Corolla swollen, two-lipped: the upper lip entire, with the tip sharpened and bent downward; the lower lip divided into two, smaller than the upper. Nectary nearly closed, swollen, fixed to the corolla, with its edge divided into four pieces: the lower one large, keeled, fleshy, notched at the tip into two parts. The two lateral ones somewhat shorter and smaller than the lower one. The fourth, upper one very small, supporting the anther, which is split below into two parts like little horns. Style filiform, passing through the anther. Stigma compressed and funnel-shaped, resting upon the anther. Capsule with three chambers, crowned with all the parts of the flower, and with many seeds in each chamber. = This plant sends up no more stem than I described before. The root is whitish and very fragrant. It is very common everywhere, and it is easy to confuse it with another that I am inclined to think belongs to the same genus, which the natives call Tamahilan or Tamohilan; but it is easily distinguished by the stripes on the leaves mentioned above. It flowered in May after the first rains. T., Barac, Lampuyang. The name of the species is taken from the blackish stripe on the leaves.
Costus luteus. Yellow Costus. Root like those of the spe-

4
cie nigricans, but they are yellow. Leaves as in the same species, but without a black stripe. = It is a plant of more than three feet in height, very common, and dyes yellow with its roots. * T., Tamahilan, Tamohilan, Tamo, Tamocausi, Tumahiba, Bolon, P., Tamo. The specific name refers to the color of the roots.
CURCUMA. Four sterile stamens, and the fifth fertile one within the nectary. Lin. Syst. veg. 8.
Curcuma longa. Large Curcuma. Root irregular, thick, with branches. Leaves somewhat lanceolate, broad, with a thin and whitish membrane along the edges, entire and smooth, and with many transverse veins, some more raised than others. Petioles notable. = A plant well known to the Indians: with it they dye yellow, though not very fast. Its raw root is prescribed by Indian physicians to those who suffer from headache, and it benefits them. It also serves to clean gold by rubbing it with the root. Indian healers claim it draws out thorns when applied crushed to the affected part. According to the curious Father Santa Maria, mixed with oil and applied to scabies, it cures it on the second application; he also says that its juice drunk in the quantity of half an egg cures typhus fever. In China it is used to provoke sneezing, and in these Islands it is also used in cooking. * T. Dilao. V. Dulao, Calavaga. Quinambov, P. Angai. Lin. ibid.
KAEMPFERIA. Corolla divided into six lobes: the three larger ones, spreading; and one divided into two others; the stigma with two small plates. Lin. Syst. veg. 8.
Kaempferia rotunda. Round Kaempferia. Sessile leaves, approaching a shape between ovate and round. Calyx (according to Jus.) very deeply split into six parts: the three outer ones very narrow and pointed. The three inner ones reach nearly to the base: the upper one larger, concave, bent backward, split at the tip into two parts, each with a sinus at the side. The two lateral ones smaller and wedge-shaped. Style, Stigma, and the rest, as in the amomun barao. Nectary: a very small tube, fixed in the larger sinus, opposite the larger segment of the calyx, and open lengthwise on the side facing that segment, with the upper end divided into two parts. Anther attached to the same nectary. = This plant sends up no stem; its root is very fragrant. The one I saw flower was part of a large root, which I placed in a pot in the month of July. In the following August, after several days of heavy rain, it put forth its flower, which perished after a few hours. I was unable to learn about its fruit. The Indians use the root in medicine. * T. Dusog, Duso, Dusod, Guisol. V. P. Cusol, Guisol, Dusol. Lin. ibid.
CANNA. Calyx of three small leaves. Corolla erect, divided into six

5
laciniae, with the lip of the nectary divided in two and recurved. Style lanceolate, united with the corolla. Lin. Sist. veg. 5.
Canna indica. Indian Canna. Root irregular, thick, with many lateral rootlets. Leaves mid-lanceolate, more than one foot long, with a great many veins that are not very prominent, some of which rise at intervals higher than others. Petioles sheathing the stem. Flowers in a spike. Calyx (Jus.) double: the outer one of three leaflets, pointed and overlapping at the edges. The inner one with six laciniae: the three inner ones more colorful, whose insertion in the flower gradually rises. Nectary as in the genus: Anther one, attached to one of the pieces of the nectary. Style a blade shaped like a sword, obtuse, attached to the same piece of the nectary where the anther also is. Inferior capsule, crowned by the calyx, with three obtuse angles, bristling with soft deciduous spines, with three chambers, and in each one many globose seeds.= This plant barely puts out a stem except when it flowers. It is easy to mistake it at first glance for Costus nigricans. The Indians make no use of it whatsoever; nevertheless, the decoction of its roots is diuretic and calms the irritation of the bladder spasm. They name it in the manner I will describe below, because its seeds, being perfectly globose and black, serve well as rosary beads, and indeed they are still used for this purpose even in Spain; while the Indians of America use them as bullets to kill their enemies. They also yield a good purple dye, though it is fugitive. Flowers in December. *T. Cacuentasan, Tiquis, tiquis, Ticas, Ticas ticas, Lin. ibid.
In Dampol de Bulacan I have seen a rare and curious variety with straw-colored flowers.
MARANTA. Corolla open-mouthed, divided into five laciniae, with the two alternate ones spreading. Lin. Sist. veg. 8.
Maranta arundinacea. Reed-like Maranta. Stem erect, smooth, somewhat flattened. Branches in an umbel, with one or more keeled, pointed, and stiff props. Leaves sheathing the stem at the base, egg-shaped, lanceolate, and smooth. Flowers in a long panicle containing many small flowers almost in pairs; each one with its own partial involucre or bract, somewhat elongated and pointed. In addition, above the ovary there is a kind of crown composed of three to five pieces that persist on the fruit. Calyx divided into six parts: the three lower ones smaller. The nectary resembles a petal divided in two, one part of which bears an anther, and at the foot of the other the pistil. Capsule slightly fleshy and firm, becoming membranous at maturity, with three chambers, each containing one seed.= A plant of one or two fathoms in height, which I have seen in the forests.
9

6

The natives use the bark to make fine hats, though not very durable. Flowers in May. — It would more likely be the species tonxat. *T. Tagbac tacbac. In Angat, Bamban. Lin. ibid.— The maranta called indica by the Authors produces edible tubers; made into flour they are very useful, tasty, and keep for a long time.

DIANDRIA.

MONOGYNIA.

BOERHAAVIA. Calyx none. Corolla of one petal, bell-shaped and folded: a single seed, naked, and below the calyx. Stamens sometimes two. Lin. Syst. veg. 14.

Boerhaavia diffusa. Spreading Boerhaavia. Stem covered with very short hairs, with many branches lying along the ground. Leaves opposite, generally one larger than the other, somewhat heart-shaped, ovate, obtuse, with a short point at the apex, finely toothed, wavy, and rough on the upper surface, with veins beneath. Lateral flowers in a kind of umbel, sometimes simple and sometimes dichotomous, placed on a very long common peduncle. Each small flower with two or three pointed scales, opposite at the base. Calyx none, unless said scales are considered as such. Corolla superior, with five lobes: each one with a fold and a notch. Stamens two in some plants, three in others. Anthers of two globes. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma broad and shield-shaped. The achene is cylindrical, crowned by the corolla, with five channels, full of short, soft spines that exude a kind of glue, with a single oblong seed that has two channels on the front. = This plant is very similar to valerian. It is common in the province of Batangas, near stone buildings. I have already noted that it spreads along the ground; its root has a rather pungent flavor. The color of the entire plant is somewhat reddish. Because of its affinity with valerian, one may, according to the Authors, try its dried root in doses of about ten grains, combined with honey or sugar, or with lemon syrup, for heart ailments, especially when the condition arises from worms. *T. Paanbalivis? I. tabtabocol ti Nuang. Lin. ibid. 15.

NYCTANTHES. Calyx in eight parts. Corolla monopetalous in eight parts. The pericarp contains two seeds. Lin. syst. veg. 23.

Nyctanthes sambac. Sambac Nyctanthes. Stem trailing along the ground, cylindrical and somewhat compressed. Leaves opposite, notched at the base, lanceolate, ovate, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Terminal flowers in a kind of pa-

7
branch of many small flowers. Cal. in eight or nine parts, very long and awl-shaped. Cor. in seven or eight parts, with a long tube. Stam. two. Pist. one. Stigma split into two plates. = This plant is known to all the natives: its flower is very fragrant, and it spreads widely over the ground: using its flowers alone and without soap, fine white linen is washed very well, and it retains a very pleasant scent. It is said in the translation of Linnaeus that the natives of India make from the tender leaves and flowers a paste which, mixed and eaten with rice, dries up scabies and other skin eruptions. The water of an infusion of its flowers is excellent for washing eyes inflamed by heat. Fl. in Dec. *T. Sampaga. V. Capopot visaya, Manul. P. Campopot, Sampagang Pougso, Culatai. Lin. ibid.
MOCORIUM. Cal. with eight laciniae. Cor. tubular in eight parts. Berry regularly twin, with two cells and two seeds. Jus. Gen. pl. 106.
Mogorium aculeatum. Prickly Mogorio. Stem round, climbing by leaning on other trees. Leaves opposite, egg-shaped, elongated, pointed, soft and smooth. Common petioles with two hard stipules like truncated spines at the base. Terminal flowers in umbel-like panicles; the individual peduncles thicken at the tip. Cal. with five or six teeth. Cor. with six or eight laciniae on the long tube. Stam. two, fixed near the throat. Two oval berries, barely compressed, very smooth, joined at the base (one frequently aborts), each with one cell and one globose seed. = A shrub unknown to the natives, which I have seen in various places. The fruit is like a chickpea. The flowers have no notable scent. It may be the Nictanthes undulata of Linnaeus. Jussieu places in the genus Mogorium all species of nictanthes that bear berries. Fl. in May. — I have seen other plants that have three stamens, one of which has a sterile anther. The berries are black at maturity. The specific name refers to the stipules of the petioles.
LIGUSTRUM. Cor. with four laciniae. Cal. with four teeth. Berry with one cell and four seeds. Jus. Gen. pl. 106.
Ligustrum quadriloculare. Four-celled Privet. Trunk with square branches at the tips. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire, soft and hairy on both surfaces. Petioles half as short as the leaves. Axillary flowers in a panicle. Cal. fleshy with five acute teeth. Cor. more than five times longer than the calyx, funnel-shaped and with five fleshy laciniae. Stam. two, fixed to the corolla and equal to each other in height. Filaments short. Anthers lying over the filaments. Style shorter than the stamens. Stigma, two awl-shaped plates. Berry dry, oval, superior, ce-

8
fused nearly to the middle with the calyx, with four chambers and in each one a single seed. = This small tree reaches a height of six feet. The Indians call it balictarin, which means something backwards, due to the peculiarity of its leaves being green on top and purple underneath. The flowers of this small tree deserve to be examined again, since I wrote about this being new to these matters, and it remains to be determined the precise insertion of the stamens, which I am inclined to think emerge from outside the tube. I leave this shrub here, although it agrees with Eranthemum in its calyx and corolla; but differs in its stigma. *Balictarin. — From its chambers I gave the species its name.
ELYTRARIA. Calyx leathery, in four unequal parts: one with two teeth. Corolla with five nearly equal lobes in the limb. Two sterile filaments. Stigma strap-shaped. Capsule oblong, with two chambers and two valves with a half-partition, without elastic claws. The peduncle of the flowers is radical and bracteate.
Elytraria amara. Bitter Elytraria. Trunk woody and short. Leaves alternate, imbricated, running along nearly the entire petiole, lanceolate, toothed below and serrate above, somewhat hairy. Radical and axillary flowers in spiked panicles: each small flower with a leathery bract, scarious at the margin, ending in a bristle. Common peduncles very long, covered with scales resembling the bracts. Calyx membranous; fitted with two opposite lanceolate pieces, and divided into four parts; the opposite ones narrower. Corolla much longer than the calyx, monopetalous, tubular, bilabiate: the upper lip divided into three bilobed parts, the middle one largest. The lower lip smaller, bifid, and with a concavity, where it conceals the stigma and anthers. Stamens two, with very short filaments, fixed at the end of the tube. Anthers as if arrow-shaped. Ovary cylindrical. Style as long as the corolla, with the stigma in the form of a lamina. Capsule oblong, without elastic claws, with two chambers and two valves, each with a half-partition. Seeds half-globose and compressed, arranged in a row. = Plant of one foot in height, common in Parañaque, on the side opposite Dongalo. The leaves are one geme long and so is the petiole. The root and even the leaves are quite bitter. The corolla is violet-colored and the calyx white and membranous. It agrees with Elytraria. It differs in having no more than two stamens, with no sign of others being sterile. By its scaly peduncles it differs from Gratiola. Flowers in December.
GRATIOLA. Calyx divided into five parts, with two accessory outer bracts. Corolla irregular, resupinate. Stamens four, two of them sterile. Capsule with two cells. Lin. Syst. 87.
Gratiola hissopioides. Hyssop-like Gratiola. Stem square, prostrate, spreading by stolons. Le-

9

leaves opposite, clasping the stem at the base, lanceolate, serrated, fleshy, and smooth. Flowers solitary in the axils. Peduncle long at maturity. Calyx inferior, divided into five or six lanceolate parts, some with two teeth. Corolla open-mouthed: the upper lip notched; the lower larger, divided into two rounded parts. Stamens four; the two fertile ones fixed at the divisions of the lips of the corolla; the two lower ones sterile, beneath the lower lip and twisted to the sides. Filaments short. Anthers one on each filament, cleft and diverging below. Ovary oval, seated within the flower. Style longer than the corolla and bent toward the middle. Stigma two small plates that disappear at maturity. Capsule twice as long as the calyx, awl-shaped, with two valves, one chamber, and many nearly round seeds fixed on a thin receptacle in the shape of a sword. = This plant, which I have seen in Pasig on land abandoned by the waters, is not known to the local people. It rises very little above the ground. Its leaves and stem are purple, and the flavor of the herb is barely bitter. — Although the flowers appear to have an egg-shaped and serrated bract, which at maturity becomes lanceolate, in reality it is not a bract but a leaf of the stem that is still growing. The calyx with its subdivided lobes, and the style with its bend, are notable features. It agrees in part with Cirtandra. The virtues of Graciola are marvelous in dropsy and other ailments. *Flowers in January. — Could this be that species? Lin. syst. veg. 37.

JUSTICIA. Corolla open-mouthed, with one anther on each stamen. Capsule with two chambers, opening by means of an elastic claw. Lin. syst. veg. 20.

Justicia picta. Painted Justicia. Trunk erect with very smooth branches. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, notched, smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary and terminal in a simple raceme. Bracts very small, somewhat elongated, pointed, entire. Calyx divided very deeply into five nearly equal parts. Corolla humped, very compressed, two-lipped, with the lips turned back and very rolled up: the upper lip divided into three parts, the middle one notched; the lower lip entire. Stamens two, attached to the corolla up to half their length: and before the expansion of the flower they are arched to the sides, and the anthers incline toward each other; after expansion they rise close together forming an arch, and bending downward, they extend well beyond the corolla. Two additional short, sterile stamens are also visible, placed above the first. Style somewhat shorter than the stamens and hidden behind them. Stigma barely bifid. Capsule conical, superior, straight, not twisted. = This small tree reaches a height of seven or nine feet. The Indians plant it in their gardens and

10
reason for the large white spots that the leaves have along their length in the middle, they call it moradong maputi: that is, white purple, because there is another congener whose leaves are purple and without spots. The leaves are used in India to resolve scirrhous tumors of women's breasts, for which purpose they are crushed and applied. I have never seen the ripe fruit. The corollas very compressed with the edges rolled backward are very particular distinguishing marks of this species and of the Echolium. There is another species with flowers in racemes, umbellate, and in every other respect like the former. Flowers in December. *Morandong maputi, Balasbas, V. Balasbas. Ant. tolang, S. Francisco. Lin. Sist. veg. 32.

Justicia ecbolium. Justicia ecbolio. Leaves opposite, broad, lanceolate, notched, smooth. Flowers axillary and terminal, arranged in umbellate racemes: each umbel of only three small flowers. Bracts very small and somewhat fringed.= A small tree common everywhere, with purple leaves. It grows to a height of twelve feet at most. The natives do not use it for anything except to cover springs with its leaves. *T. Purple leaves; Balasbas malomay, Yovas, Ataiatai, Morado, Ternate, Sarasa.

Justicia gandarrusa. Justicia gandarusa. Stem without spines. Leaves sessile, lanceolate, somewhat hairy. Flowers in terminal whorled spikes. Calyx in five parts. Corolla very long with a cylindrical tube and five lobes, two below and three above, with small purple spots. Capsule with a horizontal throat that divides it in two, each containing two seeds that spring out by means of elastic hooks.= A very common and well-known plant. There is a variety with a black, knotty stem and of greater height. An infusion of the leaves is very useful for throat ailments and for curing all kinds of sores. It is said that the deer, whose Tagalog name is usa, eats it: and from this it takes its Cebuano name. *T. cinco llagas, Silisilihan, Limang sugat. V. Mopio, Maladosdos, Panaptum, Alyopyop, and in Cebu Mandalusa. Lin. Sist. veg. 33.

Justicia nasuta. Justicia of the long snout. Leaves lanceolate, somewhat notched and hairy. Flowers in spiked panicles with awl-shaped bracts at the base of each small flower. Calyx with five awl-shaped parts, the two lower ones below. Corolla very long, thread-like with angles: limb with four lobes: three of them egg-shaped below, and the other pointed above. The two anthers protrude beyond the throat. Stigma bifid.= A plant four feet in height. The corolla has some reddish spots. *T. Tagactagac. Lin. Sist. veg. 34.

Justicia dalaora. Justicia dalaora. Stem erect, swollen at the joints and smooth. Leaves opposite, lanceolate

11
egg-shaped, pointed with small hairless notches, and rough. Petioles two-thirds shorter than the leaves. Flowers axillary. Each common peduncle terminated by an involucre of two unequal leaflets: one somewhat large, and the opposite one very small and awl-like: which supports two small pieces parallel to the involucre, each with two egg-shaped, unequal bracts enclosing up to five small flowers with their calyces. Calyx divided into five awl-shaped parts, fitted with a small scale. Corolla wide-mouthed, very long: the tube thread-like on four sides, and the limb with two lobes turned outward: especially the upper one, which has three teeth: the lower one broader, with a truncated tip. Stamens two, protruding well beyond the throat: each with an anther terminating below in a small tail. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma two thick little plates. Fruit.= A plant two feet tall, known in the Visayas: its flowers are purple or somewhat violet: the leaves are light green and five inches long, and although they appear to have no color at all, when wrung in a white cloth, they impart after about an hour a pale rose color, or something like a dirty purple. The Indians boil the green leaves in water with abaca or buli fiber that they wish to dye, and obtain the color; but since it is not vivid, today they have nearly abandoned this plant and use sapang instead. The plant takes root with great ease, as I have seen with some that I had brought from Cebu. See Dalaora.— It closely resembles the species bivalvis of Linnaeus, but also differs from it: I have therefore given it the same name it has in the country. Neither does it agree very well with the species sicundi flora, ciliata, and appendiculata of Persoon. syn. pl. t. 1. 23.

Justicia viridis. Green Justicia. Stem square, swollen at the joints. Leaves broad, lanceolate and somewhat notched. Petioles short. Flowers axillary, in a dense compound spike: the spikelets tilted, and the bracts very small and pointed. The upper lip of the corolla with three teeth and turned backward: the lower one narrower and very rolled up. Capsule with four seeds: two above the others, jumping out by elastic nails.= A semi-woody green plant, four feet tall, which I have seen in Malinta. The corollas are white and the capsules very small. Flowers in January.— It approaches the species viridis. Lin. Sist. veg. 34.

Dianthera. Corolla two-lipped. Stamens each with two alternate anthers. Capsule with two compartments and two valves, which splits open by an elastic nail. Lin. Sist. veg. 35.

Dianthera subserrata. Serrate-like Dianthera. Stem upright, with smooth branches and four not very prominent angles. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, pointed, hairless and blunt-

12
finely serrated, with small remote teeth that are barely noticeable. Terminal flowers in clusters of three sessile florets, with lanceolate bracts. Calyx with five long teeth. Corolla: the upper lip notched and pointed. The lower lip broad with a palate, and at the tip with three lobes, the middle one being the largest. The anthers, as mentioned above. = A shrub that I have seen in Bauang near the Maghinao river, and it is not very common: it is about the height of a man: the color of the stem and leaf is purple, and it has a bad smell: it is close to the species nitida of Linnaeus. Syst. veg. 35.

DIANTHERA CILIATA. FRINGED DIANTERA. Herbaceous stem, lying on the ground and rooting at the nodes. Leaves sessile, opposite, ovate, elongated, entire and slightly rough on the upper surface. Flowers in a dense regular spike. Calyx split almost to the base into four lanceolate, keeled and fringed parts, with a bract of three similar leaflets. Corolla two-lipped: the upper lip small, barely notched at the tip: the lower lip larger, with three small rounded lobes, and with parallel ribs toward the throat. Stamens two, each with two anthers (viewed from above they appear as one), the lower one with a curved tail. Ovary cylindrical, with two glands at the base. Stigma one, barely bifid; capsule with a horizontal throat dividing it into two chambers, each containing two seeds that are expelled by elastic claws. = A plant about one foot tall, common in Malinta but not well known. The lower lip of the corolla has transverse and parallel ridges toward the throat, which appear, by meeting in the middle, like so many ribs. Pers. pl. t. l. 23. among the Diantera Justicias.

CIRTANDRA. Calyx in five unequal parts. Corolla irregular, tubular, with five lobes on the limb. Stamens four: the two lower ones are abortive. Stigma with two plates. Berry oblong, with two chambers and many seeds. Jus. Gen. plant. 121.

CIRTANDRA GLABERRIMA. VERY SMOOTH CIRTANDRA. Stem erect. Leaves sessile, opposite, fleshy, slightly toothed and very smooth. Flowers axillary and terminal, either solitary or in small panicles of few florets. Peduncle proper long. Lower calyx in five deep, lanceolate divisions. Corolla two-lipped, with an angular tube and a naked throat: the upper lip linear and as long as the lower lip, with three rounded and equal lobes. Stamens four: the two sterile ones are fixed in the throat. The two fertile ones arise at the division of the upper lip, and are directed upward. Anthers shaped like a half moon: one end of one inclines downward toward the other, and both remain pressed together in this way. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma with two plates. Capsule cylindrical, awl-shaped, with two

13
valves and countless elongated seeds, fixed on a free receptacle, shaped like a sword. = Plant that I saw in Malinta, growing in waterlogged places: its height is one span. If the anthers are not examined carefully, they will appear to be two on each fertile filament. Flowers in Oct.

Cirtandra aristata. Awned Cirtandra. Fibrous roots. Hollow stem with very few branches. Leaves sessile, opposite, lanceolate, fleshy, narrow and smooth, ending in a small awn. Flowers axillary and terminal, solitary or few in number, sessile and at maturity with a short peduncle. Calyx deeply cleft into five parts, two of them to one side. Corolla two-lipped with an open throat: the upper lip short, notched; the lower in three parts, the middle one larger. Stamens two, fixed in the tube toward the throat. Anthers two on each filament, paired: (perhaps a single one split nearly in half into two). Ovary globose, seated within the flower. Style elongated. Stigma funnel-shaped. Capsule oval, with one chamber and two free receptacles, fleshy, wide and drawn close to each other, in which many elongated and somewhat fleshy seeds are fixed. = Plant of about one foot in height, growing in still water: I saw it in Malinta, and it has no notable odor, but is somewhat mucilaginous. Flowers in Oct. — Perhaps a species of Besleria.

Cirtandra personata. Palate Cirtandra. Stem square, half-creeping. Leaves opposite, sessile, clasping the stem at the base, oval, finely serrated, with the serrations ending in an awn. Terminal flowers in a raceme, with the individual peduncles opposite and short. Calyx with an awl-shaped bract at the base, inversely conical, cleft into five awl-shaped parts. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, wide-mouthed; with the tube widening upward and compressed; the upper lip small and linear: the lower much larger, with three lobes and a palate. Stamens four: two of them sterile and long-fixed in the neck of the corolla tube up to the palate, very wide with awl-shaped and twisted tips turned to the sides: the other two fertile, fixed at the division of the lips. Filaments shorter than the upper lip of the corolla. Anthers two on each filament, emerging from the tip, oval, and at maturity the one from one filament somewhat joined to that of the other. Perhaps a single one split in two? Ovary conical with a flat, egg-shaped gland at the base. Style as tall as the stamens. Stigma of two laminae. Capsule leathery, twice as long as the calyx, cylindrical, awl-shaped, curved, with one chamber and many oval seeds fixed on a lanceolate partition. = Plant that barely reaches four fingers in height. The odor of the root is somewhat unpleasant. The locals do not know it.
10

14
I saw it in Guadalupe, Malinta, and on the bank of the river of Calumpang in Batangas. The cagillas have half an inch in length, one third of a line in thickness; the leaves one inch. It corresponds closely with Besleria; but I have placed it here on account of the sterile stamens, although by the gland it ought to go with the said Besl. Flowers in October.
VERBENA. Corolla funnel-shaped, curved, nearly equal. Calyx with five laciniae (Jus.) seeds two or four, naked, with the back cortex thicker. Lin. syst. veg. 41.
Verbena capitata. Headed Verbena. Stem spreading, with barely noticeable angles, and covered with short hairs. Leaves opposite, decurrent, clasping the stem, egg-shaped on the reverse, and serrated only on the upper part and somewhat hairy. Axillary flowers on a very long common peduncle, in a tight, conical, and scaly head: each small flower with a scale at the base. Proper calyx: of two keeled and compressed pieces. Corolla somewhat arched, funnel-shaped, open-mouthed, with a very narrow throat, and the limb divided into four parts, one shorter and notched on one side, and three on the other. Stamens four, the two upper ones: filaments almost none. Anthers all four fertile, and as if of two cells, the pollen discharged. Ovary superior, half-cylindrical. Style very short. Stigma globose. Fruit two seeds covered with the membrane of the ovary. = This plant is very common in rice fields and spreads along the ground, taking root at the points where it touches the soil. Many Indians do not know it; but some drink its hot infusion as one makes tea. *T. Chachachachahan. Lin. ibid. 41.
SALVIA. Corolla open-mouthed. Filaments with a small transverse piece. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 24.
Salvia violacea. Violet Salvia. Leaves opposite, egg-shaped (the older ones obliquely) obtusely serrated, somewhat hairy and rugose. Petioles short. Flowers terminal in verticillate spikes, lax at maturity, and the small flowers with a bract nearly as long as the calyx. Calyx narrowed toward the top, with three teeth. Corolla barely emerging from the calyx, two-lipped, violet in color: the upper lip velvety and split in two, concealing the two anthers: the lower lip larger, folded downward and in three parts: the middle one broader and bilobed. Stamens two, fixed on the upper lip: each one with a thick appendage directed downward and further increased by two alternating small teeth: the two small branches brought close to each other. Two other very small filaments are seen with sterile anthers. Style with two divergent and curved stigmas: one shorter. Seeds four, naked. = A plant two palms in height, which I have only seen in the surroundings of the

15
convent of Guadalupe. It is recognized by its flowers, which are violet. The smell is herbaceous, with a mixture of pleasant and unpleasant. Flowers in January. — It has surely sprouted in Guadalupe accidentally, as I have not seen it again anywhere. At the great gathering of Chinese that takes place in that location, on the 10th of September some seeds regularly fell from one or another of them, giving rise to two plants whose leaves I took to be those of tea, and which had a good flavor.
ROS MARINUS. Corolla unequal, with the upper lip divided in two. Stamens curved, simple and with one tooth. Lin. Sist. veg. 44.
Ros marinus. officinalis. Common Rosemary. Leaves sessile, linear, obtuse, with rolled margins, and whitish beneath. Calyx tubular, two-lipped: the upper entire and pointed, the lower divided into two parts, also pointed. Corolla open-mouthed, with the tube a little longer than the calyx: the upper lip concave, divided into two parts: the lower longer, with three lobes: the middle one larger, concave, notched, and with many small teeth on the edges: the lateral ones narrow. Stamens two fertile and two sterile. Filaments of the fertile stamens curved upward with a small branch or point on each one toward the middle. Anthers elongated. Filaments of the sterile stamens, placed toward the base of the fertile ones, and are short, very slender and twisted to both sides. Sterile anthers, split into two divergent parts. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma simple. Fruit, four seeds at the base of the calyx. = This plant, which has come from Spain, never grows very large in this land, as I have observed: for at most it reaches three feet. The Indians hold it in high esteem. It is difficult to get new cuttings to take root. However, I have observed that any small branch, when placed in sea sand or river sand — that is, sand that is far from the water and in which some grasses are already growing — takes root readily if watered at the base. The sterile stamens of the rosemary I have just described are worthy of note, and for that reason I have spoken of it at length. *T. Romero. Lin. ibid.

DIANDRIA.

TRIGINIA.

PIPER. Calyx none. Corolla none. Filaments none. Anthers two, opposite. Style none. Stigmas three. Berry with one seed. Palau. Part. prác. de Lin. t. l. 159.

16
Piper nigrum. Black Pepper. Leaves oval, tapering at both ends, with seven veins that do not meet at the base, but are opposite or alternate to the midrib, with the edges turned downward. Flowers in a spike. Stigmas two, bifid. Berry globose, with one seed. = This plant was once widely cultivated in Batangas and is well known to everyone. The natives drive stakes into the ground so that the plant's feet can grip them and climb up. Pepper is native to this country. I have never heard the locals call it anything other than the corrupted Spanish name; yet it has its own proper name, though now forgotten. *T. Pimienta, Malisa. Lin. Sist. veg. 76.
Piper betel. Betel Pepper. Stem climbs upright along stakes and trees. Leaves notched at the base, egg-shaped, pointed, with veins somewhat scattered, entire and smooth. = This plant is well known to everyone, on account of the immense use made of it in the preparation of betel, or buyo as the Spaniards here call it. The buyo of Pasay, near Manila, is highly esteemed, and that of Bauang in Batangas is the most prized of that province, and perhaps even better than that of Pasay. It thrives in somewhat sandy soil, and where the sand is excessive, as in Pasay, they improve it with small fish, or with the marc of sesame or other oil-bearing fruits. It must also be watered frequently. The plants are renewed after a year, and when they are left to grow old they produce flowers and fruit like the Litlit. The natives call the fruit Poro. *C. T. Itmo, Mam-in V. Buyo, Mamon. P. Samat. Lin. ibid.
Piper obliquum. Oblique Pepper. Stem climbs up neighboring trees. Leaves obliquely lanceolate, egg-shaped, with scattered veins, entire and smooth. Flowers opposite the leaves, arranged on a common fleshy receptacle shaped like a cone, dotted with isolated scales. Calyx and Corolla none, except for the scale. Style none. Stigma with six or more lobes. Fruit, a globose seed, hidden in the receptacle. = This plant, well known to the natives, grows as thick as an arm. Its flavor and smell resemble those of betel, and its fruit resembles anise; the natives use its leaves in place of the proper betel leaves to make buyo. It is common in small woodlands. I have not seen the anthers of the flowers, and I suspect they fall off very quickly; thus anyone wishing to examine them must attend diligently at the time the plant begins to flower, which is in March. *V. Litli. litbit, Saog, Sangilo. C. Nopan. The specific name refers to the leaves.
Piper anisodorum. Anise-scented Pepper. Leaves alternate, heart-shaped, egg-shaped, pointed, with the edges turned downward and with nine veins: the lateral ones arise from the base, and the three middle ones arise higher up. = Plant co-

17
known, and used by some in betel, for its mild and pleasant smell, similar to that of anise. *T. Anise buyo. The name of the species comes from its smell.

Piper parvifolium. Small-leaved pepper. Leaves notched at the base, between ovate and lanceolate, with three or five nerves, entire and smooth. Flowers on a long conical receptacle, covered with round scales, with very thin margins close together, which separate a little at the maturity of the fruit. Stamens two. Filaments almost none. Anthers regular, two on each filament, attached along their entire length to a fleshy zone, and after shedding their pollen they become concave. I cannot confirm whether two stamens touch each floret, or whether there are more or fewer. Style the small stalk of the scale mentioned above. Stigma shield-shaped, and it is the same scale. Fruit as in the other species. = This plant, known to the natives, climbs trees; it is very common in the forests, and places are found where there is hardly a tree without one: the cut stem exudes a kind of gum. In it the flowers are more easily observed than in the other species. The smell and taste are like those of the litlit, but more pungent, especially the stem and root: I suspect that this is the plant with which, according to travelers, the people of the islands of the South Sea make an intoxicating drink. During the time of cholera morbus, the natives chewed it as a preventive. All plants of the genus piper are more or less excellent for neutralizing the venom of serpents, for which purpose it is necessary to scarify the wound first, even if only with a needle, and then apply the juice of the plant, either fresh or crushed, and change it frequently. I was called, says the author of the flora of the Antilles, to attend a black man who had just been bitten on the leg by a snake. The progress of the venom had been astonishing. All the resources of medicine had been employed in vain. A black man presented himself asking my permission to apply the local remedy. The patient had no hope of recovery: it was a matter of a man's life: I hesitated no longer; and in a few moments I saw the venom neutralized by the simple application of piper procumbens. All the symptoms yielded at the third application. Flowers in July. *T. Sabia. The specific name refers to the leaves.

TRIANDRIA.
MONOGINIA.

ANTHELIZA. Corolla monopetalous, tubular, open-mouthed, irregular, with the tube curved and cylindrical, and with six lobes.

18
Lower capsule, with three chambers and three valves. Lin. Sist.
veg. 112 Jus. Gen. plant. 58.
Antholiza meriana. Antholiza meriana. Root bulbous,
egg-shaped, compressed, with keels, with other bulbs stacked on top.
Stem short, formed by the leaves that sheathe one another
and are shaped like a sword, with six nerves and many
folds. The flower stalk barely compressed, and widened at the top
like a leaf, forming a compressed spathe
with one valve, from which the flowers emerge: sometimes there are two
spathes one over the other on each stalk. Flowers in a proliferous
panicle; that is, from some peduncles spathes also emerge.
Each group of five small flowers has two common bracts, and each
flower has its own very thin bract. Calyx or superior Corolla,
divided almost to the base into six lanceolate parts: five
on one side, and the sixth smaller and pointed, on the
other. Stamens three, fixed at the base of the corolla. Filaments very
short and broad. Anthers long, linear. Styles three, four, or
five, somewhat shorter than the stamens. Stigmas simple.
Inferior fruit shaped like a top, compressed, with four angles
or small wings, and as many chambers, each containing some
small seeds. = A plant about one foot tall,
cultivated by some curious gardeners, whose bulbs are also eaten;
they are red. A decoction of a bulb drunk
in water causes frequent urination. Flowers in November. *Persian onions.
Lin. Sist. veget. 113.
COMMELINA. Corolla of six petals. Nectaries three, cross-shaped,
fixed on their own small stalks. Superior capsule, with
two or three chambers. Lin. Sist. veg. 120.
Commelina polygama. Commelina polygama. Stem inclined
toward the ground, knotted. Leaves alternate, egg-shaped, hairy. Petioles
sheathing the stem. Calyx three-leaved, unless it is considered part
of the corolla. Corolla of three petals (or six if the calyx is
included), the two larger ones bigger than the third. Flowers axillary,
in a single-leafed, compressed spathe, numbering three;
but no more than two enlarged ones are ever seen emerging from
the spathe, of which the shorter one is hermaphrodite and the
longer one lacks a pistil; sometimes both are hermaphrodite.
Their own peduncles: that of the sterile flower very long, with a
fold in the middle. Stamens six. Filaments without hairs. Anthers three,
white, irregular, cross-shaped: the fourth is larger,
split at the base; and the two remaining longer ones are regular
and of a different color from the others. Style in the hermaphrodite
flower as long as the stamens. Stigma round and somewhat hairy.
Capsule with three angles and three chambers, with one
seed in each, oval and rough. = This plant, extremely common
everywhere, grows leaning toward the ground. The Indians

19
They know, and say that its decoction is good for eye ailments: the clouding of the eyes is removed by gently wiping them with the tender little stem of the plant, and then moistening them with a drop of lemon juice and fine powders of alum stone. This is what an Indian woman used to do. The cross-shaped anthers mentioned above do not seem to me to be nectaries, but rather true anthers, slightly different from the fourth type: and indeed if an anther splits sufficiently from below, and a little from its upper part, the resulting shape is entirely similar to what one might suspect are nectaries. In the cassias there is also great diversity in the anthers, such that some bear no resemblance to others. Flowers in August. * T. Alicbangon. V. Sabilao. P. Biasbias. Pers. Sinops. Plant. 55. — This genus is barely distinguishable from the tradescantia.

SALACIA. Corolla of five petals. Calyx in five parts. Anthers seated on the apex of the ovary. Lin. sist. veg. 107.
Salacia sinensis. Chinese Salacia. Branches round, with compressed tips. Leaves generally opposite, winged, without odd leaflet. Leaflets lanceolate, bluntly serrated, wavy and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers small, axillary, in an umbel of four or a few more small florets, with long proper peduncles. Calyx free, very small, with five obtuse lobes. Corolla of five nearly round petals, with three small teeth at the tip, alternating with the calyx lobes and nearly the same color, with short claws. Receptacle fleshy, raised and somewhat sunken toward the middle. Stamens three, fixed in the receptacle (and not on the ovary), erect at first and very pressed against the ovary, and at maturity curved backward. Filaments broad, tapering. Anthers small. Ovary partly submerged in the receptacle, with three angles. Style very short. Stigma one. Berry globose, like a cherry, crowned with the style, seated on a receptacle, with one oval seed, sometimes two, with no more skin than a thin crust. = Small trees of about three varas in height, with white, hard wood. The root is thick, irregular, very hard, and purple in color. A purgative syrup is made from it, and it is highly regarded. The Indians know it, and I have seen some in Malinta: but in Parañaque its use as a purgative is common, as I mentioned. The berry is yellow: its flesh is white, slightly sweet, and is eaten; but it is rather insipid. Flowers in January. * T. Matang-olang. — I have seen another species with flowers that smell of human excrement, which I once believed to be a comocladia.

HIPPOCRATEA. Corolla of five petals. Calyx in five parts. Three very compressed capsules with valves. Lin. Sist. veg. 107. Jus. Gén. pl. 251.

20

Hippocratea volubilis? Climbing Hippocratea. Leaves opposite, running down the petiole, lanceolate, stiff and smooth. Flowers axillary and terminal, in racemes. Calyx very small, bell-shaped, free, in five membranous, lanceolate parts, with overlapping margins. Corolla twice as long as the calyx and alternating with its parts, of five awl-shaped petals fixed to the receptacle. Stamens three, much shorter than the corolla. Anthers half-globose. Germens three, oval, divergent, large, and very compressed. Style a prominent point in the middle of the three germens, elongating somewhat with time. Stigma one. Three capsules, very compressed, obliquely oblong, heart-shaped in reverse, each with two flat valves and two heart-shaped seeds, very thin, fixed at the base of each capsule and mutually overlapping. = Small trees, which I believe are climbing, found in Malinta. The capsules have only one chamber: the seeds I saw were not ripe; but they had a membrane at the edge. Flowers in July. *T. Tatlong palad. Lin. ibid.

PISSILIA. Corolla that splits easily into three conniving petals. Calyx entire, swollen below. Stamens five, sterile. Nut covered by the calyx, with a seed. Lin. Sist. veg. 93.

Fissilia psittacorum. Parrot Fisilia. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, entire, smooth and stiff. Petioles very short. Flowers in short racemes. Calyx entire, very small at first; at maturity very large, almost entirely covering the fruit. Corolla much longer than the calyx, fleshy, stiff, of three linear petals, split at the tip into two parts. Stamens three fertile and six sterile, the sterile ones ending in a fork: all fixed to the petals: each fertile stamen has on each side one sterile stamen that is longer. Germen conical, seated inside the calyx. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma slightly thicker than the style and concave. Drupe with a small navel at the tip, formed by the calyx, with a globose and slender nut containing one chamber and one seed. = This tree is common in many places, reaching a height of five or six varas. The drupe has two fleshy rinds: one from the calyx and one its own. The flavor of the seeds, which I do not know whether they are edible, resembles somewhat that of the chestnut; but at least the rind is eaten. Flowers in March. *T. Malabaguio. I. Tadiag. Lin. ibid.

TAMARINDUS. Calyx inferior, with the rim in four parts. Corolla of three petals. Nectary of two short spurs or little horns below the filaments. Pod full of pulp. Lin. sist. veg. 94.

Tamarindus indica. Indian Tamarind. Leaves opposite, pinnate without a terminal leaflet. Leaflets twelve or more pairs, linear, with a notch at the apex, entire and smooth.

21

Flowers in racemes. Calyx inferior, divided into four parts curved backwards. Corolla of three lanceolate petals, variegated and curled at the edges; the middle one smaller and opposite one of the calyx parts; and the other two, one on each side of the same part. In addition, two very small rudimentary petals are seen, alternating with the other two parts of the calyx. Stamens monadelphous, united into a flat body, divided above into seven filaments: the three longest are fertile with versatile anthers; two short and sterile ones alternate with those; and on each side of the fleshy body and toward the upper part, another short sterile filament. Anthers incumbent. Style longer than the stamens. Legume as in the genus. = This tree is considered second-rank, and its roots are valued for certain uses in carpentry, as they are as good as or even better than ebony, and rosaries are also made from them. The pulp extracted from the fruit serves as a refresher; it also purges in doses of one or two ounces, and is a very useful remedy in bilious fevers and toward the end of smallpox. Flowers in May. *T. P. C. Sampaloc, Maca-sampaloc. B. Sampaloc, Sambac, Sumalagui, Camalagui, Sampalagui I. Salomagui. Lin. ibid.

CYPERUS. Calyx of scaly, clustered glumes facing both sides. Corolla: none. Seed one, naked. Lin. Syst. veg. 129.

Cyperus rotundus. Round Sedge. Root tuberous, oval in shape, without zones, with some prominent points that make it rough, from which some lateral rootlets emerge. Leaves sword-shaped, clasping the stem at the base. Flowers at the tip of a very long, naked, triangular stem, in an umbel composed of others: the small spikes are alternate, elongated, awl-shaped, and with distinct flowers. Calyx, or universal involucre of the flowers, of two bracts sword-shaped. Partial involucre one bract. Proper calyx a very small keeled scale. Corolla: none. Stamens three. Filaments long, fixed at the base of the ovary. Anthers long, straight. Style one, somewhat long. Stigmas three, simple, curved downward. Fruit a single oblong seed, three-sided and smooth. = This grassy plant is known to all the natives. It produces no stalk other than that of the flowers. Its root is as thick as a chickpea, and sometimes nearly a finger and a half long. It has the smell and taste of musk, and stings a little. The natives say that these roots, when eaten, are good for dysentery, and that chewed they benefit those whose teeth are decayed. This species is more suitable than others; but a friend told me it is a new species, which they have called Hydra. *T. Mut-ha. B. Botobotones. P. Mota, Malaapolid, Sursur, Onoran, Cusung, Omadiung, Galonalpas. Lin. Syst. veg. 132.

11

22
Cyperus difformis? Misshapen Sedge? Fibrous root. Leaves sword-shaped, keeled. Flowers at the tip of a triangular and bare stem with concave sides, arranged in an umbel that at first divides into more than three parts, and each of these subdivides further into others. The small spikelets are lanceolate, very small and compressed. Universal involucre of three small leaves, the two smallest being equal. = This plant is very well known, reaches the height of a man, and its stem grows to more than an inch thick. When it is tender, it is fed to horses in Manila, though I do not know whether to purge them. I am not certain that this plant is the species called Difformis. From it are made the thick mats called Bancoan, and also fine and very curious mats called Sinabatan, which are dyed various colors by preparing and boiling the leaves first with those of the Memecilon; although some say these mats are cold and harmful to the body, and that those of the Buli are preferable. * T. Titio, Tiquio, Lin. Sist. veg. 133.
— Some call it balangot, others bancoan, and others sabotan, so that even the natives themselves do not agree. The names given above are the most accurate.
Cyperus paniculatus. Panicled Sedge. Fibrous root. Leaves sword-shaped, smooth below and rough above. The petioles sheathe the entire flower stem and are long and speckled with hairs, especially toward the tip. Flowers on the said cylindrical and knotted stem, which subdivides into many small horizontal branches or ribs arranged in a star pattern, in the manner of a compound panicle, very open and lax, where all the small spikelets are turned downward, except the last ones at the top, which are ovate, very small, compressed, with distichous flowers. Universal involucre none, unless one considers as such the last leaf of the stem. Involucre of the partial peduncles a group of long hairs. Cal. glume of two valves enclosing a single flower: the outer valve ovate, concave; the inner one still more concave, compressed, also concave on the back and with two ridges each bearing a row of bristles. Cor. none. Stam. three, as long as the calyx at maturity. Ant. (dark crimson in color) split above and below into two parts. Ovary superior, middle conic. Styles two. Stigmas plumose. Fruit a small elongated seed seated within the calyx. = This delicate plant is very common and well known among the natives; it rises (that is, the flowering stems, which are very small and purplish in color) to a height of two feet. The natives make no use of it whatsoever. Flowers in October and other months. * T. Caliraorao. Lin. Sist. veg. 131.—
In Parañaque during the month of February these plants had about two finger-widths near the panicle, and even within the panicle itself, one

23
a species of fragrant gum like pine pitch or earth tar. Among those that were green, few had it. In Guadalupe I noted the same, and this will perhaps be the case everywhere; which is quite remarkable.
SCIRPUS. Scaly glumes clustered on all sides. Corolla none. One seed with three sides, without bristles, and often with down. Lin. Syst. veg. 124.
Scirpus niloticus? Scirpus of the Nile? Leaves sheathing the stem along their entire length, linear, pointed, and smooth. Flowers on a long, naked, compressed stem, with four angles, arranged in a kind of umbel that divides into more than four parts, some of which subdivide again once or twice, composed of many small ovate spikelets covered on all sides with scales that cover the florets: the spikelets at the center of the universal and partial umbel are sessile, the others have a small stalk. Universal and partial involucre of a few short, imbricated, awl-shaped bracts, the outer ones somewhat elongated. Calyx one ovate, concave, slightly keeled scale ending in a small point. Corolla none. Stamens three. Filaments very long at maturity. Anthers long, half-cylindrical. Ovary seated within the flower. Style long, thicker toward the tip. Stigmas two and more regularly three. Fruit one ovate seed turned upside down with three barely noticeable angles, without hairs or bristles. = This plant, which I have seen in waterlogged ground, rises to a height of two or three feet. The natives barely know it. I do not affirm that it is the species called niloticus by Linnaeus, Syst. veg. 126. * T. Agor.
KILLINGA. Ament ovate or oblong and clustered. Flowers with calyx and corolla of two valves. Lin. syst. veg. 122.
Killinga triceps. Three-headed Killinga. Leaves sword-shaped, clasping the stem at the base. Flowers at the tip of a long triangular stem or scape, in a (white) half-conical, very compact head, solitary, and sometimes with three smaller heads at the base of the first. Involucre of the head composed of three bracts arranged in a triangle, very long, sword-shaped. Sometimes there is one or another additional bract between the small heads and the large one. Calyx very small, a glume of two valves. Corolla persistent, larger than the calyx, consisting of a glume of two very compressed valves: the larger one with small awns on the back. Stamens three. Filaments short. Anthers long, straight. Ovary compressed. Style one, elongated. Stigmas two. Fruit one small ovate compressed seed, without any covering other than the hardened glumes of the corolla. = This plant is very common and well known to the natives. It produces no stem other than the flowering one. Flowers in July. * T. Muthang Anuang. Lin. ibid.

24
CAREX. Monoecious flowers. Spike-like catkin, imbricated, with glumes. Calyx of one leaf. Corolla none. * Females. Nectary inflated, with three teeth. Stigmas three, rarely two. One seed with three sides inside the nectary. Lin. syst. veg. 137.
Carex tuberosa. Tuberous Carex. The flowering stem without leaves, and only tightly sheathed at the bottom by two or three imbricated, cylindrical, fistulous sheaths, with knotty circles, not very noticeable at intervals, and inside with isthmuses composed of membranes; it bears at the tip a very compact cylindrical spike, composed of simple and many imbricated glumes, each covering a single small hermaphrodite floret. Calyx the glume. Corolla none. Stamens three. Filaments very short. Style compressed, cleft almost to the middle into two. Stigmas two, smooth, turned back to the sides. Nectary concave, with six or eight long bristles. Seed oblong at maturity. = This plant grows in lagoons, and is very common in Hagonoy in Bulacan, valued for its roots, which are sold in Malolos and eaten cooked, or dried and prepared in various ways. These roots are as large as hazelnuts, and with three circular lines on their surface they resemble the globe of the earth with its equator and tropics, plus the two polar caps. It is only found in December. The stems resemble the shoots of onions, and the natives call them Potoc and cibocibollasan; and the root, apulid and cabezas de negrito. The flowers must be examined in the young stems. Sometimes female flowers are mixed in the spike with the hermaphrodite ones. The plant is a new species.
Carex glomerata. Clustered Carex. The fistulous flowering stems, similar in leaves to the previous species, bear near the base many small conical, short, and clustered spikelets, furnished with closely packed glumes or scales, containing small hermaphrodite florets. Each glume covers one. Calyx the glume. Corolla none. Stamens three. Anthers half arrow-shaped. Ovary triangular with a style as long as the stamens and three short stigmas. Nectary none. One triangular seed with a hard skin, the angles slightly winged, and also furrowed with small transverse grooves. = It grows in stagnant water and is very similar to the one called Apulid, whose roots are round and edible; I have not seen that this one has them. I observed it in Mandaloyon in January.
** CHENCHRUS. Involucre cleft in many parts, bristly and of two flowers. Calyx a glume of two flowers, one male and the other hermaphrodite. Corolla a glume without an awn. Seed of the hermaphrodite one. Lin. Syst. veg. 150.
Cenchrus hexaplorus. Six-flowered Cenchrus. The flowering stalk or stem, compressed. Leaves sword-shaped, with a channel

25

in the middle, and with small hooks on both surfaces. Flowers in a long, conical spike, single on each stem. Partial involucre, split into many pointed and unequal segments, surrounded below by many stiff bristles, and containing six small flowers: two hermaphroditic, and two monoecious — that is, two male and two female — each separated by its own corolla, which is a glume of two valves without an awn. Stamens three. Anthers long, linear, split at the base into two parts. Ovary ovate. Styles two. Stigmas branched. Fruit a single seed. = A plant two handspans tall, which I have seen in Batangas. The involucres are membranous and very stiff, and as some fold inward they form something resembling burrs. Flowers in June. *T. Aguingai. I derived the species name from the number of its flowers.

TRIANDRIA.

DIGINIA.

** ANDROPOGON. Flowers polygamous. Calyx: glume of one floret. Corolla: glume with an awn at the base. * Flowers hermaphroditic. Seed single. Lin. Syst. veget. 163.
Andropogon ramosus. Branched Andropogon. Leaves sword-shaped, with long hairs on both surfaces. The petioles sheathe the flowering stem and bear a tuft of hairs at the tip. Flowers on the said long cylindrical stem, which has hairy nodes and divides into other stems, each of which bears at its tip two long, moderately rounded spikes arising from a single point; in these, three small flowers — one hermaphroditic, one male, and the third female — alternate with another set of three. The rachis or rib of the spike is hairy. * The hermaphroditic flower arises from the same point as the male and female flowers. Calyx: a glume of two valves — the outer one obliquely ovate, slightly concave, with the margins folded inward and with hairs at the base; the inner one strongly keeled.
