Corolla of three very slender petals, none bearing an awn. Stamens three. Filaments longer than the corolla at maturity. Anthers split at both ends. Ovary superior, somewhat elongated. Styles two. Stigmas hairy. Fruit an oblong seed, pointed at both ends. * Male flower? Calyx: a glume of two valves; the outer one obliquely ovate, slightly concave, with horizontal wrinkles, with the margins folded inward and with hairs at the base; the inner one like that of the hermaphroditic flower. Corolla of three very slender petals: the one nearest the inner valve bears an awn arising from the back, very

26
long, grooved, twisted, and folding toward the middle. Stamens and Anthers as in the hermaphrodite. — The three petals perhaps indicate that there is a third small flower, which aborts? = This plant, which rises to a height of three feet, is known to the Indians and grows with rice in water-covered places. They call it by the name given below, taken from the Spanish word trigo (wheat): because in effect, at first sight it bears some resemblance to it. Horses eat it eagerly, even when dry. Is it in fact this species? Lin. Sist. veg. 164. Flowers in November. * Local name: Tinitrigo.

Andropogon acicularis. Needle Andropogon. Leaves sword-shaped, smooth, very short. Petioles very long, sheathing the flower stalk, with fine hairs at the tip of said cylindrical stalk, on which the flowers are arranged in a whorled panicle: each whorl contains about eight hairy peduncles, and at the tip of each of these, three small flowers: one hermaphrodite, sessile, a little lower than the other two, which are male and paired, with a small stalk and no common glume. Universal involucre, a tuft of hairs. Partial involucre of each group of three florets, none; except for the hairs mentioned on each peduncle. * Hermaphrodite flowers. Calyx, a glume of two concave valves; the outer one with a row of stiff hairs on the edges, and with the apex split in two parts: the inner one nearly smooth and ending in a small long awn. Corolla of two oblong petals, and one smaller, egg-shaped: the innermost terminated by a long awn, with hairs bent backward. Nectary of two small transparent, concave, heart-shaped bodies with a small stalk, which encircle the stamens at the base. Stamens three. Anthers long, incumbent, barely notched at both ends. Ovary superior, egg-shaped. Styles two, shorter than the stamens. Stigmas brush-shaped. Fruit a naked seed, somewhat long, pointed at both ends. * Male flowers. Calyx a glume of two somewhat hairy valves without awns, and with entire apices. Corolla of two petals without awns. Nectary and stamens as in the hermaphrodites. Pistil none. = This plant, common everywhere, is known by the Spanish name that will be given below. Its flowers stick easily to clothing. Loureiro in his flora of Cochinchina formed from this plant a genus which he named Raphis. Flowers in August and other months. * Local names: Amores secos, Marisicos, Mariscos. Spr. Sist. veg. t. 1. 287.

Andropogon contortus. Twisted Andropogon. Stem erect, knotty. Leaves sheathe the stem at the base, somewhat sword-shaped, and very keeled. Flowers in a cylindrical, dense spike: each stem has four or five spikes: the small flowers are monoecious: the males below, and higher up si-

27
are opposite to the females. Each glume contains a single small floret. * Males. Cal. glume of two narrow, pointed valves. Cor. of two narrow petals without an awn. Stamens three. Pistil none. * Females. Cal. glume of two narrow valves, very close together, and of a different color from those of the males. Cor. of two petals, and at the base of one of them a very long awn twisted into a spiral, hairy below, and without joints. The awns of all the females come together and are twisted jointly. Styles two. Stigmas feathery. One seed. = A plant about a vara in height, with horizontal spikes, which I have seen in Malinta, near the spring. The females with their awns, which are nearly four inches long, are purple in color, and when moistened — being well ripe and very dry — with water, they exhibit a lively rotary motion. The natives do not know it. Lin. Sist. veg. 163.
Andropogon schoenanthus. Andropogon eschenanto. Root woody, thick, irregular and rough, formed by the union of many small rootlets joined together. Leaves sword-shaped, narrow at the base. Flowers.= A native plant, well known, whose leaves are about four feet tall, fragrant, and which the natives use for bathing, and for mixing with fish, to which they impart a pleasant flavor. The decoction of its root and leaves is also used with good results for those suffering from gravel in the bladder or difficulty in urinating; but the mora root seems more effective. I once saw its flowers, but they were already nearly withered. * T. Salái, Tanglad, Paja de meca. B. Baliyoco. Lin. Sist. veg. 164.
Andropogon nardus. Andropogon nardo. Roots woody, clustered, irregular: the solitary ones spindle-shaped, with circular lines. Leaves sheathing one another, forming small compressed bundles below, and are sword-shaped, with small hooks. Flowers on a knotty, compressed cane in a spiked panicle, with the spikelets in whorls of eight or ten, without hairs at the base. Each glume contains one small floret, either a sessile hermaphrodite or a stalked male: none have awns. Hermaphrodite. Cal. glume of two keeled valves: the outer one with three rows of small spiny points: the inner one with petal-like margins. Cor. of two valves: the outer one larger. Nectary trumpet-shaped. Stamens three. Styles two, brush-like. One seed. * Males. Cal. Cor. Est. and Nect. as in the hermaphrodites. Ovary none. = Native plants cultivated by enthusiasts and sold in Manila. Their roots somewhat resemble those of canes, and have a very mild fragrance, which they impart to clothing when stored with it in chests: it is also claimed that they protect clothing from moths, and likewise protect books from the small worms that destroy them—

28
yen, although for this purpose it has been observed in recent years that it is better to keep them in display cabinets with glass. The root of this herb is admirable for expelling kidney stones: for this purpose its decoction is drunk. * Nightshade, Blackberry root. Lin. Sist. veg. 166.
PANICUM. Calyx glume of one flower, and of three scales: the third very small, placed on the back of one of the others. Palau. part. pract. de Lin. t. 1. 173.
Panicum miliaceum. Millet. I have seen this plant many times, which is very common, but although I have not observed the flowers, I suspect it is the one I have described. The panicles are very large and drooping. The Indians sow it and make use of the grains, which are very small and nearly round, as good food for their taste; they are also given to canaries. In Cebu it is widely sown and serves as sustenance for those poor islanders, to whom there has fallen by lot very ungrateful and hilly land. * T., Dava, I. Bucacao.
PASPALUM. Calyx of two valves, orbicular. Corolla of equal size. Stigmas shaped like a brush. Lin. Sist. veg. 155.
Paspalum villosum. Hairy Paspalum. Leaves short, sword-shaped, rough on both sides. Petioles very compressed, long, which sheathe the flower stalk below, with small hairs at the tip. Flowers hermaphrodite and male, placed at intervals along the said long stalk, on some rachises or their own long receptacles, pressed against it, and alternating, with some directed to one side and others to the other, where the small florets are, one hermaphrodite and one male (the latter below) within a common calyx, alternating with others of similar kind in two rows, facing one side. Common calyx of the hermaphrodite and male flower, two orbicular scales, the upper one larger. * Hermaphrodite flowers. Own calyx a glume of two valves: the outer one ovate, very convex and hard, with the edges turned inward. Corolla the size of the calyx, very thin. Nectary one or two transparent laminae, heart-shaped. Stamens three, very long at maturity. Anthers of two cells, releasing pollen. Ovary superior, conical. Styles of two small ones. Stigmas brush-shaped. Fruit an ovate seed. * Male flowers. Own calyx a bivalve glume: the outer one ovate, convex on the inside. Corolla the size of the calyx, very thin. Stamens three, anthers either perfect or absent. Nectary none, and sometimes a rudiment. Styles and Stigmas none. Fruit none. == This well-known plant grows to the height of two feet. Women in labor take the decoction of the root. T., Parag-is. Lin. ibid.
STIPA. Calyx of one flower, with two scales. Corolla with the outer scale terminated by a very long awn, which has its base jointed. Lin. Sist. veg. 191.

29

Stipa spinifex. Spine Stipa. Stem three-sided, knotted, half lying on the ground, and at each node bearing many long leaflets, channeled on top, twisted backward, awn-tipped, and ending in a rigid point; these sheathe one another at the base with broad sheaths that are barely hairy at the tip. Flowers terminal, gathered into a very large head, bristling with very long awns: some of them simple and thick below, not twisted nor knotted, which are true rachises bearing a single flower at the base; the others are situated within the flowers, and are nearly as long but thinner, and weak at the base, twisting slightly there, though rarely. The head is divided into distinct groups, each with a few withered glumes, and each group contains about three hermaphrodite flowers and as many empty ones.

The hermaphrodite florets are each attached individually at the base of the rachises, or the large awns already mentioned. Cal. glume of four valves without an awn: one on one side, and three on the other — could this indicate that one flower has aborted? Cor. of two wrapped valves without awns. Nectary of two very short, truncated membranes at the base of the ovary. Stamens three. Style one. Stigmas two or three, hairy. Seed one.

The empty florets have three narrow glumes, without awns, some of them longer. Stamens and Pistil, none: only in the center of each small floret is seen a slender awn of which I spoke above.= It is a plant about as thick as a finger, knotted, four to five feet tall, and spreading low to the ground. The heads are more than a foot in diameter, and the awns a span long. The sheaths are of the same length and are quite tough. The Indians make no use of this plant, which is very common on seashores, nor do they give it a name. In Leyte, Baquibaqui? Palau, part. práct. de Lin. t. 1. 461.

SACHARUM. Cal. none, but a long tuft of hair that protrudes outward and envelops one flower. Cor. of two valves. Palau, Part. práct. de Lin. t. 1. 174.

Sacharum officinarum. Sugar of the apothecaries. Leaves sword-shaped, pointed, flat, with very short hairs on both surfaces, and barely visible small hooks along the edges. Flowers terminal, in large panicles, with crowded florets: each glume contains a single hermaphrodite flower. Cal. none, except for a long, fine tuft of hair found at the base. Cor. glume of two equal valves without an awn at the tip, with the edges rolled inward. Nectary a single lance-shaped small leaflet. Stamens three. Styles two. Stigmas somewhat bristly. Seed one small oval.= This plant, known to everyone, grows to a height of nine feet or more. A planting is made from the tips of other canes, cut to the length of a hand's breadth.
12

30
After extracting the juice of the cane by means of the mill, the Indians pour it into caldrons, which they heat until it thickens. They then take it out and put it in jars; the molasses that rises to the top they pour into other jars to sell, and what remains at the bottom, which is a dark sugar, they place in molds, leaving a space at the top into which they pack mud. The molasses still held by the sugar then drains out through a hole in the bottom of the mold, and the sugar is left hard and white, though not very much so. Instead of mud, some use the body of the banana cut into small pieces, and the result is better sugar. Purple-skinned cane yields more sugar than white cane, although the latter is thicker. There are more than twenty varieties of sweet cane in the Islands. One could write a book on the medicinal virtues of sugar. In summary I will say, citing the Author of the Flora of the Antilles, whom I shall not tire of following, that sugar is very nutritious and good for the chest. There have been individuals who have reached an advanced old age with no other food. Dissolved in water, it is useful in arthritic diseases and those of the bladder. It is excellent in putrid diseases and in scurvy. It is entirely false that sugar harms health: for the immoderate use made of it in sugar-growing districts proves the contrary. Many people have been cured of difficult diseases by eating sugar, or by chewing the cane continuously and drinking its juice. The cited Author adds that it is a valuable vermifuge, and furthermore that when powdered it is used by insufflation on ulcers, and also on opacities of the cornea of the eyes. The natives are fond of sweet things and include sugar in many of their dishes, which tend to be very simple. In this way they reach a very advanced age. I will add lastly that that paste of very low price which we call panocha, taken for a long time between meals, rarely fails to bring relief in scurvy, rheumatism, and many other diseases. Flor. en Dic. *T., Tubo Lin. Sist. veg. 152.
Sacharum koenigii. Koenig's Sugar. Leaves sword-shaped, rough on top and along the edges, and almost smooth underneath. Petioles sheathe the stem, hairy, especially at the tip. All flowers hermaphrodite, in a tight, round, long panicle, placed on a long cylindrical cane whose nodes are hairy. Each glume contains a single small floret, provided with its own little stalk, which emerges immediately from the rachis. Cal. none, but a fine and long down. Cor. glume of two lanceolate valves, without an awn, one slightly smaller than the other. Nect. two very small scales: one narrow, the other broader and with two notches at the tip. Stam. two. Filam. very long at maturity. Ant. incumbent, split in two parts at both ends.

31
Ovate superior ovary, with a small stalk. Style one. Two hairy stigmas. Fruit a somewhat elongated seed. = This plant, spread immensely throughout the islands, sometimes covers stretches of many leagues, to the exclusion of other plants. It grows to the height of a man. The natives use it to thatch the roofs of their houses. Animals eat it, and in summer, when extreme lack of water kills off the grass, I have seen oxen eating cogon that was dry, smoke-cured, and nearly rotten, having been removed from rooftops after twelve or more years. The root is somewhat sweet, and boys chew it as a treat. Flowers at the first rains. *T., B., Cogon, P. Ilib. Bálili, C. Cogon cogon.— Could this be the Imperata of the Authors? Lin. ibid.— There is another species with three stamens and a harder and taller stalk: with narrow and channeled leaves.
** SPINIFEX. Polygamous flowers. Cal. glume of two valves parallel to the rachis, containing one hermaphrodite floret and one male. Both have a blunt bivalve corolla, and the hermaphrodite has two scales. Jus. Gén. plant. 30.
Spinifex squarrosus. Sprawling Spinifex. Stem half-prostrate on the ground, with leaves gathered at the nodes, curved backward, channeled, pointed, and ending in a stiff tip, with wide sheaths at the base ending in small hairs. Terminal flowers arranged in four or more groups, distinguished by small leaflets resembling long, withered glumes: each group with about three spikes, two inches long, whose rachises end in a spine, and the flowers alternate one to one side and another to the opposite. Cal. two blunt valves, parallel to the rachis, containing two florets, one hermaphrodite and one male. Cor. in both, two blunt valves longer than the calyx. Nectary in both (often absent in the male) two small scales: Stam. three, with anthers in the hermaphrodite, and in the male (sometimes absent in the latter.) Two styles, which also are often absent, and even when present appear sterile; nor have I seen any fruit. = A common plant on sea beaches, reaching the height of three or four feet, and prostrate along its lower part. The stem is finger-thick, knotted, and ends in small heads where many spikes are gathered together. It seems to me that the flowers were late in development. The Indians do not know the plant, which resembles Stipa Spinifex, but in the heads of this latter there are no spikes. In Leyte, Baquibaqui? Palau. Part. práct. de Lin. t. 1. 496.
** HOLCUS. Polygamous flowers. *Hermaphrodites. Cal. glume of two valves and two florets, sometimes one. Cor. glume with awn. Stam. three. Two styles and one seed. * Males glume of two valves. Cor. none. Stam. three. Palau, Part. práct. de Lin. t. 1. 175.

32
Holcus sacharatus. Sugar Sorghum. A nearly round, upright cane that sends out roots toward the base. The leaves sheath the stem for a long distance, broad and reed-like, with a white line in the middle, entire and smooth. Flowers in a loose, long panicle, with the small flowers in groups of three, all hermaphrodite: each with a small, awl-shaped, colored bract. Calyx a glume of two hairy valves, the outer one harder, both with their edges rolled inward. Corolla of two very thin, hairy petals; the inner one ending in an awn that is not twisted and is twice as long as the petal. Nectary below the ovary, cup-shaped, with about four or five lobes ending in long hairs. Stamens three, with straw-colored anthers. One seed, half-lentil-shaped, hairy from the middle upward.= This well-known plant, whose canes sometimes reach nearly two fathoms in height, and often three varas. These canes are a little sweet, but not as sweet as sugarcane: the leaves of both are very similar; but those of the plant I am discussing have a white line in the middle. The Indians use the seeds as a substitute for barley. It is not to be confused with what they call Daua. The seeds are purple and larger than those of rice, and are cooked and eaten like rice and are sticky. In the Visayas a drink is also made from them that intoxicates, and is called Pangasi. * T. Batad.— There are other varieties with yellow and white grain. Palau ibid. p. 511.
** Aegilops. Polygamous flowers. Calyx a two-valved glume with or without an awn, as of three small flowers. Corolla a two-valved glume with three awns. Lin. Syst. veg. 178.
Aegilops fluviatilis. River Aegilops. Leaves sword-shaped, very pointed, covered with stiff hairs on both surfaces, especially on the upper side, along the edges and at the base. Polygamous flowers, on a hairy rachis and in sideways-leaning panicles, more than half a foot long, made up of many compressed spikes, bristling with awns placed only on the outer part of the rachis and having four rows of glumes. Each glume of two fringed valves: the outer one ending in a long awn, and the other with a short awn, and covering two small flowers, one male and one hermaphrodite. * Hermaphrodites. Corolla a membranous two-valved glume without awns. Stamens three. Styles two. Stigmas feathery. Seed oval, compressed. * Males. Corolla a single very thin petal. Stamens three. Pistil none.= This plant is found lying flat with its tips raised up, and is known to the Indians. It grows in places where there is water. The stem is as thick as the middle finger and has many nodes, where it puts out roots. A friend told me that a Chinese man used to give its decoction as a drink to those suffering from bladder ailments and to those who could not urinate, and good results were obtained—

33
The reason it is known among the natives is that the pith found inside the stem can serve as a wick for lamps, and can take the place of what the Chinese bring and sell in Manila under the name timsim; although these wicks are much longer than those from here. It grows to six feet in height, and the longest awn will have barely six lines in length, and is rough. Flowers in December. *T. Timsim.— There is another variety with small spikelets of purple color. In the inflorescence it is not distinguishable from the previous one, except in the awns of the calyx, which are not as long in this one. Neither variety fits very well with this genus, nor with others.

ARUNDO. Calyx of two valves, and many flowers. The small florets surrounded by wool. Lin. Sist. veg. 194.

Arundo tecta. Covered Reed. Stem erect, round, and hollow, with few branches. Leaves alternate, sword-shaped, sheathing the stem at the base: the sheath with long hairs at the tip. Terminal flowers in very large spiked panicles. Calyx (according to Linnaeus) one bivalve glume, or rather two scales covering four small florets: and sometimes three: the one below male, without small hairs at the base: and the two or three higher ones, hermaphrodites: each one with a group of long soft hairs at the base. * Males. Calyx one bivalve glume: the outer valve much longer. Corolla none. Stamens four per floret. Pistil none. * Hermaphrodite flowers. Corolla a glume of two valves: the outer one ending in an awn three times longer than the other valve, with the edges rolled inward. Stamens six. Styles two. Stigmas long with short hair, and rolled to the sides. Seed one, very small, oblong.= A reed four yards tall and as thick as a thumb, nothing more. It is common on the banks of rivers, where it is notable for its loose and woolly panicles: it is as hard as other reeds. Flowers in November. *T. Tambo. Lin. Sist. veg. 195.

ANTHISTIRIA. The calyx equally divided at the base into four equal lobes. Lin. Sist. veg. 194.

Anthistiria gigantea. Very tall Anthistiria. Fibrous roots, with tomentum. Stem erect, smooth, swollen at the joints. Alternate leaves that sheath the stem for a long stretch, lanceolate, smooth underneath, and with small hooks above and on the edges. Flowers in spiked, cylindrical, solitary panicles, containing two types of bivalve glumes, without awns at the tips or at the base: one glume alternating, slightly taller than the other larger one. The larger of the two glumes, with the edges of the inner valve rolled inward, contains a male flower on the outer side and a hermaphrodite flower on the inner side. * Corolla of the male: one membranous bivalve glume. Stamens three. Pistil none. * Corolla of the her-

34
hermaphrodite like that of the male. Stamens three. Long filaments. Linear anthers. Two styles. Hairy stigmas, twisted to the sides. Seed ovate, smooth. The smaller glume, bivalve, narrower than the other and containing a male flower. Corolla of three petals, two facing outward. Stamens three: and only the anthers are visible, as I believe they do not extend further. No pistil. — Do the three petals perhaps indicate that another small flower is aborted? = A plant three yards tall, and very common everywhere. The stem is slightly sweet. The leaves are three feet long. They say that by rubbing one's hands with its shoots, one can handle snakes without risk; but this is not easy to believe; nevertheless, an Indian from Hagonoy assured it was so, as he would take them in his hand, tuck them under his clothing, and throw them over his shoulder (four very venomous snakes at one time.) I saw him handle one and open its mouth with his hand, and he told me he drew them out of their holes this way: and to find out whether there was a snake in a hole, he would apply his nose to it. Nevertheless, after having opened its mouth, he rubbed his fingers carefully against the floor bricks. It seemed to me that both he and the snake were half-drunk. Even more remarkable is what a young Indian boy, still well known today, did with a snake as thick as a calf: its mouth had been tied shut with a thread, and at the moment it stuck its tongue out through its nose, he cut it off with his teeth. Many similar feats are cited, witnessed by very sharp-eyed Europeans, and some believe, among them the most learned Fr. Diego Bergaño, Augustinian, author of the Pampango Vocabulary, that this proceeds from no other principle than the quality of the blood, or a particular humor of the individual, which numbs or stupefies these terrible animals, just as there are individuals whom bedbugs do not bite, as happened to me for many years, though now I no longer have that virtue, while for others, if they are bitten, they die. Uncivilized Indians have humors that are extremely heavy and cold, and to this contribute unwholesome foods, so different from our own. *T., Talahib. — Agrees with the Andropogon. Pers. Sin. pl. t. 1. 105.

TRIANDRIA.

TRIGINIA.

MOLLUGO. Calyx of five small leaves. Corolla none. Capsule of three cells, with three valves. Lin. Syst. veg. 208.
Mollugo subserrata. Half-serrated Mollugo. Stem half erect, cylindrical, somewhat hairy. Leaves four in

35
four, all unequal, on one side of the stem, some oval,
some egg-shaped in reverse, and barely serrated. Petioles very short.
Lateral flowers in a simple umbel containing six or a
few more small flowers: each with a long peduncle, and an awl-shaped
bract at its base. Calyx inferior, of four or five
lance-shaped leaflets. Corolla none. Stamens three, somewhat shorter
than the calyx. Anthers thick. Ovary seated within the
flower, oval, with three channels. Styles three, short, divergent.
Stigmas globose. Capsule with three channels, three valves,
and three chambers, each containing many kidney-shaped seeds.=
This plant, whose leaves will be about an inch long, and which
grows in various places, in the fields where rice has been harvested,
is barely a foot tall. The natives, and even the
Europeans, eat it cooked, and call it by a name similar
to the botanical one. In other places it is called salsalida. It is
bitter, and is also known in the town of Batangas. Flowers
in January. *T. Malagoso, Molugoso. I took the name of the species
from the serrations of the leaves.— In Parañaque this
plant has three additional sterile stamens split in two. Stigmas
somewhat elongated.
Mollugo stricta. Compact Mollugo. Stem erect with
four angles. Leaves in groups of four, all unequal
in a whorl, encircling almost the entire stem, lance-shaped, narrow,
entire and smooth. Petioles none. Lateral flowers
in a long, forked, and racemose panicle. Fruit as in the
previous species. Styles none. Stigmas three, globose.=
This plant grows where the previous one does: its height is one span; the
stem and leaves, which are very small, at maturity are
reddish, and the flowers turn white. Flowers in January. *T.
Malagoso, Molugoso. Lin. Sist. veg. 208.
LECHEA. Corolla of three petals. Calyx of three pieces. Capsule
of three chambers and three valves, with as many
inner valves where the solitary seeds are found, and not in the
center. Lin. Sist. veg. 209.
Lechea minor. Lesser Lechea. Leaves alternate, sheathing
the stem at the base, lance-shaped, with a single vein, entire
and smooth. Flowers in a racemose panicle. Calyx inferior, of three
concave leaflets. Corolla of three petals larger than the calyx,
spatula-shaped. Stamens five, as long as the corolla.
Filaments broad, joined below in a membrane or hypogynous
disk, whose teeth are the filaments themselves. Anthers: the
three broader than the others. Ovary seated within the
flower. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma simple. Capsule
globose, lustrous, hollow in the middle, and with two coverings
joined to each other in five places by means of five
partitions, and in the spaces they leave the seeds are fixed,

36
lenticular, with a small stalk, numbering four or more in each partition. The capsule at maturity takes on a low color like tumbaga gold.= A plant from Cebu that I have seen dried. Although the capsule is hollow and empty at the center, the two coverings leave a certain space between them for the seeds. In a word: there are five double, overlapping valves, and the seeds are placed in the hollows they leave. See Lohod lohod.— It differs from Lechea in the stigma and in the number of seeds: it also differs from monogynous Flax in various respects. Lin. Sist. veg. 209.
POLYCARPON. Calyx of five leaflets. Petals five, very small, egg-shaped. Capsule with one chamber and three valves. Lin. Sist. veg. 207.
Polycarpon polyphyllum. Polycarpon of many leaves.
Stem erect, nearly round, and without branches. Leaves sessile, narrow lanceolate, and slightly hairy, arranged in a middle whorl, numbering five, six, or seven: half on one side, with two awl-shaped stipules at the base, and the other half on the opposite side, with another two stipules. Flowers in spike-like panicles. Calyx of five lanceolate, keeled leaflets, with membranous margins folded inward. Corolla of five lanceolate petals, truncated at the tips. Stamens three, shorter than the corolla. Anthers half-round. Ovary globose, seated within the flower. Styles none. Stigmas three, lanceolate and short. Capsule oval with three angles, three valves, one chamber and many very tiny egg-shaped seeds.= A plant I have seen in Pasig, and it reaches about four finger-widths in height. The small branches emerge directly from the root: the color of the plant is green. The leaves are arranged in a star pattern, but in the manner described above, without encircling the stem entirely. The petals are membranous and very thin. The natives do not know it. Flowers in February. New species.

TETRANDRIA.

MONOGINIA.

KNAUTIA. Common calyx oblong, simple, containing five flowers. Individual calyx simple, superior. Corollas irregular. Receptacle naked. Lin. Sist. veg. 231.
Knautia sagittata. Arrow-leaved Knautia. Stem twining, round. Leaves opposite, arrow-shaped, with teeth toward the base, soft and hairy. Petioles short. Flowers compound, axillary, in umbellate panicles, with a small bract at the base of each common calyx, which contains four small florets and is long, angular, and split nearly to the base into two parts,

37
with small teeth at the tip, one narrower than the other. Cal. proper to the adherent little flower, crowned with some bristles. Cor. longer than the common calyx, monopetalous, funnel-shaped, in five parts. Stam. two, fixed toward the middle of the corolla, and a little shorter than it: one bears three anthers and the other only two. Ant. close together but not fused, small. Style one, much longer than the corolla, passing outside the anthers. Stigmas two, long, curved to the sides. Fruit a single elongated seed with five sides, crowned with the bristles of the calyx.= Curious plants that I have seen in Pangasinan and Ilocos. They have an affinity with Scabiosa, and lack tendrils. The filaments are two: I have never seen the pistil pass through the middle of the anthers, but rather to one side. The anthers appear to be fused, but separate easily. The twisted little branches give off an aromatic scent. Flowers in January.— Although it agrees greatly with the genus Knautia and with Scabiosa, it differs from both in its proper calyx, the number of anthers, and in other particulars.

SCOPARIA. Cal. divided into four parts. Cor. wheel-shaped and in the same manner. Capsule of one chamber, with two valves and many seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 211. 254.

Scoparia dulcis. Sweet Scoparia. Central root, with lateral roots. Stem erect, branching, angular, becoming rounded at maturity. Leaves in whorls of three, lanceolate, serrated from the middle upward, obtuse and smooth. Flowers one or two, axillary. Peduncles long. Cal. of four small leaves, curved outward, persistent. Cor. barely with a tube, divided nearly to the base into four parts curved outward, and hairy at the base. Stam. four, shorter than the pistil. Ant. incumbent, shaped like a half moon. Ovary oval, seated within the flower. Stigma simple. Capsule bivalve, with many angular seeds, arranged around a fleshy lamina.= This plant, light green in color and with white corollas, reaches a height of two or three feet at most. It is very common everywhere and spreads with great speed. The flavor of the leaves is somewhat sweet, and resembles that of Abruz. Some people make a decoction of the leaves, as is done with Tea: the flavor does not resemble that which comes from China. In China itself, the infusion of various plants is drunk as if it were tea. In the general history of the voyages of Abbot Prevost, translated into Spanish, in volume 18, page 190, and even more clearly in volume 10, page 118, we are assured that it is a common deception among Chinese merchants to sell leaves of different plants as tea: and that in the most northern provinces, where little true tea is grown, the inhabitants whose palate is not very refined use everything that resembles or looks like
13

38
té. Animals do not eat this plant. The author of the flora of the Antilles states that a decoction of the root is prescribed as an astringent and antisyphilitic, and for other diseases. With the juice a pomade is made for hemorrhoids; and for prolapse of the rectum, a strong decoction of it is used. Flowers in November. *T. Chachachachachan. Lin. ibid.
PLANTAGO. Calyx in four parts. Corolla persistent, divided into four folded lobes. Stamens very long. Capsule with two chambers, superior, and which splits circularly. Lin. Sist. veg. 151.
Plantago media. Medium Plantain. No stem. Leaves lance-shaped and egg-shaped, with slight notches, five-nerved, with small hairs on the margins. Petioles long, with a large channel. Flowers in a long cylindrical spike: the lower ones somewhat separated, and the upper ones crowded, placed on a long stalk, nearly without angles. Calyx split almost to the base into four lance-shaped, concave, and fleshy parts. Corolla shaped like a small jar, with a very narrow throat, and the limb with four lance-shaped horizontal lobes. Stamens four, projecting far beyond the corolla. Anthers with a stipule at the apex, and from two cells the pollen is released. Ovary cylindrical, seated within the flower. Style nearly as long as the stamens, and hairy. Stigma simple. Capsule oval, splitting circularly, with two chambers and many oval, angular seeds.= This plant, perhaps native to the country, is known to the Indians: its leaves appear serrated, notched, and toothed, and are six inches long and more than three wide: its medicinal use is well known. Flowers in February. *T. Lantin. Lin. ibid. 252.
BUDLEIA. Corolla with four lobes. Calyx with four lobes. Stamens at the incisions. Capsule with two furrows, two chambers, and many seeds, superior. Lin. Sist. veg. 250.
Budleia virgata. Rod Budleya. Stem upright, compressed toward the nodes. Leaves opposite, lance-shaped, serrated, rough, and silvery beneath. Petioles very short. Flowers in compound racemes. Peduncles individual, very short. Calyx inferior, shaped like a vinegar cruet, with four equal teeth. Corolla longer than the calyx, tubular, divided into four equal, rounded parts. Stamens four, equal in height, and fixed at the middle of the corolla tube. Filaments very short. Anthers oval. Ovary conical, seated within the flower. Style very short. Stigma funnel-shaped. Capsule conical, with two valves split above into two parts, with two chambers, and in each one a fleshy receptacle to which many small oval seeds are attached.= A plant as tall as a man. On the river of Abra in Ilocos they use

39
the Indian women use the leaves to clean glass beads. It is also
common on the banks of the Calumpan river, in Batangas, in
Manila and in other places. The smell is herbaceous. Flowers in January.
* T. Talicnono. I. Tugnang. V. Lagundi salasa. Lin. ibid.
EXACUM. Calyx of four leaflets, or in four parts.
Corolla with four lobes, and a globose tube. Capsule with two
grooves, two chambers, and many seeds, which splits at
the apex. Lin. Sist. veg. 250.
Exacum albens. THE WHITENING EXACUM. Stem forked,
erect, square, winged, with few branches. Leaves opposite, with
three or five nerves, half-clasping the stem, running
along the petiole, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Flowers axillary,
solitary and terminal, in umbellate panicles. Universal involucre
of two leaflets. Partial of two leaflets. Calyx at maturity
deeply four-parted, keeled, erect and awl-shaped:
the two opposite ones smaller. Corolla wheel-shaped, and the tube
very short, of one petal, somewhat two-lipped, with four lobes
on the limb, lanceolate, two above and two below, and with
an open throat. Stamens four, somewhat converging, and fixed in
the divisions of the limb. Filaments very short. Anthers long, shaped
like a bird's beak, projecting beyond the tube, with perforated
apices. Ovary conical, seated within the flower. Style longer
than the stamens. Stigma somewhat thick, with a small
groove nearly invisible. Capsule globose at maturity with a
partition and a channel that serves as another partition, cutting
the first at right angles: the chambers four, and in each
one a fleshy receptacle, to which many seeds are fixed
around its contour. = Plant three-quarters of a foot in
height. The roots are slightly bitter; the flowers blue, and the
anthers yellow; the seeds round and very small. I saw it
in Tala and it is not very common. Flowers in July. Lin. ibid.
* * BRABEJUM. Polygamous. Catkin with egg-shaped and
obtuse scales. Corolla in four parts, rolled back downward, and the
stamens fixed at its base. Drupe dry, nearly round, hairy,
with one seed. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 117.
Brabejum? caliculatum. BRABEYUM WITH CALYX. Leaves nearly
sessile, scattered, lanceolate, wider toward the top, leathery,
with the edges turned downward, the veins directed slightly
upward, entire and smooth. Flowers axillary in groups
of about four sessile florets, with small scales and
slightly notable stalks on the common little stalk. Calyx of one piece,
truncate, with five very prominent angles, in the shape of a
star. Corolla of four petals, linear, rolled back downward,
and fixed in the receptacle beside the ovary. Anthers four,
sessile without filaments, a little below the middle of the
petals, with two pits in the manner of small ears on the sides. Ova-

40
men very small, globose, at the top. Style very short. Stigma simple. Fruit... = Small trees of Cebu, of which I have seen some dry branches with flowers, very whole and well preserved; and so the description is exact. I have not seen the ripe fruit, and I do not know either whether these flowers will fertilize the fruits of brabejum concatenatum. * In Cebu: Malabachao.

Brabejum? concatenatum. Concatenated Brabey. Leaves almost sessile, star-shaped, four by four, and more commonly five by five, egg-shaped in reverse and oblong, with a notch and a confused callus at the apex, smooth, membranous, with the edges turned downward, and with many low-relief veins that are nearly transverse. Axillary flowers in umbellate panicles. Each small umbel with two flowers, and at the base a receptacle of five overlapping leaflets. Cal. Cor. Stam. Style..... Two or three drupes, not very fleshy, oval, with a fragile bark, placed one on top of another in a row, and joined by a stipe or small stalk, with a similar seed in each one, endowed with a longitudinal groove (as in coffee) and covered with an aril: the last one, with a small point at the tip. = Small trees found in Cebu, whose leaves are about four inches long. The drupes are as large as cherries, but oval, and yellow when ripe. The most extraordinary thing here is that the drupes are in a row, fused together by means of a stipe; but they are not strung through, because the stipe does not pierce them. There are usually two or three, and all perfect; but sometimes the first one at the bottom is smaller and stunted. The flesh of the seeds resembles that of the areta. — I cannot say where the stamens are found; and so I think it is a dioecious or polygamous tree, and that the males are those of the preceding tree, which I called calyculatum, also from Cebu, and whose leaves are very similar in shape, though smaller. The style of the following tree called Layo in Cebu must be regularly in the last fruit, and will fertilize all those below. The males, then, of this tree are in my opinion those of the preceding one; but in it, the flowers are complete. New species.

Brabejum? lucidum. Lustrous Brabey. Leaves in whorls of three, almost sessile, lanceolate, very entire, smooth, lustrous, and with the edges turned downward. Axillary flowers, with a receptacle of two scales at the base, in a somewhat forked raceme, with very few small flowers. Cal. Cor. Stam...... Drupe almost globose, one or two in a row as in the species concatenatum. = Small trees of Cebu. The leaves are one or two inches long and lustrous. The males of these trees, I believe, are on another individual. They are called in Bolohon: Layo.

Brabejum? pinnatum. Winged Brabey. Opposite leaves, win-

41
paired. Leaflets about five or more pairs, narrow, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Petioles nearly absent. = Small trees of half a vara or more in height that grow in Cebu. Their leaves have a somewhat pleasant smell, and are three or four inches long and barely half an inch wide. The small branches are as thick as a wire. Children make a kind of neck ornament from the plant. * B. Layo.— All these species appear to be new, and I still doubt whether they belong to this genus, which has much affinity with Protea.

PAVETTA. Calyx with four teeth. Corolla with a slender, long tube, and the limb in four parts. Anthers outside the throat. Stigma thick and curved. Berry inferior, with two chambers or only one, containing one or two seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 243. Jus. gen. pl. 203.

PAVETTA SAMBUCINA. PAVETTA RESEMBLING ELDERBERRY. Leaves sessile, opposite, lanceolate, narrow, entire, smooth and membranous, with two intermediate stipules. Terminal flowers in whorled panicles. Calyx adherent, very small, with four teeth. Corolla very long, slender and somewhat curved: the tube filiform, and the limb in four oval parts. Stamens four, fixed at the incisions of the limb and outside the tube. Filaments nearly absent. Anthers linear and long, like the lobes of the limb. Style longer than the corolla. Stigma simple, thick and somewhat elongated. Berry globose, with one chamber and one seed. = Small trees that grow in Angat with whitish and opposite branches, and very thin leaves, more than five inches long and four lines wide. The flowers are white; the berries resemble a chickpea and smell bad; the seeds appear to be of a horny substance. They are unknown to the natives. Flowers in September.— I have not seen the fruit fully ripe. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 492.

IXORA. Calyx in four parts. Corolla long, superior, monopetalous, tubular. Stamens on the throat. Berry with two chambers and two seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 213. 243.

IXORA COCCINEA. SCARLET IXORA. Trunk erect, branching, smooth. Leaves opposite, half-clasping the stem, oval, very entire and smooth. Terminal flowers in an umbel. Calyx as in the genus. Corolla superior, with a long tube, and the limb flat and divided into four rounded lobes. Stamens fixed outside the throat of the corolla. Filaments none. Style rising above the throat of the corolla. Stigma thick and bifid. Drupe globose (larger than a pea) crowned with the calyx: the bony nut with two chambers, each containing one seed. = This shrub grows to a height of six feet. The natives make no use of it, although they plant it in their homes on account of its flowers, which are numerous and crimson. Flowers in July and October. * T. Santan. Santa Ana. Lin. ibid.— He

42
I have seen another species with a larger fruit, crowned with the calyx, with two bony seeds surrounded by pulp. Both these two species, and all those that I have placed under the genus Ixora on account of the bifid stigma, are barely distinguishable from the genus Paretta. The small tree Dilig. (Ixora glandulosa) may perhaps be a species of coffee.

Ixora Manila. Ixora Manila. Leaves opposite, some reverse egg-shaped, some oval, thick, entire and very smooth. Petioles very short. Axillary flowers in an umbel of some nine or more small florets. Peduncle proper absent. Calyx adherent, cylindrical, entire. Corolla funnel-shaped: long tube, throat covered with hairs, and with four half-erect oval lobes. Stamens four, at the divisions of the limb. Filaments very short. Anthers half-exserted beyond the throat. Style longer than the corolla. Stigmas two, somewhat elongated and slightly thickened. Berry small, corky, oval, crowned with the calyx, somewhat compressed: with eight angles dividing into two, with one bony seed in each half. = Small trees resembling mangroves, growing among them. Their true name is Nilad, and Manilad, denoting a place where many of these small trees grow: from this the great capital of Manila takes its name. The flowers are white, and the fruit has eight sharp angles. Nor can it truly be said that the fruit is a berry; it is rather a dry drupe whose stone can be divided in two. * T. Nilad Nilar.

Ixora arborea. Ixora Tree. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Petioles short. Flowers in an umbellate panicle. Calyx with four teeth. Corolla as in the species coccinea. Filaments long, hanging outside the corolla. Style and other parts as in the said species. = It is a tree that sometimes grows as thick as a thigh. The corollas are white and the calyces reddish. Flowers in August. * T. As-as. New species.

Ixora glandulosa. Ixora Glandulosa. Leaves with a small gland at the base of each lateral vein. Axillary flowers in groups of about five small florets. Calyx adherent, with four teeth. Corolla very long, tubular, with the limb in four parts, and in the incisions four nearly sessile anthers. Style somewhat elongated. Stigma cleft in two. Fruit. = A small, somewhat known tree. * T. Malapatopat. New species.— In the Abra of Ilocos I have seen other similar small trees as thick as a calf of the leg: their leaves have no glands; the petioles have intermediate stipules; the fruit is black when ripe and edible. I. Dilig.

POLYOZUS. Calyx adherent, top-shaped, with dark teeth on the deciduous limb. Corolla with a cylindrical tube shorter than the lobes, which are four or five, and with a hairy throat. Anthers alternating with the lobes and barely ex-

43
lient. Style short. Stigma bifid. Berry like a semi-globose drupe with two chambers and solitary stones.
Polyozus bipinnatus. Twice-winged Polyozus. Leaves with intermediate stipules, entire, and drawn out to a point; twice winged without an odd one. Leaflets from three to six pairs, nearly sessile, broad, lanceolate, and very pointed, entire, membranous and smooth. Axillary flowers in an umbel of three or a few small florets, with rather long peduncles. Calyx adherent and with five lobes. Corolla. Stamens. Style.... Berry crowned with the calyx lobes, club-shaped, with a partition, two chambers, and two oval stones, flat on the inside and with solitary seeds. = Little-known small trees found in Angat, as thick as a calf of the leg. The leaves are an inch and a half long, and the fruit is smaller than a cherry and yellow in color. Flowers in June.— This species belongs to Laureiro; Decandolle excludes it from the genus Polyozus. I leave it here for now, while its true place is determined.
SPERMACOCE. Corolla tubular. Cagilla inferior, with two chambers. Seeds solitary with two teeth at the apex. Lin. Syst. veg. p. 214.
Spermacoce mutilata. Mutilated Spermacoce. Stem erect and square; with rough hairs on the angles. Branches opposite below: one shorter than the other; and above there is only one, the opposite one being absent, and from this peculiarity I have taken the name of the species. Leaves nearly sessile, united at the base by means of a scarious sheath ending in four bristles, oval, and sometimes egg-shaped, wavy, with the veins directed upward ending in a small point at the apex, with rough and very short hairs on both surfaces, more so on the upper. Sometimes the leaves are four in a whorl: the two that arise within the sheath are smaller and opposite and are slow to emerge. Flowers, four in number, sessile within the sheath. Calyx adherent, with four small lanceolate bracts at the edge. Corolla cone-shaped, inverted, with four entire laciniae, turned slightly outward. Stamens four, at the divisions of the corolla, with the anthers fixed at their midpoint. Style one, with two short stigmas, nearly horizontal and somewhat rounded. Cagilla oval, thicker in the middle, hairy, crowned with the calyx teeth, with two chambers formed by a double septum and solitary oval seeds, coiled before maturity. = Plant about two palms tall, common in Parañaque. The leaves are an inch long and half an inch wide, and are somewhat rough. The corollas are small and of a medium violet color. The seeds before maturity look like thick, slightly coiled membranes.— It does not correspond well with the species Philippensis of Decand. prod. p. 4. 556.

44
Spermacoce muriculata. Spermacoce with small soft spines. Stem erect, very branchy, with disordered branches, square, with small soft and widely spaced spines at the four angles. Leaves opposite and joined by means of a sheath ending in a few points, oval, pointed at both ends, with veins directed upward, rough with small hooks at the margins and dotted with hairs on both surfaces. Axillary flowers in a very tight whorl of very numerous sessile florets. Calyx with four teeth. Corolla white with four woolly lobes at the tips. Stamens four, fixed near the divisions. Capsule of two membranous pods, diverging when opening, each crowned with two teeth, and with solitary, half-round seeds with a navel. = Plant about one foot tall, in Guadalupe. — It closely resembles the species muriculata of Decand. Prod. p. 4. 554.
OLDENLANDIA. Corolla tubular. Calyx adherent with four teeth, widely separated, or with a large sinus between them at maturity. (In this it is distinguished from Hediotis.) Capsule twin, with many seeds in two chambers, which splits between the teeth. Dec. Prod. vol. 4. 424.
Oldenlandia paniculata. Panicled Oldenlandia. Stem erect, square. Leaves opposite, clasping the stem at the base, obtuse, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short, and on each side with a stipule split into two or more lobes. Flowers terminal, in umbel-like panicles. Calyx adherent, bell-shaped, compressed, and with four teeth. Corolla shaped like a cruet, with a hairy throat, and four oval lobes. Stamens four, shorter than the corolla, fixed in the incisions of the limb. Anthers oval (black). Style very short. Stigma simple. Capsule crowned with the calyx teeth, compressed, half twin, of two chambers, with many seeds, and opening at the top. = This plant grows anywhere, even in flower pots, and its height does not reach a hand's breadth. When the green fruit is crushed between the fingers it smells bad, and I have observed that when the plant is passed over cockroaches, they first run, but afterward remain as if stupefied, though they do not die. In India a beautiful crimson dye is obtained from a species of oldenlandia. Flowers over several months. Lin. Sist. veg. 264.
Oldenlandia affinis. Allied Oldenlandia. Stem herbaceous, erect, with opposite branches, square and smooth, even at the angles. Leaves opposite, somewhat fleshy, with intermediate sheaths, ending in four or five bristles, the middle ones longer, nearly without a petiole, lanceolate, egg-shaped, elongated, with ridges on both surfaces, with small spines on them, slightly rough on the lower surface, and with barely hairy margins.

45
Flowers lateral and terminal in a panicle, irregularly subdivided: the small lower florets very distant from the upper ones: the individual stalks half as short as the leaves. Calyx with four teeth widely separated by broad sinuses. Corolla twice as long as the calyx (white) with four laciniae, narrowed at the throat which is hairy. Anthers four, nearly round, black, and not projecting beyond the throat. Stigma one, thickened. Cagilla twin, with two chambers and very many seeds, opening between the teeth. = A plant four fingers tall, found in Parañaque, and the whole plant is grayish in color. The common peduncle of the panicle is one inch long. The fruits are whitish or grayish, with a slight purplish sheen, and they grow and ripen quickly. The roots are whitish and yield no color. Flowers in May. — It agrees in part with the doubtful species affinis of Decandolle, vol. 4, Prod. 428.

Oldenlandia capensis. Cape Oldenlandia. Leaves opposite, linear, very narrow. Flowers axillary, solitary, with very short peduncles. Calyx with four teeth. Corolla in four parts. Stamens four. Stigmas two, somewhat elongated. Cagilla slightly more rounded than in the previous species, opening from above. = It is barely a quarter of a foot tall. I saw it in Mandaloyon. Flowers in March. Lin. Sist. veg. 263.

ORIXA. Calyx inferior, in four parts. Corolla of four lanceolate, flat petals. Stigma in a small head. Cagilla? Lin. Sist. veg. 255.

Orixa ternata. Ternate Orixa. Trunk erect, with opposite branches. Leaves opposite in threes, on a long common petiole. Leaflets lanceolate, entire, smooth and soft. Individual petioles very short. Flowers axillary. Calyx and Corolla as in the genus. Stamens four. Ovary girdled at the base by a zone, and above square with four channels. Style short. Stigma somewhat thick, square and striated. Cagilla with four chambers, each containing one seed. = This little tree, which is not known to the natives, grows to a height of twelve feet. Both the branches and the leaves, when rubbed, emit a strong odor somewhere between pleasant and disagreeable. It has no tendrils, and the fruit is a cagilla. It is the genus Othera according to Pers. Sin. pl. t. 1. 145. Flowers in July. New species.

SERINGIA. Corolla of four petals. Calyx inferior with four lobes. Stigma one. Samara with two chambers. Spre. Sist. veg. Lin. t. 1. 369.

Seringia lanceolata. Lanceolate Seringia. Trunk erect. Leaves alternate, obliquely lanceolate, smooth and notched at the apex. Petioles very short. Flowers in a panicle. Individual peduncle very long. Calyx of five leaflets, inferior (sometimes
14

46
split almost to the base into five parts.) Cor. of five petals fixed on the receptacle, each one with two small teeth toward the lower part and with small claws. Stam. six, shorter than the corolla, fixed on the receptacle. Ovary oblong, compressed, with a channel in the middle. Style awl-shaped, very long, persistent and somewhat twisted. Stigma simple. Samara, with a small stalk, thin, membranous, round, compressed, more swollen in the middle, bordered along the edge by a wing, with a channel in the middle and a partition dividing it into two, and in each chamber two small ovoid seeds, fixed to the same partition and with a small aril at the base.= This tree rises to the height of about four fathoms. The corollas are green. The Indians use the wood in the construction of their houses. Its bark, pounded and thrown into the water, intoxicates fish. From its seeds an oil is extracted. * T., Poas. Ioas, New species.— It has much in common with the Ptelea. In terms of stamens it agrees with neither of the two.
AMMANIA. Cor. of four petals inserted in the calyx, or none. Cal. inferior with folds, and with eight teeth. Capsule in four chambers. Lin. Syst. veg. 264.
Ammania ramosior. More branched Ammania. Stem erect, four-sided, with straight branches. Leaves opposite, sessile: barely clasping the stem, lanceolate, very narrow below, smooth, and very slightly notched. Flowers axillary, solitary. Cal. shaped somewhat like a jar, with eight awl-like teeth on the border: the alternating ones small, and four folds. Cor. none. Stam. four, fixed to the walls of the calyx. Ant. of two globules. Ovary seated within the calyx. Style somewhat long. Stigma globose. Capsule ovoid, in three or more chambers, each containing many very small, ovoid seeds.= This plant barely reaches the height of one foot. Flowers in Oct. Lin. ibid.
Ammania debilis. Weak Ammania. Stem erect, square, branched. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, somewhat fringed. Petioles very short. Flowers in the axils of the leaves, in small clusters. Peduncles short. Cal. inferior, bell-shaped, with eight angles on the border: the four alternating ones larger. Cor. none. Nect. surrounds the ovary, and is bell-shaped, shorter than the calyx, with four small teeth which, lengthening, form the filaments of as many stamens. Ant. with four chambers. Ovary globose, seated within the flower. Style almost none. Stigma somewhat thick, with striations. Capsule globose, splitting horizontally, with more than fifteen angular seeds fixed on a common axis.= This plant, whose height is about a quarter of a vara, I have seen in flooded terrain. The Indians barely know it. The stems are red: the flowers very

47
small, and the seeds even more so. *T., Bias pogo.— Lin. ibid. Could this belong to this genus?
FAGARA. Calyx with four laciniae. Corolla of four petals. Capsule of two valves, one or two chambers, with solitary and lustrous seeds. Lin. Syst. veg. 248.
Fagara piperita. Pepper Fagara. Trunk with spines. Leaves winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets ovate, pointed, obtusely serrated, with transparent blisters on the surface, and spines on the midrib and common petiole. Flowers as in the species Pterota.= Trees of about five or six fathoms, and their properties are those of the Cayutana. They have an affinity with the genus Zanthoxylum. The common petioles are purple in color. Zanthoxylum is reputed to have virtues equal to Guaiac in syphilitic diseases. But great caution is necessary in taking the bark of these trees internally, as the Indian designates them in general by the names of Cayutana, and others listed below. Since the descriptions by Botanical Authors do not agree very well, there is reason to doubt the identity, and consequently the use of this plant. The Author of the Flora Medical of the Antilles speaks of Zanthoxylum as an innocent tree, whose bark he says can be administered like that of Cinchona. Furthermore, in his description, he grants it a polypetalous corolla, rarely absent: the other Authors deny this; and only in one species is it granted. I have also seen that the illustration that said Author provides corresponds very well with the Fagaras I am discussing. All this confusion arises from the great resemblance that exists between Zanthoxylum and Fagara. I return to the matter above. Father Ignacio de Mercado indicates to those with intermittent fevers the weight of one drachm of the bark of the root of the Cayutana taken internally as a substance; but a very small quantity of the bark of the tree is very caustic. It is true that the very thick bark of the tree is not so caustic, and even less so that of the root. It may be inferred, therefore, that among the Cayutanas there is a good one and a bad one. Therefore it is not advisable to use any of them internally. The wood is whitish and hard; but that of the root is so hard and of such fine grain that it can perfectly substitute for boxwood. The bark of the root is of a beautiful yellow. I have heard that a branch of this tree, even after being dry for several years, will take root when placed in the ground; and this has been confirmed for me by an event that occurred in Hagonoi. I consider it very doubtful.
* T. Cayutana and others cited in the following species. Lin. ibid.
Fagara pterota. Winged Fagara. Trunk covered with spines. Leaves opposite, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets ovate, oblong, smooth, notched along the edges and at the apex. Common petioles dotted with small spines

48
on the upper part. Cal. very small, monophyllous, in four
parts. Cor. twice as large as the calyx, with four petals.
Stam. four, fixed in the receptacle, of the same length as the
corolla. Superior ovary with four angles. Style none.
Stigmas two. I believe these trees never bear fruit. But
in others I have seen that it consists of a small lenticular
capsule (solitary) with many dots, which splits open on
one side, containing one seed. = These trees, well known to
the natives, rise as I have seen to a height of eighteen
or more feet. The trunk and branches are full of spines. Its fruit
gives off a singular and very pleasant scent, somewhat resembling
that of the lemon. The bark of the tree is bitter, and of it
as well as of the wood, many extravagant things have been said
and even written. Nevertheless, it is certain that the bark is very
good for various uses in Medicine. Flowers in Feb. * T.
Cayutana. V. Salay Marbar, Baga tambal. P. Cayutana, Sa-
lay Cangay. Lin. ibid.
Fagara decandra. Fagara with ten stamens. Leaves heaped
at the ends of the branches, obtusely lance-
olate, entire, smooth, and somewhat stiff. Petioles short, com-
pressed. Flowers at the ends of the branches, in compound
racemes. Cal. very small, in five pointed parts.
Cor. of five linear petals, bent downward. Stam.
ten, as long as the pistils, fixed in the receptacle and below
the nectary. Sometimes a few more sterile stamens are seen.
Nect. swollen, fleshy, channeled, with many small teeth
on the edge, enclosing the pistils within. Ger-
mens five, pressed close together, oblong, with one alone
larger and hairy. Styles short. Stigmas somewhat thick. One
drupe (the other four abort) compressed, lentil-shaped,
with one chamber and a similar seed. = This tree,
whose fruit is the size of a small cherry, and is found in the
forests of Batangas and in those of S. Mateo, rises to a height
of seven or more yards. The natives know it. Its wood is
very white and fairly soft. When the bark is wounded, it exudes a
blackish gum with no notable odor (the fruit is also not fragrant), and
I do not know whether it would be good for varnishing wooden furniture; but
it should be noted that the liquor or resin used in the Philippines
to give luster to paintings is not obtained from this tree. Flowers in
Jul. * T. Balinhasa and in the environs of Manila.— In order to
understand well the fruiting of this tree, it is necessary to wait
until the fruit appears. New species.
Fagara octandra. Fagara with eight stamens. Leaves opposite
in groups of three, on a common petiole. Leaflets lanceolate,
with a notch at the pointed apex, nearly entire, and with
transparent dots on the lower surface. Common petioles long.

49
Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in loosely compound racemes. Calyx free, small, divided into four pointed parts. Corolla of four petals, much longer than the calyx, pointed, and somewhat reflexed downward. Stamens eight, attached to the receptacle, and nearly below the ovary. Filaments compressed, all united in a common membrane of little note, and shorter than the ovary. Anthers small, rounded. Ovary seated within the flower, oval, with four grooves. Style rather long. Stigmas four, very short, thick, and horizontal. Four capsules separate from each other on a single peduncle. = Trees of medium size, without thorns, which the Indians use as pillars for their houses. The bark and especially the fruit, which I have not seen ripe, have a very gentle and aromatic smell. The leaves are about six fingers long and two wide. They are common in San Mateo. Flowers in June. * T. Matang arao. — Note that the resin called Tahamaca, according to some authors, comes from Fagara octandra. It differs from the octandra species of Linnaeus in that the leaflets are not tomentose, and in that it has four stigmas. Compare with Amiris? Tecomaca of Dec. vol. 2. 82.
AZIMA. Calyx membranous, with three or four laciniae. Petals four, alternating with the laciniae of the calyx. Capsule with one compartment, and two seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 262. Jus. Gén. pl. 425.
Azima nova. New Azima. Trunk erect, square. Leaves opposite, ovate, entire and smooth, with one spine at the tip. Petioles very short, with two spines at the base. Flowers axillary and terminal in racemes. Calyx small, membranous, horizontal, irregular, sometimes oblong, with three or four rounded lobes. Corolla of four petals, upright, lanceolate, separate from the calyx. Stamens four, alternating with the petals, and as long as them, attached to a small membrane that encircles the ovary and has four points. Filaments at the points of the membrane. Anthers arrow-shaped. Ovary superior, globose, seated within the flower. Styles two, broad, fleshy, and reflexed to the sides. Berry juicy, with one compartment, and one to three half-heart-shaped seeds: compressed, fixed on a central axis. = A stiff little shrub, about one vara tall, and even four or five when leaning against other trees. I have seen it in many places: the fruit is like a small cherry, white and half-transparent. Since the leaves are opposite and each one has two spines at the base, there result four spines at each node. It therefore strongly resembles Monetia Barlerioides of Linnaeus. The description of Azima in Jussieu is very similar to the plant in question. Flowers in March. Lin. ibid.— I have seen other shrubs with a pointed scale at the base of each small flower. The calyx bell-shaped, free, with four pointed lobes. Corolla of four petals, not

50
fixed to the calyx. Stamens four, very close together, in the center of the flower. The membrane to which they are fixed, and the germ, are slow to appear.
EVODIA. Calyx with four or five lobes. Petals four or five. Stamens four. Nectary cup-shaped. Capsule of four small pods joined at the base, with two valves and one or two seeds. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 724.
Evodia triphylla. Three-leaflet Evodia. Leaves opposite, ternate. Leaflets lanceolate, entire, smooth, and soft. Individual petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in a panicle. Calyx deeply divided into four obtuse parts. Corolla of four petals, much longer than the calyx, lanceolate. Stamens four, fixed to the receptacle, and alternating with the petals. Filaments the length of the corolla, compressed, and awl-shaped. Anthers long. (In another species I have seen they are small.) Germ with a rim attached around its base, seated on the calyx, with three or four lobes. Style one, short. Stigma with four lobes. Four egg-shaped pods, joined only at the base, and afterward separated, inflated, with one chamber, and one or two seeds fixed in a suture. — Trees reaching five or six yards in height. The smell of the leaves is unpleasant. The Indians scarcely know them. Flowers in July. — Compare with the Zieria of Decandolle.
Evodia bintoco. Evodia bintoco. Branches compressed at the tip. Leaves opposite, ternate. Leaflets broad, lanceolate, entire, hairy, soft, and dotted. Common petioles long and rounded. Individual petioles absent. Flowers hermaphrodite, axillary, in a racemose panicle. Calyx in four parts. Corolla of four petals, alternating with the calyx parts. Stamens four. A glandular disk with four lobes, in the center, surrounding the germ. Germ of four lobes, top-shaped. Styles four, very short. Stigmas somewhat thick. Pod very small, of four capsules and solitary seeds. — Small trees found in Bohol and Samar: their leaves are about a hand's length and very fragrant: from the tree is extracted a fragrant resin or varnish, which is used to paint wood, leaving it very lustrous. Flowers in October. * B., Bintoco, Tancapan.
Cisus vexicatorus. — A vine whose leaves the Indians use as caustics. — * P. Pirapit angin.
CISSUS. Calyx and Corolla in four parts. Berry with one seed, surrounded by the calyx. Lin. Sist. veg. 255.
Cissus acida. Acid Cissus. Stem twining, dotted, and with simple tendrils on the leaves. Leaves ternate. Leaflets oval, serrated, and covered with very short hair on both surfaces. Common petiole long, striate, and with two stipules at the base. Individual petiole very short. Flowers axillary, in um-

51
bela, which regularly divides into three parts. Common peduncle very long. Individual peduncle very short. Calyx very small, entire, sometimes with small blunt teeth. Corolla of four concave petals, longer than the calyx, with the tips folded inward. Stamens four, very short, emerging from beneath the edges of the fruit, fixed on a barely noticeable disk. Ovary very flattened, with thin margins and four lobes. Style none. Stigma short, thick, and conical. Berry superior, seated on the said disk, very juicy and flattened, with four three-sided seeds, the outer side convex. = This plant, known to the natives, is extremely common everywhere, particularly along the fences of cultivated fields. It grows with great speed, climbing and twining around everything it encounters by means of its tendrils, forming a very pleasing vista, and at the same time an impenetrable canopy against the rays of the Sun, and would serve perfectly as a bower. The flavor of the leaves is acidic, and even some poor natives say they use the most tender ones in place of vinegar in their food, when they lack it. The naturalists of the country claim (I believe without foundation) that this plant is very effective in curing scirrhous tumors, by applying the crushed leaves on top. The fruit is acrid and caustic, of a violet color, and might perhaps serve for dyeing. This color turns green with soap. The corollas are also green. Flowers in September. * T., Calit calit, Cavilan, Pacopol, V. Lupo, Langingi, Lagini, Caguindi. P., Culutpamo. Lin. Sist. veg. 256.

Cissus arborea. Tree Cissus. Trunk erect, with drooping branches. Leaves opposite and ternate. Leaflets lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Calyx with four teeth. Corolla of four petals. Stamens four, longer than the corolla. Pistil and the rest as in the previous species. Berry globose. = This tree grows thicker than a thigh and rises to a height of five to eight varas. The smell of the bark is unpleasant, but that of the leaves is somewhat agreeable. The Chinese seek its wood to dye paja cloth. I have seen it in Batangas and in Malinta. The boys in that place call it matang diablo, that is, devil's eyes. Lin. ibid.

Cissus alata? Winged Cissus? Stem climbs by means of bifid tendrils, opposite the leaves. Leaves ternate. Leaflets somewhat heart-shaped, lanceolate, serrated, and hairy. Flowers semi-lateral, in umbellate panicles. Berry globose, somewhat flattened, sometimes white, sometimes somewhat flesh-colored or rose-colored. = This species sometimes becomes a tree, and the fruit is said to be edible, though quite insipid, and in Pampanga they say they make a sweet from it; but this is false. * T., Sampang. P., Lobas. Dec. prod. p. 1. 63. Could this perhaps be that species?

MISSOURI
BOTANICAL
GARDEN.

52
Cissus pedata. Ramose Cissus. Stem climbs by means of simple tendrils. Leaves branching, in groups of five, and sometimes seven, on a common petiole: two or three on each side, and one in the middle. Leaflets lanceolate, serrated, and smooth. Everything else as in the acid species. The fruit is globose and of a superb violet color. = I have heard that cotton, prepared as usual for dyeing red with the Nino, takes on the said violet color, and permanently. There are some varieties of this plant whose leaves are more or less small, and more or less sharp in taste. Those under discussion are somewhat so. There is also another variety with whitish fruit. The roots of these plants when boiled provide a very diuretic drink, which the Indians use to cure mange; but Europeans should try it with caution. *T., Ayo. Pers Syn. pl. t. 1. 143.
Cissus latifolia. Broad-leaved Cissus. Stem climbs, twining around neighboring trees by means of tendrils opposite the leaves. Leaves simple, alternate, heart-shaped, pointed with small teeth along the serrations, soft and hairy. Petioles long. Flowers opposite the leaves, in umbels. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 142.
Cissus quadrangularis. Four-angled Cissus. Stem jointed, with four concave sides; sometimes the two opposite ones wider. Leaves heart-shaped, toothed, serrated, with opposite tendrils. = It rises to a height of somewhat over a vara, leaning against other objects. It is common in San Juan del Monte. Some Indians call this plant dugdungahas, and say that snakes cure their wounds with it; but others give this name to a different plant. Lin. Sist. veg. 256.— There are many other species of Cissus, among them one which the Tagalog Vocabulary calls Bica, and many have believed it to be a species of ubas, and have made brandy from it. Its whole appearance is that of a grapevine; but the shrub dies every year and renews itself from the root. The fruit is black and somewhat spicy. I have not seen the flower. Moreover, the buds of the true vine end in a small tuft of wool, which resembles tinder: in the bica there is no such thing. Perhaps it is the species Vitigenea of Dec. Prod. p. 1. 627.
CANCIERA. Calyx between globose and jar-shaped, with four teeth. Corolla none. Anthers enclosed. Ovary superior, girdled with four scales. Stigma in a small head. Lin. Sist. veg. 280.
Cansiera rhedi. Cansiera of Rhedi. Leaves ovate, somewhat lanceolate, entire, and hairy on both surfaces. Petioles very short. Flowers in racemes, very small. Calyx inferior, hairy, with four blunt teeth. Corolla none. Stamens four, with a gland between each one. Filaments slightly longer than the calyx. Anthers shaped like a half-moon. Style

53
long at maturity. Stigmas three, four, or five: sometimes three, bifid. Drupe globose, fleshy, with a compressed nut, with pits, and one seed.= This small tree, like that of the following species, reaches a height of three or four yards. It flowers in April. *T., Bignay pogo. Lin. ibid.

Cansiera pentandra. Five-stamened Cansiera. Leaves oval, soft, and hairy. Flowers like those of the previous species, very hairy. Calyx with five blunt teeth. Stamens five in this species.= Everything else as in the previous species. *T., Bignay pogo. New species.

Cansiera grossularioides. Gooseberry-like Cansiera. Leaves elliptical with a small point at the apex, entire, and with fine hairs, especially on the margins. All flowers hermaphroditic, terminal in long and dense racemes. Calyx, Glands, Pistil and Fruit as in Cansiera Rheedi. Stamens four.= This tree, known to the natives, grows to eight yards tall. They use it as charcoal for forges, and it throws off many sparks with noise. The racemes are two inches long. The fruit is sour like that of the other species.— These trees are related to the genera Antidesma and Stilago. *T., Cabogbog. New species.

FUSANUS. Description of the genus. Calyx top-shaped, with four segments. Corolla none. Stamens four, opposite the calyx segments. Ovary inferior, glandular above. Style none or very short. Stigmas four. Drupe? top-shaped, with one seed. Jus.

Fusanus? parasitus. Parasitic Fusanus? Leaves opposite, oval or lanceolate, with three veins, smooth above and woolly below. Flowers axillary and terminal in spikes. Calyx superior, with four small teeth. Corolla none. Stamens four, opposite the teeth, and fixed to the receptacle. Filaments almost absent. Anthers rounded. Ovary inferior, oval and somewhat four-sided. Style very short. Stigma somewhat thick. Berry? with one seed.= Small trees found in Angat, and the one I describe had grown upon a Pterocarpo. The leaves are one inch long, and the fruit, which I have not seen ripe, resembles an anise seed. The natives have no name for it. It has an affinity with the Thesio of Lin. Flowers in Feb.— Could it perhaps belong to this genus?

ELÆAGNUS. Corolla none. Calyx in four parts, bell-shaped, superior. Drupe below the calyx. Lin. Sist. veg. 275.

Elæagnus angustifolia. Narrow-leaved Eleagnus. Trunk upright, without thorns, with drooping branches. Leaves alternate, lance-shaped to ovate, somewhat toothed on the margins, with raised dots above, and whitish below. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, often solitary. Peduncles very long. Calyx superior, square, wrinkled, speckled with
15

54
with salient points, and in four egg-shaped parts. Cor. none. Stam. four. Filam. none. Ant. at the divisions of the edge of the calyx. Style awl-shaped, and somewhat shorter than the calyx. Drupe oblong, fleshy, crowned with the calyx, angular, with small pits, with the nut also angular, and a seed surrounded by wool.= A shrub that grows at most to the height of three varas. The fruit is red when ripe, and its taste is not disagreeable; but it has a certain roughness, which might perhaps disappear with cultivation. It is very common in the town of S. José de Batangas, on the roadsides. Fl. in Oct. *T., Alingáro. Lin. ibid.

CHLORANTUS. Cal. none. Petal one with three lobes, fixed on the side of the germ. Ant. fixed on the petal. Berry with one seed. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 148.

Chlorantus inconspicuus. Invisible Chloranthus. Stem square. Leaves opposite, broad, lanceolate, serrated, with hard points at the serrations, and somewhat rough underneath. Petioles very short, sheathing the stem at the base, and with two intermediate stipules, ending in two awl-shaped points. Flowers axillary in a compound spike: the spikelets bear distichous florets, each with a keeled bract. Cal. none notable, unless it be a simple line barely raised on the belly of the germ, and then adherent. Corolla, (if it may be so called) a fleshy lamina of three lobes, fixed on the line of the calyx. Anthers, four, with two valves, and fixed without filaments on the surface of the corolla or lamina. Germ globose below, and compressed above, ending in a barely notable point. Berry globose, with one seed covered with a somewhat hard and fragile membrane.= Common plants in Calauan, in La Laguna, where Mr. Azaola has seen them, and from whom he has sent me some small branches with flowers and fruit. The leaves are about four inches long. With the flowers and the trunk, which have a pleasant smell, the Chinese, it is said, flavor their tea. Fl. in Sept. Pers. ibid.— It is the Nigrina of other Authors.

GIROCARPUS. Descr. of the gen. Flowers polygamous. Cal. in four unequal parts. Cor. none. Nectaries four. Stigma sessile. Capsule of one chamber and one seed and with two to five wings at the tip. Pers. Sin. pl. t. 1. 145.

Girocarpus lobatus. Lobed Girocarpus. Leaves alternate: the lower ones broad with three to five lobes; the upper ones lanceolate, with three veins and smooth. Petioles long. Flowers monoecious. * Male flowers in a racemose panicle, with very many tiny florets, with their own very short peduncles. Cal. bell-shaped with six lobes, and hairy. Cor. none. Stam. four, fixed on the receptacle. Filam. much

55
longer than the calyx. Anthers round, with the pollen discharged, having two small ear-like projections. Four glands on the receptacle; some or all with a small stalk, surrounding three small hairy bodies; the largest of these appears to be a rudiment of a deciduous germ. No fruit. * Females in a lax panicle with long proper peduncles. Calyx attached to the germ with two very long lobes, rarely three. Corolla none. Style none, but only a short and hairy stigma. Nut oval, somewhat compressed, with a bony covering and crowned with two very long wings, which are the lobes of the calyx, rarely three. The embryo of the nut contains about four chambers, only one of which persists at maturity with a single seed. = This genus is new and the wings number five in Person; but other Authors give the fruit no more than two. The trees I speak of are known in Tagudin; but I have also seen one in Parañaque near Manila. They produce no resin. They are about half a fathom in thickness: the leaves are lobed and broader than the palm of the hand, and they have a bad smell. The wood is soft and serves for making shields. The wings of the fruit are two inches long and are not reticulated, as in the dipterocarps. The fruit is like a chickpea. The stigma is barely perceptible because it is surrounded by fine hairs.
