Flowers in December and at no other time. * I., Lapolapo.— Persoon does not give a description of the species he titles Jacquini, and so I have taken the name of this one of mine from the lobes of the leaves.

Gyrocarpus pendulous. Pendulous Gyrocarpus. Leaves opposite, and also alternate, obliquely oval, entire and smooth, with short petioles. * Females on the branches, in a compound and pendulous spike. Calyx superior, with four lobes in the manner of wings: the three upper ones oval and membranous, semi-transparent, with fine veins and a nerve in the middle. The middle wing longer: the fourth opposite to the other three, very short, rounded and its tip folded inward and drawn up to the base of the three. Corolla none. Stamens four. Filaments attached to the style and formed by a production of the covering of the ovary with anther-bearing tips? Style long, glandular, split into two long parts, which are further subdivided into two more. Stigmas four. Nut like a pea, globose, hairy, with two chambers and solitary seeds. = A tree I have seen in Angat, in the forest called Pangisihan, ten fathoms tall and larger in girth than a man's body. The flowers, which resemble butterflies, are on long pendulous spikes. The wings are whitish, semi-transparent, and the largest is one inch long. The leaves, some two or three inches. I doubt whether the tips of the filaments are anther-bearing, in which case these flowers would be hermaphrodite. They call

56
some to the Tree, Pingol.— I have incorporated it with the Girocarpo
because of its great resemblance to it, and it seems to me there should be
separate male flowers, although I have not been able to find them.

TETRANDRIA.

TETRAGINIA.

COLDENIA. Corolla funnel-shaped. Calyx of four pieces. Styles four. Four nuts with a fungous bark. In summary, seeds two from two chambers. Lin. Sist. veg. 288.
(Four united cagillas. Jus. Gen. pl. 130.)
Coldenia procumbens. Prostrate Coldenia. No stem.
Branches arise from the ground, dividing in a star pattern. Leaves alternate, obliquely egg-shaped in reverse, toothed, with facets on the upper surface, and hairy. Petioles very short. Flowers sessile, solitary, a little above the axils. Calyx inferior, in four lanceolate and hairy parts. Corolla cylindrical, a little longer than the calyx, monopetalous, in four rounded parts. Stamens four, shorter than the corolla, fixed toward its base. Anthers triangular. Pistil conical, seated within the flower. Styles two, short, thick. (At maturity they are four.) Stigmas somewhat turned to the sides. Cagillas or dry pyramidal berry, with four lobes at the base, corky, which splits in two parts, and in each one two chambers, and one seed in each, convex on the outside and angular on the inside.= This plant, which grows close to the ground and is barely known to the natives, I have seen frequently in places where rice has been harvested after the land has dried. The spaces between the veins of the leaves are raised and the sides look like facets. The natives say that the dry leaves cause sneezing. Flowers in January. * T., Tapiasin, Hojas de Calamba. I., Tabtabocol. Lin. ibid.
TILLAÆA. Calyx in three or four parts. Petals three or four, equal. Cagillas three or four, with many seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 289.
Tillaea rubella. Somewhat reddish Tilaea. Stem erect, branching, round, hairy, with joints on the branches. Leaves sessile, opposite, lanceolate, serrated, hairy, with two awl-shaped and hairy stipules at the base. Flowers nearly sessile in the axils of the leaves, in a kind of umbel. Individual peduncle short. Calyx inferior, membranaceous, in five lanceolate, hairy parts, with a colored border on the edges. Corolla of five obtusely lanceolate petals, fixed to the calyx, and of the same length. Stamens now three, now four, fixed at the divisions of the

57
calyx, and nearly as long. Filaments curved inward. Anthers thick. Ovary globose, seated within the flower. Five very short styles. Stigmas somewhat thick. Five small capsules joined together: each with one chamber, many small seeds.= This plant, about a quarter of a vara tall, and with a reddish hue, which I have seen in the marshy places of Pasig, has almost no name among the Indians. They confuse it with the one commonly called by them golondrina, which is a species of Euphorbia, to which it bears a strong resemblance at first sight. What is peculiar about it is that the small branches appear to have movement at the nodes, so that after the plant is uprooted (and perhaps even while still alive in the ground) they bend in different directions. It bears much resemblance to the genus Crassula, and I would consider it one of its species; but it lacks the five scales that Linnaeus attributes to the genus, although Jussieu does not mention them. Flowers in November. New species.

PENTANDRIA.

MONOGINIA.

MIRABILIS. Corolla monopetalous, funnel-shaped, superior. Calyx inferior. Nut very small, globose beneath the corolla. Lin. Syst. veg. 291. 377.
Mirabilis longiflora. Marvel of long flowers. Root tapering and blackish. Stem smooth, with forking branches. Leaves opposite, between lanceolate and heart-shaped, pointed, somewhat hairy along the edges and upper surface. Petioles short. Flowers terminal, in umbels. Proper peduncles very short. Calyx persistent, in five acute parts. Corolla superior, very long, with the tube somewhat hairy, funnel-shaped, and with five lobes on the limb. Stamens five, longer than the corolla. Style longer than the stamens. Stigma globose. Nut small and globose, with many ribs, and filled inside with a starchy substance.= This plant grows to a height of three feet: its flowers open at four in the afternoon and close at eight in the morning of the following day, and it gives off a notable fragrance. Its root, though very similar in appearance and texture to that of Jalap, is not the same, for Jalap is a convolvulus. The fruit is black when ripe. The Indian calls it oracion (prayer) because of the peculiarity of its flowers being open at prayer time. It is easy to recognize by the globose ovary upon which the corolla is seated. It is very common everywhere, and it is the one that medical authors designate as a substitute or surrogate for Jalap: it is known by the name-

58
named Diego de noche or bella de noche, but this one I speak of hardly purges at all. It is always in flower, and the flowers are of various colors even on the same plant. Indian embroiderers use the flour of the fruit dissolved in water to form designs on fabrics: for this reason they call it albayalde. Likewise, with the juice of a variety that constantly produces crimson flowers, boys write; and the color of the letters is firm and pleasing. *T., oracion, Guilalas, Popol señora. In Manila, suspiros. Lin. ibid.
PLUMBAGO. Corolla funnel-shaped. Filaments of the stamens, dilated at the base and arched. Stigma in five parts. Superior capsule, with one chamber and one seed. Lin. Syst. veg. 337.
Plumbago viscosa. Sticky Plumbago. Stem inclined toward the ground, angular. Leaves lanceolate, ovate, running along the petiole, entire, and somewhat hairy. Petioles clasp the stem at the base. Flowers axillary, in a spike. Each flower with its own involucre of three small ovate bracts, the lowest being the largest. Calyx long, divided almost to the base into five linear segments, covered with small stalked glands that exude sticky gum at their tips. Corolla twisted, with a very long and square tube, a naked throat, and a limb with five ovate lobes that are reversed and terminated by a small style-like point. Stamens five, fixed toward the base of the corolla, and nearly as long as the tube. Style somewhat shorter than the stamens. Stigma in five parts. One long seed, covered with a membranous skin, with five angles, and enclosed within the calyx. = This plant is well known to the native people, who call it sangdigcquit, from digcquit meaning to stick; because in fact the calyxes of the flowers, by means of the gum exuded through their glandular spines or bristles, stick to everything that comes near them. The flowers are white, and the corolla is twisted. This plant is not found in many places, but it is very common along the roadsides of the town of Bauang and in Ilocos. The root is used in medicine as a caustic, at least in Bauang: also applied for a short time, and from time to time, it destroys warts. I have read that one of the species of Plumbago is used as a dye. It is also used to treat mange by means of a decoction, which must be prepared by mixing with water an equal weight of mallow leaves, since otherwise it is too caustic. The cure is certain and without risk. This secret, awarded a prize in Paris by the Academy of Medicine, is known to the Ilocanos. *T. Sangdigcquit. I. Bangbanh, Talaucao. Lin. ibid.— In Pasig I have seen a variety with crimson flowers, which may be the species rosea of Lin.
AEGICERAS. Calyx bell-shaped, with five divisions-

59
leathery. Corolla with five laciniae, rolled downward. Cagilla elongated, sickle-shaped, with one chamber and one curved seed, in the form of a horn. From living specimens.
Aegiceras corniculata. Aegiceras of horn shape.
Leaves semi-opposite, approaching the shape of a wedge, with a notch at the apex. Flowers axillary, in a simple umbel of more than twelve small florets. Common peduncles none. Individual peduncles long. Calyx inferior, twisted, of five imbricated and persistent pieces. Corolla deciduous, jug-shaped, with five lanceolate laciniae, rolled downward. Nectary small-jug-shaped, fixed at the base of the corolla, monophyllous, with a woolly margin, formed by the corolla itself, whose tube, after reaching the bottom of the calyx, bends in the opposite direction and turns upward. Stamens five, fixed on the woolly margins of the nectary. Filaments as long as the corolla. Anthers versatile, arrow-shaped. Ovary conical. Style long. Stigma simple. Fruit, a single seed, long, cylindrical, curved, pointed, seated on the calyx, covered with a membrane that ruptures on the convex side. = This tree reaches a height of eighteen feet: it is common on beaches, and is usually found mixed among Rhizophoras. The fruit greatly resembles that of those plants, but is smaller. The native makes no use of it at all. The leaves have marbled streaks along the midrib, and small spots along the edges. The calyx also has them on the lower part, which is green, while the upper part is white. Furthermore, the anthers have spots or little marks on their backs, before the flower opens. Flowers in May. * T. Tingang baguis, Pipisic. I believe neither of these two is its true name. More certain is that of snguing-saguingan. — It is the plant that Linnaeus called Rhizophora corniculata. Syst. veg. 747.
HELIOTROPIUM. Corolla salver-shaped, with five laciniae; and between these, five folds, with the throat closed by arched scales. Four nuts without a hole.
Heliotropium parviflorum. Small-flowered Heliotrope.
Stem erect, somewhat square, with channeled branches, sprinkled with hairs. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, ovate, running down a long petiole, notched, very wrinkled, hairy on both surfaces. Flowers in very long spikes, curved downward, sometimes simple, and at other times divided in two, containing two rows of small florets, placed on one side only of the peduncle. Calyx in five deep parts. Corolla longer than the calyx, tubular, with the tube somewhat swollen below, the limb divided into five blunt lobes with five folds, and the throat naked. Anthers fixed in the middle of the corolla. Stigma with four lobes. Upper cagilla divided at the top into two broad, tapering parts,

60
and notched, diverging from one another, and separating easily at maturity: the capsule divides into four parts, each containing one seed. = This plant, which is found everywhere, grows to the height of one foot. Its juice applied topically removes warts, and even gout, according to Father Delgado: two or three seeds ground up and drunk in wine cure tertian and quartan fevers, taking the medicine one hour before the onset. Some Indians remove cloudiness from the cornea of the eyes by applying, from time to time, a drop of the plant's juice mixed with a grain of ordinary salt. The color of the flowers is violet: the throat is open, without scales or teeth; not even the plicas close it. Flowers in July. *T., Hinlalay-on, Cotingcotingan. Lin. ibid.
BORAGO. Corolla wheel-shaped, with the throat closed by filaments. Four closed nutlets. Lin. Sist. veg. 321.
African Borago? African Borage? Stem hairy with opposite branches. Leaves opposite, clasping the stem at their base, lanceolate, veined beneath and very hairy. Flowers pendulous, terminal, in a compound raceme. Calyx swollen, divided into five deep lobes without small ears. Corolla with the tube shorter than the calyx: the limb flat, divided into five heart-shaped and pointed laciniae: the throat covered with a dense network of fine threads, and with five flat, awl-shaped scales that rise upward, joined and twisting into a spiral. Anthers hidden inside the corolla, long. Style shorter than the stamens. Four very smooth nutlets without a hole, attached on their inner side to small cavities of the receptacle. = This plant, which does not agree well with the African species nor with the others of Linnaeus, grows to the height of three feet. The Indians hardly know it, although some call it Sigangdagat; they also give this name to another plant. It is common in the towns of Lipa, San José, and in Bauang in the cultivated fields; but it is not seen in many places. Flowers in December and in other months. *T., Sigangdagat: and others call it Dilan usá, Olongain. Lin. ibid.
Borago indica. Indian Borage. Leaves opposite, sessile, clasping the stem at the base, between linear and lanceolate, covered with small hooks that make them very rough. Flowers axillary, solitary, with long peduncles. Calyx divided into five sharp, straight lobes, with five angles prolonged downward in the form of small ears that separate from the base. Corolla flat, with five groups of yellow glands placed near the throat of the corolla and opposite the laciniae. = This plant is barely two hand-spans tall and I have seen it in Parañaque, among the peanut plantings. The calyces, on account of that continuation of the angles downward, appear arrow-pierced. The leaves are two and a half inches long, and barely one

61
wide. The small glands of the corolla are absent in the other species
described before. Fl. in September. Lin. ibid.
STRYCHNOS. Cal. in five parts. Cor. tubular, with the
limb in five parts. Stam. fixed at the throat. Stigma
in a small head. Berry with one or many seeds. Lin. Syst. veg.
by Spreng. t. 1. 511.
STRYCHNOS PHILIPPENSIS. STRYCHNOS OF THE PHILIPPINES. Root cen-
tral, with some lateral rootlets. Trunk with bark very
close-fitting. Branches opposite, smooth, with square extremities.
Leaves run along the petiole, opposite, oval, very pointed
at the ends, with three very notable nerves, and veins in
a network, entire and smooth. Petioles very short, channeled
on top. Flowers in panicles of many small florets. Cal. infe-
rior, very short, with five teeth. Cor. six or seven times
longer than the calyx, funnel-shaped, with five lacin-
iae. Filaments: none. Anthers five, fixed at the throat of the
corolla. Ovary very small. Style filiform, as long as the
stamens. Stigma truncated and somewhat thick. Drupe globose, and
sometimes oval, large, smooth, with a woody and
thick covering, of one cell, filled with small nuts pressed tightly together,
leaving no gap between them. Seeds of various shapes, of
solid, horny, and very hard substance. = This shrub, whose
flowers described here were sent to me from Bohol by Fr. Narciso de Jesus
Maria, Augustinian Recollect, a person very devoted to na-
ture, grows as tall as the largest trees. It is common in some
towns of the Visayan provinces of the Philippines, such as Catba-
logan, from where it takes its name, and it grows as thick or thicker
than a thigh. I have had a small dried specimen the height of a
man, which showed no sign of being a climbing vine. The Indians have told me
that it is one; and others worthy of trust say they are trees like the
oak; but I agree with the Botanists that these trees climb up
neighboring bodies, either by means of tendrils that some
have, or by means of the ends of their branches. The use of
the nuts is great in fevers and in other illnesses.
Applied to the place where a snake or other
venomous animal has bitten (first scarifying the skin with a needle or
lancet so that blood appears) they adhere with great force
and draw out the venom. This virtue of dispelling venom is prodig-
ious and most certain: as I have seen in myself, not just once
alone. At the same time that the seed is applied to the bite,
the patient is given to drink warm water in which
another piece of the seed has been soaked: normally one does not taste its
bitterness: and when the patient says it tastes bitter, he is already out of
danger: this too is very true, and I have experienced it
myself. On this occasion I should mention that for snake bites
the Indians have many medicines. One of them
16

62
most admirable is fire, as I have seen myself. When the poison, according to the healers, has taken hold of the most vital parts of the body, they place a live coal or a burning brand at the back of the head; and in this state the bitten persons remain with the greatest calm, without the fire causing them any sensation at all: when the burned part bursts open, the Indians assure that there is no longer any danger; which I hold to be true in some cases, though not in all. Returning to the seeds of Saint Ignatius, I say: that much prudence is needed in their internal use; for carelessness in this matter has led to many deaths and misfortunes. For no reason whatsoever should they be put in the mouth, as some do, to swallow the bitter saliva; for if one should accidentally swallow them, death is certain, if vomiting cannot be achieved. How many have perished from this! In such a case they say it is good to take the honey that drips from the sugar loaves. It is not advisable to drink wine of any kind: it is good to wet the face, hands, and thighs with cold water: it is also effective to drink vinegar diluted with sugar. The nuts have two cotyledons, and they are seen very clearly when they have been in vinegar for some time. Although I have often obtained fresh nuts, I have never been able to make them germinate: they only produced a small root if placed in vinegar; in soil or sand, they rot immediately. Father José Delgado, a learned Jesuit, in his history of the Philippines, says that very hard seeds are sometimes found, like stones, and at the same time brilliant: he says they possess the same virtues as the others. *T., Pepita, Fruta. P., Pepita sa catbalogan. V. Pangaguason, Aguason, Canlara, Mana-naog, Dancagi, Catalonga, Igasud. Spreng. ibid. 672. — It is the genus Ignatia of other Authors.
(CAMOTAIN.) Leaves opposite, entire, smooth and slightly stiff. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in a panicle. Calyx cleft almost to the base into five parts. Corolla nearly the length of the calyx, cleft almost to the base into five parts hairy below. Stamens five, fixed between the divisions of the corolla. Filaments none. Anthers shaped like arrowheads. Germen conical, inside the flower. Style the length of the corolla. Stigma slightly thick, compressed and lightly cleft into two parts. Fruit.....= A shrub that the Indians barely know, nor make use of. The leaves bear some resemblance to those of Laurus Culilaban. I have not seen its fruit, and so I leave it undetermined.
SPHENOCLEA. Calyx inferior, with five laciniae. Corolla with five laciniae and smaller than the calyx. Capsule compressed, with two chambers, breaking open horizontally. Seeds numerous and semi-rounded. Pers. Sin. pl. t. 1. 173.
Sphenoclea zeylanica. Sphenoclea of Ceylon. Stem—

63
straight, with spongy bark. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, nearly entire and smooth. Flowers axillary, in a very compact conical catkin, where the small flowers are sessile but separable (and not as in Morinda) with four small leaflets between each floret. Calyx of four or five rounded, fleshy, persistent lobes. Corolla above the ovary, bell-shaped, with a connivent limb and five lobes. Stamens five, attached toward the base of the corolla. Filaments very short. Anthers thick. Ovary globose, depressed, seated within the calyx. Style very short. Stigma funnel-shaped. Capsule globose, depressed, wrapped in a membrane, and almost entirely covered by the calyx, with two chambers formed by an imperfect partition, and in each a fleshy receptacle where the slightly elongated, rough seeds are fixed. = An aquatic plant, about half a meter tall, which I saw in Malinta and Hagonoy. The bark of the stem contains a white, soft, and spongy substance about a finger's thickness. Flowers in October. *T. Silisilihan. Pers. ibid. — It is the Pongatium of Jus. Gen. pl. 423.

MENYANTHES. Corolla hairy. Nectaries five at the base of the ovary. Stigma with two lobes. Capsule with one chamber. Lin. Sist. veg. 329.

Menyanthes Indica. Indian Menyanthes. Leaves fleshy, shield-shaped, circular, notched, deeply cleft at the base, with many nerves radiating from the center and branching twice, smooth above and somewhat rough below. Petioles very long. Flowers on the side of the petiole, in a simple umbel. Calyx in five parts. Corolla woolly inside, with the wool very neatly arranged, funnel-shaped, in five deep divisions. Stamens five, fixed at the base of the corolla, with anthers bifid at the base. Ovary conical, with five very small glands at the base. Style awl-shaped. Stigma in two oval portions, each with two wings on the back. Capsule conical, with one chamber and many small, lenticular seeds fixed to the walls. = This plant is common in Laguna de Bay, where I have seen it. Its leaves are a foot and a half in diameter, and can scarcely be distinguished from those of the Nelumbo: they rise from the water, and the roots are fixed in the bottom. I do not know that the Indians make any use of it; but the decoction of the roots and leaves of the species of Menyanthes, especially the one called Trefoil fibrin, in doses of half an ounce and in a suitable quantity of water, is excellent for rheumatic pains; but it must be taken with caution, as it is harmful to some. Flowers in August. *T. Lauas. I. Locloquisin. Lin. ibid.

PORANA. Corolla bell-shaped, in five parts. Calyx shorter than the corolla, in five parts. Style one, bifid. Stigmas globose. Fruit of two valves. Jus. Gen. pl. 420.

64
Porana? volubilis. Porana? voluble. Stem erect, with alternate, lax, and smooth branches. Leaves alternately spaced, egg-shaped, with five veins, very pointed, entire, and smooth. Long petioles. Flowers terminal, very small, in a racemose panicle. Calyx bell-shaped, with five laciniae (some overlapping others), somewhat woolly and spotted. Corolla somewhat longer than the calyx, between bell-shaped and wheel-shaped, with small spots, woolly, and deeply divided into five parts rolled outward. Stamens five, fixed at the divisions of the laciniae. Filaments very short. Anthers inside the corolla, oval and compressed. Ovary between superior and inferior. Style single, very short. Stigma thick, with striations. Fruit...= Shrubs that grow as thick as a calf of the leg, and are common in Cebu and other places, and exude a milky sap. Although they are called bulacan, they must not be confused with other plants of the same name. The flowers I saw were dried. The bark is filamentous, soft, and seems to have some tenacity: it separates by itself from the branches.— The insertion of the stamens is at the divisions of the parts of the corolla, and not in these parts themselves. Perhaps the flowers described are sterile: for I have seen others on other specimens with smooth calyx and corolla, and without spots or color patches. It closely resembles Porana. Lin. Sist. veg. 339.
ALLAMANDA. Corolla twisted, funnel-shaped, with a very wide limb and five lobes. Stigma with two lobes. Capsule bristly, with many seeds provided with a membranous wing. Lin. Spr.
Allamanda cathartica. Purgative Allamanda. Trunk twining. Leaves in fours, lanceolate with rough hair. Flower in a compound spike. Calyx in five parts, cylindrical below, with a very large limb of five lobes. Anthers five, arrow-shaped, in the throat. Ovary superior. Style thread-like. Stigma cylindrical, ending in two small points. Capsule....= A shrub made known by Mr. Azaola, which grows in Calauang. The flowers are yellow.
OPHIORHIZA. Descr. of the gen. Corolla funnel-shaped. The style girded at its base with a small tube. Stigmas two. Capsule widened and compressed, nearly miter-shaped, crowned with the teeth of the calyx, with two chambers and many seeds. Lin. Syst. Veg. 333. Dec. prod. t. 4. 415.
Ophiorhiza oblongifolia. Ophiorhiza with oblong leaves. Central root fibrous. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, egg-shaped, and sometimes elongated, obtuse, slightly hairy on both surfaces and margins. Petioles short, with two intermediate stipules on each side, joined at the base and split in two at the tip. Terminal flowers in umbellate panicles, with the peduncles

65

partial clusters adorned with small lateral flowers, upright and nearly sessile. Cal. adherent, compressed, with five teeth. Cor. much longer than the calyx, monopetalous, funnel-shaped, with five lacinae, and a hairy throat. Stam. five, shorter than the corolla, and fixed toward its base. Ant. long, straight. Nect. surrounding the style at the base, top-shaped, somewhat fleshy, and two-lipped. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma two long, narrow, and close-set laminae. Capsule compressed and widened, crowned with the teeth of the calyx, with two chambers and very many seeds. = A plant the height of a hand's breadth and up to one foot, sent to me by Mr. Azaola, who found it in Calauan. The leaves are dark green above, pale below, and range from one to two and a half inches in length. The root and flowers are very small and dark yellow; and the root is somewhat bitter and disagreeable to the taste. Flowers in June.

Ophiorhiza triandra. Three-stamened Ophiorhiza. Stem erect. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, slightly hairy. Petioles short. Terminal flowers in simple opposite racemes, of small lateral florets, all directed upward. Cal. adherent, with five teeth on the margin. Cor. long, with five teeth. Stam. six: the three alternating ones sterile, all fixed to the corolla. Filaments somewhat long. Ant. long. Style none. Stigma a single lamina, wide and short: presumably two united. Fruit depressed and elongated on the sides, nearly oval, very compressed, with five lobes on the upper margin, which are the teeth of the calyx, and which contains some small seeds. == I have seen this small plant of three inches in height, at Punta Mal Abrigo. In its inflorescence and fruit it resembles a hydrocotyle; and I indeed believed it to be such when I first saw it, thinking it was a rare monopetalous species: the stamens are remarkable, of which three are sterile and the other three fertile. Flowers in December.

CONVOLVULUS. Cor. bell-shaped, with folds. Nectary a crown or ring encircling the ovary. Stigmas two. Capsule with two or three chambers, each containing two seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 339.

Convolvulus pes caprae. Goat's-foot Convolvulus. Root branching. Stem prostrate, rooting. Leaves with two lobes, or with a very large notch at the tip, and two small glands at the base. Flowers axillary in a panicle: the individual peduncles long. Cor. very large, bell-shaped, with five angles on the limb and five nerves forming a star. Stam. five, unequal in height. Stigma globose, marked with a line along which it eventually divides in two: another line is faintly visible crossing the first one at the middle, but it does not reach the margins.

66
Capsule ovoid, with two cells, and in each one two hairy seeds, convex on one side and angular on the other. = This plant, although not twining, spreads widely along the ground: its flowers and glands are rose-colored. It is very common on the seashore. From the ashes of this plant, I have observed that a very good soap can be made, better than that obtained from the ashes of coconut fronds; but inferior to that obtained from the Rhizophoras. Its leaves have, according to the Indians, a singular virtue for consuming the excrescences or fleshy growths of sores. Flowers in January. *T., B., Catang-catang, Lagayrai. Lampayong. Bagasua, Camigang, Daripay, Tagaray, Arodayday, Lambayong. I., Lambayong.— It corresponds with the convolvulus brasiliensis in the two glands of the leaves. Lin. ibid. 344.

Convolvulus dentatus. Toothed Bindweed. Root branching. Stem round, somewhat hairy, and twining. Leaves heart-shaped and pointed, somewhat hairy, with some teeth on the sides of the base. Petioles as long as the leaves. Axillary flowers on a long peduncle that supports seven or more small flowers in an umbel, which divides into three parts. Calyx with five deep divisions. Corolla as in the species pes caprae. Filaments curved. Capsule with two cells, and in each one two seeds.— A very common plant, which does not correspond well with any of those described by Linnaeus, and so I have named it dentata (toothed).

Convolvulus hederaceus. Ivy-like Bindweed. Root long and fibrous. Stem twining and hairy. Leaves heart-shaped, hairy and soft: others with three lobes. Axillary flowers in groups of three, or many more, on a very long peduncle. Calyx with five deep, ovoid, soft, and erect divisions: the two outer ones larger, covering the others. Corolla bell-shaped, and toward the base on the inside of a purple color. Pistil surrounded by small hairs at the base. Stigma divided into two oval and divergent parts. Capsule somewhat flattened, hairy, with two cells and in each one two large seeds.= It is an unknown plant. Lin. ibid. 340.

Convolvulus colubrinus. Snake Bindweed. Stem twining, milky, with soft spines. Leaves alternate, heart-shaped, slightly hairy, with red and prominent veins beneath. Petioles as long as the leaves, with two dark glands at the tip. Flowers solitary: Calyx with five overlapping and pointed divisions. Corolla straw-colored on the outside, and on the inside purple and tomentose, with five angles and five folds. Ovary with a ring. Stigma globose, divided as into two globules. Capsule with compartments and white, smooth seeds.= A plant three feet tall, native to China (so they say), brought to Pangasinan, and from there to other parts.

67
Its virtue is said to be prodigious for neutralizing the venom of snakes. A man already dying as a result of a bite from that reptile had placed in his mouth a little of the saliva of someone who had chewed a seed of this convolvulus, and the rest was applied to the site of the bite, and he soon recovered. It bears fruit quickly.

Convolvulus boerhaavioides. Convolvulus resembling Boerhaavia. Stem twining. Leaves alternate, notched at the base, elongated-ovate, pointed, wavy-edged and smooth. Petioles short. Axillary flowers in umbellate panicles. Calyx free in five parts: the three outer ones larger, covering the two smaller inner ones. Corolla bell-shaped with five pleats and five pointed lobes. Stamens separate below forming an arch and drawing slightly closer together above. Anthers regular, ending in a small stipule. Ovary globose. Style longer than the stamens, divided in two down to its midpoint. Stigmas simple, bending inward to form an arch. Seed capsule globose with four chambers, each containing one seed. = A small plant with bluish flowers, somewhat resembling Boerhaavia. I place it here, although it differs from the convolvuluses in its stigmas. It does not exude milky sap. I saw it at Punta Santiago. — It approaches the genus Evolvulus fairly closely.

Convolvulus reniformis. Kidney-shaped Convolvulus. Stem creeping, rooting. Leaves alternate, kidney-shaped, with some teeth. Petioles long. Axillary flowers, solitary, nearly sessile. Calyx free, divided into five ovate parts with very thin, fringe-like margins. Corolla bell-shaped, with five pleats and as many lobes. Stamens five, attached at the base of the corolla, each with a small fringe-like membrane at its base. Filaments equal, somewhat inclined inward. Anthers oblong, versatile. Ovary conical. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma in a small head, with a barely visible line that appears to divide it in two. Seed capsule globose, protruding, with two chambers, each containing two seeds. = A creeping plant with yellow flowers. A decoction drunk from it reduces fever in the sick and causes much urination. I have seen it in many places. *T., Batobato. I., Cupitcupit.— The small membrane found at the base of the stamens distinguishes this species from the others of the genus.

Convolvulus maximus. Greatest Convolvulus. Stem twining, with four angles. Leaves heart-shaped. Axillary flowers, numerous, in umbels. Calyx deeply divided into five parts, imbricate, ovate and very fleshy. Corolla bell-shaped, with pleats. Stamens as in the genus. Ovary with a nectary encircling it at the base as in the genus. Stigmas two, globose. Seed capsule square, with two coverings: the

68
only one covers the upper part, and it is separable, with two chambers each containing two seeds. = A climbing plant that grows very tall and spreads widely. The Indians make no use of it. The two coverings of the fruit are notable. It is common in Ba-uang and Pasig, and resembles the Turbit species. Flowers in November. Lin. ibid. 341.

Convolvulus muricatus. Soft-spined Convolvulus. Twining stem, covered with soft spines. Leaves heart-shaped, sometimes with three lobes and smooth. Calyx of five scales or small leaflets ending in spines, the three larger ones longer than the others. Corolla funnel-shaped, very large. = The flowers of this plant, which are white and whose limb measures five inches in diameter, should be examined early in the morning. The Indians call this plant Camocamotihan, because they notice a certain resemblance between its flower and that of the sweet potato. Flowers in December. *T., Camocamotihan. Lin. ibid.

Convolvulus repens. Creeping Convolvulus. Stem hollow and spreading. Leaves arrow-shaped, with the two lobes sometimes rounded and sometimes not, with two glands at the base, entire and smooth. Flowers up to three in number on a common peduncle. Stigma with two globes. = A plant two feet tall, with white flowers, known everywhere; for it grows and spreads widely in watery places, and is mildly purgative: the natives and Europeans eat it cooked, and it is not unpleasant. Flowers in November. *T., P., Cangcong, V., Tancong. Lin. ibid. 343.

Convolvulus nil. Nil Convolvulus. Stem rounded, twining, hairy. Leaves heart-shaped, with short hairs, three-lobed: the middle lobe broad and lanceolate; the lateral ones with right-angle sinuses, and with petioles as long as the leaves. Flowers axillary, solitary or in pairs, with peduncles much shorter than the petioles. Calyx hairy, in five long parts. Corolla bell-shaped with five lobes and five slight incisions in the limb. Ovary with a ring. Stigma globose, with a line dividing it in two. Capsule globose, depressed, with three chambers and two seeds in each. = A climbing plant that I have seen in Manila, and which does not produce latex. Its flowers are violet. Flowers in August. Lin. ibid. 340.

Convolvulus batatas. Batatas Convolvulus. Root tuberous. Stem trailing, hairy, and rooting. Leaves heart-shaped, somewhat arrow-shaped, with nine veins and two very small glands at the base on the underside, sometimes quite entire, sometimes with small angles as numerous as the veins. Petioles as long as the leaves, hairy. Flowers axillary, two to four in number, on very long, smooth, angular peduncles, thicker toward the top. Calyx and the rest as in the convolvulus

69
Pes capræ. Nectary with five lobes.= This plant spreads widely, and at the points where the stem touches the ground, it puts out roots and small branches. From each root emerge oblong tubers, of unequal sizes. Their number, then, is four, or six, or more if they are small, hanging from the main root by small rootlets. These tubers are what constitute the principal merit of the plant, and they sometimes reach six inches in length or much more. Their preparation in the kitchen is very varied, and according to each person's taste. They serve in place of soup all the way to chocolate, cut into thin slices and toasted over the fire. When people want to make a planting, they do not use the buds of the roots, but pieces of branches, which they insert into the ground. At other times they spread a long branch over the prepared soil, and press it down with the hand, burying only the nodes, where the buds are located. I have been assured that in Camarines there is a species called ticsi, which produces a camote of monstrous size. Although the camote closely resembles the Batatas species, I am inclined to think it is not the same, but rather a variety. When the Indians intoxicate fish in the rivers with the fruit of the Menispermum, they say its potency is weakened by throwing the leaves of the camote into the water. Father Antonio Mozo, in his valuable book on the Missions of the Calced Augustinian Fathers of the Philippines, states that the camote seed came from New Spain. Notwithstanding this testimony, which carries much weight, it is more credible that many species or varieties known in the islands are native, and these would take long to recount and describe, as they number more than thirty. The differences are taken from the color and shape of the leaves, the color of the skin and flesh of the roots, and their flavor and size. The skin varies in color: black, purple, white, yellow, and mottled; the flesh is either white or purple, and also yellow. All these camotes have their own names among the Indians. T., Camote. Lin. ibid. 341.
Convolvulus longi florus. Long-flowered Convolvulus. Root long, woody, and fibrous. Stem twining, producing much milky sap, woody at the base. Leaves heart-shaped, ovate, pointed, smooth, sometimes three-lobed. Petioles long, with two small purple glands at the tip. Flowers solitary. Peduncles very long. Calyx smooth, of five concave leaflets. Corolla white, very long, compressed, monopetalous, funnel-shaped, with five lobes on the limb. Stamens five, shorter than the corolla. Anthers small, regular. Style somewhat longer than the stamens. Ovary with a small ring at the base, appearing to have five lobes. Stigma divided into two oval parts. Capsule with two chambers, and in each two seeds with three sides, one convex and the others flat and fringed on both edges.= This plant, which I have ordered to be brought
17

70
from Cebu, and it grows in Manila; I have seen it at Punta Santiago and on the beaches of Manila Bay. It spreads extensively and produces a great deal of latex, which is a resin that turns black and is soluble in alcohol like that of Jalapa, whose properties it shares. Its woody branches, which are about as thick as an arm, purge reliably at a dose of one real. The flowers are white and long, about a hand's span. This plant must not be confused with another called bulacan in Tagalog, a species of Chironia. The resin of that plant is very caustic and should not be used. Flowers in March. * Bulacan.— There is also found in Cebu another plant called Bulacan, whose description I will give shortly, celebrated for the abundant water it distills, which the natives use very effectively as a purgative.

Convolvulus distillatorius. Distillatory Convolvulus.
Leaves heart-shaped, nearly round, with about five nerves, with small teeth barely noticeable along the edges, suddenly very pointed at the tip, and silky on both surfaces. Flowers in a kind of umbellate panicle, of about eight or more small florets. Individual peduncles thickened toward the square-shaped tip. Calyx of five oval, smooth leaflets: the two outer ones partly covering the three inner ones. Corolla... Stamens five. Anthers regular, not in a spiral. Pistil conical, seated on a ring. Stigma split into two oval parts. Capsule egg-shaped, splitting into three or four parts, with two chambers each containing two three-sided seeds, one side convex and the other two flat, covered with soft hairs, and still fringed along the two outer angles. = It is a climbing plant, known in the Visayas and highly valued for the water it distills, which, drunk in the quantity of a cup, purges very gently. It is called, like several others, bulacan or buracan. It should be noted that in the Conv. with the long flower, the seeds are fringed only at the angles and smooth on the rest. The leaves of this species I am describing are nearly round. I have seen other convolvuluses with hairy and fringed seeds, as described above, but whose leaves are not round. A new species.
Convolvulus paniculatus. Paniculate Convolvulus. Root with many spindle-shaped, pendulous tubers. Twining stem that appears to have three angles. Palmate leaves; smooth: the older ones with seven lanceolate lobes. Petioles as long as the leaves, with two small glands barely visible at the tip. Axillary flowers in panicles of six, eight, or more small florets. Common peduncle very long. Individual peduncle long. Corolla funnel-shaped, with five angles on the limb. Anthers rather long. Pistil with a fleshy border at the base. Two globose stigmas. Capsule with four seeds. = Common in Pasay and other places. The flowers are red. The natives use

71

of the infusion of the root for purging; but when dry it has little virtue. The tubers are the same shape as the sweet potato, and I have seen them as large as a man's head. Flowers in July. * T., Puntaspuntas. — It will more likely be Ipomoea tuberosa! Lin. ibid. 342.

CHIRONIA. Calyx with five laciniae, swollen after flowering. Corolla salver-shaped. Anthers twisted after flowering. Capsule with the valves folded inward, forming a partition. Lin. Sist. veg. ed. 16 by Spr. t. 1. 505.

Chironia lanosanthera. Chironia with woolly anthers. Stem twining. Leaves ovate, sinuous, smooth, with some veins united at the base. Flowers in a sort of panicle. Calyx split almost to the base into five concave parts, placed one over another, and very fleshy at maturity. Corolla very large, bell-shaped, monopetalous, with five angles on the limb. Stamens five. Anthers with channels, and at maturity spirally twisted and covered with wool. Ovary superior with five angles, surrounded by a thick zone. Style longer than the stamens. Stigmas two, globose. Capsule juicy, with two chambers, each containing hairy seeds. — A plant that spreads more than four fathoms with its long roots. It grows to the thickness of an inch and exudes much milk, which soon turns black. The leaves are one foot long, and the flowers are yellow. When a small branch is twisted, a very pleasant smell is perceived. What is singular about the flower are the anthers, which besides being twisted after maturity, each appears like a little tuft of wool. The parts of the calyx are very thick and juicy. The resin of this plant dissolves in alcohol and is very caustic. It should not be confused with others also called Bulacan, which are purgatives. Although it appears to have tendrils, they are not really such, but rather the tips of the branches, which shed their leaves in time. * T., Bulacan. New species.

Ipomaea. Corolla funnel-shaped. Stigma globose. Capsule with three chambers. Lin. Sist. veg. 345.

Ipomaea pes tigridis. Ipomea tiger's foot. Stem prostrate, hairy, with twining tips. Leaves alternate, palmate, with seven lobes, lanceolate, and hairy. Flowers clustered on a common, very long peduncle. Common calyx composed of ten bracts, the outer ones larger, containing four or more small flowers. Proper calyx in five sharp-pointed, very deep parts. Corolla funnel-shaped, with five notched lobes at the stamens, erect, unequal. Ovary conical, with a rim at the base. Stigmas two globes pressed against each other. Capsule with two chambers, each containing two seeds; sometimes with three chambers and solitary seeds. — This plant, which is not co-

72
known to the locals, it spreads along the ground, and its flowers are
white. Flowers in September. Lin. ibid. 347.
Ipomoea hepaticifolia. Ipomoea with hepatica-like leaves. Leaves
three-lobed, or halberd-shaped; the middle lobe much
longer and lanceolate, the others truncated, toothed,
smooth on the underside and somewhat hairy above, and more so on the
veins. Flowers axillary in very short panicles bearing about three
small florets. Ovary without nectary. Stigma globose.= A creeping plant
found in Parañaque, with straw-colored flowers. The leaves
are one inch long. Flowers in January.
Ipomoea quamoclit. Ipomoea quamoclit. Stem striped and
twining at the tip. Leaves laciniate, with winged segments.
Flowers in groups of three, in a panicle. Calyx in five very
deep parts. Corolla very long, funnel-shaped, with the limb
divided into five pointed segments. Stamens five, attached at the
base of the corolla, and as long as it. Ovary encircled
at its base by a small ring. Style as long as the
stamens. Stigmas in two globose parts. Upper capsule,
twisted in a spiral at maturity with four partitions, four
chambers, and in each one a long seed.= This plant twines
and climbs trees. The Indians in Batangas call it agoho,
although in other parts of the Islands this name
refers to a tree that is a casuarina. The leaf segments of
this plant are one inch long and half a line
wide. Flowers in December. * T., Agoho. Linnaeus ibid. 345.—
The two genera Ipomoea and Convolvulus have much affinity with
each other. Some authors have joined the former with the latter.
DATURA. Corolla funnel-shaped, with folds. Calyx
tube-shaped, with angles, and which falls with the corolla. Capsule
with four valves. Lin. Syst. veg. 378.
Datura metel. Datura metel. Trunk with knotty branches,
approaching a forked shape. Leaves obliquely egg-shaped,
angular, somewhat hairy, and with pointed tips. Flowers
axillary, solitary. Calyx tube-like, with five angles
and five teeth, which falls at the maturity of the fruit,
breaking apart horizontally, with a circular portion
remaining attached to the fruit. Lower corolla funnel-shaped: the
limb with five angles, five folds, and on its edges bearing
five long, pointed teeth. Stamens five, the length of the
calyx. Anthers long, compressed. Stigma thick, oblong,
blunt, and which can be split into two plates. Capsule globose,
somewhat inclined downward, bristling with spines, with two
complete partitions and two incomplete ones that cross the
first, and with four valves, seated on the base of the
calyx. Seeds very numerous, compressed and kidney-shaped.= This plant, very similar to henbane, rises to

73
sometimes reaching a height of five or six feet. The Indians call it Talamponay: its properties are both good and bad. The flowers are very large and white, and the fruit does not have very clear or well-defined valves. I have seen that sheep devour it whole with great eagerness, but not goats. In medicine, I have not seen the natives make use of it. Despite how harmful this plant is, I find it recommended by Authors for the treatment of cancer: the leaves are applied to tumors of women's breasts and to hemorrhoids. The pills taken internally, and the leaves first soaked in hot water and applied between two cloths to scirrhous tumors, are extremely useful, and in the Philippines they admirably substitute for Hemlock: let anyone who wishes verify this, and they will find nothing exaggerated in what I have said. The appropriate amount of fresh leaf is the width of a two-real coin (which weighs eight grains of rice), and it is ground in a ceramic cup with a small stick, and pills the size of peas are made, which are dropped into a tablespoon of cold water and swallowed whole. The leaf must not be chewed; for in that way, even a quantity of eight grains will cause dizziness; but taken as I described above, absolutely nothing bad is felt: I have taken them many times myself. Whoever wishes to use these pills for some ailment or disease should not take a large amount from the first day; rather, they should begin with the weight of eight grains, as I said above, and then may gradually increase the dose each day, as long as they notice no ill effect. Pregnant women must not take it. Some asthmatics find relief by smoking the dry leaves. This plant should also be tried for cataracts of the eyes, especially if they are recent, making use of lotions made from its infusion (kept weak), as some authors affirm it is very useful in that disease. * T., Talamponai. P., Talamponai. V. Tacbibung. Lin. ibid. 379.
Datura fastuosa. Datura fastuosa. Stem and leaves like those of Datura metel. Corolla doubled, or one placed inside the other, with rudiments of others. Fruit erect, and with few spines. = This plant grows to the same size as the other. The trunk, corolla, and leaf stalks are purple in color. The Indians plant it in their gardens and use it to repel abscesses. * T. Talamponai na itim. Lin. ibid. — I have seen in the town of Pasig a variety of Datura with the leaf stalks and stem spotted, like hemlock. It is used as I described when speaking of the metel species. — In Agoo I have also seen another species with a wavy stem. Leaves obliquely egg-shaped, oblong, entire, and soft. Flowers simple. Fruit slightly drooping, and with smaller points than in the metel species.

74
NICOTIANA. Corolla funnel-shaped, with folds on the limb. Stamens inclined. Capsule with two valves, two chambers, and many small seeds, kidney-shaped in form. Lin. syst. veg. 380.

Nicotiana pusilla. Little Nicotiana. Herbaceous stem. Leaves opposite on the branches, alternate, obtuse, lanceolate, running down the petiole, entire and somewhat fuzzy. Petioles short. Flowers in racemose panicles. Proper peduncle short. Calyx half-globose, monophyllous, obliquely truncated, with five unequal angles; the upper one largest (this is better seen at maturity). Corolla between tubular and bell-shaped, much longer than the calyx, with five folds and five lobes. Anthers conical, hollow underneath. Stigma thick, shield-shaped. This plant was born in a garden in Manila. Its height is one foot. The calyx is clearly cut at a slant. The flowers are yellow, and the anthers resemble the capitals of compass needles. Flowers in March. Perhaps this is the species? Lin. ibid.

Nicotiana fruticosa. Shrub Nicotiana. I can say no more of this species than that this small tree existed, not many years ago, in San José de Batangas, in a place called Bongahan. I do not know whether it had come from elsewhere. It may also have happened that the natives took it for tobacco, when it was not. Lin. ibid.

Nicotiana tabacum. Common Tobacco. Herbaceous stem. Leaves alternate, clasping the stem, linear at the base and afterwards oval, pointed, one foot long. Petioles absent. Flowers whitish and rose-colored on the limb, in racemose panicles. Calyx swollen below and narrowed above, with five sharpened lobes. Corolla funnel-shaped, widening from the middle upward, with five folds and as many pointed lobes on the limb. Stamens five, attached at length toward the base of the corolla. Anthers half-exserted. Ovary superior, conical. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma shield-shaped with a line down the middle. Capsule egg-shaped, with two notched valves at the tip, two chambers and many small seeds. = An annual plant reaching the height of a fathom, which produces the tobacco sold in the government shops. In these islands, as everywhere else, tobacco varies in flavor according to the region. That which is generally held superior to all others comes from Gapan. Also highly prized and aromatic is that from the towns of Passi, Laglag and Lambunao in Iloilo, that from Maasin in Leyte, and that from Cagayan, especially when aged for some years, since otherwise it burns the mouth, as does that from the island of Negros and others. Tobacco is narcotic and serves to repel recent tumors. Taken as smoke, it is very healthful, and almost a necessity in these countries. It consumes

75
phlegm, and protects against dampness and the ill effects of morning dew, and so those who take it do very well; but too great an excess can cause illness. Tobacco in powder form relieves headaches and eases a head heavy with humors. When applied to the nose of the lizard we call here chacon, a small piece of already-smoked tobacco placed on the tip of a small stick causes it to drop dead immediately. It would be better, rather than killing them, for everyone to take care that these most useful reptiles are never lacking in their homes: for they kill cockroaches, centipedes, and mice. They also comfort the timid with their song, as those people believe that while lizards are singing there tend to be neither earthquakes nor excessive rains. Lin. ibid.
POLEMONIUM. Upper calyx with three cells. Corolla in five parts. Stamens placed over certain valves that close the bottom of the corolla. Stigma cleft in three parts. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 185.
Polemonium obscurum. Dark Polemonium. Twining stem that exudes milk. Leaves alternate, broad, heart-shaped, with three lobes and slightly toothed, with seven nerves and two indistinct glands at the base below, soft and hairy. Long petioles. Axillary flowers in a compound, dense raceme. Calyx in five deep parts. Corolla much larger than the calyx, vinegar-flask shaped, very narrowed at the throat, with five folds and as many lobes notched at the small limb. Stamens five, shorter than the corolla. Filaments arched and placed over five concave laminae below, in the manner of fleshy and glandular hoods, which are outgrowths of the corolla and close it at the base. Anthers arrow-shaped. Superior ovary, girdled to the middle by a membrane furnished with eight notches at maturity. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma very thick, granular, pyramid-like and three-sided. Fruit with two chambers, each containing two seeds. = A plant not very common, which grows up to the height of two fathoms, and whose flowers are white with a straw-colored tint. In Bauang, Batangas, I saw one individual, and some others in the port of Santiago de Ilocos. The natives do not know it. It closely resembles this genus and the species dubium, and differs from it: for that reason I have called it obscura. Flowers in January. New species.
NERIUM. Corolla twisted. Two straight follicles. The tube of the corolla terminated by a lacerated crown. Seeds with a feathery pappus. Lin. Syst. veg. 435.
Nerium oleander. Oleander. Straight trunk. Leaves in threes, in a star pattern, lanceolate, narrow, entire and smooth. Flowers in an umbellate panicle. Calyx in five parts, inferior. Corolla of fifteen petals: the inner ones larger, arranged in groups of five in three bodies: all with small claw-

76
the latter slightly united, and on each of the ten petals, a flat gland with a groove, and some three or four bristles. Stamens ten, fixed to the receptacle. Filaments short. Anthers notched, terminating in a thread, and all five twisted together into one. Ovary split into two parts. Style shorter than the stamens. Stigma a zone. Two follicles (six inches long) sharp-pointed, with striations, and many imbricated seeds with a pappus. = Small trees of about two varas that I have seen in some places; their flowers are as described, full, and flesh-colored. They are given the name Adelfa, and in other places are called Baladre. In the Spanish translation of Linnaeus it is said that their leaves are acrid, and that the oil in which they have been boiled is very useful for mange. Lin. ibid.
TAYOTUM. Calyx with five teeth and narrowed toward the end. Corolla with five laciniae. A single-chambered carpel enclosed within the calyx, which splits with it in two parts along the belly. Seeds arranged on two plates, numerous, fixed to some bristles. New genus.
Tayotum nigrescens. The blackening Tayoto. Leaves opposite, notched at the base, oval and sharp-pointed, hairy below, and above all embossed with many small wrinkles. Axillary flowers in an umbel of many small florets. Common peduncle short, compressed, and thick. Individual peduncle long. Calyx hairy, inferior, narrowed in the middle; the border bell-shaped and with five teeth. Corolla much longer than the calyx, hairy on the outside, funnel-shaped, with five concave laciniae. Stamens five, fixed in the throat of the corolla. Filaments very short. Anthers long, thick, not protruding beyond the corolla, and split below in two parts. Style very long. Stigma thick, oval. Carpel oval, single-chambered, enclosed in the lower part of the calyx, which remains narrowed toward the end, opening together with the calyx along the belly, in two parts, with very many seeds tightly packed, on two separate plates. Seeds globose, joined together in the middle by some bristles, split below in two parts. = A shrub found in Angat: the leaves are more than four inches long, and are beautifully embossed with many small veins, and seem varnished with an unctuous, blackish liquid. The seeds are less than half the size of basil seeds. Flowers in June. *T., Saguing saguing, Tayoto. = It has seemed to me a new genus, and so I have given it the name by which some Indians called it; but many do not know it, and others use that name to designate other plants.
(HINGUIO.) Stem twining. Leaves opposite, broad, egg-shaped, tapering, entire, smooth above, and hairy below. Petioles short. Flowers in half-umbellate panicles.

77

Short proper peduncle. Cal. of five lanceolate pieces. Cor. very large, monopetalous, with a short cylindrical tube, the throat covered by the stamens, and the limb bell-shaped, with five oval lobes. Stamens five. Filaments attached nearly their entire length to the tube of the corolla, widening and free at the tip. Ant. large, arrow-shaped, and pressed together. Germen hidden at the base of the calyx, divided in two parts. Style one, very long, rising laterally between the anthers and continuing upward in a spiral with many coils. Stigma slightly widened and compressed. Fruit.= Small shrubs, which I do not know whether they are climbing. They exude a milky sap. The corollas are white, very large, and at night give off a very sweet fragrance like that of a lily. The Indians use them for tying. Fl. in August *T., Hinguiong Calabao.— It certainly belongs to the Apocynaceae; but because of the style twisted in a spiral, it does not fit any genus treated in my books, and so it remains thus.

ECHITES. Cor. regularly funnel-shaped, with a naked throat. Two long, straight follicles, and seeds with a pappus. It belongs to the twisted group. Lin. Syst. veg. 436.

ECHITES CAUDATA. TAILED ECHITES. Leaves opposite, oval, pointed at both ends, entire, and hairy beneath. Petioles short. Flowers terminal, in umbellate panicles. Cal. very small, swollen, with five pointed teeth. Cor. twisted, twice as long as the calyx, salmon-colored, somewhat inflated in the middle, woolly from the open throat to the tip, with the limb divided into five woolly sections, each ending in a long oblique appendage. Stam. five, attached toward the middle of the corolla. Filaments nearly absent. Ant. arrow-shaped. Nect. five erect, linear glands at the base of the germen. Germen hidden in the calyx, divided into two hairy parts. Style one, shorter than the corolla. Stigma simple, placed on a small cylindrical body.= A small shrub whose flowers are white and which exudes a very sticky juice when the bark is cut. The Indians know it because it is excellent for tying. There are species with smooth leaves beneath. Fl. in Jul. * T., Hinguio. Lin. ibid. 437.— Compare with the gen. Strophantus.

ECHITES SCHOLARIS. SCHOLAR'S ECHITES. Trunk covered with small protuberances that resemble vestiges of spines. Branches in a star pattern. Leaves in a whorl, numbering five, six or more, approaching an elliptical shape and pointed at the tip. Petioles very short, with a sharp-pointed gland on the inner part of the base. Flowers terminal, in umbellate racemes. Cal. very short, in five parts. Cor. twisted, tubular with the limb divided into five half-rounded parts: the throat open, and

18

78
with a hairy ring. Stamens five, hidden within the throat of the corolla, and fixed to its tube. Filaments nearly absent. Anthers shaped like arrowheads. Style long like the stamens, somewhat compressed, with a barely visible line running along its length. Stigma bifid, placed upon a small disc or cylindrical zone. Two follicles twisted like a cord, in which the seeds are lodged arranged in a row, and not overlapping one another. Seeds cylindrical, with a hairy pappus at each end. = This tree rises in the forests to a height of eighteen or more varas. The fruit is more than a foot long, and barely more than a line in thickness. Its leaves are about five inches long. It is a remarkable thing that the seeds are furnished with pappus at both ends. The flowers are white. When the bark of the tree is wounded, it exudes a sticky and very bitter sap, as does the bark itself, which is whitish, and thick and granular. The praises I can bestow upon this precious tree will always fall short; it suffices to say that it serves most perfectly in place of quinine; and thus for every kind of fever, and to guard against the tendency toward corruption in malignant diseases, it may be used with hope of the best results. For my part I recommend it as strongly as I can to those who care for the welfare of the poor Indians, who cannot afford or obtain quinine. If anyone should be so squeamish as to fear taking the bark of this tree internally, I must inform them that some women take the milk of the tree itself, on the advice of Indian healers, for the ailments particular to their sex; and that this is precisely the worst and most dangerous way in which it can be taken. As for the rest, and with regard to the bark, I myself have seen the most admirable results in tertian fevers, in putrid and malignant fevers, in thrush, and in other diseases. Its preparation is very simple: one need only sun-dry the bark of the tree for a few days; it is then ground into powder and administered at half the dose that physicians prescribe for quinine, or even less (since it is very bitter.) The Indians use its wood to make small troughs, as it is white and easy to work. In India, children use small tablets made from this tree to write on, and erase what they have written; hence it gets the name Scholaris. It flowers only in April and not in other months. *T., Dita. I., Dallopaven. Lin. ibid.— The tree called Tanitan in Iloilo, whose bark is bitter and highly esteemed, can barely be told apart at a glance from the Dita: only its leaves are somewhat hairy. I have seen no more than the tree itself, but not its flowers.
Echites procumbens. Prostrate Echites. The trunk either spreads along the ground or climbs over other trees, and is round

79
with many small excrescences. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, egg-shaped, entire, smooth, with the margins rolled downward. Terminal flowers in panicles. Calyx pyramidal, in five keeled and awl-shaped parts. Corolla four times longer than the calyx, somewhat swollen, with a flat limb and five linear lobes. Stamens five, fixed below the narrow throat of the corolla. Anthers arrow-shaped. Ovary cleft into two conical parts, surrounded by a membrane at the base. Style one, thickening upward and finally narrowing at the tip. Stigma simple. Two very long follicles, with many seeds in a row, furnished with down at one end. = A shrub that grows as thick as an arm and spreads widely. The follicles are more than two feet long and a finger's breadth thick. This plant is called the same as the one said to yield vanilla. *T., Malayantoc. In Angat, Ginguiu. Lin. ibid. 346.

Echites trifida. Echites of three parts. Branches star-shaped. Leaves in whorls of four, lanceolate, wavy along the margins, smooth above and hairy below. Terminal flowers in a kind of umbel that divides into three parts? Calyx in five parts. Corolla twisted, three times longer than the calyx, funnel-shaped, with five lanceolate lobes and the throat closed with wool. Stamens five, fixed near the throat of the corolla. Filaments almost absent. Anthers arrow-shaped. Ovary superior, of two conical, approximated pieces. Style one, marked along its length by a line, along which it easily divides in two. Stigma thick, conical, with a bifid tip. Fruit. = A tree that grows larger than a man's body and in my opinion comes very close to Linneo's Trifida species, although it would be necessary to examine its manner of flowering more carefully. I have not seen the fruit either. From its wood looms and other things are made. The bark is bitter and the leaves very long. Flowers in September. *T., Cayaoyao, Batino? Lin. ibid.

Echites spiralis. Spiral Echites. Twining stem, with slightly raised, very inconspicuous dots. Leaves opposite, oval, very entire, smooth. Short petioles, with many pointed stipules in the axils and around the stem. Flowers in an umbel, divided twice into three parts. Calyx in five or six parts, appearing as if attached to the corolla. Corolla twisted, more than three times longer than the calyx, somewhat fleshy and swollen below; the limb in five parts, with the throat open and bare. Stamens five, arising from the base of the corolla. Filaments twisted in a spiral. Anthers long, arrow-shaped, and joined to one another above the throat of the corolla. Ovary superior, appearing divided into two parts, and at the base surrounded by five glands. Style one, marked with a line along its length. Stigma thick, conical, and terminating

80
in two small laminae. Fruit. = This climbing plant, which I have seen in Bauang, is generally unknown to the Indians. The corollas are greenish. I leave it in this genus, although the twisted stamens argue against it. Perhaps it is a new genus.
PLUMIERA. Corolla twisted. Two follicles turned to the sides. Seeds inserted in their own membrane. Lin. Syst. Veg. 237.
PLUMIERA ALBA. WHITE PLUMIERA. Trunk, with forked branches. Leaves alternate, broad, lanceolate, very entire, smooth, and with the tips twisted downward. Petioles short, with two glands toward the base, on the upper part. Flowers in umbels. Calyx with five teeth. Corolla twisted, funnel-shaped, with a very large, upright limb, divided into five oval parts, each with a fold at the base, and the throat closed and hairy. Stamens five, hidden at the very bottom of the corolla tube. Filaments almost none. Anthers arrow-shaped. Style very short and thick above. Stigma in two parts. Two horizontal, cylindrical and long follicles, which join at the base, with many seeds placed in the hollows of a corky receptacle proper to it, which runs the length of the follicle. Seeds with a wing all around. = It is a well-known tree, and rises to a height of four or six yards. Its bark is bitter and purgative, and is used in Ilocos for this purpose: even its milk placed on the navel also purges; and applied externally, it is a great remedy against scabies and ringworm, according to Hernandez. The syrup of its bark expels tapeworms, and the infusion of its leaves drunk for a long time is said to cure venereal disease. It is always in flower, and the flowers are fragrant. It very rarely bears fruit: I have only managed to see it once, and as it was not ripe, I could not form an exact judgment of it. Nevertheless I believe I have not been mistaken in the description given. Father Ignacio de Mercado, in his treatise on the herbs of the Islands, highly recommends for dropsy the bark well ground in doses of two drachms, boiled in seventeen ounces of water until, after filtering, eight remain. Of this infusion, he says, a portion is to be taken after eating little and early: and to mitigate the bitterness, one may eat candied anise. This water may be drunk three or four nights in a row, or once every three days. If after having taken it nine times the dropsy does not disappear, after resting some ten days, it is taken again as many times as the patient can tolerate, but it is always advisable to act under the advice of a physician. It is believed that this tree has come from America. *T, Carachucha, Calachuchi, Calasusi. Lin. ibid.
ANASSER, Calyx small with five laciniae, Corolla longer, funnel-shaped, with five lobes, Stamens five, alter-

81
nos with the lobes of the corolla. Style one. Twin stigmas. Cagilla like two joined follicles, two valves and two compartments. Jus. Gen. pl. 150.
Anasser laniti. Anaser laniti. Trunk erect. Leaves opposite, twice pinnate without a terminal leaflet. Leaflets numbering four pairs, more or less, broadly lanceolate, entire, very soft and hairy, especially beneath. Petioles very short. Flowers terminal, in panicle-like racemes. Calyx inferior, bell-shaped, split almost to the base into five ovate parts, with six nectariferous scales fixed near their midpoint, rounded, with a notch at the apex, arranged in pairs at alternate parts of the calyx. Corolla twisted, swollen, very constricted at the throat, with the limb divided into five oval lobes. Nectary of five scales attached near the middle of the limb, with their ends split in two, and with two small horns at their base, also split at the ends. Stamens five, fixed at the throat of the corolla. Filaments very short. Anthers large, woody, projecting beyond the tube, arrow-shaped and pressed against each other even at maturity. Ovary seated inside the flower, conical, with a channel in the middle. Style as long as the stamens, ending in a globe, and also marked with a line. Stigmas awl-shaped. One follicle, striate, woody, somewhat compressed and pointed, with two opposite channels along which it splits and divides into two at maturity, forming two compartments, each with two rows of imbricated seeds, oblong, with irregular angles, and adorned with a hairy pappus at one end. = A tree of medium size, well known, because its wood, which is very white, soft, and easy to work, is used to make chairs, benches, and other things. It exudes considerable latex. The fruit, which in reality consists of two joined follicles, is about a hand-span long, and at times many flies are found inside, lodged there in a row: and for this reason some natives believe that this tree produces flies as its fruit. What actually happens is that the female fly bores very finely into the fruit and deposits her eggs there, which in time develop, and the insects are born, which remain inside until they either bore their way out by themselves, or the fruit bursts open as it dries. The little hole made by the fly is extremely small and is immediately sealed by the latex that the fruit exudes, making it very difficult to detect. I have seen these flies many times; they are as large as ordinary flies, but they can grow even larger. Flowers in August. *T., Laniti.—There is another species with axillary, solitary flowers.— Spreng. Syst. veg. t. 1. 588 places these trees in the genus Geniostoma, but his description does not agree with the one above, which is accurate.

82
TABERNAEMONTANA. Corolla twisted. Two horizontal follicles, with the seeds submerged in a kind of pulp. Lin. Syst. veg. 443.

TABERNAEMONTANA LAURIFOLIA. TABERNAEMONTANA WITH LAUREL LEAF. Trunk straight, forked, and without spines or thorns. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire, with nearly invisible down. Flowers in umbels. Calyx pentagonal, with five teeth. Corolla very long, with the tube twisted and the limb flat with five lobes, and the edges wavy. The throat very narrow and bare. Stamens five. Filaments attached nearly their entire length to the tube of the corolla. Anthers arrow-shaped, distant from the throat. Ovary in two parts, surrounded at the base by a single-layered, entire membrane. Style one, marked along the middle by a groove. Stigma bifid, placed on a small cylinder. Two fleshy, oval follicles, pointed at both ends, diverging from each other, angular, with many seeds convex on one side and angular on the other, stacked one upon another and enclosed in a soft pulp. = This small tree, which exudes a milky latex, grows to a height of six to twelve feet. Its roots and leaves are considered celebrated and highly medicinal in this country for certain ailments. Applied to wounds, they kill the worms and close the wounds quickly, according to local authors: a decoction of the roots drunk is used for stomach and intestinal complaints and for women after childbirth. The leaves, pounded and applied, cause the afterbirth to be expelled, according to the Tagalog vocabulary. I do not know whether the effects live up to the reputation. Its flowers are purgative. * T., Campopot, Pandacaqui. V., Alibubut Toar, Pandaya. P., Pandacaqui. I., Curribuetbuet. Lin. ibid.

TABERNAEMONTANA POLIGAMA. TABERNAEMONTANA POLYGAMOUS. Branches forked. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire, soft and downy. Petioles very short. Flowers in a dichotomous panicle, with very long peduncles. The greater number are female flowers, small and without corolla; the others, few in number, are hermaphrodite, complete, and much larger. * Hermaphrodites. Calyx fleshy with five lobes, provided on their inner surface with four to six veins that branch off only at the top. Corolla fleshy, much longer than the calyx, cylindrical, monopetalous, with five straight, rounded lobes, terminating in a beak curved inward. Stamens five. Filaments none. Anthers oval, fixed in the middle of the tube. Ovaries two, joined together. Styles two, thick. Stigmas short. Fruit.... * Females. Calyx with five keeled lobes and the veins mentioned above. Corolla none. Stamens none. Styles two, very long. Two follicles diverging as in the laurifolia species, but smaller and with many irregular seeds in a row. = Small trees

83
extraordinary in form compared to the previous ones, but more slender. The most singular thing about them is that the greater part of the flowers are female, and lack a corolla and stamens; but they produce fruit when fertilized by a few hermaphrodite flowers that are much larger than the others. The calyx of the hermaphrodite flowers becomes very fleshy, to the point of almost entirely losing its shape; and sometimes these do not produce fruit; for once fertilization is complete, they fall off; at least I have never seen a large one with ripe fruit; even though the pollen is very abundant. The follicles of the female flowers are the size of almond seeds. In Paranaque and Mandaloyon. Flowers in May.

Tabernaemontana elliptica. Tabernaemontana elliptica. Leaves opposite, notched at the base, broadly oval, suddenly pointed at the apex, with margins rolled downward, and with small pits following the outline, soft and hairy. Short petioles. Terminal flowers, in a panicle of few small florets. Calyx with five angles and five teeth. Corolla much longer than the calyx, twisted, with the tube swollen below, then funnel-shaped: the throat open and bare, and the limb flat, with five long, oblique laciniae. Stamens five. Anthers arrow-shaped, hard and pointed, almost sessile at the base of the corolla, and all united. Ovary in two parts, surrounded at the base by five scales. Style as long as the anthers. Stigma over a zone, with five angles, ending in a point. Fruit....= A small shrub that climbs over trees. The leaves are a quarter of a foot long and are almost rounded. The flowers are much larger than those of the Pandacaqui: they smell very pleasant and are white. I cannot say with certainty that it is the species cited. It is found in Tula. Flowers in July. Lin. ibid.

Tabernaemontana cirrhosa. Tabernaemontana with tendrils. Stem twining. Leaves opposite, obtuse-lanceolate, with a stiff point at the apex, leathery and smooth. Two fleshy follicles, oval, very large, angular, ending at their tips in a small curled horn, or tendril. Seeds wedge-shaped, very compressed, with hairy edges, and a half-pappus at the tip, imbricated, and attached around a corky receptacle.= This curious little tree is not very common, nor known to the natives. The fruit in appearance is indistinguishable from that of the pandacaqui species; but it is much larger. It is climbing and I saw it near Bauang in places flooded by seawater. The tendril of the fruit is a singular thing. New species.

Tabernaemontana globosa. Tabernaemontana globosa. Branches forked. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Flowers in an umbel. Calyx long, cylindrical, with five teeth. Corolla twisted, large, fleshy, funnel-shaped,

84
with the tube curved, and the limb in five parts turned back downward, one half green, the other white, with the throat open and bare, and the divisions with a black spot. Filaments attached along their entire length to the corolla, with thick ends. Anthers shaped like arrowheads, hidden inside the tube. Ovary bilobed. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma small, awl-shaped, placed on a small head with lobes. Two globose follicles, somewhat compressed, resembling berries, turned slightly downward, with many bony, irregular seeds wrapped in a kind of pulp. = This tree, which produces a milky sap, grows to a height of nine feet. The Indians know it, but not all of them, and they call it bayagusa, that is, testicles of deer. Flowers in August. New species. *T., Bayagusa. — In the pulp and shape of the seeds it much resembles the campopot, but differs in other respects.

VINCA. Corolla twisted. Two straight follicles, and naked seeds without pappus. Lin. Syst. veg. 435.

Vinca rosea. Rose-colored Vinca. Leaves opposite, semi-elliptical, with a small point at the apex, very entire, and both surfaces covered with short hairs. Petioles short, with two small stipules at the base. Flowers axillary, two in number. Calyx in five awl-shaped parts. Corolla very long, angular, funnel-shaped, with the tube ending in a hairy crown, and the limb salver-shaped, with five broad, rhomboidal lobes. Stamens five. Filaments almost none. Anthers placed near the throat of the corolla. Ovaries two, each with two glands at the sides, persistent and shaped like small horns. Style filiform, the single one that rises above the two parts of the ovary. Stigma one, on a zone. Two straight follicles, with many seeds fixed in the cavities of two laminas, joined together and following the suture of the follicle. Seeds elliptical, with channels and prominent small dots, and without pappus. = This plant grows to a height of two feet. It has a very disagreeable smell, but similar species do not. I have not seen the Indians make any use of it; but in former times, as may be inferred from the Tagalog vocabulary, they cultivated it in plantations: many of them do not know it either. Its flower is very showy on account of the beautiful rose color that makes it visible from a distance. It agrees with the Nerium only in the lacerate crown; but in everything else it much more closely resembles the Vinca Rosea of Linnaeus, and so I leave it here: the anthers have no thread. This plant must not be confused with another they call Cantotay. Bears fruit in November. *T., Cantotan. Lin. ibid.

MASDENIA. Corolla with five divisions: five simple scales. Anthers terminated by a membrane. Two smooth follicles: seeds with pappus. From Beauvois. = Another description by R. Brown.

85
