Corolla urn-shaped, divided into five parts, sometimes wheel-shaped. Staminal corona of five compressed, undivided leaflets, simple on the interior. Anthers terminated by a membrane, with the pollen masses erect and fixed at the base. Follicles smooth. Seeds with a pappus.

Marsdenia akkar. Marsdenia acar. Trunk twining at the tip, rough and branched. Leaves opposite, elongated-ovate, tapering, with a cluster of dry small glands at the base of the upper surface, and with the margins rolled downward, entire and smooth. Petioles joined together, short, channeled above. Lateral flowers in umbellate clusters of many small florets. Common peduncle long. The individual floret's peduncle also long. Calyx-Perianth inferior, small, bell-shaped, monopetalous, deeply divided into five ovate, concave lobes overlapping one another at the margins. Corolla twisted, erect, fleshy, twice as long as the calyx, cruet-shaped. The tube with five indistinct angles, adorned on the inside with five small bundles of conniving hairs. The throat closed by a membranous corona, divided in many parts, with the limb divided into five ovate lobes, slightly notched at the tip, bending slightly outward and overlapping one another at the margins. Receptacle isolated, globose, somewhat pointed, containing the nectaries, stamens and pistil, with five barely noticeable angles and five slits. Nectaries: five simple, small horns without ear-like projections, awl-shaped, united along almost their entire length to the receptacle and applied over the stamens. In addition, at each angle there is a small red body to which two small oval glands are attached by two small threads. Stamens fixed to the walls of the receptacle and leaning against it. Filaments: five short, broad and thin scales. Anthers simple, linear, attached to the inner side of the scales. Pistil. Ovaries two, ovate, close together. Style one, thick, crossing through the receptacle and projecting slightly above it. Stigma single, conic, irregular. Fruit two follicles with seeds bearing a pappus. = This shrub, which at another time so greatly attracted the attention of the Royal Society of Manila, which is common in the forests of Samar, Camarines, and other regions, and whose discovery is owed to the diligence and curiosity of Father José de Mata of the Order of Saint Francis, grows according to accounts sent in by various members to the thickness of a thigh. It climbs by coiling its tips around neighboring trees, and yields a milky sap. It thrives and grows quickly when planted from a cutting. Its leaves are more than three inches long and two inches wide. The trunk is somewhat rough and cracked, but in its native soil it is smooth. The flowers I have seen on the specimen sent to me by the Society in a

19

86
in the cluster, some are white, and others have a light yellow color,
(Fr. Mata says that in Samar they are somewhat purple) and they barely
have any notable scent. The small horns of the receptacle are green
and very tender. The five clefts of the receptacle are seen better
when the flower is almost dry. The fruit consists of two oval follicles,
pointed and with seeds that have a pappus. The Indians of
Camarines have used its leaves since ancient times to
dye Abaca a beautiful blue. For this they boil them in water,
adding a little lime, until they can tell by the vein or
midrib of a banana leaf, which they use to stir it,
whether the color has reached its proper point. From some samples I have
of the starch of this plant, which some knowledgeable persons
in the indigo trade have examined, it can be seen that it is able to compete
with second-quality indigo, but not with first-quality. In
compensation, cultivating the plant takes no effort;
nor need one fear losing it: moreover, its growth
is much faster than that of indigo; the leaves are much
larger, and the color they yield is very abundant. I have learned that
this plant was known in other times by Mr. Marsden,
and that it takes its name from him. This shrub flowered in Manila
in September. * See Payanguit, Aringit.
Marsdenia parasita. Parasitic Marsdenia. Parasitic stem.
Leaves opposite, very fleshy, lanceolate, or nearly tongue-shaped,
with edges rolled downward, entire and smooth. Lateral flowers, in a simple umbel. Calyx monopetalous, in five
parts. Corolla shaped like a vinegar cruet, monopetalous, in five
parts, with the throat closed by a membranous crown,
cleft in many parts, and the tube without brush-like hairs.
Receptacle, Nectaries, Stamens, Pistil, etc., like the Pa-
yanguit. Two follicles two inches long, very nar-
row and pointed, flat on one side and convex on the
other, with many oval imbricate seeds, furnished with
a pappus. = This parasitic plant grows on mango trees, and I have also
seen it on an Erythrina. The flowers are flesh-colored, and
resemble those of the Payanguit, but lack the small brush-like hairs.
It yields much milk, and an infusion of the leaves does not
impart any color to water. The anthers do not terminate in threads,
as in the Nerium. Flowers in April, and bears fruit in June.
Marsdenia tagudinia. Marsdenia of Tagudin. Stem round,
twining, exuding latex. Leaves opposite (about one hand's length),
oval, elongated, entire, with a cluster of hairs at the base
of the upper surface, with a spine-like tip far from
the base, and on the midrib above, and the edges
slightly rolled downward. Petioles slightly twisted at
the base. Calyx in five rounded parts. Corolla with five laci-
niae; a membranous crown, cleft in many parts, in

87
the throat: and the tube with small tufts of bristles. The five anthers rise above the receptacle. Two conical follicles (one aborts) about an inch thick at the base, with many clustered seeds and pappus.= This plant, which I have seen in Taguding in Ilocos through the active curiosity of Fr. Juan Sorolla, Augustinian, is worthy of being known and propagated, since it can bring great benefits. It is as thick at the base as an arm, and called there tayomtayom. Cotton is dyed blue with it very well, and durably, by boiling it or steeping it for two days and adding a little lime; though I am not very well informed about these procedures as practiced by the natives. I have easily dyed some pieces of cotton cloth myself, well washed beforehand and without any other preparation; but I have not been able to dye abacá as is done with the other species from Camarines. The spine is sometimes absent from the leaves. Local name: Tayomtayom.

CORDIA. Corolla funnel-shaped. Style cleft in two parts, each of which subdivides into two more. Drupe with a nut of two to four cells. The inferior calyx grows over the drupe. Lin. ibid. 295. 392.

Cordia sebestena. Cordia sebestena. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, broad, pointed, entire, somewhat rough, and with little hair on both surfaces. Petioles long. Flowers, some sterile and others fertile, mixed together and arranged in umbellate panicles. * Sterile flowers. Calyx inferior, top-shaped, without striations, with three or four teeth, and which splits open at the expansion of the flower. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, with a cylindrical tube, a hairy throat, and the limb regularly cleft into five, and rarely six, lobes, curved downward. Stamens five, attached at the divisions of the corolla limb, longer than the corolla, and equal in number to those divisions. Ovary globose, with a groove at the upper part, and girdled to its midpoint by a membrane. Style none. Stigmas two, almost invisible. The fruit does not reach maturity in these flowers. * Fertile flowers. Calyx persistent, splitting unevenly at the expansion of the flower, and with many divisions at maturity. Corolla as long as the calyx, with the limb cleft into five or six lobes. Stamens five or six. Anthers sterile. Ovary fills the entire calyx and has channels at the tip. Styles two (which are clearly visible at the maturity of the fruit), each one still cleft into two parts. Drupe covered (but not fused) by the calyx to its midpoint, fleshy, containing a nut that holds one large seed, with chambers for others.= This well-known and very common tree reaches a height of thirty or more feet. Its leaves are regularly full of caterpillars, and for this reason there has been no shortage of people in the islands who have written that it is a mulberry tree. The scrapings

88
the fine inner bark of the branches instantly heals mouth sores when held inside the mouth; and the juice of the tree, applied to the affected area, cures erysipelas. The decoction of the bark, taken as a drink, is also good for soothing the heat of the blood and stomach. The only use I have seen the natives make of the fruit, which gives off a very sticky juice, is to use it in place of glue for sticking paper. The two stigmas of the sterile flowers must be examined in those that have been open for some time: the stigma in the fertile flowers has an irregular shape, and sometimes none is visible at all; but in the ripe fruit they are clearly distinguishable. Its wood is used for musical instruments and drums. Flowers in March. *T., Anonang. V., Anonang, Bibili. Lin. ibid.—I am persuaded that it is a variety of the species Sebestena.

Cordia dichotoma. Forked Cordia. Broad, lanceolate leaves, bluntly serrated, with the margins rolled downward, smooth. Flowers in a dichotomous panicle, all fertile. It is like the previous one and I have seen it in Mandaloyon. *T., Anonang. Lin ibid.

Cordia? olitoria. Cordia? of the kitchen garden. Straight trunk. Leaves opposite, ovate, oblong, barely notched, grayish in color, and smooth. Short petioles. Terminal flowers in a corymbose panicle. Common peduncle long. That of the small flower short, with two awl-shaped bracts at the base, one below the other and on the opposite side. Calyx inferior, fleshy, monophyllous, bell-shaped, with the margin rolled outward and finely notched. Corolla none. Stamens six, seven, or eight, fixed on a fleshy ring located below the little foot of the ovary, of which some others protrude beyond the calyx, with the alternating ones longer. Filaments awl-shaped. Style the same length as the stamens. Ovary oval, with a small stalk. Stigma shield-shaped, with four or five teeth, sometimes two laminae each split into two or three parts. Berry? with a small stalk, and with one oval seed. = This tree, very well known and which very rarely bears fruit, rises to a height of twelve or fifteen feet. It is notable for the whitish-green color of its leaves. These can be eaten cooked: they are heavily attacked by caterpillars, as are those of the Anonang. The cordia dichotoma corresponds fairly well with the Maluco; although I have seen nothing but the description that Linnaeus gives in his Systema Vegetabile. *T. Maluco, Coles Maluco.— On reflection, it does not appear to be a cordia: perhaps a Dirca, or a Buginvillaea; or more likely a new genus.

Cordia? ignota. Unknown Cordia. Leaves somewhat lanceolate, and smooth. Calyx persistent, inferior, cylindrical, with six or seven small teeth. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, bell-shaped with five lobes. Stamens six

89
or seven, fixed to the corolla. Style one. Stigma in two parts,
and each of these subdivides further into two small laminae. Drupe!
with five angles at the upper end, one chamber, and many angular seeds.= This little-known tree, which I saw many years ago on a beach at Bauang and could not examine well at the time, grows until it becomes taller than a man's body: its wood is easy to work, fragrant, and of a dirty black color; it is very suitable for gun-stock boxes, for which purpose it is sought. The calyx of the flower is almost half an inch long. Fl. in Jul.
* T. Banalo; but this name is also given to a species of Hibiscus.— It does not correspond well with Cordia.
CERBERA. Nectary at the mouth of the corolla, with five angles and five teeth. Filaments short. Two compressed nuts. Wernisch. cited by Lin. in the pract. translation of Palau. vol. 2. 485.
Cerbera manghas. Cerbera manghas. Branches in forks. Leaves clustered at the ends of the branches, lanceolate, very entire, and glabrous. Flowers in a kind of umbellate spikes. An involucre proper to each flower, a lanceolate scale. Calyx of the same color as the corolla, divided into five very deep, long, lanceolate parts: the two smallest. Corolla twisted, cylindrical, with the limb salver-shaped, cleft into five rhomboidal parts, with the throat cut in the form of a star, covered with wool. Stamens five. Filaments attached to the corolla, with thickened tips. Anthers arrow-shaped. Germen bifid. Style one, as long as the stamens. Stigma thick, conical, with lobes. Two drupes, very large, oval, fleshy, united at the base (one regularly aborts), with a nut between woody and fibrous, containing one compressed seed.= It is a small tree that produces latex, and is not common in the forests. The natives scarcely know it. The corollas are white, and the drupes are purple in color. Linnaeus supposes the drupe to be one: I have seen that the described tree has two, and I consider it to belong to this genus. Fl. in Jul. * T., Toctoc calo. Lin. Syst. veg. 433.
Cerbera thebethia. Cerbera thebethia. Leaves almost sessile, scattered, and partly clustered at the ends of the branches, lanceolate, entire and glabrous. Calyx in five parts. Corolla cylindrical, very narrowed below: with the limb very large and widened, and cleft into five parts overlapping each other at the edges, which are of a different color from the rest. Nectary with five small horns at the throat of the corolla, and two lateral pits. Germen cleft in two parts, and surrounded at the base by a rim of five lobes. Style one, thickened at the tip into a rhomboidal shape, with a notched rim at the underside. Stigmas two, short. Drupe one (the other aborts), very fleshy,

90

depressed and elongated horizontally in a rhomboid shape, with four grooves in a cross, and a hollow at each end, with a very hard nut, shaped like a half-moon, compressed, with four valves and as many chambers, and solitary seeds. = Small trees of three varas in height, common on seashores, known in Manila and of poisonous properties: the bark in proper doses causes vomiting. Their flowers are two inches long and straw-colored; but the margins of the laciniae are greenish: the fruit resembles a small apple and is not eaten. Mr. Alcedo says that the bark of a species of Cerbera serves to make sandals. * In Manila: Campanelo. Lin. ibid.

BLADHIA. Corolla wheel-shaped, deciduous. Berry with one seed bearing an aril. Lin. Syst. veg. 404.

Bladhia japonica. Bladhia of Japan. Leaves clustered, doubly serrate, glabrous. Petioles very short. Flowers in a compound raceme. Calyx of five lanceolate pieces, inferior and persistent. Corolla wheel-shaped, almost without a tube, divided nearly to the base into five lanceolate parts, with an open throat. Stamens five, attached at the base of the corolla. Filaments short. Anthers pointed, connivent, with some small glands on the inner surface and many more on the outer. Ovary conical, seated inside the flower. Style longer than the corolla. Stigma awl-shaped. Berry? globose with one seed. = A tree smaller than a man's body. I do not know of any use made of it. The flowers are very beautiful, crimson, but small. Flowers in August. * T., Tacpong dalaga. Lin. ibid. = I could not observe the shape of the leaves well. For the rest, I believe it belongs to this genus.

EHRETIA. Calyx with five laciniae. Corolla with five lobes on the limb. Berry with four seeds, splitting into two hemispheres, each with two chambers. Stigma bilobed. Jus. Gen. pl. 128.

Ehretia virgata. Ehretia of small rods. Leaves alternate: the older ones somewhat heart-shaped, ovate-oblong; the newer ones lanceolate, serrate, and rough with short hairs. Petioles short. Flowers terminal in a panicle. Calyx small, in five obtuse and hairy parts. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, divided nearly to the base into five lanceolate parts. Stamens five, shorter than the corolla, and fixed at its base. Filaments flat, awl-shaped. Anthers broad, heart-shaped. Ovary conical, seated on the receptacle. Style thick, short. Stigma divided into two parts. Fruit.... = A tree that grows barely larger than a man's thigh. Its wood is hard and is used for plows. Although I have not seen the fruit, I am persuaded it belongs to this genus. Flowers in Aug. * T., Onava. Lin. Syst. veg. 393.

91

Ehretia beurreria. Ehretia beurreria. A trunk that climbs over other trees. Leaves alternate, oval, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Terminal flowers in umbellate panicles, nearly corymbose, without any bract. Calyx inferior, smooth, half as short as the corolla tube, and in five parts. Corolla with five lobes, the margins folded downward and the throat open. Stamens five, fixed at the incisions of the corolla. Filaments long and exserted. Ovary globose. Style as long as the corolla. Stigmas two, somewhat elongated, and truncated. Berry globose, with four small stones: each with two chambers and solitary seeds, one of which regularly aborts. = Small trees two fathoms tall and slender, that climb over other trees, which I have seen in Mandaloyon. Their thickness is like an arm, and the leaves are about four or five inches long; the flowers are white, fragrant, and resemble those of the coffee plant. The berries are like chickpeas, yellow, and are not eaten. Flowers in September. * Itmong dalaga. Lin. ibid. 394.
TOURNEFORTIA. Pulpy berry, pierced at the tip, with two to four stones, each containing two upright seeds. Lin. ibid. 295 324.
Tournefortia hirsutissima. Very hairy Tournefortia. The trunk rises, leaning over neighboring trees. Branches square. Leaves scattered, ovate, elongated, curly-edged, and with the margins rolled downward. Petioles very short. Flowers in a compound spike, curved downward, with paired small flowers placed only on the upper side. Calyx in five parts. Corolla twice as long as the calyx: the tube with four angles, and the limb with five flat, pointed lobes. The throat of the corolla naked. Filaments none. Anthers fixed to the walls of the corolla. Ovary conic; stigma thick, apparently divided into four parts. Berry globose, conic, without a hole, and in other respects as described above for the genus. = This shrub rises to a height of nine feet, leaning against other trees. Its leaves are used to rub fishing lines; but for that purpose the Hanarion is better. The small branches, twisted in the hand, give off a smell that is at once pleasant and unpleasant. The Indians say that its leaves, when crushed, kill the worms in the sores of animals, and from this it takes the name given below: in America they are also used to achieve the same effect on humans. Flowers in December. * V. Patai ood. I. Sallacapo. Lin. ibid.
Tournefortia arborea. Tree Tournefortia. Leaves clustered at the ends of the branches, lanceolate, thick, and hairy. Flowers sessile, in two paired rows on the common peduncle, bent in an arc downward. = Straight small trees, about four varas tall, which I have seen on a beach of an island

92
from Negros, called Manaul. The flowers resemble those of the Heliotrope. New species.
SIDEROXYLON. Corolla with five laciniae and five alternate appendages, and with five or ten stamens. Stigma simple. Sometimes there are no appendages. Berry with five seeds. Lin. Syst. veg. 296. 396.
Sideroxylon duclitan. Sideroxilo dulitan. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, entire, smooth. Flowers with a small stalk, arranged in groups along some long common peduncles. Calyx in five obtuse and concave parts. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, with ten concave, egg-shaped laciniae: the five alternate ones very small. Stamens five, fixed to the corolla. Ovary globose, hairy, placed inside the flower. Style very short. Stigma simple, awl-shaped. Pome oval, with one or more seeds also oval, pointed, with a leathery covering and a wide, long scar. = It is a first-class tree, very well known to the Indians. The fruit is about one inch in diameter and is eaten. Canoes are made from the tree, whose wood tends toward a flesh color; but it is not very durable for that purpose. The common peduncles almost all end in a kind of club, which is the effect of insects. Flowers in September. *T., Duclitan. Hence the name of the species.
Sideroxilon balitbitan. Sideroxilo balitbitan. Leaves are broader than in the Duclitan; but in the flowers and in everything else it is indistinguishable. = A first-class tree, whose soft and whitish wood the Indians use in their houses. *T., Balitbitan. Hence the name of the species. — These two trees are without doubt of this genus Sideroxilon, which belongs to the family of the Zapotes, as do the Achras and the Palaquium: the seeds of the latter are entirely similar to those of the trees above.
TEKTONA. Corolla funnel-shaped. Stigma with teeth. Drupe dry, spongy, placed inside the swollen calyx. Nut with three cells. Seeds solitary. Lin. Syst. veg. 337. Jus. Gén. pl. 108.
Tektona grandis. Teak. Leaves nearly round, running down the petiole, entire, and rough especially on the upper surface. Petioles very short, compressed. Flowers in a panicle. Common peduncle square. Calyx inferior, bell-shaped, very large at maturity, with five laciniae at the border, downy. Corolla longer than the calyx, white, bell-shaped, hairy, with five obtuse laciniae. Stamens five or six, fixed to the corolla. Filaments compressed, somewhat longer than the corolla. Anthers half-globose, with a yellow band, grooved below and with a black ring above. I have not seen a nectary. Ovary seated inside the flower, oval, hairy.

93
Style as long as the stamens. Stigmas two, somewhat thick and short. Drupe globose, corky, depressed, covered by the calyx, very large, membranous and swollen, containing a very hard nut with four chambers and one seed in each. = The only Teak tree about which I first received notice is the one found in the town of Tanay, on the Laguna de Bay. There were once two, and a Franciscan Father had planted them. It is not known from where he brought the seed. The people of Tanay call it Ticla. In the history of the travels of Abbot Prevost, it is said that the leaves of this excellent tree, which measure two palms in diameter, are used to dye red, because they exude a purple sap. This resin dissolved in water and taken as a gargle is very good for ulcers of the throat. But the principal use of the tree is in buildings, and also in boats, because besides being of superior girth, it is incorruptible. It is common in some provinces of the Visayas, on the Island of Negros, Zambales, Mindanao and Butuan, as has been ascertained recently. The tree whose flowers I have seen is at Tanay, and it took twenty-three years to flower. Flowers in September. * Ticla, and in the Visayas Da london, Yate, Calayate. Lin. ibid.
FAGRAEA. Calyx bell-shaped, with five lobes. Corolla funnel-shaped with the limb in five parts. Stigma shield-shaped. Berry fleshy with two chambers and many seeds.
Fagraea scholaris. School Fagraea. Branches four-sided. Leaves opposite, somewhat heart-shaped, oval, abruptly pointed, entire, smooth and stiff, grayish in color. Petioles very short, sheathing the stem at their membranous base. Flowers terminal in umbellate racemes, with the partial stalks opposite and with a bract at the base: each one with five or more small flowers, and each with three very small bracts. Calyx inferior, oval at maturity, bell-shaped, with five rounded lobes, their membranous edges overlapping at the apex. Corolla five or six times longer than the calyx and the same color, funnel-shaped, with five entire lobes in the limb, smooth. Stamens five, attached below the middle of the tube. Filaments as long as the corolla. Anthers oval. Ovary conical. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma thick and depressed. Berry with a partition; two chambers and two fleshy receptacles, as in the Datura, and with many seeds along their edges. = Trees found in Angat and in the Laguna, as thick as a thigh. The leaves are one foot long; the corollas are white and one inch long. The smell is somewhat unpleasant. The leaves are leathery, and for this reason schoolchildren use them to cover their primers. Flowers in July. * T., Cabal. — By the arrangement of the seeds, it approaches the family of the Solanaceae.
20

·94
WILLUGHBEIA. Corolla twisted, salver-shaped. Anthers arrow-shaped. Style four-sided. Stigma between ovate and head-shaped, with two dots, seated on a flat zone. Berry ovate, with one or two chambers, and many seeds. Lin. Syst. veg. 434.

WILLUGHBEIA MULTILOCULARIS. WILLUGHBEYA WITH MANY CHAMBERS. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, blunt, very smooth, and very hairless. Petioles almost none. Flowers in half-umbellate panicles. The primary peduncle with two edges. Calyx inferior, in five rounded parts, overlapping one another at the margins, and spotted. Corolla (somewhat twisted before opening) wheel-shaped, almost without a tube, in five ovate and pointed parts. Stamens five, fixed in the bare throat of the corolla. Filaments short. Anthers very large, arrow-shaped, leathery, convex, and spotted on the back, and grooved within. Ovary five-angled, superior, seated on a small lobed disk, filling the hollow of the corolla's throat. Style longer than the stamens, dotted with many small glands, and angular at the base. Stigma as if divided into two parts: one is a point, and the other is elongated. Berry globose, depressed, hairless, with many chambers, and in each one two or three ovate seeds. = It is a tree that rises to a height of two fathoms. The flowers are rose-colored. The taste of the leaves is slightly acid and astringent. Flowers in August. *T. Malabatoan. New species. = It differs from Willughbeia in the stigma.

WILLUGHBEIA DRUPACEA. WILLUGHBEYA THAT BEARS DRUPES. Branches swollen at the base. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, very smooth, without veins, and very hairless. Petioles short. Calyx and the rest as in the previous species. Drupe globose, depressed, with a thin and fragile stone, and one seed. = This tree grows as large as the previous one: its flowers are dark red. I leave these small trees here because I believe they belong to this genus rather than to the genus Ardisia, with whose calyx and corolla they do not agree. I find no more descriptions of these genera than those that Linnaeus gives in his Sistema vegetabilium. New species. — I have seen another tree taller than the previous ones and differing considerably from them. Leaves scattered, almost sessile, one span long, and a finger's width wide. Flowers terminal in a compound raceme. The corollas are violet in color. The anthers break open by two pores at the tip. — There is yet another, whose leaves are alternate, sessile, lanceolate, cleft, serrate, and very hairless. Flowers in drooping, simple, and dense racemes. Ovary globose, with small dots, seated on a disk of five pointed lobes, the same color as the corolla. In all other respects, like the flowers of the previous species. = It is a tree like the

95
the body of a man, which grows in the mountains of Tala. The leaves also have small dark spots. The Indians do not know a name for it.

BASSOVIA. Berry ovoid, with an uneven surface. Calyx in five parts. Corolla hypogynous, with a short tube and a limb in five parts. Germен superior, seated on a disk. Juice.
Bassovia silvatica. Forest Bassovia. Leaves alternate, sometimes lanceolate, sometimes ovoid, obtusely serrated, smooth, with short petioles. Flowers axillary in a compound raceme: each small flower with a bract of two small leaflets at the base of the calyx. Calyx inferior, with five obtuse teeth. Corolla monopetalous, bell-shaped, with five obtuse lobes. Stamens five, fixed near the base of the corolla and opposite its lobes. Filaments very short, with very small anthers. Pistil on a disk. Style and Stigma one. Berry, like a pea, globose, with one chamber and many seeds confusedly heaped in a pulp. = Small trees found in Angat, an inch thick and known to the Indians. Flowers in February.
*T., Solinao.—It is much closer to this genus than to the genus Tachia.

CAPSICUM. Corolla wheel-shaped. Berry corky, hollow, with two chambers. Anthers close together. Lin. Sist. veg. 296. 387. Palau. Traduc. t. 2. 10.
Capsicum minimum. Very small pepper. Stem square. Leaves opposite, lanceolate-ovoid, entire, and with small hairy glands in the axils of the lateral veins. Petioles short. Flowers drooping, in a cluster. Fruit erect, very small, conical, with a long peduncle. = This plant grows on its own anywhere and is native to the islands. The fruit is slender, conical, and barely an inch long. Although it is extremely hot, it is used in kitchens, especially for certain kinds of dishes, to which it gives a very pleasant seasoning. I have been told that by boiling the leaves of these peppers or chiles with a little alum, one obtains a very good and fast yellow dye. I have also seen them applied crushed to wounds made by a rabid dog. I must mention here in passing that an Indian from Dumangas, in Iloilo, who had the curiosity to smell the blood of a rabid dog that had stuck to the iron of a lance with which they had killed it, paid for it with his life: for he died raving within four hours. Flowers at all times.
*T., Pasitis. New species.— Peppers were known in ancient times among the Tagalogs by the name lara, which has now been almost entirely forgotten; but the Pampangos still retain it.

SOLANUM. Corolla wheel-shaped. Anthers apparently fused, opening by two pores at the tip. Berry with two chambers. Lin. ibid. 382.

96
Solanum nigrum. Black Nightshade. Stem erect, half-forked, with three or four half-winged angles, and with soft tips. Leaves lanceolate, running along the petiole, with the edges having small angles terminated by tiny points. Lateral flowers in a distichous raceme. Calyx inferior, with five persistent teeth. Corolla in five parts, somewhat reflexed downward. Berry small, black at maturity. = This plant grows to a height of two feet. It is known to the Indians, who eat its cooked leaves; but it is not very good food, as it causes dizziness in delicate persons. In Spain it is known by the name of yerva mora, and is used in medicine. It is repellent, induces sleep, and refreshes. It is very useful in cancerous ulcers, phlegmons, scirrhous tumors, and erysipelas. The fruit is smaller than a chickpea. Flowers in January and other months. *T., Cunti, Onti, Gamagamatisan. V., Lagpacum, Bolagtob, Lubilubi. C., Cuti, Lubilubi. In Leyte, Hutabtub. Lin. ibid. 384.

Solanum mauritianum. Mauritian Nightshade. Trunk erect, dichotomous or trichotomous. Leaves lanceolate, entire, and downy. Terminal flowers in an umbel, with glandular peduncles. = This small tree grows to a height of six feet. The Indians do not know it. It is not very common; but I have seen it in the vicinity of the town of Bauang, and it lasts for several years. Flowers in January. * In Cebu, Noog noog. Lin. ibid. 383.

Solanum lycopersicon. Lycopersicon Nightshade (Tomato). Stem wavy, or bending in different directions, covered with hairs, and appearing to have three angles. Leaves interruptedly pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets unequal, notched along the edges. Lateral flowers in distichous racemes. The individual peduncles are bent near the flower. Calyx in five parts. Fruit globose and smooth at maturity. = This plant, which is always found in the Philippines wherever there are people, grows to a height of one or two feet: the fruit is four or five lines in diameter. The natives make immense use of the fruit, which they incorporate into almost all their foods. With its leaves they dye cotton cloth a dirty green. Flowers in all months. *T., Camatis, Tomatis, Lin. ibid. 384.

Solanum melongena. Eggplant Nightshade. Stem erect, smooth, with downy extremities. Leaves obliquely egg-shaped with large obtuse angles on the edges, downy. Flowers solitary. Stamens numbering five, six, or seven. Fruit more than three inches long and one inch thick, smooth. = It grows to a height of three feet. It has no thorns. All the Indians know it, because they frequently mix the fruit, which is violet in color, into their foods, and it pleases many. Flowers in January and other months. *T., Talong. Lin. ibid. 384.

97

Solanum coagulans. Coagulating Nightshade. Stem moderately inclined many times toward the ground, cylindrical, covered with spines. Leaves somewhat heart-shaped, oval, rounded at the tip, with large sinuses, and very finely toothed at the edges, with spines along the veins, and hairy, the hairs forming little stars. Leaf-stalks also covered with spines. Flowers one or two in number, lateral at the axils. Calyx covered with spines. Fruit approaches a globose shape, and smooth. = This plant grows to a height of six feet, and the leaves become very large; but in grounds frequented by people, it grows very little. Many Indians know it, and eat the fruit with pleasure in Ilocos, even when it is not yet ripe: introduced into the nose on a small moistened feather dipped in its juice, it causes violent sneezing. It also resolves recent tumors, and quickly relieves pain when applied to the affected part. Its seeds thrown on hot coals, and receiving their smoke through a paper funnel directed toward aching teeth, brings much relief. Flowers in January and other months. *T., Tarambulo, Tangantangan. Lin. ibid. 385. — Some people, including the indefatigable and learned Father Clain, have wished this plant to be the Belladonna; but it is not.

Solanum zeilanicum. Ceylon Nightshade. Stem round, upright, speckled with spines. Leaves obliquely oval, with large angles at the edges, woolly and soft, and covered with spines along the veins above and below. Flowers lateral in distichous clusters. Calyx with some additional prickle. Fruit globose, bristling with hairs. = It is a small tree with leaves a foot long, which rises in the forests to a height of nine feet: it agrees with the species ferox in its fruit. The Indians hardly know it, but in Pasig they eat the raw fruit after removing the hairs, and some call it Forest Eggplant. Flowers in January. *T., Talong gubat. In Pasig, Tarambolo. Lin. ibid. 387.

Solanum serratum. Serrated Nightshade. Stem upright, branching, and without spines. Leaves lanceolate, serrated. Leaf-stalks on the older leaves, very long. Flowers solitary. Calyx swollen, in five parts. Corolla longer than the calyx, tubular, with five rounded lobes. Stamens and Pistil as in the genus. Berry oval, covered by the calyx, without compartments, and with many kidney-shaped seeds, submerged confusedly in the pulp of the berry. = I have seen it in Pasig, and it is not known to the Indians. Its height is four fingers. By its anthers it belongs to the genus Solanum: but by its calyx it resembles Physalis. Flowers in January. New species?

Solanum tuberosum. Tuberous Nightshade. Stem upright, three-sided, with three barely noticeable wings, and somewhat hairy. Leaves semi-opposite, interruptedly winged, with the terminal leaflet the largest.

98
Leaflets notched, and with one or two small ear-like lobes at the base, egg-shaped, elongated, pointed, wrinkled, nearly entire, and somewhat hairy. Proper petioles very short. Flowers in a kind of raceme, which divides into two parts with the proper peduncles set to the side. Calyx oval, narrowed toward the top, and with five pointed parts. Corolla in five very deep parts, oval, shorter than the calyx, and somewhat woolly on the outside toward the tip. Stamens five. Filaments very short, fixed between the divisions of the corolla. Anthers oval, with striations, and separated. Upper ovary oval. Style very short. Stigma thick, somewhat lobed. Berry large like a cherry. = A plant native to China, about two feet tall, which is planted in this country for its roots, which are highly valued. I do not know whether this plant might perpetuate itself on its own, without the need to bring roots from China annually. My experiments and those of others have been fruitless; for the plants do not increase. These resemble those of Spain, and the skin is whitish. Some people like them very much. They are multiplied by planting the upright or trailing branches (as I have been told) or by the buds of the roots, dividing the latter; but I am not certain of this. In this country, neither one way nor the other yields any result. But in the district of Pangasinan in the valley of Benguet, where the cold reaches six degrees above zero on Reaumur's thermometer, a good harvest has been obtained a few years ago, as I have been informed. The size of the largest Chinese roots is about half a fist. The leaves are more than an inch long, and among them there are other smaller ones, as in the local tomatoes. The flowers are white, and very small. Lin. ibid. 384.
PHYSALIS. Corolla wheel-shaped. Stamens inclined. Berry inside the calyx, inflated and two-chambered. Lin. Sist. veg. 381.
Physalis peruviana. Peruvian Physalis. Root central, fibrous. Stem erect, hairy. Branches forked. Leaves alternate, lateral at the fork, egg-shaped, pointed and downy. Petioles shorter than the leaves. Flowers solitary, axillary. Peduncles long. = It grows to a height of three feet, and is well known. It appears to be close to the said species. Children burst the fruit noisily against their hands; and from this comes the name they give it. Flowers in January. T., Potocan. Lin. ibid.
Physalis pubescens. Hairy Physalis. Stem erect, with slightly noticeable angles. Leaves obliquely lanceolate, broad, somewhat hairy and sticky. Flowers lateral, solitary, pendulous. Calyx cylindrical, with five pointed teeth. Corolla a little longer than the calyx, bell-shaped, with five pointed lobes. Stamens five, shorter than the corolla. Anthers erect and distant. Ovary inside the flower, oblong. Style of the length

99
of the stamens. Stigma thick, compressed. Berry covered by the calyx, oblong, with two chambers and many egg-shaped seeds. = This plant is unknown to the natives; it grows in Pasig, and its height is about one palm-span. The corolla has small purple spots. Flowers in February. Lin. ibid. 382.
Physalis angulata. Angular Physalis. = This plant, which I have not been able to examine to my satisfaction, I place here solely because a Spanish gentleman who had spent many years in America, having seen its fruit, assured me it was this species. It is common in Batangas, in a place called Pinamoc-can, and in Ilocos. It is what they call in Spain the tomatoes of Brihuega. The height of the plants I have seen is about two palm-spans; they are very branchy; the fruit is covered by the calyx, and is handsome, of a color between green and violet, and like a cherry. The natives of Batangas do not know it. The physalises have very medicinal properties: they cause frequent urination without stimulating the organs of the bladder. They are useful in jaundice and ischuria, and have even been used successfully in epilepsy. Some dropsical patients have been cured by eating up to eight fruits a week; they have likewise greatly benefited those with gout, eaten in the same way. Since on these islands we have several species, and they have not yet all been tested, one should proceed with caution in this matter; though not so much with the last species, which grows in Batangas, and which it is a pity does not spread more widely. I., Tuttullacac. Lin. ibid. 382.
MENAIS. Corolla salver-shaped, with five laciniae. Calyx of three pieces. Berry with four chambers and four seeds. Stigmas two. Lin. ibid. 376. Jus. Gen. pl. 128.
Menais mollis. Soft Menais. Leaves alternate, half-lanceolate; entire, soft and hairy. Petioles very short. Flowers terminal, in umbellate panicles. Calyx small, in five pointed parts. Corolla four times longer than the calyx, tubular; the throat open, and the limb in five parts turned downward. Stamens five, fixed at the divisions of the corolla, and protruding from it. Anthers arrow-shaped. Ovary conical, seated within the flower. Style one, split at the top in two. Stigmas obtuse. Berry (like a pea) with four small hard seeds. = Trees I have seen in Mandaloyon of more than eight varas in height. Their wood appears to be hard. It differs from the genus only in the calyx; but it perhaps fits better with the genus Porana. Flowers in May. *T., Taglocot. New species.
RANDIA. Berry dry, with two chambers and many seeds. Calyx superior with five laciniae. Lin. ibid 296. Jus. Gen. pl. 199.
Randia aculeata. Spiny Randia. Trunk straight, with many solitary spines. Leaves sessile, arising from the buds, gathered three by three, bluntly lanceolate, entire and smooth. Flowers either solitary or in pairs. Cal.

100
with six small teeth. Corolla twisted, arched, swollen in the middle, with a bare throat, and with five large, smooth lobes. Stamens five. Filaments short, fixed to the corolla. Style one. Stigma bifid. Fruit inferior. = This small tree, which I saw many years ago and could not examine well, was about twelve feet tall. The flowers are very fragrant and fall at night. I saw it in a place in Bauang called Lagundi on the seashore. Flowers in May. * T., Sinampaga. Lin. Sist. veg. 335. — It bears much resemblance to the Gardenia and to the Canthium.

NAUCLEA. Corolla funnel-shaped, above the fruit, which has two cells. Common receptacle globose. Translated from Lin. Sist. of veg. 123.

Nauclea glaberrima. Very smooth Nauclea. Leaves opposite, broad, lanceolate, obtuse at the tips, wavy, entire and smooth. Petioles short, with broad intermediate stipules. Terminal flowers, gathered in very great numbers on a globose receptacle (not two, nor three) covered with a single-leaved, deciduous spathe, full of pits or alveoli, whose walls are divided at their upper part into four or five woody small teeth. The common calyx is the spathe. Belonging to the small flower are the four or five small teeth of the alveoli. Corolla longer than the calyx, funnel-shaped, with the limb in four or five obtuse and concave parts. Stamens four, or more regularly five. Filaments none. Anthers fixed in the divisions of the corolla. Style much longer than the stamens. Stigma thick, conical. Fruit, many very tiny seeds beneath the calyx, placed in a kind of small branches or panicles, all hidden within the woody receptacle. Could this perhaps be the work of insects? = A tree larger than a man's body, common in many places and well known. Its leaves are half a foot long and more than three inches wide. The fruit, that is to say the receptacle, is as large as a walnut, and when ripe has a somewhat pleasant smell. The flowers offer a very beautiful sight. The root has a very bad taste. The wood is used by the natives for various purposes, especially in the vats for indigo: its color is yellow. History tells us that before the arrival of the Spaniards in the islands, the Visayans made coffins from these trees for their dead, which were of long duration. The toughness and fine color of the wood make it valuable even for making chairs and writing desks. The arrangement of the seeds is so unusual, as I said above, as I noted very well in a tree between the towns of Anilao and Banate, in the province of Iloilo. Considering this strange mode of fruiting so different from what it ought to be, I have believed that the fruit aborts and that those

101
seeds (apparently) arranged in a panicle, are the work of insects or a trick of nature. In the Mambog the seeds are inside the calyx, at least that is how it seemed to me. V. Spec. stipulosa Dic. Prod. p. 4. 336. I have observed that cotton thread, prepared with a mordant of lye and sesame oil, can be dyed with the bark of the root of this tree, ground to powder. The color obtained is a dirty yellow, but fast; and if this thread, thus dyed, is put into an indigo vat that does not have a very deep color, it will come out a very fine green, and as fast as any I have seen in the fabrics of India. Flowers in May and June. * T., Bangcal, V. Bancal, Cabag Hanbabalos. P., Bancal. I., Bulala, Dec. Prod. P. 4. 344. — It differs from the species Orientalis of Dec. ibid. 345, which is the Bancalus of Rumphius, in that this my bancal is a tree.

Nauclea glabra. Smooth Nauclea. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire, and smooth, with a small concave gland at the base of the veins that branch from the midrib. Flowers as in the species glaberrima. Calyx and the rest as in the same species. Fruit: the globose receptacle is covered with small cases of inverted pyramid shape, separable from one another, each crowned by its own calyx, with two compartments, and in each compartment many seeds, egg-shaped, compressed, with a sort of pappus at both ends. = A second-order tree, well known. Its wood is the color of molave; fairly clean and tough, and takes a moderate polish. As the tree is tall and straight, very long timbers are obtained from it for buildings, and they last many years as long as they are not exposed to rain. The flowers in this species are terminal, and the globose receptacles in which they are set usually number three in this and the following species; but in the preceding one that I called glaberrima, there is usually only one. Flowers in September. * T., Bagarilat. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 344. Perhaps the same as the escelsa species of the same Author. ibid.

Nauclea calycina? Calyced Nauclea? Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers terminal, gathered in great numbers in globose receptacles, without pits, each covered by a single-leaved deciduous spathe. Proper calyx angular, of five thick pieces terminated in small claws. Corolla divided into five lanceolate parts. Stamens fixed at the base of the corolla. Filaments almost none. Anthers oval. Ovary hidden in the lower part of the calyx. Style rather stout, the length of the corolla (before it opens). Stigma globose. Fruit a single seed. = A tree which in appearance cannot be distinguished from the other. * T., Bagarilao na itim. — Perhaps this is the species of Dic. Prod. p. 4. 346?

Nauclea obtusa? Blunt Nauclea? Leaves opposite, lanceo-
21

102
lanceolate, broad, blunt, entire, smooth. Terminal flowers, gathered in large numbers in globose receptacles each covered by its own deciduous spathe. Calyx proper bell-shaped, small, with five awl-shaped, soft divisions. Corolla long, funnel-shaped, with five lobes. Stamens five. Filaments almost none. Anthers rather long, attached near the divisions of the corolla. Ovary hidden in the lower part of the calyx. Style as long as the corolla. Stigma thick, ovate. Fruit two seeds hidden in the lower part of the calyx. = A tree as large and of the same uses as the other members of its genus. Its roots yield a dull yellowish color. In the vicinity of Manila they do not know the Balod, nor the Bagarilao; but they do know the Mambog. See Tapogomea in Decandolle, Flor. en Ag. *T., Balod. It will be the species of Dec. Prod. p. 4. 345.
Nauclea luzoniensis. Nauclea of Luzon. Leaves opposite, somewhat indented at the base, ovate, elongated, very wavy, entire, smooth, stiff, with broad intermediate stipules. Terminal flowers in globose heads on a small stalk, bearing at its tip one or two opposite bracts, and containing more than forty small florets. Common receptacle full of bristles. Common calyx none. That of the individual floret very small, tubular, angular, with five teeth, and at the lower part with a glandular ring. Corolla very long, very hairy inside, funnel-shaped, with five lanceolate lobes turned outward. Stamens five. Filaments short, at the divisions of the limb. Anthers oval. Style filiform, very long. Stigma very thick, half cylindrical, and half lateral to the style. Inferior capsule oval, two-valved, with two compartments, each containing two or more oval seeds terminated below by a tail, and at the apex by two small horns: the seeds have no woolly covering. The capsules separate from one another at maturity. = A first-class tree, well known, from which tables and other things are made: although it resembles the Nauclea, it is distinguished from it, among other things, by its bristly receptacle. For this reason I would have placed it in the genus Cephalanthus, were it not for the five-part division of its flowers being contrary to that. I have added it to the Luzonian variety of Dec. Prod. p. 4. 345. *T., Mambog.
Nauclea adina. Nauclea adina. Leaves somewhat heart-shaped, ovate, widening above, somewhat downy and veined below. Receptacle with spatula-shaped bracts and bristles. It agrees with the genus Adina of Dec. Prod. p. 4. 349, which some Authors incorporate into Nauclea. *T., Mambog.
Nauclea digitata. Digitate Nauclea. Leaves alternate, digitate. Leaflets ten, broad, lanceolate, entire, smooth, with prominent midribs and wavy margins. Petioles long, one third the length of the leaves. Flowers in a globose head (as in the Naucleas). Style

103
almost none. Stigma thick with five lobes. Cagilla of the floret, below the flower? in the shape of an inverted pyramid of four or five sides, which opens at the top with one chamber and about five or six seeds, half-oval, thin on one edge, as in the species Luzoniensis.= Trees found in Angat, the location of which I am unaware, and they are not known. The leaves are more than three inches long. The flower heads one inch thick. The style is notably absent.
CEPHÆLIS. Flowers in a head with an involucre of about five or more small bracts. Calyx with five teeth, very short. Corolla tubular. Stigma divided in two. Berry of two seeds. Receptacle chaffy. Pers. Syn. pl. 202.
Cephælis expaleaccea. Cephælis without chaff. Branches with four angles. Leaves opposite, oval, entire. Petioles short, with three angles: one sharpened at the back, and two above forming a channel. Flowers clustered in common receptacles, sessile, without chaff, and each containing more than fifty florets, and bearing at the base an involucre of many imbricated scales; those above larger, linear and obtuse. Calyx proper to the floret none. Corolla proper to the floret very long, funnel-shaped, monopetalous, with five or six lobes, which at maturity curve downward. Stamens five or six, the length of the corolla. Filaments fixed at the middle of the corolla lobes. Anthers long, straight. Ovary wedge-shaped, four-sided. Style the length of the stamens. Stigma slightly thickened. One seed wedge-shaped, four-sided, below the floret.= A small tree found in Cebu. The flowers are flesh-colored, and are more than one inch long. I do not know what use is made of it. Flowers in April. * V. Mampel.— The receptacle of the flowers has no chaff, and thus it does not fit well in this genus. I have therefore formed a new species; and among those brought by Dec. Prod. p. 4. 533. in the Tapogomeas, and other sections, I have not seen any similar one either.
DENTELLA. Corolla tubular, in five parts; each with three teeth. Calyx in five parts. Stigmas two. Cagilla globose, inferior, with two chambers, and in each many seeds. Lin. Syst. veg. 370.
Dentella repens. Creeping Dentella. Stem with two opposite channels. Leaves opposite, coherent, oval, fleshy, entire and dotted with hairs on the upper surface. Flowers axillary, solitary. Calyx adherent, with five teeth. Corolla cylindrical, with five lobes, each with three teeth, and with club-tipped beards in the tube. Stamens five, fixed at the base of the corolla. Filaments very short. Style short. Stigmas two, long, glandular, forming an arch inward

104
tro. Cagilla with white bristles on the outside, with two chambers and many seeds fixed around two fleshy receptacles attached to the partition. = A small and very common plant, which spreads by means of small roots emerging from the sides of the leaf nodes, which are very tiny; it is usually found on the ground and only between the stones of buildings. * T., Dilaug butiqni. Flowers in July.— There is another species with somewhat larger leaves and smooth little cagitas. Lin. ibid.

WENDLANDIA. Corolla with a round tube and a spreading limb with five slightly pointed lobes. Calyx with a half-globose tube and four or five very short teeth on the limb. Anthers and Style exserted. Stigma with two thick laciniae. Cagilla ovate, globose, crowned with the calyx, with two awns, two chambers and many seeds. Dec. Prod. p. 4 411.

Wendlandia exerta. Wendlandia exerta. Leaves opposite, broad, lanceolate, very pointed, entire and somewhat hairy. Petioles short; with two intermediate stipules, heart-shaped and buckler-like. Flowers in racemose panicles, terminal, very large, with two lateral fulcra and two others at the base of the partial peduncles. Calyx very small, adherent, with the limb hairy in five parts. Corolla four or five times longer than the calyx, funnel-shaped, with a flat limb, divided into five rounded parts. Stamens five. Filaments very short, fixed at the divisions of the limb. Anthers conspicuous on the outside. Style a little longer than the stamens. Stigma thickened and divided into two parts. Cagilla crowned with the calyx, nearly round, with two chambers and many seeds. = Small trees found in Angat, and hardly known. The leaves are one span long, and the petioles one inch; the panicles one span, by about as much in width; the calyxes one line long, and the corollas, which are slender and of a light rose color, four or five lines. The wood is hard. Flowers in March. Dec. ibid.— This genus has recently been separated again from Rondeletia, from which it is barely distinguishable.

SCAEVOLA. Corolla monopetalous, with the tube split along its length, with a lateral limb and five laciniae. Drupe inferior, fleshy, with two chambers. Seeds solitary. Lin. Syst. veg. 361.

Scaevola lobelia. Scaevola lobelia. Trunk erect, branching and dotted with points. Leaves crowded at the ends of the branches, sessile and partly clasping the stem, wedge-shaped, very entire, soft and smooth. Flowers axillary, in dichotomous, racemose panicles. Calyx cylindrical, adherent, bell-shaped, compressed, with five teeth. Corolla very long, fleshy, monopetalous, with the tube split throughout its entire length: the cleft filled with wool, and the limb with

105
five lanceolate, curled lacinae. Stamens five, fixed to the receptacle, much shorter than the corolla. Anthers large, oval, pressed together before the flower opens, and separating afterward. Ovary adherent. Style thick and wavy. Stigma very wide and compressed, divided into two lobes densely covered with hairs. Fleshy drupe, crowned with the calyx teeth, with channels, two chambers, and in each one a seed. = A tree of two fathoms. From its new branches, by means of a small stick inserted at one end, a soft, very white pith is extracted, as thick as an inch or more, which the Chinese and Visayans cut with great delicacy to make paper a few inches wide, from which they make very beautiful flowers. This pith also serves as a wick for lights, and even as tinder. In the Visayas the leaves are also used as tobacco, although they say that for this purpose the leaves of the Malacbalac are better, which I do not know what it is. In Camarines I believe it is called Bosboron or Mosboron. In Tagalog it seems to be called Boto, which is not to be confused with another tree they call boto (Excacaria). Its decoction, when drunk, serves to cure venereal disease in the Visayas, and the juice of the root, also drunk, they say is useful in cases of dysentery. Flowers in June and January. *T., V., Boto, Bosboron, Mosboron, Bocaboc, Panabolong, Pangangtolong. In Zambales, Linog. Lin. ibid.
MORINDA. Flowers clustered, monopetalous, funnel-shaped. Stigma bifid. Many drupes clustered together, inferior, angular, and with four chambers. Lin. ibid. 298. 371.
Morinda royoc. Morinda royoc. The trunk sprawls over neighboring trees. Leaves opposite, ovate, oblong, keeled. Petioles very short. Flowers and fruit as in the culit. = A shrub common in Malinta, but little known to the natives. Its root is used to make ink, and when powdered it serves as a gentle purgative in doses of one dram, for diarrhea, worm-related diseases, and intermittent fevers: in infusion two drams are necessary. Applied externally it is used to arrest the progress of gangrene. *T., Tumbong asong hapay. Lin. ibid.
Morinda ligulata. Morinda de cintillas. Branches opposite, square at the tip, channeled, and broader on the two lateral sides. Leaves opposite, broad, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Petioles very short, with two intermediate stipules, broad, lanceolate, and bent outward. Flowers opposite the leaves, placed on globose, solitary receptacles without bracts, from which the small flowers emerge successively. Proper calyx very short, monophyllous, from whose edge springs a small lanceolate leaflet. Corolla tubular, woolly toward the middle on the inner surface, and divided into five parts. Stamens five, fixed to the walls of the corolla. Filaments almost none.

106
Anthers somewhat long, slender, and incumbent. Pistil slightly longer than the corolla. Stigma split into two lobes, curved to the sides. Fruit: the receptacle, where the flowers were attached, grows large until it takes the shape of a globe bristling with the small bands of the calyxes, often irregular, but continuous, and somewhat like a berry with many stalks, and at the site of each flower there is a seed embedded in the flesh of the receptacle, four-angled and tapered at the lower part. = Dye trees, whose height is twelve or more feet. Their leaves are eight or more inches long. The fruit, shortly after being picked, gives off a very bad smell. No animal eats it. It appears to be the same tree known in some parts of the East Indies under the name of Abegaste. General History of Voyages by the Abbot Prevost, Madrid edition in Spanish, volume 20, page 129. *T., V., Bancudo, Pancudo, Bangcoro, Nino, Culit, Tumbong aso, Lino, Mambog, Tacpus. P., Taliantar. I., Apatot. In Tahiti in the South Sea it is called Nono, a word that differs little from Nino. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 447.— By the small bands of the calyxes, this must be a new species.

Method of dyeing with the Nino. The roots, which are removed from only one side without felling the tree, are those that the Indians use for dyeing red. Their procedures are the following, which I have seen practiced many times by the Indian women, who are the ones engaged in this work. I should note that the roots of some trees (usually the coastal ones) do not yield a red color, but rather purple; these are not valued, and perhaps belong to a different species. It should also be noted that the root causes itching in the hands of those who handle it. Once the bark of the roots is removed, it is left to dry very well in the sun, having first washed it in water to remove any dirt that may be clinging to it. If the roots are left to mold, they will not yield a good color. After the bark is dry, it is ground very well in a wooden mortar and passed through a sieve with very small holes, and the coarser parts are ground again. This powder is kept well covered in a dry place, and it is what is used for dyeing red, first preparing the skeins of cotton by washing them in clear water and beating them a little so that the thread swells, before giving them the following mordant.

Mordant for dyeing with the Culit or Nino. This is made from a lye of ashes and sesame oil. The women who engage in this trade differ in their choice of the plant that is to supply the ash; but they generally choose any of the following: the cotton bolls after they have shed their seeds; the fruit of the calumpan (sterculia) or else

107
the plant known here by the name of oraye or quiletes (a species of amaranth) or else those of the catuit (Euphorbia tiraculli.) I was told that these last ones were used in the Visayas; but I believe that is false. The ashes of plants that grow on the seashore, and which approach in their properties those of barilla, are not good for the purpose: because their lye is mild and lacks the energy needed to raise the color; at least that is what I have inferred from my own experiments. Over whichever of the said ashes one chooses, sufficient water is poured, and everything is left to rest overnight. I think it would be important to add to the above some goat or sheep dung, as they do in India, as we shall see later. By morning the water is very clear; it is decanted into a wide vessel, and over it a small quantity of the oil called sesame oil is poured little by little: the liquid then takes on the color of milk, and if it does not, that is a sign that the lye is weak, and it is then necessary to add more ash. In this milky liquid, which the native calls tobal, and which is the result of the combination of oil with lye, the skeins are stirred very well for a few minutes, because this mordant then penetrates the cotton marvelously. Once this is done, the skeins are left to dry, and then they are put back a second time into the same mordant: this is repeated up to seven or eight times, over as many days, and this is the best approach. Once done, they are left to dry for at least eight to fifteen days. After this, if one wishes to proceed to dyeing, it is necessary to prepare a weak lye, which must be made from ordinary ashes, or from the same kind of ashes used at the beginning, provided they yield a very clear lye, which contributes greatly to the brilliance of the future dye. No oil is added to this lye. The skeins must then be placed in it without rubbing, in order to remove the excess oil, which would spoil the beauty of the color. This is how the native women explain it, and they call this operation tugas; and in India the same thing is done.

Dyeing. When one wishes to dye the skeins (which is done on the same day the excess oil was removed), a spoonful of Nino in powder is taken for each skein, and a little water is added — just enough to wet the skeins and no more — and they are rubbed and worked with it until they take on color; but on the first occasion one takes care that the dose is weak. They are left to dry in the sun; and if one wants a very fast dye before dyeing them again, they are passed through clear water. The same operation is repeated up to five or six times, always being careful to use very little water, and never enough to wet all the skeins at once, since the color must spread to all of them through the rubbing that the thread undergoes. At six months after a skein has been dyed, according to the method

108
exposed, even if washed with lemon juice, it loses none of its color, as I have seen myself. The color given by the roots of the Culit or Bangcoro, which is what has been described, is so good and fast that from a distance it cannot be distinguished from that of India; but it is also known that it is not the same, and that in those countries the ingredients are different. I do not know what they are; but on one occasion I received a letter from a Religious friend, who, in a certain small work he was able to find on the subject, told me he had read the true method for dyeing scarlet, which is as follows — and note that the procedures are almost the same as those used in these Islands.

Method for scarlet dye in India. The mordant for the dye is a mixture of hard water (1), ash of Nayourivi (2), goat dung, and sesame oil: this mixture is left to ferment for forty-eight hours. A little of it is taken out and dissolved in a sufficient quantity of Nayourivi lye; then a little sheep dung is dissolved in it, and above all, sesame oil is added. The whole mixture then becomes like milk, and the cloth is soaked in it, stirred well, and left there for an entire night. In the morning it is stirred well again, then taken out, wrung, shaken, and placed in the sun. Once dry, it is returned to the mordant, a practice repeated for eight days, taking care to add more lye when the liquid thickens. Once this is done, and the cloth is dry, it is washed in ordinary ash lye one or two times, then in the hard water mentioned above, and placed in the sun. While these operations are going on, the leaves of Cacha are set to dry and ground into powder. (3) About nine or ten ounces of this powder are taken —

(1) Hard water. The hard water so widely used by the Dyers of India is Natron, which is found distributed throughout all the lands of that country. (a)
(2) Nayourivi. This is a plant that grows on its own everywhere; and although the natives use it in their remedies, just as they do with all others, it is claimed that it could be counted among the weeds, were it not so usefully employed in those regions for dyeing. (b)
(3) Cacha. This is a large tree, very common in the Indies, whose leaves are of a consistency quite similar to those of the Laurel, though softer and more spongy, shorter and more rounded at the tip; its flower is blue. (c)

(a) What is called Natron here, I think it would be difficult to lack in these Islands, if one looks for it carefully.
(b) The Nayourivi, in this country, is what is called Quilites or Orayi. Even the word Orayi differs little from Nayourivi, and perhaps Nay is just the article.
(c) Cacha is certainly what they call in the Islands of the Negroes Saguingsing, in Tagalog Colis, and in Ilocos Candong, with whose cooked leaves the natives prepare their mats, dyeing them all colors. Its flower is blue. In the provinces near Manila, this tree is well known and belongs to the genus Memecylon. In Ilocos they mix these powdered leaves with Nino; but the color comes out dirtier and duller than what is made in Tagalog regions, where that ingredient is left out — which might well produce a good effect, were it not for the lack of Chaya or Chaiver. It may also happen that the Morinda used in Ilocos is a different species from that of Batangas, which is where they dye best.

109
a cloth of five cubits: they steep it in rough water, and place the cloth in it, turning it over and leaving it there for a whole night. In the morning they wring it and put it out to dry in the sun, after which it takes on a yellowish tinge. They then take nine ounces of powder from the bark of the Nouna tree: (1) they dissolve it in water, and also immerse the cloth in it, as was done with the Cacha, except that this second operation is repeated for two days; and then the cloth takes on a vermilion color. After this they take the powder of the root of Chayaver or Chaya: (2) they dissolve it in nine azumbres of pure water, and in it they stir the cloth very well, leaving it there afterwards for a whole night. In the morning they wring it tightly, put it out to dry in the sun, and repeat this same process for eight days. After these are done, they take eighteen ounces of the same powder of Chaya or Chayaver: they place it in an earthen vessel with ten azumbres of water, which they heat over a moderate fire until it just begins to boil, and when it has cooked well, they remove the firewood that remained beneath the vessel, and leave it for eighteen hours over embers, without touching it or giving it any more fire. During this operation, they take care to stir the cloth very well on all sides with a stick, so that the dye penetrates better throughout. After the eighteen hours have passed, the cloth is taken out, washed in clear water, and upon being left to dry, it comes out dyed a scarlet of the first class. This is the method reputed to be the best on the coast for scarlet dye, it being worth noting that the mordant used there and the one used in the Philippines are very similar. It remains now to give the explanation of the ingredients of the dye, taken from the aforementioned work.
Morinda litoralis. Shore Morinda. Opposite leaves,

(1) Nouna. This is a large and stout tree, whose leaves are about three and a half inches long, and fifteen lines wide. Its fruit is the size of a small walnut, covered by a skin, and containing in various compartments five or six seeds. (a)
(2) Chaya or Chayaver. This is a plant that grows on its own, and is also cultivated because of how necessary it is for dyeing. It does not rise above half a foot in height, and its leaves are of a light green, two lines wide and six lines long. The flower is very small and bluish. Its root sometimes reaches four feet in length; but the better one is that which has no more than one foot, or a foot and a half at most. It is central, and puts out only a few other small rootlets to the sides. When it is still fresh, it is yellow; but upon drying, it becomes brownish in color. The Chaya appears to be a species of Gallium. What is certain is that both one and the other cause milk to curdle.
This is essentially what the cited book (whose author I was told was Mr. Povre or Porben) said about scarlet dye. (b)

(a) The tree called Nouna is the Nino of the Philippines; also called Nono, Bangcoro, and Culit; but the one here is not large.
(b) The Chaya is what is lacking in the Philippines for achieving a scarlet equal to that of India. I say it is lacking because it is not sought; for I do not believe it would fail to be found there. But let it be noted that it is not a species of Gallium, but rather the Oldenlandia umbellata of Linnaeus.
22

110
oval, pointed at both ends, smooth on top, and with a tuft of hairs in the axils of the cross-veins underneath. Very short petioles with two intermediate stipules, short and pointed. Flowers opposite the leaves, in solitary receptacles, without bracts on the peduncle. Occasionally two receptacles are joined below into one by the peduncles, and then they are axillary. Calyx entire and without a rim; rarely having one. Corolla in five lobes, hairy at the throat. Stamens five. Stigma cleft in two. Berry without rims and with four seeds. = Trees of two fathoms that grow on beaches. The leaves are a hand's-length long, and the corollas are white as in the other species I have discussed. I do not know whether their roots yield any dye. It is very probable that this is the same plant used for dyeing in Ilocos, and that it never gives as good a color as that of Batangas. It resembles the species nodosa, and Corcia of Decand. Prod. p. 4. 448. — In the vicinity of Manila, tumbong aso.
Morinda umbellata. Umbellate Morinda. Leaves opposite, oblong, entire, very smooth and leathery. Petioles very short. Terminal flowers in an umbel of four receptacles arranged in a cross. The peduncles of the receptacles each with two deciduous bracts. The calyces of the small flowers, entire and without a rim. Seeds compressed. = Small trees that grow in Angat, whose leaves are lustrous, black at maturity, and about four inches long. Pers. Sin. pl. t. 1. 201.
COFFEA. Corolla funnel-shaped, with the limb in five parts. Stamens above the tube. Berry below the flower, with two seeds covered by a thin membrane, and having a lateral groove. Lin. Sist. veg. 365. Jus. Gén. pl. 204.
Coffea arabica. Arabian Coffee. Trunk straight, with long, drooping branches, thicker and more compressed below the point where the leaves originate. Leaves opposite, and rarely whorled, in threes, egg-shaped and oblong, wavy, with small glandular leaflets in the axils of the primary veins that branch from the midrib, and with intermediate stipules at the base. Axillary flowers on each side, from four to twelve, in clusters on a common peduncle that is very short and thick. Individual peduncle very short. Calyx adherent, with five angles, ending in five small teeth. Corolla as in the genus. Stamens five, projecting beyond the corolla. Anthers long. Stigmas two, long, somewhat thick. Berry globose, with two oval, flat seeds, with a groove on the inner side; convex on the other side, and covered with an aril. = This well-known tree reaches a height of eight or nine feet. I do not know whether it is native to the Islands, though I am inclined to think it is. It grows in the Province of Batangas, and spreads on its own with great ease; especial-

111
mente in the town of S. Pablo. Much has been written, with great variety of opinion, about the drink made from coffee, which is so widely used. Some say it causes trembling in the hands, takes away sleep, and shortens the sight. This last effect I have experienced myself, after having taken it for a period of two months. Some have also written that it causes sterility. But other Authors acknowledge that coffee has cured chronic asthmas and melancholies; that it clears the head, and counteracts the effects of spirits. Administered as an enema, it dispels the torpor that causes apoplexy. It is known that a King of Spain published a remedy against intermittent fevers, which consists of taking a cup of strong coffee into which the juice of a lemon has been squeezed. (In the Philippines it is necessary to use three or four lemons, as they are very small.) Many Indian women afflicted with hysteria have recovered immediately upon drinking a cup of coffee into which two spoonfuls of brandy had been added. It also reduces, and even cures, scabies. * Café. Lin. ibid.

Coffea volubilis. Climbing Coffee. Climbing trunk. Leaves arranged in threes, rarely opposite, egg-shaped, entire, with their edges rolled downward, with a small glandular pit at the base of each lateral primary vein, and in the axils of the secondary veins. Petioles very short, channeled above, with three intermediate stipules; and if the leaves are opposite, only two stipules. Flowers axillary and terminal. The axillary ones more than six in number, gathered on a single very long common peduncle. The terminal ones in a kind of corymbose panicle. Calyx adherent, very small, cylindrical, with barely noticeable teeth. Corolla very long, funnel-shaped, split almost to the middle into five parts rolled downward, with five angles and as many grooves in the tube. Stamens five, attached along nearly their entire length to the corolla, projecting slightly outward at the top. Anthers very long, arrow-shaped, and half-incumbent. Style a little shorter than the stamens. Stigmas two, long and somewhat thick. Fruit crowned with the calyx teeth, and similar to the other species, but a little smaller. Seeds two or more, lenticular, and somewhat concave on the inner side. = A climbing shrub that grows thicker than an arm, reaching six or more varas in height. Its flowers, which I observed in August of 1824, are in every way similar to, and as fragrant as, those of the common coffee plant. The Indians do not know it, although some call it Halon; but I note that the local people here use that name for a species of Amaranth. The said shrub was flowering vigorously in a place in Bauang called Munting tubig, on the bank of a small stream, a stone's throw from the sea, and in another place called Baguilaua, in the month of August.

112
It is unfortunate that both this individual plant and some others I have seen do not bear fruit until many years have passed. Only old trees produce it; and I have seen only about twenty seeds, whose infusion was somewhat similar to that of the usual coffee; but the smell and taste not as good. The singular shrub discussed in this article takes root easily from a cutting. * T., Halon.— A singular phenomenon is observed in the fruit of this vine: although I have said it has two seeds, three or four are commonly found, placed confusedly and ordinarily covering one another. They are smaller than those of the usual coffee, roundish, lentil-shaped; but somewhat concave on their inner side. The reason there are more than two is that the flowers are very tightly packed, and two or three come together to form the misshapen fruit. Indeed the berries regularly have two, or three, or more stalks, which are the vestiges of the flowers that joined together to form the fruit. The arils are thick and adhere strongly to the seeds. New sp.
PAEDERIA. Cal. small, with five teeth. Cor. funnel-shaped, with five lobes, and with rough hair inside. Ant. long, half-sessile, not projecting beyond the tube. Berry small, oval, fragile, with two seeds. Jussieu Gen. pl. 205.
PAEDERIA FOETIDA. FETID PAEDERIA. Twining trunk. Leaves opposite, ovate, oblong, tapering to a stiff point, entire, somewhat rough above and tomentose below. Petioles short, with two intermediate stipules, straight and pointed. All flowers hermaphroditic, axillary, in a loose, dichotomous panicle. Own peduncle very short. Cal. small, adherent, with five teeth. Cor. much longer than the calyx, cylindrical, rough on the outside, purple, and full of wool inside, with five lobes edged on the flat limb. Stamens five. Filaments fixed along their length to the tube of the corolla; the three lower ones hidden within it. Ant. long, arrow-shaped. Ovary inferior, conical in reverse. Style surrounded at the base by a small five-sided body, with as many confused channels; short, and deeply cleft in two parts. Stigmas simple, projecting beyond the corolla. Berry juicy even at maturity, globose, somewhat compressed, crowned with the teeth of the calyx, with two chambers, and in each one a large seed, convex on one side and flat on the other, without grooves. = I have seen this little shrub in many places, and it is well known to all the natives, for the bad smell it gives off and for the indecent name they give it. There are some other species with leaves more or less whitish below. It closely resembles the Psychotria. The flower is not twisted, nor funnel-shaped; and the fruit is crowned with the calyx. * T., Cantotai-

113
V., Lilitan. P., Cantotai, Dicuta maboloc, Matabang dicut.
Lin. Sist. veg. 432.
Paederia tacpo. Pederia tacpo. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire, smooth, and somewhat fleshy. Petioles very short, with intermediate stipules. Terminal flowers in a cluster containing about six long peduncles that subdivide into an umbel. Calyx adherent, very small, with five small teeth that disappear at maturity. Corolla bell-shaped, with five groups of hairs at the throat, and opposite the lobes of the limb, which are five in number, pointed, curved downward, and ending in two barely noticeable small teeth. Stamens five, fixed opposite and near the divisions, and straight. Anthers oval, fixed in front of the filaments, and projecting slightly beyond the tube. Style one, longer than the stamens. Stigmas two thick plates, curved to the sides. Berry globose, marked with five or more lines, which at maturity form just as many small angles, somewhat compressed, with a channel, a single chamber, and two oval seeds, narrowed and compressed at the base, mutually pressed together, with a membranous covering, and without a groove on the flat face, as in coffee. = Small trees common in Angat, Bulacan, Batangas, and other places, about the height of a man: I do not know whether they grow larger; nor do they have a bad smell. The leaves are five to seven inches long, without glandular dots, as in coffee. The flowers are white and without notable scent. The five groups of hairs are visible when looking at the flower from above, and when it is in its fullest vigor. The fruit is like a small yellow chickpea and has only one cell: children eat it as a treat, but there is nothing particularly pleasant about it. Flowers in November. * T., Tacpo. New species. Perhaps the coffea luzoniensis of Dec. Prod. p. 4. 502?
EXOSTEMMA. Calyx regular, with five teeth. Corolla tubular. Stamens inserted at the top of the tube and projecting outward. Stigma entire. Capsule oblong, with two chambers. Seeds winged, with an entire margin. Spreng. Sist. veg. t. 1. 513.
Exostemma philippicum. Philippine Exostemma. Leaves opposite, oval, entire, pointed, and hairy. Petioles long, flat on top and with two intermediate stipules in one piece.
