Flowers axillary in whorled and compound racemes. Calyx adherent, with five teeth, very soon deciduous, replaced by a navel-like structure that also vanishes shortly after. Corolla much longer than the calyx, funnel-shaped, with five lobes. Stamens five, fixed toward the middle of the tube. Filaments almost absent. Anthers with two chambers, and somewhat ear-shaped. Style longer than the corolla. Stigma globose. Capsule somewhat rough, egg-shaped, compressed, with two chambers through which it opens (not through the partitions), with two receptacles in which are found

114
fixed many imbricated circular seeds, surrounded by a whole wing, (in maturity lacerated) and notched at the base. = Small trees known in Angat, three varas in height. They exhale a very strong odor, sometimes like vinegar, sometimes like tobacco, and occasionally it also seems pleasant. They are not used for anything. — They agree with the genus Cinchona, and are the species Philippica of Cavanilles. I must note that at another time, when I was still new to these matters, I had in my hands on two occasions branches with fruit of some species of Quina, according to what I had seen in the Flora Peruana; some were brought to me from the mountains of Bauang, in Batangas, and others from those of Angat. Flowers in August. * T., Huliganga.
RONABEA. Corolla with five laciniae, with a long tube, swollen toward the throat. Stamens do not extend beyond it. Stigma two plates. Berry with one chamber, (not crowned by the calyx — Jussieu, Gen. pl. 205,) and containing two nutlets with solitary seeds. Linnaeus, Syst. veg. 365.
Ronabea arborea. Tree Ronabea. Trunk straight, with horizontal and opposite branches. Leaves opposite, ovate, elongated, entire, with a small glandular pit at the base of the lateral veins, and two intermediate stipules at the base of the petioles. Flowers axillary in umbels. Calyx adherent, very small, bell-shaped, with four or five teeth. Corolla much longer than the calyx, swollen, with five laciniae turned outward, and the throat filled with wool, arranged in two series, one directed downward and the other upward. Stamens five, at the divisions of the limb. Filaments almost none. Anthers ovate, incumbent, and exterior. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma thick, depressed, and slightly cleft in two parts. Berry crowned by the calyx, globose, fleshy, with two bony and separable seeds. = A well-known tree, very abundant with horizontal branches, and quite common in the Province of Batangas, and in other parts: it rises to a height of two or three fathoms. The flowers are not fragrant. The berries are as large as cherries. The natives call it by a name meaning: Buffalo Rib, perhaps on account of the shape or arrangement of the branches. I have noted that the fruit boiled in water gives a dull green color; but the crushed seeds dye it the same color, stronger and more vivid. The true form of the stigma must be observed in flowers that are already fully open: for otherwise it will appear globose and angular. * T., Tadiang anuang. I., Pamalatanguen. New species.
REMIJIA. Calyx with five laciniae. Corolla in five linear parts. A fleshy disk at the base of the style, and separate from it. Stamens fixed in the middle of the corolla tube. Two stigmas. Capsule ovate, with two chambers, and a receptacle in each

115
one, which bears many imbricated seeds and has a membranous wing. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 357.
Remijia olorata. Remigia olorosa. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Very short petioles, with two intermediate keeled stipules that sheathe the branch. Flowers axillary, sometimes solitary, and sometimes in a panicle with few small flowers. Common peduncle very long. The proper peduncle also long, with two bracts at the base. Calyx adherent, top-shaped, with five obtuse teeth whose edges partly overlap the nearest ones. Corolla much longer than the calyx, fleshy, with five rounded lobes, and from the middle of the limb to the throat filled with hair. Stamens five. Filaments almost none. Anthers very long, projecting beyond the corolla, and fixed between the divisions of the limb. Pistil surrounded at its base by a very small crown with four or five angles. Style filiform. Stigma thick, club-shaped, very hairy and split into two twisted laminae. Capsule globose, crowned by the calyx, with two separate axes, and around them many chambers; in each one a seed. These two axes are undoubtedly the receptacles of the seeds, as in quinine. = Small trees frequent in Bauang, and unknown to the natives, which rise, as far as I have seen, to a height of two fathoms. The smell of the bark and wood, when dry, is somewhat similar to that of nutmeg. The flavor is also pleasant, though slightly pungent. The wood is hard. The leaves are nearly half a foot long. New species. — Although it differs somewhat from the Genus in having a hairy corolla, it agrees in the disk of the style. Note that this Genus concurs with quinine in its characters and virtues.
Remijia angatensis. Remijia of Angat. Trunk with the ends of the branches square. Leaves opposite, sessile, lanceolate, narrow and somewhat fringed, with two intermediate stipules that are pointed and soft. Flowers axillary, solitary, with long peduncles, and two bracts close to the calyx. Calyx adherent, with four teeth hairy on the inside, and rarely five. Corolla funnel-shaped, with a hairy throat and four or five oval lobes. Stamens four or five. Filaments very short, fixed in the incisions of the corolla. Anthers fixed by their midpoint on the filaments, with one side projecting upward in the manner of a tooth. Style longer than the stamens, surrounded at the base by a disk. Stigmas two, rather long, hairy, and thick. Capsule globose, crowned by the calyx, with a confused partition, and more than eight seeds, bony, ovoid, compressed, and clustered. = Small trees known in Angat, with branch bark the color of cinnamon. The leaves are about three inches long and half an inch wide. The Ca-

116
berries are somewhat fragrant, and at maturity are red in color. The tree so closely resembles the one described in this book under the name Mirtus communis that at first glance they appear to be the same. Flowers in August. * T., Caragli.

REMIJIA OSCURA. Remijia oscura. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, egg-shaped, elongated, wavy, entire, and smooth. Very short petioles, with two intermediate stipules, as in the coffee plant. Flowers axillary, solitary, or in groups of two to four in a cluster, with long common and individual peduncles, and a bract of two small leaves toward the tip. Upper calyx with five rounded lobes. Corolla funnel-shaped, with a hairy throat, a saucer-shaped limb, with five rounded and somewhat two-lobed lobes. Five anthers, nearly sessile, at the divisions of the limb, placed outward. One style, which extends slightly beyond the corolla, and from the middle divides in two. Hairy stigmas. Capsule globose, crowned with the calyx, of one chamber, and two central axes, on which many oval, compressed seeds are fixed. = A shrub as thick as an arm, which I have seen in S. Isidro. *T., Caragli. P., Pagbut. Might it belong to this genus? For this reason I gave the species the name oscura. — I have seen another with opposite branches, lanceolate leaves, with two intermediate stipules, and star-shaped flowers; but it is the same as the other, since the flower peduncles elongate with time.

CANTHIUM. Calyx with five lobes. Corolla tubular, short, open, with five lobes. Stamens hidden inside the corolla. Stigma in a small head. Berry egg-shaped, crowned with two chambers, and in each one a single seed. Jussieu, Gén. pl. 204.

CANTHIUM HORRIDUM. Horrible Canthium. Leaves already gathered in groups of two or three, alternately opposite, egg-shaped, pointed, entire, and smooth, with two lateral stipules, and two axillary spines, placed opposite at the base of the very short petiole. Flowers with a small stalk, axillary, two or three. Calyx adherent, top-shaped, compressed with five small teeth. Corolla longer than the calyx, roughly funnel-shaped, with a narrow throat, surrounded by a hairy crown, and divided into five lanceolate parts, very much recurved downward, together with part of the corolla tube. Stamens five. Filaments rather long, fixed at the divisions of the limb. Anthers long and incumbent. Ovary conical, inverted. Style long. Stigma with two thick little plates. Berry compressed, top-shaped, crowned with the calyx teeth, with two chambers, and solitary bony seeds. = It is a small tree of two or three varas, which I have seen in many places, and horribly bristling with spines. T., Suliac daga. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 472.

CANTHIUM PEDUNCULARE. Stalked Canthium. Leaves oppos-

117
clustered at the nodes, numbering about six, almost sessile, oval, sometimes pointed-oval, fringed, with two opposite spines in the axils. Flowers solitary, hanging from very long peduncles. Corolla strongly recurved downward, with five laciniae. In other respects, like the preceding species, from which it is barely distinguishable. = It is a very thorny small tree, about three yards tall. — This species and the preceding differ from the Gardenia Spinosa in that the tree I speak of has only two seeds. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 475.
STIGMANTHUS. Calyx with five thread-like divisions. Corolla funnel-shaped, with five open lobes. Stamens five. Stigma very large with furrows. Berry without juice, compressed, with one chamber and many seeds. Dec. Prod. t. 4. 469.
Stigmanthus cymosus. Cup Stigmanthus. Leaves opposite, ovate, almost sessile. Branches climbing. Flowers above. Peduncles bent downward. Calyx and Corolla as in the genus. Stamens five. Anthers erect. Stigma very large. Berry with five seeds. A shrub found in Caluan, made known by Mr. Azaola. Loureiro gave it the name above on account of the large stigma.
VANGUERIA. Calyx open, with five teeth. Corolla globose, bell-shaped, with five laciniae, and hairy inside. Anthers barely protruding. Berry with a navel, five chambers, and as many seeds. Stigma with two plates, according to Vahl, and with 4-5 lobes according to Roxb. Lyn. Syst. veg. 367. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 454.
Vangueria stellata. Star Vangueria. Leaves arranged in a star pattern around the trunk, three in number, lanceolate, almost entire, very rough on top, and whitish and somewhat soft beneath. Petioles very short. Flowers in a panicle. Calyx adherent, bell-shaped, with the margin cleft in five parts. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, bell-shaped, with five very woolly laciniae. Stamens five, fixed at the base of the corolla. Filaments long and twisted disorderly. Ovary cylindrical. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma bifid. Berry dry, oblong, crowned with the parts of the calyx, very large at maturity, with a half-leathery covering that has four chambers, each containing one seed pointed at the ends. = A tree I saw many years ago and was unable to examine well. It grows in the forests to the size of a man's body. Its wood is as hard as that of the molave. The leaves are very rough, and that is where the first name below comes from. Its fruit resembles that of the Culasi. Flowers in August. * T., Malaas-is, Madoudon. = New species.
MUSSAENDA. Corolla funnel-shaped. Calyx in five parts: one of them sometimes extended in the form of a broad leaf.
23

118
Two thickish stigmas. Oblong berry below the flower, with two compartments and seeds arranged in four rows. Lin. Syst. veg. 376.

Mussaenda frondosa. Musenda frondosa. Trunk erect, branching. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire and hairy. Petioles very short, and at the base with two intermediate stipules, divided at the tip into two. Flowers in umbellate panicles. Calyx adherent, with five awl-shaped teeth, equal to one another, except in the last flower, which is at the center of the final division of the umbel, in which one of the teeth is very large, lanceolate, egg-shaped, with five nerves, and white. Corolla much longer than the calyx, funnel-shaped, with a flat limb, split into five lobes, convex in the middle, ending in an awl-shaped point, and with the throat closed with hairs. Stamens five, hidden inside the tube of the corolla. Filaments none. Anthers long. Style one, shorter than the tube of the corolla. Stigma in two parts. Berry hard, with one compartment, and two half double partitions, with their ends curved to the sides, with many seeds placed along the edges of the partitions, and around the rind of the berry. = This small tree grows to a height of seven or eight feet, and in forests can reach fifteen. The tooth mentioned above has no notable scent; and because it is white and as large as a leaf, it creates a striking appearance. The Indians therefore call this plant by a name meaning that the milk of the Virgin fell upon it. Fl. in Jun. * T., Tingatinga. I., Balailamoc. Lin. ibid.—In Capis and Iloilo there is another variety with oval leaves, with fine hairs on the nerves and margins, and also on the panicles. The white tooth has five nerves and is one to two inches long. There has been no shortage of people who have suspected that this small tree indicates the presence of gold where it grows; and the reason is no other than that it has been found in places where gold is actually extracted in granules: which is very weak evidence. In Capis it is called Agboy.—I have also seen in Angat the following species. Leaves opposite with very short petioles, lanceolate, entire, smooth and wavy. Flowers terminal in a dichotomous umbel. Calyx with one white tooth of about three lines in length, the other teeth having fallen along with the corolla. Fruit identical to that of the preceding species, even in the arrangement of the seeds, and it contains a very fragrant balsam. It is a small tree about as thick as an arm, and the Indians call it Cahoi dalaga. The white tooth seems to me to have been small from the start, and not a piece broken off from a larger one. Fl. in Jan.
Diosma. Fruit of three to five capsules. Calyx in five parts, with a hypogynous disk at the base, with five scales

119
or notches. Five petals, alternating with the parts of the calyx, and opposite the scales of the nectary, attached below the disk. Five stamens, fixed at the same point, and alternating with the petals. Juss. Gen. pl. 298.

Diosma serrata. Serrated Diosma. A weak trunk that leans upon trees. Scattered branches, surrounded at the base by hard scales resembling glands, with dots that make them rough. Leaves scattered, half-oval, and suddenly pointed at the tip, serrated and smooth. Petioles very short. Terminal flowers in a racemose panicle. Calyx free, bell-shaped, with five lobes at the edge. Corolla flat, with five oval petals the color of the calyx, and twice as long as it, alternating with its parts, and fixed to the outer walls of the nectary. Nectary shorter than the calyx, fused to it below, bell-shaped, with five rounded teeth opposite the petals. Five stamens, fixed between the teeth of the nectary, alternating with the petals. Filaments very short. Anthers compressed, arrow-shaped. Ovary globose, seated upon the nectary. No styles. Three stigmas, very short and thick, with two lobes. Capsule the size of a chickpea, with the beginnings of three partitions, with three chambers, each containing a small compartment with its own cover and partition, two chambers and solitary seeds fixed at the base of the capsule. = Small, weak trees, two or three varas tall, whose branches are at most one inch thick, and which lean upon other trees. Their leaves are about six or seven inches long and about five inches wide. I have seen them in Malinta, and they are barely known to the natives. Flowers in April. * T., Bilogo? New species.

RHAMNUS. Calyx tubular, with scales (petals according to some) that support the stamens. Corolla none. Berry with three or four seeds. Stigmas one, two, up to four. Lin. Syst. veg. 398. Pers. Syn. pl. 238.

Rhamnus carolinianus. Carolina Buckthorn. Trunk erect, very branchy, without spines or prickles. Leaves alternate, egg-shaped, pointed, serrated, with regular veins, smooth. Petioles short. Axillary flowers, hermaphrodite, usually two. Peduncles long. Calyx conical inverted, with five teeth that fade at maturity. Corolla of five petals (those which Linnaeus calls scales) smaller than the calyx teeth, inserted between them, oval, without claws, with a notch at the tip, and compressed. On the receptacle there is a fleshy, smooth, and somewhat concave disk. Five stamens, hidden within the petals. Filaments flat. Anthers round. Ovary rises from the base of the same fleshy calyx. Style short. Three stigmas, divergent. Berry oval, adherent by the base to the calyx, erect

;

120
at maturity, with three seeds convex on the outside, and angular on the sides. = Small trees commonly seen on seashores, three or four varas in height. Their leaves are eaten cooked; but they do not agree with everyone, because they cause dizziness. Fl. in Jul. and Oct. *T., Cabatiti in Batangas. Lin. ibid; 399.—There is another species, which differs from the former only in that the leaves have three veins united at the base. It is also called cabatete.—There is yet another with leaves of similar three veins, and a nearly globose drupe, with a nut of four chambers, each containing one seed. In China the poor use the leaves of a species of Rhamnus in place of tea, and take its infusion.

ZIZYPHUS. Calyx with five divisions. Five petals. Disk fleshy, orbicular, surrounding the pistil. Drupe with a nut of one or two seeds. Styles, two. Pers. Syn. pl. 240.

Zizyphus jujuba. Jujube Azufaifo. Trunk with spines spread apart and widely spaced: one pointing upward, and the other downward. Leaves alternate, oval; obtuse with a small sinus, with three veins, finely serrated, white and hairy beneath. Petioles very short. Flowers lateral, in small, somewhat umbellate clusters. The common peduncle divides in two. The proper one is long. The receptacle has a disk of five lobes. Style one, cleft to the middle into two. Drupe oval, with a nut of two chambers, each with one seed. = A tree cultivated by some enthusiasts, and which has been brought from the mountains, since it grows wild in Sta. Cruz de Ilocos, and probably in other places. The fruit, called manzanitas, is eaten and is moderately tasty. Fl. in Sept. * Manzanitas Dec. Prod. p. 2. 21.—It differs from the jujube species in having twin spines.

Zizyphus zonulatus. Banded Azufaifo. Trunk with solitary spines. Leaves alternate, narrow, egg-shaped, with three veins, finely serrated, and somewhat hairy. Petioles very short, with two spines at the base. Calyx inferior, in five parts. The disk at the center of the flower with five notched lobes. Petals five, fixed between the teeth of the calyx and hood-shaped. Stamens hidden within the petals. Style one. Stigmas two. Drupe globose, fleshy, with a very hard nut, which is divided into three parts: the middle one is a zone, narrowed in one part and wider in others, which serves as a partition for the other two parts, which form two lids of the nut: one at one lateral end, and the other at the other (the zone corresponding to the insertion of the peduncle), and each contains a compressed, heart-shaped seed. = A first-order tree, which I have seen in Batangas and in other places. When the nut is stripped of its flesh, it remains clearly—

121
manifest the dissepiment, which has the two lids as if glued to it. The flesh of the Drupe is edible, sticky, and the infusion of the tree's bark is quite red. Flowers in August. * P., Balacat. In Angat, Bigu. New species.

Zicyphus lotus. Lotus Jujube. Trunk with thorns arranged in pairs: the lower one erect, and the upper one curved downward. Leaves alternate, notched at the base, obliquely egg-shaped, elongated, barely serrated, and hairy, with three veins. Petioles very short, with two thorns at the base. Axillary flowers, hermaphrodite, in umbellate panicles, which subdivide three or four times. Calyx as in the cabatiti. Corolla of five very small petals, with small claws between the calyx teeth. Stamens five. Stigmas two or three, rounded. Globose drupe, adherent below to the calyx, which curves downward. = Small trees of four to six varas in height, whose fruit is not eaten: the Indians know them by the name duclap, and they are very common on the seashores. In Ilocos, from this species or from another that has thorns, very good chairs are made: its wood is white and fine, and they call it there lanoti. It is very close to the species Zeciphus of Lin. and also to the one called Lotus, whose fruit when eaten, some European authors claim without foundation, causes one to forget past things. The fruit of the trees above is not eaten, and if one speaks of forgetting, without any need to eat the lotus, the phenomenon observed in the Philippines is remarkable: for Father Sta. María tells us, and I have also observed, that some Indians forget even the number of their children and the names of these and of their wives. * T., Duclap. I., Labba labba, Lanoti. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 240. Differs from the lotus of Dec.

Zicyphus dalanta. Dalanta Jujube. Trunk without thorns. Leaves alternate, obliquely egg-shaped, with seven veins, obtusely serrated. = A tree I saw in Bonbonon on the Island of Negros. The fruit is eaten. * V. Dalanta.

Zicyphus latifolia. Broad-leaved Jujube. Trunk without thorns! Leaves alternate, obliquely egg-shaped, lanceolate, with three veins, notched and downy underneath. Axillary flowers in dichotomous racemes. Globose drupe, with a bony nut, of two chambers, and solitary seeds. = A first-order tree, known in the forests of S. Mateo, of white wood, from which canoes are made. The seeds of the fruit are eaten toasted. The branches have no thorns: I do not know whether the trunk has them: the leaves resemble those of the Cabatiti. * T., Talanas. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 20.

Paliurus. Calyx with five laciniae. Petals five, scale-like, inserted on a glandular disk as in the Zicypho. Five stamens inserted at the anterior base of the pe-

122
talos. Ovary surrounded by a disk. Styles three. Fruit orbicular, bony, surrounded by a broad membranous wing, with three cells and three seeds. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 22.
Paliurus lamiyo. Paliuro lamiyo. Leaves sometimes alternate, sometimes opposite, slightly heart-shaped, ovate, oblong, with barely notched margins, smooth. Common petiole with two long spines placed above and away from the base. Axillary flowers on a common, very long peduncle, arranged in a kind of racemose panicle. Calyx small, leathery, with three obtuse lobes. Corolla more than three times longer than the calyx, cleft nearly to the base into three keeled, fleshy, and leathery parts. Nectary cup-shaped, hairy, with six lobes, surrounding the ovary. Stamens six, longer than the corolla, fixed at the base of the nectary on the outside. Anthers straight. Ovary superior, hairy. Styles none. Stigmas three, thick. Drupe fleshy, globose, depressed, with one small rib encircling the belly and five others very thin and somewhat indistinct, which start from the ends (where they divide in two) down to the belly where there are five small points, with a very depressed, extremely hard nut having five lobes on the rim, five cells, and one seed in each. = A tree of great height, which some call Lamiyo and others Malaihao or Malaiyao. Its wood is whitish and soft; but it has the property of not splitting even when exposed to the sun, and is therefore useful for certain purposes. The fruit is an inch and a half thick; it is eaten and is bittersweet, though it slightly irritates the tongue at the end; silver is also cleaned very well by boiling it with the fruit. Canoes are made from the tree. Flowers in August. * T., Lamio, Malaiyao. V., Batoan. New species. — This tree and the following ones belong, in my opinion, to this genus.
Paliurus dao. Paliuro dao. Leaves semi-opposite, obliquely ovate, elongated, pointed, entire, and smooth. Drupe globose, as in the lamio, but much smaller and the nut very depressed. = It is a well-known tree, some reaching forty-five fathoms in height, whose fruit is eaten and is the size of a cherry; the flavor is like that of the lamio. Some natives call Dao the one described in the genus Poupartia; but the true one is this, which I am treating here. Note and compare these two genera, as they may perhaps be the same thing. New species.
Paliurus perforatus. Palivro agugereado. Branches with two hooks at the base of the common petioles. Leaves opposite, generally approaching a lanceolate shape, serrated from the middle upward, hairy beneath. Flowers in a raceme. Calyx inferior, very small, with four or five obtuse teeth. Corolla cleft nearly to the base into six parts. Stamens.

123
thirteen, fixed at the outer base of the nectary. Filaments compressed at the base, thicker above and full of wool. Germen globose, depressed, surrounded by the nectary, which is a small membrane, thicker at its upper part. Style thick, perforated along its length. Stigma with four or five small teeth. Berry depressed, with one rib that encircles it horizontally at the middle; in addition to others that emerge from above and below, terminating at that middle one, with five chambers, each containing one ovate, bony seed, with a small hole at the upper part. = The small trees that produce these little fruits, larger than a cherry, and on the outside very similar to those of the Lamium, rise to a height of eight or nine feet. Their leaves are one inch long. The small bones of the seeds are very hard. They are not very common; but I have seen them in Bauang at a place called Mailayin, and in Malinta. Fl. in January. * T., Asimao. New species.

PALIURUS DUBIUS. DOUBTFUL PALIURUS. Trunk erect, with two hooks at the origin of the small branches. Leaves opposite, sometimes oval, sometimes ovate-oblong, obtusely serrate from the middle upward, slightly hairy, with their own petioles nearly absent. Flowers terminal in clusters of two or three small florets. Calyx inferior, flat, with six or seven pointed teeth. Corolla of six or seven lanceolate petals, much longer than the calyx. Nectary a cup-shaped tube, woolly, terminated by as many teeth as there are stamens. Stamens about twelve or fourteen, longer than the petals, attached and fixed along their length and at the outer part of the said tube, from whose extremity they separate. Anthers oval, compressed; the alternating ones smaller. Style shorter than the stamens. Stigma broad, depressed. Berry globose, depressed, with more than five chambers, and in each one an oval, bony seed, with a small hole at the tip, and in all else like the Pal. perforatus. = Small trees I have seen in Mamdaloyon of about two varas in height. Fl. in May. * Laiya. New species. — I am certain that these small trees are the same; but how is it that in one the stamens are separated, and in the other they are attached to the nectary? No doubt that with time they detach from the outer part of the nectary and become free and woolly, as in the other small tree I mentioned before. In the fruit the two are identical, as they are in the hooks and leaves. In Namacpacan in Ilocos I have seen another species, with the common petiole of the leaflets winged, and two hooks at the base; one of them deciduous. Petals five. Stamens eleven or thirteen fixed on the outside of a glandular and woolly body that encircles the germen, and which is cleft into four or five parts. Berry as in the Asimao.
BURSARIA. Calyx with five teeth. Petals five. Cagilla

124
compressed, heart-shaped on the reverse, with two chambers and two valves. Seeds covered in resin. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 347.

BURSARIA INERMIS. BURSARIA UNARMED. Leaves alternate, without stipules, ovate, acute. Calyx inferior, of five sepals. Five hypogynous petals, appearing united. Stamens five, alternating with the petals. Ovary single, appearing divided in two. Style one. Stigma simple. Capsule somewhat heart-shaped, dividing into two with four seeds, resembling the silique of the Haspi. Seeds round, black. = Trees thirty feet tall in the mountains of Calanan, seen by Mr. Azaola, to whom the description belongs. New species.

VENTILAGO. Calyx with a short tube, half-attached to the ovary at the base, and with five lobes. Petals five, scale-like, fixed between the lobes of the calyx. Stamens below the petals. Style very short. Stigmas two. Capsule without valves, half-round, terminating in an oblong membranous wing, containing one seed. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 38.

VENTILAGO MONOICA. MONOECIOUS VENTILAGO. Trunk without spurs or thorns, with branches in forks, climbing over trees. Leaves alternate, ovate, lanceolate, somewhat blunt, barely serrated, smooth, and slightly twisted to one side on a very short petiole. Flowers monoecious; males separated from females on different branches. * Males in dense racemes. Calyx with five lobes. Corolla of five very small petals, fixed between the divisions of the calyx. Stamens five, at the base of the petals. Style sterile. * Female in a loose panicle. Calyx inferior, fused with the base of the fruit, with the margin free, and five or more inconspicuous ribs and as many small teeth. Corolla of five or more very tiny petals, which fall off very quickly, with as many stamens, also very small, sterile and deciduous. Drupe dry, globose, with a leathery and somewhat hard covering, which suddenly extends into a broad and long membranous wing, with one chamber and one globose seed. Styles two, very small, at the central tip of the wing. Stigmas simple. = It is a curious and delicate shrub, which climbs over neighboring trees. The branches are somewhat forked, and the small branches coil at their base upon themselves. The Indians use it for tying. It is known in the mountains of San Mateo, but by various names. The fruit, which is barely larger than a pea, has no particular smell, and is crowned with a wing more than an inch long; its width is two or three lines, and it is very thin. Flowers in April. * T. Salapao, Silipao. — The description given is exact, and so it should form a new species: for the two that the Authors present, they consider hermaphroditic. It is what I called enrila at another time.
QUILESIA. Calyx inferior, in five parts. Corolla of five

125
petals, without little claws, alternating with the parts of the calyx, and bifid at the tip. Stamens five, alternating with five scales opposite the petals: the five filaments bearing rounded anthers. Berry somewhat compressed, elongated at the sides, with two chambers and solitary nuts, heart-shaped. New genus.
Quilesia sericea. Silky Quilesia. Trunk straight, branching. Leaves alternate, broad, lanceolate, entire, somewhat rough above and silky below. Petioles very short, with two small stipules. Flowers in a compound raceme. Calyx free, tomentose on the outside, and in five straight parts. Corolla of five oval petals, cleft at the top into two lobes, somewhat longer than the calyx, and alternating with its parts. There are also five very short scales opposite the petals. Stamens five, as long as the petals, alternating with them, with rounded anthers, white in front. Ovary seated within the flower, lentil-shaped and hairy. Style very short. Stigma slightly cleft in two. Berry elongated at the sides, with a groove that divides it in two at the partition wall, and in each chamber a nut that is heart-shaped and resembling a chickpea, with a bony and rough covering, with some other small points. = Small trees found in Ilocos, brought to notice by the diligence of Father Antonio Quilez, Augustinian, to whom I have thought it just to dedicate them, because they form a new genus. They are the height of a man, and their thickness much less than that of a wrist. The fruit in color and consistency of the flesh resembles a small apricot. When fully ripe, it is eaten and is tasty. Transplanted to gardens, I believe it would grow larger and sweeter. It is attached at the middle of its length, and is cylindrical, somewhat compressed, with a shallow channel that divides it from top to bottom in two. The chambers are always two, and the partition is fleshy. The nuts are flat below and convex above, with a pointed tip, and for that reason very similar to a chickpea. The flowers are small, and I have not seen any disk at the base. Flowers in January, Dec. New species.—Although this genus, upon closer examination of the flowers, I find has an affinity with the genera Rinorea, Conohoria, Riana, and Corynocarpo of Jussieu, it differs from them in having bifid petals, in that the stamens alternate with the petals, and in the fruit which is a berry with two small nuts. The following small tree, which in appearance resembles the Quilesia, but not in its fruit, is closely related to the genus Riana.
RIANA. Calyx in five parts. Petals five, and on their inner side, with as many smaller alternate scales. Stamens five, fixed at the bases of the small scales. Cagilla oblong, with one chamber, three compressed valves, and three seeds in the middle. Jus. Gen. pl. 287.
24

126
Riana? tricapsularis. Riana? with three little capsules. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, narrower on one side, hairy, especially underneath. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in a compound raceme. Calyx inferior, in five deep, hairy parts. Corolla of five regular, oval petals with small claws, alternating with the parts of the calyx, split at the top into two parts. Stamens five, alternating with the petals, and fixed at their claws. In addition, there are five small scales, opposite the petals and of similar color, and still other tiny scales alternating with them. Ovary with three angles, hairy. Style short. Stigma thick. Capsule with three chambers, or perhaps three small capsules joined together, with three angles and solitary seeds: one or two of these often abort, and then the capsules are compressed.= Small shrubs found in Angat, resembling the Quilesia. The leaves are a dirty straw color, and the fruit is much larger than a hazelnut, with three chambers; and although the chambers are full, it is always compressed more or less; but if one is missing, it looks like a legume to the eye. The fruits I saw were not fully ripe, and with my hand and with care I separated three complete capsules from one of them. The description was made from small branches sent by Father Antonio Llanos, parish priest of Angat, to whom I am indebted for the acquisition of not a few remarkable plants from the mountains of that town. Flowers in July. Species new.
LEEA. Calyx with five teeth. Stamens five, fixed to the outside of a five-lobed tube shaped like a jar, which bears the anthers between its lobes. Dec. Prod. vol. 1. 655.
Leea sambucina. Leea resembling elderberry. Branches swollen at the joints. Leaves twice pinnate with an odd leaflet: those of the secondary petioles at first in threes, and later simply pinnate. Leaflets somewhat lanceolate, serrate, smooth, with very prominent veins on the lower surface. Flowers in a very broad umbel-like cluster. Calyx very small, with five persistent lobes. Corolla the color of the calyx, deeply split into five parts that curl downward, and attached to the nectary nearly to its middle. Nectary globose, fleshy, ending above in a narrow mouth with five slightly notched teeth. Stamens five, fixed to the outer walls of the nectary by means of short filaments that curve inward passing between the teeth of that same nectary, to unite inside and support the anthers, which are oval, two-chambered, and united with each other only at the lower part. Ovary superior, conical, attached to the nectary. Style short and thick. Stigma simple. Berry depressed, juicy, with ridges, six chambers and as many small seeds.= Small trees with crimson flowers, which rise to

127
at a height of four to six varas. The umbel offers a very beautiful sight, being more than two feet wide: its wood is very soft and easy to work; and therefore the Indians seek it out for certain uses. The berries are large like cherries. It is known by the two names given below. Others call Abangabang a large tree that produces legumes. Fl. in August. * T., Caliantang, Abangabang.—The description given is exact, and the stipes of the anthers of which Lin. speaks are nothing but the filaments, by which they are fixed to the outer walls of the nectary, and thus hang inside its mouth. It is the Aquilicia of Lin. Syst. veg. 421.
Leea aculeata. Spiny Leea. Trunk erect, round, fistulous, with circular nodes that are not very prominent, swollen at the joints, and full of spines. Leaves opposite, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets about three pairs, ovate-lanceolate, serrate and glabrous. Petioles short. Flowers terminal, opposite the leaves, in an umbel that subdivides four or five times. Calyx inferior, very small, bell-shaped, with five small teeth. Corolla with a short tube, attached up to its midpoint to the nectary, split into five long parts, rolled back downward, and with as many grooves. Nect. a cylindrical tube, attached to the corolla, with five teeth. Stamens five, fixed at the base of the tube on the outside. Filaments rise along the length of the tube and leave their five anthers united at the base, hanging inside the nectary: among them one can see some other sterile anther. Style short and slender. Stigma simple. Berry globose, depressed, with two to four chambers, and in each one an oval seed covered with a hard membrane. = Very spiny shrubs of about five varas in height, which I saw in Arayat. They climb over neighboring trees. Fl. in Jan. * P., Malimali. New species.
MANGIFERA. Corolla of five petals. Drupe kidney-shaped. Lin. Syst. veg. 418.
Mangifera indica. Mango. Branches form a spherical crown. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, with very wavy, entire, stiff, and glabrous margins. Petioles very short. Flowers in a verticillate, racemose panicle. Calyx hairy, divided into four, five, or six pointed parts. Corolla of four, five, or six petals, twice as long as the calyx and alternate with its lanceolate parts, with the tips rolled back downward, and marked on the inside with about five or more colored (yellow) veins. Nect. cup-shaped, with five or more obtuse lobes, which are clearly visible when the flower is nearly dry. Stamens emerge from between the teeth of the nectary, numbering five; but in some flowers only one is visible, in others two, and in others three fertile ones: sometimes one is seen with two anthers.

128
Filam. very wide at the base, and the longest one projects slightly above the germen. Ant. small and oval. Germen globose, seated on the receptacle, and rising above the nectary. Style to one side of the germen, inclined toward the long stamen. Stigma simple. Drupe large, fleshy, egg-shaped and somewhat compressed with the tip twisted to one side: the nut very compressed, covered with fibers, and containing one seed.= This tree, so common in the Philippines, is generally said not to be native to the country, but to have come from India; I believe that some other variety may indeed be from there, but not all of them. Its leaves sometimes reach ten inches in length. It grows to a height of more than ten varas. It takes many years (I believe ten) to bear fruit; and in order to make it do so sooner, the Indians are accustomed to make many incisions in the trunk. They also light fires beneath the tree and in front of some thick branch during the calmest hours of the morning, hoping that the heat of the smoke will produce early mangoes, on account of the high price they fetch: in this way mangoes are sometimes available in January. During that month, or before it and continuing through June, the tree produces an infinite multitude of flowers whose pleasant fragrance can be perceived from a distance. The corollas are white. Most of them fall, and even much of the fruit that remains is lost, particularly if it rains heavily. For this reason the Indians say that when there is an abundance of mangoes, the rice harvest is poor, and abundant when there are few mangoes; and this forecast usually proves correct. Also, when there are many mangoes, there tend to be diseases, which is a consequence of the scarcity of rains. However tasty the mango fruit may claim to be, it falls far short of the excellence of some fruits of Spain, which leave nothing to be desired in terms of flavor and aroma. Spaniards, especially those recently arrived in this land, who are the ones best qualified to judge the matter, find in the mango a slight odor like that of bedbugs, according to some, or like onion, according to others; but in reality it is like tar, and perhaps from this comes the very notable empyreumatic odor of excrement during this season. Nevertheless, it is the foremost fruit of the country, and very wholesome.
The sap of the branches of the mango is caustic. Its leaves, rubbed between the fingers, give off a very pleasant smell. The young shoots and the already yellowed leaves, boiled in water, give it a flavor like tea, and some women sell it as such. In some places white cotton cloth is dyed black using mango bark, which when afterward dipped in mud (such as that found in buffalo wallows) acquires the desired color, though not a very fine one. The roots boiled in water yield a straw-yellow color, which becomes deeper with the addition of lye. Some people believe the mango fruit to be heating, without giving any reason

129
for that purpose. What is certain is that it causes drowsiness and tends to produce slight skin eruptions, similar to those sometimes caused by oranges and lemons taken frequently in the same season. This eruption, called a rash, goes away with bathing, and better still if done with rainwater or cistern water. * T., Manga. Lin. ibid.

Mangifera anisodora? Mango with anise scent? I speak of this singular mango only by hearsay, knowing at least that it is found in Sinait, a town in the north of Ilocos. It is the largest of the known mangoes and gives off an anise scent that can be perceived from a distance. The people of Sinait say that the seed has made its way to the Tagalogs; but here I have had no news of it. * Anise mango. — Others do not recognize this species of mango.

Mangifera altissima. Very tall mango. Leaves lanceolate, entire, smooth and flat. Flowers and everything else as in the common mango. The fruit is much smaller. = This tree grows taller than the mango, and without having a spherical crown like that one. The Indians eat the fruit after soaking it in a vinegar infusion, and it is sold everywhere in this manner. If it is left to ripen on the tree, they say it is as flavorful as the common mango. Flowers in January. * T., Pajo. I., Pao. Sp. distinct?

Besides the Manga and Pajo there is another variety called Pahohotan. I have not seen this tree, but I have seen the fruit, which is larger than that of the Pajo, or like a small mango. Its flavor strongly resembles that of tree pitch, and for this reason it is not prized. — There is also another species, with leaves clustered at the tips of the branches, lanceolate, entire, smooth and flat. The fruit is like that of the pajo. In Manila it is called Paopauan, and it is a large tree. To gather the edible pajos, the Indians sometimes fell the trees, cutting them down. They do this because of the great abundance of them in the forests. They do the same with the alpai. The Chinese, who are more observant and careful with their trees, I have read, make a hole in a thick root in order to gather the fruit without having to climb the trees, into which they pour a certain quantity of salt, causing the fruits to fall by themselves.

Mangifera rostrata. Beaked mango. There is still known in some places a variety of mango they call "pico" (beak): because indeed the tip of the fruit is very much bent to one side, forming a point sharper than in the other mango. The leaves are narrower. Calyx, corolla, nectary, and the veins of the petals, the same as in the other. The fruit has a slightly different smell, color and flavor; but also agreeable. The tree is smaller.

Mangifera pinnata. Winged mango. Leaves opposite, winged

130
without an odd one. Leaflets sessile, lanceolate, serrated. Flowers in a panicle. Calyx very small, with five or six teeth. Corolla of five lanceolate petals. Nectary very short, jar-shaped, woolly, with ten small teeth, nearly covering the ovary. Stamens ten, fixed at the extremities of the nectary. Filaments as long as the petals. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma thick, depressed. Fruit...= It is a tree barely known.
*T., Tagapi.
GERUMA. Calyx flat with five teeth. Petals five, truncated. Filaments united at their inner base in a ring. Stigmas three. Capsule with four or five chambers, and in each one or two seeds, fixed in a three-sided pulp. Jus. Gen. pl. 264.
Geruma? subtriloba. Geruma? THREE-LOBED TYPE. Leaves either ovate or nearly three-lobed, narrowed, serrated, with a small cluster of hairs at the base above. Petioles short. Flowers in clusters. Calyx jar-shaped, with five lobes on the limb. Corolla of five spatula-shaped petals. Stamens five, united in a cylindrical tube, and at the tip five thick anthers. Style one, very short, or nearly absent. Stigmas five, long. Upper capsule with five chambers and in each one seed.= A small tree about one vara tall, unknown to the natives. Common in Manduloyon. Flowers in July.— Could it belong to this genus?
CEDRELA. Calyx deciduous. Corolla funnel-shaped, of five petals, united from the base to their third part to the receptacle. Capsule woody, with five chambers and as many valves. Seeds clustered downward, with a membranous wing. Lin. Syst. veg. 416.
Cedrela odorata. Fragrant Cedrela. Leaves either opposite or alternate, winged. Leaflets obliquely ovate, entire and smooth. Flowers in a loose panicle. Calyx very small, one-leaved, with five teeth; at first bell-shaped, becoming flat with time. Corolla of five petals, much larger and longer than the calyx, lanceolate, hairy within, and united at the base to the lower part of the receptacle. Stamens five, close to the pistil and of equal length, fixed to the receptacle, which has five angles and is attached to the lower part of the ovary. Anthers long, incumbent, arched. Ovary globose, hairy, attached to the receptacle. Style rather thick, shorter than the corolla. Stigma shield-shaped with five angles and as many similar lines radiating from the center. Capsule nearly round, with five chambers, and in each many ovate seeds, compressed and furnished with a membranous wing.= This tree, very well known in the Islands, and called Cedro in America, though it is not a true cedar, is of the first order. The seeds have

131
one inch long, and the wings four inches from one end to the other. Its wood is flesh-colored, fragrant, and the natives use it for their small boats, because it is very durable. When burned it gives off a very pleasant smell, like juniper. I believe there are some varieties, and that the one called Alam in Mindoro is one of them. Flowers at the end of December. *T. P. Calantas. V. Lanigpa, Lanigda. Lin. ibid.

Cedrela taratara. Cedrela taratara. Leaves sometimes opposite, sometimes alternate, pinnate with or sometimes without a terminal leaflet. Leaflets about seven pairs, obliquely ovate, sometimes oblong and pointed, stiff, entire, and barely hairy underneath, and very smooth and glossy above. Petioles very short and hairless. = Large trees, well known in the islands, especially in the Visayas. I have had a piece as thick as a thigh, whose bark was flesh-colored, and the wood very hard, heavy, and pale in color, resembling that of the Asana: the leaves are about two inches long. It was sent to me from Bohol by Fr. Narciso de Jesus Maria, Augustinian Recollect. Both the wood and the bark and resin give off a smell similar to juniper. *T., Taratara. V., Sandana. C., Balongcauit.

HELICONIA. Spathe universal and partial. Calyx none. Corolla of three petals. Nectary of two leaflets. Capsule of three cells. Lin. ibid. 423.

Heliconia... There is a species of Heliconia in the Islands. A very curious person told me he had seen in Camarines a plant resembling the Musa, and that each fruit, he said, had a small leaf, which agrees very well with the characteristics of Heliconia. Fr. Delgado affirms that in Leyte there grows a species of Musa, about a fathom tall, that bears no fruit and is considered useless. Surely when he saw it, it was not the time for it to bear fruit. They call it there Manalisid, and it is very likely the same as the one from Camarines.

ARGOPHILUM. Corolla of five petals. Nectary pyramidal, with five angles, and as long as the corolla. Ovary half inferior. Lin. ibid. 418.

Argophilum pinnatum. Winged Argophilum. Leaves commonly opposite, pinnate without a terminal leaflet; rarely with one. Leaflets about seven pairs, slightly notched at the base, ovate, very elongated, entire, hairless (when mature) above, and hairy below. Petioles very short. Flowers terminal in compound spikes, with striated common peduncles. Calyx half superior, with five round, leathery leaflets, very hairy on the outside. Corolla of five round petals, converging, leathery, without claws, and of the interior color of the calyx. Nectary a small bladder somewhat shorter than the corolla, globose, with five sides and a small hole at the tip. Stamens five, more

132
shorter than the nectary, and fixed within it, on the receptacle. Filaments very short. Anthers large, oval, and simply appressed. Germen submerged in the calyx, with a conical and superior apex. Style very short. Stigma rounded. Fruit...= A small tree found in Angat and not well known. The wood is hard; the leaves are long, about a hand-span, and nearly two inches wide at the base, very densely covered underneath with down. The spikes are terminal and numerous; the spikelets are one inch long. Flowers in March. New species?

GRONOVIA. Five petals and five stamens, inserted in a bell-shaped calyx. Berry inferior, dry, with one seed. Lin. ibid. 420.

Gronovia ternata. Ternate Gronovia. Stem twining, striate. Leaves alternate, ternate. Leaflets broad, oval, pointed, with very small hooks underneath, with five veins, and tendrils in the axils. Flowers axillary, in compound racemes. Calyx half-colored, bell-shaped, divided nearly to the base into five parts. Corolla of five petals, fixed at the divisions of the calyx margin, lanceolate, lined with down on the inside. Stamens five, shorter than the corolla, fixed on the receptacle, alternating with the petals, with two small stalked glands between each filament. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma globose, with many lobes. Fruit inferior, with two or three chambers.= A twining plant, which I have seen in Malinta. Its smell is between pleasant and disagreeable. It is not known to the natives. Perhaps the same species. Scandens of Lin. ibid.

BALINGAYUM. Calyx adherent, split into five parts. Petals five, ending in two lateral appendages. Style one. Stigmas three, with two lobes. Capsule crowned with the calyx and with six seeds.

Balingayum decumbens. Prostrate Balingayo. Stem herbaceous, round, lying on the ground. Leaves alternate, sessile, oblong and narrow, smooth, with some remote small teeth and another lobe at the base. Flowers solitary. Peduncles rather long. Calyx adherent, with the margin split into five lanceolate segments. Corolla of five petals, linear, ending in two lateral appendages that close together, forming a sort of hood. Stamens five, fixed on the receptacle, shorter than the corolla. Anthers compressed, ending in a beak. Style one, short and thick. Stigmas three (the middle one shortest), very broad, each with two fringed lobes. Capsule oval, single-chambered, with six compressed seeds.= A rare plant, small, lying on the ground, and smooth. I saw it in Malinta, and it is not well known; it grows in very damp places. * T., Balingayo.— The said plant seems likely to form a new genus;

133
although it closely resembles the Jussiaea, and the Oenothera. I have given it the name by which the Indians called it.
(MALULUCBAN.) Leaves alternate, lanceolate, wavy, stiff, entire and smooth. Petioles very short, without stipules. Flowers axillary, very small, in compound clusters. Calyx monophyllous, in five parts. Corolla none. Stamens five, fixed at the lower part of the calyx, shorter than it, and opposite its lobes. Filaments short. Anthers oval. Ovary seated within the calyx, and surrounded at the base by a ring of five lobes. Style thick, very short. Stigma thick, and at maturity with about eight or ten rays. Drupe oval, crowned with the radiating and deciduous stigma, slightly fleshy, with a thin, bony stone containing one uniform seed. = Small trees of two or three fathoms in height, of white wood, and common in Malinta. The flowers are very small; the fruit smaller than a cherry, and of a pale color. The stamens are not fixed on the ring, but on the calyx. Flowers in January. *T., Malulucban. — It does not correspond to any genus in my way of thinking.

ACHYRANTHES. Calyx of five leaflets. Corolla none. Stigma in two parts. Seeds solitary. Lin. Syst. Veg. 423.
Achyranthes Aspera. Rough Achyranthes. Stem angular and hairy. Leaves opposite, hairy, clasping the stem at the base, lanceolate, very blunt, and wavy. Flowers turned downward, placed in a very long and semi-whorled spike, with many small florets. Calyx of five scales, stiff, awl-shaped, and pressing against one another, with three other scales at the base, resembling the calyx, lanceolate, and colored. Corolla none. Nectary much smaller than the calyx, monophyllous, cleft in five parts, with frayed ends. Stamens five at the ends of the nectary. Ovary top-shaped, with the upper part somewhat concave. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma thick, and appearing divided into two parts. Fruit a single seed covered with two membranes, one that covers it entirely, and another outer one that adheres only at one point. = This plant grows to a height of three feet. Its leaves, crushed and applied to sores infested with worms, kill them. The calyxes cling to the clothing of those who brush against it. Flowers in November. * T. Hangor, Hangot, Docotdecot, Libai. V. Hangor. P. Angud. Lin. ibid. — I believe this is the plant that the learned Fr. Clain calls Salimbagat, Salimbangon, Calimbangon.
There is another species, with opposite leaves clasping the stem at the base; lanceolate, blunt and hairy. Flowers in a spike: each partial peduncle, which is very short, bears two or three small flowers, and not just one. Calyx cleft almost to the base into five blunt, soft parts. Ovary cylindrical. Stigma in two parts. — Plant like the previous one. T. Hangor.
25

134
There is yet another, with flowers bearing two bracts, formed from two small bundles of flesh-colored awns, like spines. There is also another with two bracts composed of small bundles of awns arranged in a star pattern. I am inclined to consider these as belonging to the species echinata.
Achyranthes Villosa. Woolly Achyranthes. Stem square, barely branched. Leaves sessile, opposite, half-lanceolate, clasping the stem at the base. Flowers axillary, in an egg-shaped, oblong spike, with many small flowers, closely packed, and woolly at the base. Calyx compressed, of five lanceolate leaflets; three flat, and two keeled, with a bract of three leaflets at the base, the same color as the calyx. Nectary: a membrane surrounding the ovary up to its midpoint, single-veined, with six teeth, which are the filaments of the stamens. Stamens: three complete, and three rudimentary, all fixed to the said membrane surrounding the ovary. Filaments flat, awl-shaped, and shorter than the corolla. Anthers of the three fertile stamens, nearly oval. Ovary seated within the flower, heart-shaped, very compressed. Style single, very short. Stigma single, obtuse. One kidney-shaped seed, covered with a membrane. = This plant grows in Pasig. Its height barely a quarter-span. The natives scarcely know it. Flowers in January. *T, Bonga bonga. Lin. ibid. 424. — By reason of the opposite leaves, it does not appear to be the Achyranthes lanata of Linnaeus.
CELOSIA. Calyx of three leaflets, resembling the petals, which are five. Stamens united at the base, with a folded Nectary. Capsule that splits horizontally. Lin. Syst. Veg. 425.
Celosia Lanata. Woolly Celosia. Stem erect, somewhat hairy. Leaves alternate, between round and oval, hairy. Petioles short. Flowers axillary, in divergent spikes, very closely packed, full of small flowers that form spiral lines. Calyx bell-shaped, divided into five deep, pointed, very hairy segments. Nectary: a membrane with ten teeth, which are the filaments of the stamens, of which two are perfect and eight are sterile. Fruit a single seed. = It is a plant one foot tall; the spikes very fluffy, white, and about one inch long. It is common in various places. Flowers in May. Lin. ibid. 425.
Celosia Coccinea. Scarlet Celosia. Stem erect, striate. Leaves alternate, clasping the stem at the base, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Flowers in very densely packed, conical spikes, terminating in a large, fleshy, half-moon-shaped blade, also covered with small flowers. Calyx (if it should be considered as such) three small lanceolate colored scales. Corolla (according to others the calyx, in which case there is no corolla) of five lanceolate colored scales. Nectary encircling the ovary, single-veined, with five or six teeth, which are the filaments of the stamens. Stamens five or six, shorter than the calyx.

135
Anthers elongated, versatile. Ovary globose, seated within the flower. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma somewhat thick. Capsule that breaks open horizontally, with many lenticular and lustrous seeds. = This plant, which I have seen in gardens, has a very beautiful appearance, owing to the unusual arrangement and vivid crimson color of its flowers. I do not know whether it is a native plant. Flowers in December.* Palonpalongan. Lin. ibid.
Celosia Glauca. Glaucous-colored Celosia. Stem erect. Leaves alternate, green above and purple below, lanceolate, glabrous. Petioles very short. Flowers almost sessile, in axillary racemes. Calyx inferior, with five laciniae reaching halfway. Corolla none. Nectary a small tube with five small teeth, which are the filaments of the stamens. Ovary globose, seated within the flower. Style none. Stigmas three, broad and very short. Capsules with many small seeds, attached to a central axis. = A small plant, which I saw at Punta Mal-abrigo, and is found in many places. Its leaves, which are green above and purple below, are used by the indigenous people to heal wounds. It may perhaps be a variety of the glauca species of Pers. Syn. plant. t. 1. 260.
Celosia Argentea. Silver-colored Celosia. Stem with striations. Leaves alternate, sessile, lanceolate, nearly entire, and glabrous. Flowers in a long, conical head, and sometimes, though rarely, interrupted with sessile florets. Calyx (see cel. cristata) of three lanceolate bracteoles, barely colored, keeled; the lower one smaller. Corolla of five lanceolate, keeled, and membranous petals. Nectary bell-shaped, single-leafed in five parts, folded at the edges and awn-tipped, which are the five filaments of the stamens. Ovary nearly globose, seated within the nectary. Style one. Stigma somewhat thick, depressed with two lobes. Capsule club-shaped, breaking open horizontally, with one chamber and more than twenty very small, lenticular seeds, cut with 6 faces or facets, and very glabrous. = A common plant in cultivated fields, known to the indigenous people in Batangas. It grows to a height of five feet. The cooked leaves are eaten, but women who are menstruating should abstain from this food. The spikes are more than two inches long and are white, with a slight rosy tinge. Flowers in September.* T. Cadayohan, Quindayohan. Lin ibid.
DEERINGIA. Calyx with three bracts, and in five parts. Filaments united below in the shape of a cruet. Style in three parts. Berry with many seeds. Spr. Syst. veg. t. 1. 522.
Deeringia Celosioides. Celosia-like Deeringia. Trunk spreads over neighboring trees, with furrowed, grooved branches. Leaves scattered, lanceolate, ovate, sinuate,

136
and somewhat hairy. Short petioles. Axillary flowers, in long, compound racemes. Very short proper peduncle. Calyx fitted with three scales; the most distant one with five linear leaflets, which curl downward at maturity. Corolla none. Stamens five, divergent, the length of the corolla. Filaments are the elongated angles of a proper membrane, single-leafed, surrounding the germ. Germ seated within the flower, globose, and lobed. Style short and thick. Three stigmas, turned downward. Berry with three angles, very small, hollow, fleshy, globose, red at maturity, with four or six heart-shaped seeds, compressed, and fixed by small stalks at the base of the berry. = This weak shrub, of some two or three yards in height, is little known among the natives. I have seen it in many places. It ought to be made known in the same way as other similar plants, on account of its dyeing properties. Its leaves, pounded and placed in water, impart within less than two hours a more or less black color, which I believe could serve in place of China ink for shading. Flowers in December. * V Hanlilimocon. T. Hagorilis. Spr. Syst. veg. 816 — it closely resembles Celosia baccata of Linnaeus. — The one called Hanlilimocon in Cebu, which serves the schoolchildren for writing, has smooth leaves with a red petiole. This is common in many places, and it is impossible not to notice it in the month of December, owing to the abundance of its flowers.
There are other small trees with finely notched leaves. Could no use be made of these trees, even if only for dyeing paper?
QUILAMUN. Calyx inferior, with five laciniae, rarely four. Corolla none. Stamens five, rarely four, fixed in the incisions of the calyx. Cagilla? compressed, with two compartments and many seeds. Style longer than the flower, with the stigma in a small head. New genus?
Quilamum Luteum. Yellow Quilano. Trunk straight, tree-like. Leaves opposite, broad, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Very short petioles. Axillary flowers, in compound racemes. Calyx bell-shaped, fuzzy, with five laciniae; rarely four. Corolla none. Stamens five, rarely four, fixed in the incisions of the calyx. Filaments the length of the calyx. Anthers oval, flat, and single-celled. Germ superior, conical, compressed, with two grooves. Style twice as long as the calyx, curved. Stigma in a small head. Cagilla? seated on the calyx, compressed, with two grooves, two compartments, and many small seeds fixed on the axis of the cagilla. = Small trees that grow in Angat, as large as a thigh. The wood is hard, and the leaves are about four inches long. The flowers are small and pale-colored, and from here

137
taken the name of the species. As in my view it does not belong to any known genus, I have formed this new one, giving it the name that some Indians use for tala, although I am not sure whether they may have been mistaken. It differs from Calicot in that this one barely has a style, and possesses only two seeds in the drupe; but the quilamum has many, and moreover the fruit of this one, although I have not seen it ripe, seems to be more of a cagilla than a drupe. Flowers in April. * T. Quilamo.
(CALICOT.) Branches star-shaped. Leaves opposite, winged without an odd one. Leaflets three or four pairs, egg-shaped, oblong, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in racemose panicles. Calyx inferior, bell-shaped, in five parts. Corolla none. Stamens five, fixed at the divisions of the calyx. Filaments exserted and long. Anthers with two chambers. Ovary globose, seated within the flower. Style none. Stigma a prominence. Drupe somewhat fleshy, round (smaller than a pea), compressed, with a bony and thin nut, two chambers, and in each one a seed. = Trees that I have seen in Agoo, and they are almost unknown to the natives. — It does not agree with the Hedycrea of Linnaeus or the Licania of other authors because its fruit has two chambers. They also differ from Amanoa and other genera. For this reason I leave them thus.
** PISONIA. Flowers polygamous, either dioecious or trioecious. Corolla (calyx according to Jussieu) bell-shaped, cleft in five parts. In hermaphrodite flowers. Stamens five or seven. Superior cagilla, with one chamber, without valves, and with one seed. Lin. Syst. Veg. 431.
Pisonia aculeata. PISONIA WITH SPINES. Flowers dioecious, in compound racemes, with opposite and horizontal peduncles. * Males. Trunk with alternating middle spines, on the opposite branches. Calyx (corolla according to Lin.) with six teeth and fitted with two or three small leaflets already in the form of a calyx; or, when there are two, nearly opposite. Stamens six, fixed on the receptacle; the three alternate ones longer, all exserted. The anther of one of the three shorter stamens is the largest. Ovary oval. Style short. Stigma small. Fruit none. * Females. Trunk with opposite hooks. Leaves heaped at the nodes, broad, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers in compound racemes with opposite peduncles. Calyx like that of the males, with five teeth on the rim, striate, with five double rows of globose glands, and with a small stalk that secretes gum. Corolla none. Stamens none. Ovary oblong, enclosed within the calyx. Style one, short. Stigmas two, thick, each subdividing into four or five. One oblong seed, covered entirely by the calyx, which is bristled with the same gummy hairs. = Shrub of the al-

138
the height of a man, which I have seen in Malinta and in a place in
Batangas called Pinamoccan, in Mandaloyon and in Ilocos. The
calyxes stick to clothing and to the hands, by means of the
gum or birdlime they secrete, in which respect this plant greatly resembles
the one called Sandicgquit, a species of Plumbago. Boys
scatter some grains of rice in a convenient spot, interspersing
some small branches bearing fruit, and in this way turtledoves
and quails, called pogos, which happen to get a seed
stuck to their feathers, are lost, because instead of being able
to shake it off, they become more and more entangled, and thus they are caught.
Flowers in January. *T., Digquit digquit. I., Puriquit. in Angat, Pa-
nacla. Lin. ibid.
GOVANIA. Calyx with five laciniae. Corolla of five petals,
in the manner of scales. Stamens five, wrapped with the scales.
Style divided into three parts. Fruit inferior, with three sides or
three wings, and three chambers and solitary seeds. (Dec. Prod.
p. 2. 38.) Male flowers are found among the hermaphrodites. Lin.
ibid. 432. Jus. Gén. pl. 381.
Govania domingensis. Govania of Santo Domingo. Trunk
branching, which spreads over neighboring trees. Leaves alternate,
ovate, with five nerves, with small serrations, and somewhat
hairy. Petioles short, with two stipules at the base. Flowers
in racemose panicles, with a simple tendril at the base of the common
peduncle of the flowers. Calyx superior, bell-shaped,
(whitish) divided into five pointed parts, and with
five small scales, opposite the laciniae, and fixed near
their base. Corolla of five small petals, hood-shaped,
inserted in the divisions of the edge of the calyx (as in
Rhamnus.) Stamens five, placed inside the hoods,
and with globose anthers. Ovary conical. Styles three, turned
to the sides. Stigmas blunt. Capsule with three sharp
angles, and three small separable compartments, without wings, and with
solitary seeds. = A shrub which I have seen in Angat, reaching the height
of three varas. The Indians give it no name. Flowers in December.
Lin. ibid.

PENTANDRIA.

DIGINIA.

** CELTIS. Male flowers mixed with hermaphrodite
ones, on the same plant. Corolla none. * Hermaphrodite flowers.
Calyx in five parts. Drupe with one chamber and one enclosed seed.
* Male flowers. Calyx in six parts. Stamens six. Lin.
Syst. veg. 456.

139
Celtis philippensis. Philippine Hackberry. Branches somewhat forked. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, entire, smooth, stiff, with three veins. Axillary flowers in panicles. Calyx free, in five very deep, concave divisions, somewhat hairy at the edges. Corolla none. Stamens five, nearly the length of the calyx, fixed between its base and the receptacle. Ovary cylindrical, very thick. Style none. Stigmas two thick, short laminae, curved inward. Drupe (like a chickpea) globose, thicker in the middle, slightly fleshy, with four indistinct angles and some ridges, with a bony nut bearing a black line dividing it from top to bottom into two chambers, with one seed. = This tree is of the second order. The natives use it for various purposes; because its wood is very good, white, clean, and quite hard. They call it Malaitmo, because its leaves resemble those of the Itmo or Betel. It is very common in various places and quite well known. * T., Malaitmo. New species.

Celtis lima. Lima Hackberry. Leaves alternate, with two angular notches at the base, ovate, very pointed, finely serrate, very rough on top, with short hairs, and hairy underneath. All flowers hermaphrodite, axillary, in half-umbellate racemes. Calyx inferior, deeply cleft into five keeled, hairy divisions. Corolla none. Stamens five, fixed to the receptacle, the length of the calyx. Filaments awl-shaped. Anthers with two cells, projecting slightly beyond the calyx after shedding their pollen. Style shorter than the stamens. Ovary thick and compressed. Stigmas two points, and when the fruit is somewhat large, they become elongated, broad, hairy, and curved inward. Drupe fleshy, ovate, appearing to have four sides, the two most notable of which contain a rough nut with one seed. = This tree is of the third order: its fruit is small: the Indian fishermen on the sea of Batangas know it well; because they rub their cotton fishing lines with its bark, which then become dyed with a beautiful, dark crimson varnish, very slippery and impenetrable to water. The crimson color turns black when the lines are wetted. I have not seen male flowers. Flowers in May. * T., Hanarion. Lin. ibid.

GOMPHRENA. Calyx colored: the outer part of three small leaves; the two keeled ones pressing against each other. Petals five, poorly formed and hairy. Nectary cylindrical, with five teeth. Style split halfway in two. Capsule with one seed. Lin. ibid. 455.

Gomphrena globosa. Globe Amaranth. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, joined and hairy. Terminal flowers, arranged in numbers of more than fifty, in a globose head, with two

140
small leaflets, egg-shaped at the base. Cal. of the small flower with
three scales, leathery and colored: the two that approach each other,
with a very sharp back; the third very small and exterior. Cor. of
five very narrow, stiff, flat, straight, awl-shaped petals, bordered with
wool along the edges. Nect. funnel-shaped, very small, with the edge
divided into five notched parts. Stam. five, fixed near the edges of the
nectary. Filam. nearly none. Ant. fixed by their middle. Germen
egg-shaped, very small. Style one, rather long. Stigmas two, turned
downward. One lenticular seed, very small, covered by the membrane
of the ovary. = This well-known plant, whose flowers are called in Spain
Perpetuas, is annual and grows to a height of two feet. The calyxes are
flesh-colored, which makes the flower quite showy. There is also a
white-flowered variety. Fl. in Jan. *T., Buquingan. Lin. ibid.—The
third small leaflet of the calyx is more properly a scale, which each
small flower has at its base.

Gomphrena volubilis. Twining Gomphrena. Stem round,
twining. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, egg-shaped, entire, smooth,
fleshy, and running along a very short petiole. Flowers axillary,
in a simple, cylindrical raceme, surrounded by countless small flowers,
with their own very short peduncles. Cal. membranous, compressed,
of two keeled pieces along the back, where they have a wide semicircular
wing. Cor. in five oval parts, somewhat shorter than the calyx and the
same color as it. Stam. five, fixed on a membrane of their own, situated
below the germen, divided into five awl-shaped parts that form the
filaments. Ant. split into two diverging parts. Germen seated within the
flower. Style one, very short, divided into three long parts. Stigmas
fork-shaped. One seed covered by a membrane, within the persistent
calyx, and with two wings. = A plant with a red, twining stem, that
smells bad, about one or three fathoms tall, common in Parañaque. It is
notable for its racemes, which rise perpendicularly. Fl. in Nov. A new
species, and perhaps a variety of the arborescens of Lin. or of the
vermicularis of Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 257.

CHENOPODIUM. Cal. of five leaflets, with five ribs. Cor. none.
Seed one, lentil-shaped, superior, and covered by the calyx. Lin. ibid. 448.

Chenopodium ambrosioides. Chenopodium like Ambrosia.
Stem with many angles, scattered with hairs. Leaves lanceolate,
serrated, with large and widely spaced teeth. Flowers sessile, axillary,
in small clusters. Cal. in five concave parts forming five angles. Cor.
none. Stam. five. Filaments compressed, fixed toward the center of the
flower, and opposite the parts of the calyx. Anthers as if divi-

141
divided into two globose parts. Ovary superior, globose, de-
pressed. Styles none. Stigmas two, three, or four, short,
diverging from one another. Fruit a single lenticular seed, covered
by the skin of the ovary. = This plant reaches a height
of two feet. It has a very strong odor; and although
it is pleasant, it soon becomes disagreeable. An Author states that this plant
preserves books from worms; and if this is true, it must be held in
high esteem in these Islands. The Indians eat it cooked. The whole
plant promotes sweating, urination, and menstruation, and is very
useful in moist asthma and in chronic pulmonary catarrh. The
decoction of the root, drunk by one suffering from tertian fever, at the
time the chill comes on, and after this operation is performed two or three
times, wrapping oneself up afterward to sweat, is said to cure it:
its seeds drunk in wine dull and prevent the feeling of
blows or lashes: this is what has been written about it in the islands. The word
Apasotis is from America, and the true name according to the Spanish
translation of Linnaeus is Epazolt. Flowers in May. * T. V. P. Apo-
sotis. Lin. ibid. 449.
PERGULARIA. Corolla twisted, salver-shaped. Nectary surrounds
the stamens and pistil; and ends in five half arrow-
head-shaped points. Lin. Syst. Veg. 440.
Pergularia glabra. Smooth Pergularia. Stem prostrate
on the ground. Leaves opposite, heart-shaped, ovate, pointed,
with a cluster of dry glands at the upper base.
Petioles short. Flowers in umbels. Calyx half as short as
the corolla, deeply cleft into five parts. Corolla twist-
ed, inflated, in five horizontal parts, with the margins
rolled downward, and the throat hairy. Nectary of five simple
hornlets, flat on the back. Stamens five. Fila-
ments five pointed scales, hidden beneath the nectary, bearing
five anthers on their inner surface. In addition, between each
anther there is a small black body with two little threads, carrying
two small oval glands. Ovary divided into two parts. Style
one. Stigma one, thick, conical, compressed. Fruit . . . = This
plant sprawls on the ground and is known in Manila by the name of
mil leguas (thousand leagues), because it extends over a great distance: its flowers are
barely fragrant. * Mil leguas Lin. ibid.
Pergularia glandulosa. Glandular Pergularia. Stem twining,
with swollen nodes. Leaves opposite, heart-shaped,
with the margins rolled downward, with a small cluster
of glands at the base of the upper surface. Petioles
with two very small, stiff glands or points at the
base. Flowers very numerous, in umbels that divide twice.
Nectary of five hornlets, concave on the back. Calyx,
Corolla, Stamens, and the rest, as in the previous species. = This plant
spreads widely along the ground. Its flowers do not

142
they have no smell. I have seen it in Bauang. Flowers in June. New
species.

STAPELIA. Corolla twisted and flat. Nectary: two little stars of
five pieces that cover the genitals. Lin. ibid. 447. Jus.
Gen. pl. 146.

Stapelia quadrangula. Four-angled Stapelia. Stem twining; and when old, angular and cork-like. Leaves heart-shaped, egg-shaped, entire, somewhat hairy, with a group of small glands at the base of the upper surface. Petioles nearly as long as the leaves. Flowers lateral, in a simple umbel, with five or more small florets. Calyx very small, in five parts. Corolla fleshy, flat, smooth. Nectary: a star with five pointed lobes, placed flat on the corolla, and with five very small horns at the tips of the lobes. Two cylindrical follicles, pointed at both horizontal ends, with many imbricated seeds, membranous, and with a pappus. = This plant climbs the tallest trees; and when the stem is already very large and old, it has four or five very large angles, with the appearance of cork. The flowers have no notable smell; they are green on the outside and yellow on the inside. The calyces are very small. * Local name: Bini-guasan. — It may rather be the Cinancho Suberoso of Linnaeus? Lin. ibid.

Stapelia meliflua. Honey-producing Stapelia. Stem smooth, twining. Leaves opposite, egg-shaped, oblong, stiff, very fleshy, smooth, with the margins rolled downward, and with a gland at the base. Flowers very numerous, lateral, in an umbel. Calyx in five oval parts. Corolla flat, lined with down. Nectary of five egg-shaped, pointed, flat pieces, laid upon the corolla, with a slit below through which much honey distills. = I place this plant here on account of the corolla and nectary: it spreads along the ground. A decoction of it is used for women after childbirth; but I do not know in what manner. Flowers in June. * Local name: Balicbalic. New species?

HOYA. Corolla wheel-shaped. The column containing the pistils (gynostegium) surrounded by depressed, fleshy scales, with a small tooth that covers the pollen mass from within. Spr. Syst. Veg. Lin. t. 1. 525.

Hoya carnosa. Fleshy Hoya. Stem twining. Leaves oval, fleshy, smooth, with small glands on the upper base. Flowers in an umbel of many small florets, with long little stalks. Calyx in five parts. Corolla flat in five parts, and inside five pieces, enlarged at the center with five erect scales that cover the ovary from below. = An exotic creeper that spreads greatly, and which curious people cultivate in gardens. * Called "Flor de piedra" (stone flower), flowers in July. * = In Paris, Hoya Azaola.

143
CYNANCHUM. Corolla twisted. Nectary cylindrical, with double angles, and with five teeth. Two follicles, and the receptacle elevated. Lin. Syst. Veg. 441.
Cynanchum viminale. Osier Cynanchum. The stem extends along the ground and climbs trees, curling around at the tips. No leaves; but instead of these, the branches are fused to one another at the tips, or as if jointed; unless one wishes to say that the leaves are cylindrical and fused to one another, as in the Opuntia. Axillary flowers, in a simple umbel, with about seven small florets. Calyx very small, in five parts. Corolla much larger than the calyx, in five deep, lanceolate parts. Nectary a disk with ten angles; the five alternating ones are smaller, and in the center five small horns rise up. Ovary of two small conical bodies. Styles two. = This plant is common at Punta de Azufre. Its flowers are very fragrant, and resemble those called "mil leguas" in Manila. Flowers in February. Lin. ibid.
Cynanchum? hirtum. Stiff-haired Cynanchum? I place here the following plant; (although, not having seen its flowers, I am not very certain of the genus.) Stem twining.
