Leaves opposite, somewhat heart-shaped, ovate, elongated and pointed: One follicle large (the other aborts), nearly pyramidal, warty, with four angles running from one end to the other, with uneven edges and teeth. Seeds compressed, imbricate, and with a pappus. = A plant I have seen in Manila. Should flower in May.
Cynanchum tenellum. Slender Cynanchum. Leaves opposite, lanceolate. Fruit two small follicles, with many seeds, with a pappus. = A twining plant, with a very slender stem, and very small, crimson flowers. Its virtues for curing wounds, however mortal they may be, are said by the Indians to be astonishing; but all of this has no foundation whatsoever. Lin. ibid. 442.
APOCYNUM. Two follicles. Corolla bell-shaped. Nectaries five glands, with as many bristles.
Apocynum mucronatum. Pointed Apocynum. Leaves opposite, ovate-lanceolate, with a small notch and a tuft of hair at the base, terminating at the apex with a stiff, fleshy point, with the edges rolled downward. Petioles very short. Lateral flowers, in an umbel dividing into four or more parts. Calyx inferior, of five ovate, pointed pieces. Corolla much longer than the calyx, twisted, somewhat rolled downward, funnel-shaped, somewhat swollen, in five linear and pointed parts, and with the throat open and bare. Receptacle isolated, nearly globose, which con-

144
it has the nectaries, stamens, and pistil. Nect. five double, fleshy scales, one over the other, the outer one larger. Filam. none. Ant. five, with two chambers, placed at the end of the receptacle, and covered by the scales of the nectary. Germens two, egg-shaped. Style one, thick, marked with a line that crosses the receptacle and projects far beyond it. Stigma with two lobes. Two follicles, somewhat woody, long, linear, tapering to a point at the tip, flat on one side, with many tightly packed seeds, and a pappus. = This twining plant, which exudes a milky sap, and whose seeds were sent to me from China, rises to the height of a man, coiling around everything it encounters. Its stem is about a line thick; the leaves two inches long. When steeped in water, they impart no notable color to it. The throat of the corolla is very wide and bare, and has no crown. Therefore it cannot belong to the genus Norium as I had been assured, and so I have placed it in Apocynum, because it seems to me not to differ from it as much as from others. Flowers in May.
ASCLEPIAS. Cor. twisted. Nect. five, egg-shaped, concave, each producing a small horn on the outside. Two follicles and the receptacle free. Lin. ibid. 444.
Asclepias Syriaca. Syrian Asclepiad. Root fibrous, whitish. Stem erect, smooth, and barely branched when the plant is old. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire. Petioles very short and channeled. Flowers lateral in an umbel, or simple parasol, containing from eight to eleven small florets. Common peduncle of the umbel very long; the individual ones also very long. Cal. of five leaflets, inferior. Cor. cleft almost to the base into five egg-shaped lobes, drooping downward. Receptacle isolated, containing the nectaries, stamens, and pistils. Nect. five small tubes, cut diagonally, in the manner of a sleeve or hood; and from the center five small horns emerge, flesh-colored, inclined toward each other, and nearly meeting in the middle. Stam. five. Filam. membranous and firm. Ant. a black point, with two appendages hanging from small threads at the sides, approaching an oval shape. Germens two, beneath the nectaries. Styles none. Stigma a thick little body. Two lanceolate follicles, swollen in the middle and pointed at the end (one regularly aborts), which split lengthwise along a suture. Seeds very numerous, imbricated, compressed, elliptical, with a large, long, hairy pappus. = This plant, with very beautiful flowers, rises to a height of six feet. The corollas are flesh-colored; the nectaries are saffron-colored; and the leaves are five inches long. Those who wish to learn about the benefits this plant can provide, let them hear the Abbot Ro-

145
zier in his Dictionary of Agriculture, vol. 3, entry Asclepiade.
"When the fruit begins to open, he says, it is cut and left to dry; the seed is then separated from the floss or down, and stored in sacks.
In 1757, the Agricultural Society of Brittany undertook the cultivation of this plant; and in 1762, Fontanes, a member of the Agricultural Society of La Rochelle, made two hats in Niort from the down of an asclepias that grows naturally in the sandy lands of Lower Poitou. This down is shorter than that of the Syrian asclepias, and so the hats came out somewhat thick.
La Rouviere, a manufacturer of woolen fabrics from the Ney region in Paris, carded and spun it; and with it he currently makes velvets, baizes, and flannels superior to those of England, fabrics resembling those of the Indies, baizes, stockings, caps, and, in a word, every kind of woven goods. He presented all of this to the Academy of Sciences in Paris in the year 1760.
In order to card this down, which is so light that the slightest breeze would scatter it, it is necessary to keep it enclosed in a sack and expose it to steam from hot water. I do not know whether Rouviere managed to card it alone; but it is a very easy thing to do by placing one layer of cotton or silk, then one of down, and so on alternately. The silk or cotton gives body to the down.
The down of the Asclepias does not take black dye as perfectly as wool or silk do; but it is certain that if we knew the methods that Folie used to dye linen and hemp black, we could achieve that color with it as well.
Even if this down were not used to make fabrics, it would still be very useful to cultivate the plant, for stuffing blankets, etc.
The stalk, retted like that of linen and hemp, and then prepared in the same way, yields a very long, very fine fiber of brilliant whiteness. This plant deserves in every respect to be cultivated."
So far the Abbot Rozier; but it seems to me that the preparation and processing of the stalk is not as easy as Rozier implies. Moreover, some authors say that today this plant has fallen into disuse and is not highly regarded. There are other species of Asclepias in the Islands whose floss, and even whose leaves, can be spun.
The seed of this plant was brought from Manila to the town of Bauang some years ago, and the natives planted it in pots, tending it with care; but today it has multiplied enormously everywhere. Its root is purgative.* T. Bulac Castila.

146
This species is very close to the Curas savica. Much has been written, with varying opinions, about the medicinal virtues of the asclepiads — some granting them such virtues, others denying them, and still others regarding even some celebrated species with suspicion.

GIANT ASCLEPIAS. VERY TALL ASCLEPIAD. Stem erect, branched, and very woolly. Leaves sessile, opposite, cleft at the base, oval, fleshy, and downy. Lateral flowers in a simple umbel, with three or more small florets. Calyx of five sepals. Corolla monopetalous, divided into five pointed parts. Nectaries five, united along their length to the receptacle: the bases coiled most elegantly in a spiral outward, then curving back inward in the opposite direction, perfectly imitating the sides of a fleur-de-lis: at the upper part, each nectary has two small prominences placed at its sides; above the nectaries there is a crown of five angles forming the tip of the receptacle, and at each angle a black anther. Two large follicles, somewhat tapered at the ends, downy, and with the apex bent somewhat to one side, containing many imbricated seeds furnished with long pappus. = It is found in Bauang and Taal, and is not very common: it grows to a height of seven or eight feet, and the leaves are about six inches long. The pappus or fluff of this species is easier to spin than that of the previous one, but is not as white. The most remarkable thing about this plant is its flowers, on account of their very beautiful and most unusual shape. They are entirely white. Flowers in April.* Local name: Capal capal. Lin. ibid. 445.

WANDERING ASCLEPIAS. WANDERING ASCLEPIAD. Stem twining, angular. Leaves opposite, ovate, oblong, entire, with a cluster of small glands at the base of the upper surface. Axillary flowers, few in number, in an umbel. Calyx in five parts. Corolla flat, in five parts. Nectary of five scales placed on the upper part of the elevated receptacle, alternating with the stamens. Two large follicles, oval, woody, with a wing also woody, running from one side from one end to the other, containing a chamber, and inside many imbricated seeds, without hair or pappus. = This singular plant is twining. It is found in waterlogged terrain near the sea, in Bauang. The scales of the nectary can be bent easily outward, but then return to their former position, and so they appear to have a small foot.
It does not agree with the apocinaceous plants lacking pappus; but on account of the receptacle I have placed it here. Perhaps it will prove to be a new genus.

DAEMIA ASCLEPIAD. DEMIA ASCLEPIAD. Stem twining, smooth. Leaves opposite, somewhat heart-shaped, oblong, entire,

147
and smooth: the upper ones approach a lanceolate shape. Flowers in a lateral umbel, from which other umbels successively emerge, also lateral. Nectaries straight. Two follicles (one almost always aborts) very pointed. = This plant climbs, twining around everything it encounters. The pappus of the seeds is shorter than that of the Asclepias syriaca; but it is fine and very white. The fruit is about two inches long. Flowers in November. Lin. ibid. 444.

Asclepias Carnosa. Fleshy Asclepiad. Trunk twining, smooth. Leaves lanceolate, somewhat fleshy and smooth. Flowers in a simple lateral umbel, containing more than twelve small florets. Nectaries straight, pointed at both ends, and joined in the middle. Fruit... = A shrub whose fruit I have not seen. It climbs by twining around neighboring trees. Both the bark of the stem and the leaves themselves contain fibers so soft that I believe this plant could be of great utility. The leaves are thick, but not as much as those of Stapelia Meliflua. Flowers in March. Lin. ibid. 446.

CARMONEA. Calyx persistent, in five parts. Corolla wheel-shaped. Styles capillary. Drupe globose, with six chambers and solitary seeds. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 290.

Carmonea Heterophylla. Diverse-leaved Carmonea. Trunk erect, very branchy. Leaves sometimes alternate, sometimes clustered at the nodes in groups of three or four; sometimes lanceolate and broader toward the tip, sometimes spatula-shaped, with three teeth at the apex, the middle one larger and rounded; sometimes serrated toward the tip, covered with short, stiff hairs. Petioles almost absent. Flowers axillary, in a kind of racemose panicle, with few small florets. Common peduncle long. Individual peduncle short. Calyx free, bell-shaped, persistent; split almost to the base into five lanceolate, narrow, and hairy lobes. Corolla bell-shaped, with five oval lobes. Stamens five, fixed at the base of the corolla. Filaments shorter than the corolla and corresponding to its incisions. Anthers long, sessile, with four furrows, and with a confused stipule at the apex. Ovary oval, seated within the flower. Style one, split to the middle into two parts longer than the stamens, and at maturity splitting further, so that there are then two styles. Stigmas simple, truncated. Drupe globose, with a hard, bony nut with small furrows, six chambers, and solitary seeds: two of them abort many times at full maturity. One partition is thick, and crosses the nut from side to side, opening at the extremities into two rhomboidal chambers; the other two partitions perpendicular to this one are thin. = Small trees the height of a man, common in Malinta, in Visayas, and in many par-

148
tes. At first glance they resemble a malvaceous plant called escoba: the bark is extremely tough, like that of this plant. The leaves are barely distinguishable from one another, except in color, and in the short hairs that make the one I am now discussing very rough. It is therefore very strange that in these times people have wished to give it such celebrity, even claiming that it was the true tea of China, with similar properties. It was enough to dispel the error simply to compare one set of leaves with the other, since they bear no resemblance. In the provinces of Leite, and others that we call Visayas, its bark and wood are used to dye things a dirty black. Its leaves, from very ancient times, have also been taken by the local people as tea in infusion, but dried in the shade; and even so, they have nothing agreeable about them. For this reason some call it wild cha or wandering cha. Chewing its leaves and the buds of the lagnob (the lacquer fig) makes the saliva turn red. Flowers in January and in other months. * T. V. Manguit, Alañgitñgit.— The genus Carmonea, which I find described in Persoon, was formed by Mr. Cavanilles. Ordinarily the seeds number four; but others are found sometimes upon examining the larger fruits, which are like peas.
HYDROLEA. Calyx in five parts. Corolla wheel-shaped and bell-shaped. Filaments heart-shaped at the base. Capsule of two valves and as many chambers. Receptacle very large, central, bearing seeds. Seeds small. Lin. Syst. Veg. 458. Jus. Gen. pl. 134.
Hydrolea zeylanica. Hydrolea of Ceylon. Stem erect, without spines. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, decurrent. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in panicles. Calyx free, divided into five very deep parts. Corolla bell-shaped, in five lanceolate parts, and of violet color. Stamens five, fixed at the divisions of the laciniae. Filaments with a very broad and oval base. Anthers notched at the base, in two rolled-up parts. Ovary oval. Styles two. Stigmas slightly thick. Capsule oval, with six grooves, the two deepest of which contain a fleshy axis, fused with it at two or more points, and between the spaces an infinite number of small oval seeds, fixed to the axis. = A plant two feet tall that I have seen in Arayat, near the water. Flowers in January. Pers. Syn. pl. 289.
NAMA. Calyx in five parts. Corolla tubular, in five parts. Capsule bilocular, bivalve, superior, with many seeds. Lin, ibid. 456. Jus. Gen. pl. 134.
Nama jamaicensis. Nama of Jamaica. Stem creeping. Leaves crowded at the nodes, the lower ones very long and oval, entire and smooth. Flowers opposite the leaves, solitary, with rather long peduncles. Calyx inferior, bell-shaped, with five laciniae. Corolla wheel-shaped, with five di-

149
oval visions in the blade. Stamens five, in the divisions of the corolla. Filaments broad at the base. Anthers split in two, greatly twisted to the sides. Ovary oval, seated within the flower. Styles two, thick. Stigmas funnel-shaped. Capsule bivalve, with two cells and very tiny seeds like sawdust. Flowers in February. == It is a spreading plant and very similar to the genus Hydrolea and to the Steris of Java. Lin. ibid.
HYDROCOTILE. Simple umbel with a small stalk. Involucre of two to four leaflets. Petals entire. Fruit compressed, gibbous, and that can be split in two. Lin. ibid. 467.
Asiatic Hydrocotile. Hydrocotile of Asia. No stem. Leaves heart-shaped, kidney-shaped, and forming something like a funnel, notched at the margins and with teeth (whose tips turn white), sprinkled with small hairs. Petioles very long, which sheathe one another by means of two wings they have at the base. Three or four sessile flowers, which emerge directly from the root, placed in a horizontal row on one and the other side of a very short common peduncle. Common involucre of two or three leaflets. Calyx adherent, compressed, with small dark teeth. Corolla of five small oval petals that incline toward one another. Stamens five, equal in height, fixed on the receptacle, alternate with the petals and likewise inclining toward one another. Filaments short. Anthers globose, split at the base into two divergent parts. Ovary below the corolla, heart-shaped, very compressed with a channel in the middle. Styles two, awl-shaped, very short and twisted to the sides. Stigmas simple. Fruit truncated and oval, hairy, that does not open, marked with furrows (not swollen), compressed, divisible into two, with two chambers each containing one seed fixed in the wall of the channel (there is room for another or more). = A plant very well known to the Indians. I have seen it frequently in coconut groves and in shady, humid places. It has no stem, and its leaves rise to the height of a span, or more than a foot. The Indians use its juice on wounds of the eyeball, and they also remove cataracts from the eyes with it, or with the petioles of the leaves, drawing them to the sides. With a bundle of the herb boiled in two bottles of water until reduced by half, and adding an appropriate amount of sugar, a very useful syrup is made that purges and refreshes, and is very beneficial according to Father Mercado for catarrh settled within the body. The flavor of the leaves is slightly pungent and resembles that of watercress. Flowers in June, after the first rains. * T., Taquip suso, Taquip cohol. Lin. ibid.— It is the Azorella of Lamarck.
DAUCUS. Calyx with five teeth. Petals inversely oval, emarginate. (Dec. prod. 4. 209) the leaflets of the involucre divided. Lin. Syst. veg. 474.
27

150
Daucus anisodorus. Anise-scented Daucus. Leaves three times pinnate. Leaflets cleft with flat, awl-pointed segments. The common petiole simply clasps the stem at the base. Flowers in a flat umbel, with the central umbellets shorter, all florets fertile. The partial peduncles number about twelve, more or less, and the florets of each umbellet exceed sixteen. Universal involucre apparently of one piece, cleft nearly to the base into about six flat, awl-pointed parts, some of them still subdivided into three segments. Partial involucre of one piece, cleft into about six flat, awl-pointed parts. Calyx proper of the florets, superior, with five globose teeth. Corolla of five equal, keeled petals, folded inward, with two rounded lobes. Stamens five. Filaments longer than the corolla. Anthers (reddish) three-angled. Ovary with tubercles. Styles two, straight, very short. Stigmas somewhat thick. Two seeds joined together, rather long, striate, and nearly smooth at maturity. = This plant, which curious natives plant in their gardens, grows to a height of two feet. The seed is smaller than that of the Haras (see Anethum) and has the taste and smell of anise, pungent and aromatic; they mix it with betel. Its seeds, though small, I have noted do not rot easily in waterlogged ground, even after three months. It is a native plant. Flowers in October. *T., Lamudio, Damoro. V., Lamudio. P., Damoro.

ANETHUM. Calyx entire. Petals entire, folded inward. Fruit half egg-shaped, with ridges. Jus. Gen. pl. 219.

Anethum foeniculum. Anise Fennel. Stem erect. Leaves three times pinnate. Leaflets cleft with plump, awl-pointed segments. Common petiole with two long wings toward the base, by which it sheathes the stem. Flowers in a flat umbel; the central umbellets shorter, all florets fertile. The universal umbel has more than six or ten peduncles. Universal and partial involucre, none. Calyx proper of the florets, superior, entire. Corolla of five keeled petals, folded inward. Stamens five. Ovary bilobed. Styles two, broad, and bent to the sides. Stigmas somewhat thick. (The styles are only noticeable once the fruit has grown large.) Fruit: two joined seeds, oblong, striate, and without hair. = This plant, known to the natives and indigenous to the country, grows to a height of five feet. The flavor of the seeds is sweet (though at the last it stings a little) and very similar to that of anise, for which reason I believe it could substitute for it in the Philippines. The natives grow it as a curiosity in their gardens, and I saw it in flower in May. *T. Haras. Lin. Syst. veg. 491.

151

PENTANDRIA.

TRIGINIA.

SAMBUCUS. Calyx superior with five lobes. Corolla wheel-shaped, with five lobes. Style none. Stigmas three. Pulpy berry with three to five seeds. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 321.

Sambucus javanica. Java Elder. Leaves............Flowers in a thyrse. Calyx superior with five small lobes. Corolla monopetalous with five lobes. Stamens five, projecting, fixed at the divisions of the corolla lobes. Filaments flat. Anthers oval. Styles none. Stigmas three, somewhat thick. Berry round, very small, crowned with the stigmas, with one chamber and three seeds.= Small trees found in Laguna. I have only seen the flowers and the fruit sent to me by Mr. Azaola, who named the species Javanica; I have not seen the leaves. Flowers in October.

BASELLA. Calyx none. Corolla (calyx according to Jus.) divided into seven lobes; the two opposite ones broader, becoming a berry at maturity. Seed one, covered. Lin. Syst. veg. 507.

Basella rubra. Red Basella. Stem twining. Leaves alternate, lance-shaped to oval, running down the petiole, and somewhat fleshy. Flowers axillary in a spike, with three scales at the base of the small flowers. Calyx none, other than the said scales. Corolla somewhat swollen and cylindrical (unless one wishes to call it a calyx) with seven lobes, inclined inward: the five inner ones more colorful than the two outer ones. Stamens five, united halfway at the base, fixed toward the middle of the corolla. Filaments shorter than the corolla and thick at the base. Anthers versatile, elongated. Ovary with sides. Style one, very short. Stigmas three, hairy, a little shorter than the stamens. Berry globose, formed by the same corolla, with one chamber and one seed.= This plant, whose flowers are all hermaphroditic, is common in the small woodlands. It is eaten with pleasure, cooked in salad, and has the flavor of chard. The juice is sticky; the root is caustic and is used for mustard plasters. The berries are purple in color. I have read that a species of Basela (I believe this one), when eaten, makes women fertile. Flowers in October. *T., Libato. L., Ilaibaquir. Lin. ibid.

Basella lucida. Shiny Basella. Leaves decurrent, almost heart-shaped, lance-oval, entire, hairless, and somewhat fleshy. Petioles very short. Flowers in compound racemes. Styles three. Stigmas oval. The corolla turns into a

152
a globose berry with lobes, containing a uniform seed with rolled flesh. = This plant is very common in Pasai and is a climber. The stem is flesh-colored, and the berries give a very beautiful purple color, highly prized by the Chinese: they say that silk is dyed purple with them. Flowers in June. In Baliwag it is called grana. Lin. ibid.

SEMECARPUS. Corolla of five petals. Nut superior, heart-shaped, seated on a large, fleshy receptacle and containing one seed. Lin. ibid.

Semecarpus anacardium. Cashew Semecarpus. Trunk rough, with many branches. Leaves lanceolate, stiff, entire, smooth above and downy below. Petioles very short, swollen at the base and compressed. Flowers terminal in a panicle. Own peduncle very short. Calyx persistent, with five teeth. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, of four or five petals. Stamens as many as the number of petals. Anthers drooping. Pistil: on the receptacle the embryo of the future nut can be seen, large and globose. Styles three, twisted to the sides. Stigmas oval, with dots that make them rough. Nut oval, seated on a large, fleshy, and inversely conical receptacle. One seed. — The receptacle rises together with the calyx, becoming very large and fleshy, and retaining its five small teeth. In this it differs from the Anacardium, which will be described later. The fruit of this tree is also seated on a very large receptacle and not immediately on the calyx. = This tree produces the fruit known in pharmacies under the name of Official Anacardium: others call it Oriental Anacardium, and some give this same name to Avicennia tomentosa of Lin.

It grows regularly to a height of nine or twelve feet, and I have seen it as thick as a man's body. It is very common in the Islands, and the natives eat the fruit — that is, the receptacle, which is red at maturity and is astringent. Neither the nut nor the receptacle is more than an inch long. The local people know this tree very well, because of the harmful properties it has, of which they are often victims.

If, after a rain, drops of water that have run over the leaves fall on someone, or if one happens to be moistened by the dew drops that often cover the trees in the morning, the affected area becomes covered with painful sores. The cure is difficult; but I believe the ailment clears up on its own within a year. Some people are simple enough to undress and dance around the tree, saying certain rather indecent words at the same time, hoping thereby to be cured; but the more civilized do not practice this superstition. I have heard from one person that the quickest and surest remedy is to rub the rash with a piece of Trichosanthes. It is also removed

153
rubbing it with salt, or washing it with salt water or with a decoction of lagundi leaves. In the Spanish translation of Linnaeus it is said that the juice of Semecarpus can be used to paint black on cotton fabrics without fear of the paint fading; and I have seen that this is true. This tree is the one known in Ilocos by the name Camiring. It is extremely poisonous, and exudes a sap that blackens with time, and perhaps it is the Urusi of the Japanese, whose juice is used in lacquer. I have not noticed that all of them yield this sap; but I have seen large trees at Punta Santiago that produced it abundantly.
Let us hear what Kaempfer says in his Exotic Amenities, which I find inserted in volume 18 of the General History of Voyages by Abbot Prevost, printed in Madrid, page 161.
"The Urusi (he says), or the lacquer tree, is no less admirable for its usefulness. It yields a whitish juice which the Japanese use to varnish all their furniture, bowls, and plates. Even at the Emperor's table, lacquered tableware and utensils are preferred over the most precious metals. Another species of lacquer tree is known, which has narrower leaves and is called Faasi. It grows on hills and mountains; but its juice is not as good as the other, nor as plentiful. The true Urusi is a particular species of Japan. That of Tamatto is the most esteemed, although it also grows in the Provinces of Figo and Tsi Koku." Kaempfer observes that the lacquer tree found in the Indies is entirely different from the Urusi of the Japanese, which according to him is the Anacardo. In light of this, those curious about such matters may conduct their own experiments. On page 108 of volume 10 of the cited History, mention is also made of the lacquer tree of China, called Tsi-chu, which I believe to be the same one I am discussing in this article, known among Tagalogs by the name Ligas, and among Ilocanos as Camiring. The Chinese plant many of them intentionally, and make incisions in them every seven inches, in which they place shells during summer, where the sap drips overnight; during the rainy season the juice would not be pure. These shells are collected with iron tools by men wearing gloves, leather boots, and an apron of the same material, hung from the neck, with no openings except for the eyes, having first rubbed their hands and face with oil in which one ounce of the fleshy fibers found between the lard of a pig has been cooked, per pound of oil. The sap from the trees is filtered without touching it by hand, through a cloth that is wrung out, so that little is lost. From a thousand trees, it is considered good when twenty pounds of lac-

154
nish: that is to say, from one tree, not even half an ounce is obtained. The varnish is applied over the works, or pieces, adding to it whatever color one desires; and in order for it to come out well, it is applied more than twice, since with only two coats the work does not turn out properly. See the aforementioned History. I will now add some details brought by the little work of the painter, Gilder and Lacquerer Mr. Riffault, translated from French into Spanish by D. Lucio Franco de Salva. He states as follows: "The varnish of China is not a particular secret composition, as many have believed; it is a resin that flows from a tree called by the Chinese Tsi-cheu, or varnish tree, similar to turpentine. In this tree they make incisions, and beneath each one they place a shell to collect the liquid. It is said that the exhalations of this liquid are poisonous, and that those who decant it take care to avoid breathing them. When the resin comes out of the tree, it looks like liquid pitch; exposed to air, its surface first acquires a reddish appearance, and then turns black. Placed in tightly sealed vessels, it has the property of keeping for more than forty years.
Once this resin is collected, it is poured into a large earthen vessel, over which they place a frame with a clear cloth. After the most liquid part strains through on its own, they wring the cloth to let more pass, and the harvest is considered very abundant when a thousand trees produce twenty pounds of resin in one night.
Before the Chinese use this resin, they place sixty ounces of it, with an equal amount of water, in a wooden vessel, stirring this mixture for one day in summer, and two in winter. Once thus prepared, this varnish is kept in a porcelain vessel covered with a bladder.
When the Chinese wish to make their beautiful black varnish, they allow their varnish called nieu-tzi (that is, the mixture of resin and water just described) to evaporate in the sun until it is reduced to nearly half, and then add one pound of pig bile per pound of varnish. Without this addition the varnish would have no body, and would be too fluid.
To varnish common works, the Chinese apply no more than two or three coats; for the most perfect ones, they apply a greater number. Once the varnish is dry, they paint whatever they wish upon it; and then, to preserve it and give it more luster, they pass over it one more light coat of varnish.
This varnish takes on all sorts of colors: it is mixed with gold and silver leaf; figures, mountains, palaces are painted on it, in short everything one desires; cabinets, tables, boxes, etc. are covered with it."
I should note that from the Balimhasai (a species of Fagara) flows a liquid very similar to that of the Semecarpo, and that it would be worth testing: it is a fairly common tree. This tree flowers in the

155
Islands in Feb. * T., Ligas. I., Camiring. In Cebu, Langas.
Lin. ibid.—V. Cassuvium.
Semecarpus cuneiformes. Wedge-shaped Semecarp.
Leaves wedge-shaped, sharply notched at the tip, stiff, entire, smooth
on top and fuzzy underneath. Calyx as in the previous species. Corolla
regularly of five petals, and often six. Stamens as many in number as
the petals. Germen: the embryo of the nut, compressed, rises in the
middle. Style with some projecting points. Fruit as in the previous
species. * T., Ligas. New species.
Mr. Azaola has seen another species in the mountains of Calauan.
Leaves opposite, egg-shaped, oblong, petiolate, entire, with very
prominent transverse veins. The receptacle fleshy, six to eight lines
thick, globose, and red: the drupe or green nut, more than one inch
long. It is a tree ten varas in height.
REICHELIA. Calyx in five parts. Corolla bell-shaped, with five
lobes. Anthers curved, and split above and below into two parts.
Capsule that splits circularly, superior, with three chambers, three
sides, and many seeds. Lin. ibid. 311. 499.
Reichelia palustris. Marsh Reichelia. Stem erect, smooth.
Leaves decurrent, alternate, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Petioles
very short. Terminal flowers in a conical, very compact head. Universal
involucre, none. Belonging to the little floret, three very small
leaflets. Calyx semi-globose, with five rounded parts. Corolla longer
than the calyx, bell-shaped, in five oval parts, folded and wrinkled
from the middle upward. Stamens five, fixed at the divisions of the
limb of the corolla. Filaments broad at the base, compressed, very
short. Anthers twin, concave, and versatile. Germen globose, seated
within the flower. Style shorter than the stamens. Stigma thick,
shield-shaped. Capsule that splits circularly, with two chambers, rarely
three, and in each one many seeds, fixed on a semi-globose receptacle;
and they are very tiny and cylindrical. = This plant, about two feet
tall and hardly known, I saw on the banks of the Mandaloyon river.
The heads are about an inch and a half long. To examine the flowers,
one must look for the heads while still small. Flowers in April. * Lin.
ibid.—It differs from Pongatium in that the corolla in that genus is
above the germen.

156

PENTANDRIA.

TETRAGINIA.

EVOLVULUS. Calyx of five leaflets (in five parts, Jus.). Corolla wheel-shaped, with five laciniae. Capsule with four chambers, each containing one seed. Lin. Syst. veg. 312. 508.

Evolvulus linifolius. Flax-leaved Evolvulus. No stem. Branches hairy, spreading along the ground. Leaves nearly sessile, alternate, ovate, oblong, entire, and hairy. Flowers solitary, axillary. Peduncles long, with two bracts. Calyx in five parts, with a small tuft of hairs at the divisions. Corolla wheel-shaped, with five notched lobes and five folds bearing small hairs at the tip. Stamens five, long. Styles four, long. Capsule superior, with four seeds.= This plant spreads its small branches along the ground and has no stem. The Indians do not know it, nor do they make any use of it. The flower is bluish. It is common in the place called Punta de azufre. Flowers in January. Lin. ibid.—I have seen at Mandaloyon a variety with a white flower.

(LONGAYAN.) Trunk erect. Leaves alternate, ovate, oblong, with small teeth along the margins, smooth. Petioles short. Flowers axillary, in spike-like panicles. Calyx ovate, with five teeth. Corolla slightly longer than the calyx, somewhat bell-shaped, and divided into five rounded parts. Stamens five, attached at the middle of the corolla tube. Filaments thick, very short. Anthers broad. Ovary globose, seated within the flower. Styles none. Stigmas four, thick, and linear. Berry? globose, with one chamber? and many small, kidney-shaped seeds.= It is a small tree found in Pasig. The Indians barely know it. The flowers are very small. Flowers in March. Might it perhaps belong to the genus Geniostoma?

PENTANDRIA.

PENTAGINIA.

* * PANAX. The umbels on one plant are hermaphroditic; on a separate plant they contain only males. * Males. Calyx entire. * Hermaphrod. Calyx superior with five teeth. Berry with two seeds. Lin. Syst. veg. 466.

Panax fruticossa. Shrubby Panax. Leaves about three times pinnate with an odd leaflet, or doubly compound. Leaflets lanceolate:

157
the new ones, serrated, with spiny serrations, the old ones with lobes. The common petiole sheathes the stem at the base. Flowers in a compound umbel of small florets, all hermaphroditic. Calyx adherent, with five small teeth, not very notable. Corolla of five lanceolate petals, curved downward. Stamens five, fixed to the receptacle. Anthers regular. Styles two, shorter than the stamens. Stigmas awl-shaped. Berry half-lenticular, with two bony seeds.= A shrub of about one fathom in height, very common in Manila and other places. Flowers in May. * T., P., Papua. V., Macan, Papua. Lin. ibid.
ARALIA. Involucre of the umbellule. Calyx with five teeth above the ovary. Corolla of five petals, and berry of five seeds. Lin. ibid. 509.
Aralia? bipinnata. Aralia? doubly winged. Leaves twice pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets sometimes lanceolate, other times irregular; and they have now one lobe on one side, now three or four, with spiny teeth on the margins. Flowers in a compound umbel, all hermaphroditic. Calyx adherent, very small, with as many teeth as there are petals. Corolla of five, six, or seven small petals. Stamens as many as the petals. Styles numbering two, three, and sometimes four. Fruit...= This well-known small tree reaches a height of nine or twelve feet. I do not know whether it has thorns on the trunk: and if it does, it may perhaps be the species Spinosa of Lin. ibid. The Indians eat the young leaves cooked. Flowers in Feb. * T., Potat. This name is also given to the Stravadium.
Not having seen the fruit, I cannot state with complete certainty whether it belongs to this genus, or to Polyscias or Cussonia: all belong to the family of the Aralias.
Aralia? pendula. Aralia? drooping. Branches swollen at the joints, and clustered at the top of the tree. Leaves inserted below the middle of the branch, and drooping, opposite, egg-shaped, very elongated, obtusely serrated, and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers in racemes, composed of very small sessile florets, globose and gathered in likewise globose clusters: in each one there are seven or eight, on a fairly long partial peduncle: the common peduncles with a large, heart-shaped bract. Calyx adherent, with five lobes barely visible at the margin. Petals five, egg-shaped, and concave. Stamens five, sometimes up to seven, and an equal number of petals. Styles five, short and flat. Stigmas simple. Berry globose (like a pea) with five chambers and bony, solitary seeds.= A tree known in Bauang and in the vicinity of Manila, which sometimes grows as thick as a man's body, and eight or more varas in height. Its wood is soft, and wooden clogs are made from it. It puts out no branches except at the top:
28

158
the leaves hang downward, and for that reason I have called it pendulous. The fruit has a balsamic odor, mixed with an unpleasant one. Fl. in Sept. * T., V., Bongliu, Bingliu, Biasbias, Malapapaya. New species. — Perhaps a species of Cussonia?
Aralia? octophilla? Aralia? with eight leaflets? Leaves digitate, numbering eight or more. Leaflets lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Common petioles very long. Individual ones short. Flowers in compound racemes, umbellate, very long. I have seen no involucre. Calyx adherent, shaped like a top, with as many small teeth as petals. Corolla of seven or eight petals, broad below, fixed between the edge of the calyx and the receptacle. Stamens equal in number to the petals, fixed at the edges of the receptacle, with very short filaments, and the anthers double and arched downward, in the shape of a half-moon. Styles none. Stigmas as numerous as the stamens, and they resemble small horizontal points that converge at the center. Berry formed by the same calyx, with as many chambers as there are stigmas, and in each one two seeds. = A tree whose height I do not know: it is found in Cebu, and its wood is soft. The fruit was not ripe. Fl. in Sept. * V., Tagima. — This species may belong to Dec. Prod. p. 4. 250, or perhaps to the genus Paratropia of the same. ibid.
PARATROPIA. Everything as in Aralia; but the stigmas are sessile and submerged in a hypogynous disk. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 200.
Paratropia crassa. Paratropia with fleshy leaves. Trunk parasitic, dotted with spots, branching, which clasps the trees. Leaves digitate, five in number on a common long petiole, swollen at the base, which clasps the stem. Leaflets fleshy, lanceolate, very entire and very smooth. Individual petioles shorter than the leaves. Flowers terminal in umbellate panicles. The secondary peduncles bear many small flowers and concave scales ending in an awl-shaped point. Calyx adherent, entire, very small. Corolla fixed at the edges of the calyx, of three, and more regularly of six petals, concave, pointed, and inclined inward. Stamens three to six, according to the number of petals. Filaments longer than the corolla. Anthers lying flat. No style: only five or six rays arranged in a star are observed at the base. Berry small, globose, with four to six somewhat elongated and compressed seeds. = A parasitic shrub, twining, and which climbs very high. The trunk is at most three inches thick. It is very well known among the natives. The use they make of it is to cure scabies: for this purpose they pour the water from a decoction of the leaves over the affected limbs using a cup, taking care not to reuse the water that has already passed over them once. This remedy causes the scabies to break out

159
with great force; but it disappears afterwards. They also use the decoction of the leaves to bathe women who have recently given birth.
The wood of the shrub, enclosed in a box so that the scent becomes concentrated, gives off an extremely pleasant fragrance. It also distills a white, very aromatic resin. Flowers in February. * T., Limalima, Galamai amo. V., Cayangcan, Taguima, Galamai amo, Calangcang, Carangcang, Limalima, Taguilma, Tuglima. P., Limalima.

Paratropia obtusa. Paratropia obtusa. Leaves as in the previous species, except that they are lanceolate and obtuse. Styles five or six protruding points, very short, in the middle of the fruit: and in this it is distinguished from the former, in which those points are not notable. Berry round, with ridges that are not very prominent, enclosing five or six seeds. = Parasitic shrub. — The genera Poliscias, Aralia, Cussonia, and Panax have much affinity with one another.

DROSERA. Calyx in five parts. Five petals. Capsule with one chamber, and at the apex with five valves. Very numerous seeds, fixed to the walls. Lin. Syst. veg. 514. Pers. Sin. pl. 336. This species has three, six, and nine styles.

Drosera hexaginia. Drosera with six pistils. Stem erect, round, without branches; and both the stem and the leaves are bristly with hairs; those of the stem and the lower part of the leaves are very short and buckler-shaped; and those of the upper part of the leaves are longer, and end in an oval, transparent gland. Leaves sessile, alternate: the new ones coiled in a spiral, as in ferns; the old ones long, very narrow, and with a channel beneath. Flowers to one side, and distant from the leaves, in a simple raceme, and at the tip, a compound one. Individual peduncles long. Calyx free, cleft almost to the base into five lanceolate parts, which alternate with the petals, which are five (sometimes six), spatula-shaped, attached to the calyx, and twice as long as it. Stamens equal in height and equal in number to the petals, and alternate with them, attached to the calyx. Anthers half arrow-shaped. Ovary oval, seated at the center of the flower. Styles six, arranged in pairs over the ovary, and very close to the center, and appearing as if joined there: at other times they appear very separate; but always twisted irregularly to the sides. Stigmas simple. Capsule globose, with one chamber and many ovoid, rough seeds, fixed on three excrescences that form a triangle among themselves, and arise from the walls of the capsule, running from top to bottom. = An extremely rare plant, a hand's span tall, which I have seen in Malinta in humid places. Since it is not found in flower, anyone would be mistaken and would take it for a fern. The fruit is larger than a pea. The leaves are three or four inches long, and at most two lines wide, and have a channel

160
from below. The roots are fibrous, regular. Fl. in Oct. *
T., Hintipalo. New species.
COMMERSONIA. Calyx of one piece, which bears the corolla. Five petals. Nectary in five parts, and within the stamens. Capsule of five bristly cells. Lin.
Commersonia echinata. Bristly Commersonia. Leaves alternate, with winged veins, notched at the base, ovate, pointed, serrated and tomentose beneath, and somewhat rough above. Petioles very short. Flowers half-lateral to the leaves, in a dichotomous panicle. Calyx inferior in five pointed parts. Corolla of five petals, alternating with the parts of the calyx, narrow, linear, widened at the base with two small concave ear-like lobes. Nectary placed inside the stamens, monophyllous, bell-shaped and in five parts. Stamens five, very short, fixed at the outer base of the nectary, and opposite the petals. Anthers round, compressed. Ovary with lobes. Style one, short, (when the flower dries, there are five) with the stigma in a small head. Fruit with long tomentose awns, (as in Adelia) with five small nuts joined together. = A tree as large as a man's body, common in Pangisihan de Angat. The fruit is the size of a hazelnut, and resembles that of Sparmannia. Fl. in Feb.— When the flowers are dry, there are five styles, although before there appeared to be only one. It has affinity with Buttneria.

HEXANDRIA.

MONOGINIA.

CORYPHA. Calyx of six pieces. Corolla none. Drupe superior, with one seed. Lin. ibid. 559.
Corypha umbraculifera. The Umbrella-bearing Corypha. Trunk very thick and straight. Leaves form the crown of this species of palm: and are fan-shaped, with folds ending in a point. Petioles long, with spines on the edges. Flowers come out only at the very end of the tree's life, and form a panicle so large that it looks like a small tree placed at the top. Cal. Cor. Stam. Pistil.... Drupe globose with a membranous nut, without scales, and at maturity, hard; with one chamber and one globose seed, horn-like. = This palm rises to a greater height than coconut palms, and is also of greater girth. The leaves are so large that with a single one more than four men can be covered: the natives use them to make mats, and many useful and curious things. From the midribs boiled in water, they also extract certain fibers

161
which they use to make a kind of mat called Sagoran. By cutting the stalk of the flowers found at the tip, and making a hole there, a large quantity of sweet liquor called tuba is collected every day, similar to that of the coconut, and considered to have equal virtues to those of the black cabo for consumptives. From it vinegar is also made, and a kind of yellow honey called Pacascas in that land. The vinegar is obtained by the same procedures used with the coconut. To make the honey, the tuba is boiled in a cauldron, adding a little shell-lime (others do not add it), and when the tuba has thickened, it is poured into molds of cane. The Buli flowers only once and then dies. I have not been able to see the flowers, but I have seen the fruit, whose outer flesh is eaten by thrushes and even by children. The drupe is smaller than a hazelnut, and it is difficult to break with a hammer: for this reason, when the Indians want the seeds to germinate quickly, they first toast them a little in a pan over fire. The inner flesh burns the tongue. From the pith of the trunk is extracted the flour called yoro by the Indians, and sago by Europeans, which in former times was brought to Manila and was much eaten by the Spaniards, especially during Lent, mixed with sugar. From its ripe fruits very beautiful rosaries are made, with great ease, because the little hole is almost already formed. The bindings made from Buli leaves have great fame among the Indians for protecting against plague, bad winds, and other diseases. There are times when entire villages are seen full of these necklaces; but for all that, those who wear them die just as the others do.
* T., Buri, Buli. Lin. ibid.
Coripha minor. Lesser Corypha. Leaves fan-shaped, with folds ending in a point. Petioles without spines. Flowers in a spathe. The spadix, one braza long, containing many small flowers in compound clusters. The stalk very short and thick. Drupe globose (like a large cherry) with a scaleless rind and a hard seed, horn-like. = This palm, commonly called Palma brava, grows as tall as coconut palms and areca palms. It is found in forests, not in settled areas. The trunk is black and very straight: the wood very hard, with a soft pith inside, like other palms. The seed when young is edible; but it is very astringent, and only tolerable for savages. The Palma brava is used in palisades, in channels to carry water, and in other things, because it is very durable. The leaves serve to cover the roofs of houses. Flowers in February. * T., Anahao. V., Anahao. P., Anao, Bolong luyong. Lin. ibid. — I leave this Palm here, guided solely by the leaves, since I have not been able to see its flowers.

162
BROMELIA. Calyx with three lobes, superior. Three petals, with nectaries in the form of scales at the base of the petals. Berry with three chambers, inferior. Lin. ibid. 529.

Bromelia ananas. Bromelia ananas. Stem nearly absent. Leaves tongue-shaped, very pointed, with hooks along the edges. Flowers gathered on a common receptacle, elliptical, large, scaly, crowned with a tuft of imbricated leaves. Proper calyx, a thick, pyramidal scale, split in three parts, one smaller, at whose base there is a lanceolate support, with hooks along the edges. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, of three linear petals, with two lateral appendages like wings, toothed higher up from the base. Stamens six, shorter than the petals; three opposite them, and three alternating. Anthers arrow-shaped. Ovary inferior. Style longer than the stamens, split at the tip into three parts. Stigmas thick. Strobilus oval, with the scales and carpels edible and fleshy. The proper carpel, with three fleshy partitions, three chambers, and in each one two seeds, shaped like a half-moon, compressed, and resembling those of apples. = This famous plant grows easily everywhere. The fruit is celebrated for its agreeable flavor. It is asserted that those who eat this fruit to excess sometimes spit blood. I have no great difficulty believing this, because one can perceive in it some hint of pungency. It is for this reason that Linnaeus perhaps advises that it be forbidden to pregnant women. From the leaves of these plants, the natives extract very fine threads, from which they make cloth of astonishing delicacy. The pineapple given to children to eat in the morning, especially when it is not yet perfectly ripe, expels roundworms. Flowers in April. * T., Piña. Lin. ibid.

TILLANDSIA. Calyx inferior, persistent, split in three parts. Corolla (inner calyx according to Jus.) bell-shaped, split in three parts. Carpel with one chamber, and seeds with pappus.

Tillandsia pseudo ananas. False ananas Tillandsia. Stem erect, spongy, covered with scales from the deciduous leaves. Leaves clustered, sword-shaped, with three folds, and as many rows of hooks directed upward, one in the middle on the underside, and the others along the edges. Flowers on a long triangular peduncle, with some remote scale, in oval, alternate spikes, without scales, where the small flowers are found in great number, very tightly packed, and fused together at the base. Proper calyx of the small flower, inferior, split at the tip into three parts. Corolla... Stamens six or more, with very stiff filaments. Style... Fruit superior, with many seeds bearing pappus. = Plant as thick as an arm, and

163
at a height of five or six yards, found in the forests of Angat. The leaves are more than a fathom long; the flower stalk is one yard; the receptacles of the flowers, about three inches: they are red or yellow in color like pineapples, but they lack the scales and the tuft that crowns the fruit of those plants. The little flowers are joined to one another below, and above are conical, making it difficult to determine (due to the mucilage in which they abound) into how many parts the calyx divides above. It is also difficult to discern the corolla or inner calyx, and to count the stamens and pistils. Only about six or more hard veins can be seen, which can be divided in two. The fruit was still in embryo; but many very small seeds were visible, ending in a long little hair. The leaves resemble those of the Paudan sabotan and could serve the same purposes. See the genus Pitcarnia in the Authors. Flowers in August.

TRADESCANTIA. Calyx three-leaved. Corolla of three petals. Filaments of the stamens, with articulated hairs. Capsule with three chambers, superior. Lin. Sist. veg. 532.

Tradescantia cristata. Crested Tradescantia. Stem prostrate on the ground. Leaves sword-shaped. Petioles sheathing the stem. Axillary flowers, in many imbricated, compressed spathes arranged in a row; of two leaflets, half-moon shaped, or like a torn hood. Calyx and Corolla as in the genus. Stamens six, a little longer than the corolla. Filaments with a thick, conical appendage at the apex, and with a section of articulated hairs toward the tip, with a single article. Anthers small, all regular. Ovary superior, oval, with three angles. Styles as long as the stamens. Stigma thick, oval, with the tip cleft with many teeth. = This plant is known to the natives, and its decoction is said to be good for eye ailments. Flowers in August. * T., Alicbangon. Lin. ibid. 533.

Tradescantia discolor. Two-colored Tradescantia. Stem knotted, prostrate on the ground. Leaves clasp the stem at the base, sword-shaped. Axillary flowers, in a compressed spathe of three leaflets, shaped like a torn hood; the smallest one below. Calyx and Corolla as in the genus. Stamens six, sometimes seven, and occasionally a small extra petal serves as a filament and bears its own anther. Filaments with articulated hairs. Anthers shaped like an inverse half-moon. Ovary superior with three angles. Stigma with teeth. Capsule with three chambers, each containing one elongated seed, convex on one side and flat on the other. = This plant, which I have seen in various places, is hardly known to the natives. The leaves are very large and purple underneath. This may perhaps be the species of Lin. ibid. Flowers in September.

164
LORANTHUS. The calyx tube egg-shaped, or rarely top-shaped. Petals four to eight, most often five or six, sometimes distinct, sometimes more or less united. Stamens as many as the petals and opposite them, fixed at their base and separated at the apex. Stigma in a head, or conical in reverse. Berry with one seed, crowned with the calyx limb. Dec. Prod. p. 4. 286.= In Section 3 of the Surrula 301, it adds: Petals four or five, united in a tubular corolla, and at the tip with four or five lobes, gibbous at the base and split along its length like the lobelia.
Loranthus Philippenses. Philippine Loranthus. Parasitic trunk. Leaves opposite, notched at the base, nearly oval and downy. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary in umbel-like clusters, each small flower with a very small, circular bract at the base of the calyx. Calyx adherent, bell-shaped, entire. Corolla much longer than the calyx, monopetalous, tubular, fleshy, the same color as the calyx, split longitudinally almost to the base (like the Scaevola) and with the limb divided into four lanceolate lobes, bent backward. Stamens four, sometimes equal in height, sometimes irregularly unequal, as long as the corolla, and attached to it along their length except at the tip. Anthers regular, straight. Style filiform, longer than the stamens, with a small disk toward the tip. Stigma globose. Berry crowned by the calyx, with one seed surrounded by pulp. = I saw this shrub growing on a species of vitex. Its branches and flowers have no notable scent. The Indians call it Dapo, as they do other parasitic plants. The filaments of the stamens and the pistil are black. The leaves do not yield a blue dye. It agrees closely with the species cited by Dec. ibid. 302.= There is another species, with scattered leaves: stamens five or six: the corolla split all the way down; and the style with a fleshy rim at the base: the flowers are flesh-colored, and arranged in an umbel. It is also a parasitic shrub.
Loranthus tomentosus. Tomentose Loranthus. Parasitic trunk. Leaves opposite, approaching a lanceolate shape, blunt at the apex, notched, and with a cottony fuzz on the margins and on both surfaces, in the form of small stars. Flowers axillary, in clusters of three or four small blossoms. Calyx adherent, very small, with six blunt little teeth, barely noticeable. Corolla more than five times longer than the calyx, cylindrical, fleshy, with six petals. Stamens regularly six. Filaments none. Anthers fixed near the tips of the petals. Style somewhat longer than the corolla, surrounded at its base by a rim with six angles. Stigma somewhat thick. Berry with one seed.= This shrub grows on the trunks of trees, and I have seen it on that of Spondias. I have not noticed that the Indians make

165
its use. The corollas are green above and flesh-colored below. = In Ilocos I have seen individuals with alternate leaves. Stamens five, which separate from the corolla, which has five laciniae. *T., Dapo sa cáhoy. I., Binbinguay. The first approaches the species Patulus of Dec. Prod. p. 4. 317.
HILLIA. Corolla very long, twisted. Calyx superior with an involucre of two or four small leaves at the base, (Dec.) and the limb of two or four parts. Stigma thick, bifid. Capsule of two chambers, without wings and with many seeds bearing a pappus. Lin. Sist. veg. 576.
HILLIA? LONGIFLORA. HILLIA? WITH LARGE FLOWERS. Leaves opposite, decurrent, lanceolate, nearly entire, smooth and fleshy. Flowers axillary and lateral, in racemes, with three small leaflets at the base of each small flower. Calyx crowning the fruit, with five barely noticeable small teeth. Corolla large, shaped like a small jar, with six angles on the belly, and six linear laciniae, curled outward. Stamens six, the length of the corolla. Filaments attached along nearly their entire length to the corolla, and separated from it at the tip. Anthers rather long. Style the length of the stamens, with a throat toward the base. Stigma globose. Capsule? with six seeds. = This shrub grows on the species of Mango called Pajo. Flowers in April. *T., Dapo sa Pajo. Lin. ibid.
ACHRAS. Corolla egg-shaped, cleft in six parts, with as many alternating lower scales. Calyx of six inferior pieces. Pome of twelve seeds, solitary, with a scar on the margin and a claw at the apex. Lin. ibid. 573.
ACHRAS SAPOTA. ACHRAS ZAPOTE. Leaves clustered, lanceolate, keeled, entire, and smooth. Flowers solitary, or in pairs, terminal, with very long peduncles. Calyx of six pieces, three inside the others, inferior persistent. Corolla jar-shaped, with the border in twelve parts; the six smallest ones alternate, and inside the other six. Stamens six, fixed near the divisions of the corolla, and opposite its outer parts. Filaments very short. Anthers arrow-shaped. Ovary woolly at the base, conical and seated upon the flower. Style long. Stigma obtuse. Pome globose, crowned with the hardened style, with more than ten chambers, and in each one seed. Seeds oval, compressed, with a scar that bears a sharp point at one end, and fixed to a central fleshy axis. = They are very well-known small trees, which grow to a height of twelve feet. They exude a very sticky sap. Their fruit, which is of middling flavor, resembles a small pear, and is nonetheless prized in this country where good fruits are rare. The outer bark is somewhat rough and dark: that of the tree is febrifugal, and its seeds are diuretic. I do not know whether it is
29

166
a native tree, or whether it has come from elsewhere. Flowers in April and
in other months. * Chicos. Lin. ibid.

Achras lucuma. Achras lucuma. Branches with soft down
at the tip. Leaves clustered at the ends of the branches, lanceolate, somewhat broader from the middle upward, wavy, slightly tomentose, especially on the veins, which are prominent underneath. Petioles very short, swollen at the base. Flowers in a spike? Calyx divided into ten parts, in the manner of rounded, concave, somewhat hairy scales, overlapping one another: the inner ones larger, and nearly the color of the corolla. Corolla shaped like a bell, leathery, divided to about halfway into five rounded lobes at the top. Stamens five, fixed toward the middle of the corolla tube, opposite its lobes, and of the same length. Anthers marked with a groove above and below. In addition, five small horns are visible, inserted in the incisions and alternating with the stamens. Ovary superior, globose and hairy. Style conical, as long as the corolla. Stigma of about four or five barely visible points. Pome egg-shaped, elongated, with a rough and woody rind, with one perfect seed (three or four abort), very large, oval, pointed, with a covering that is half bony, lustrous, convex on the outer part, and on the inner side flattened along its entire length and somewhat hollowed out. = Beautiful trees, about five fathoms tall, which exude a milky sap and which seem to me to be native to the islands, although similar ones exist in New Spain. The fruit, which is entirely similar to that of that country, and which I have eaten there without seeing its flowers, is sold in Manila and is about five inches long. The flesh is a color between yellow and red; the seed covering is very smooth, blackish, and its hollowed part is of a lighter color. The calyx scales are thick and whitish, and the corolla is white. The leaves are fifteen or more inches long and two inches wide; the veins have a reddish tinge. The Tagalog Indians call the fruit of these trees mamei, although it is not. The flowers I have described are from a Manila tree, and I have seen others similar to them on trees found in Bauang. They are also found in Balanga and in other places. It is the same tree described in the Flora Peruana, vol. 3, p. 17, under the name Achras lucuma; although the seeds of this Philippine variety are somewhat different, being pointed rather than rounded at the ends. Flowers in September.

CORONG. Leaves alternate, egg-shaped, oblong, entire and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers on the branches. Calyx. Corolla. Stamens. Pistil. Berry superior, globose, with two or more nuts, veined, triangular; one angle very obtuse, and on the opposite side hollowed out with a broad scar. = Trees of medium size in Angat, whose leaves are four or five inches

167
in length. The fruit is like a large plum, but globose, and with very red, edible flesh, and it is somewhat tasty. I note that it stains clothing the same color, which is difficult to remove. The seeds are hard, as large as those of plums, flat, veined and hollowed out on the inside, and on the exterior with an obtuse angle. The Indians of Angat confuse it with the binucao (Cambogia), though it is not that. Since I have not seen the flowers, I cannot say what genus it belongs to; but from the excavation of the seeds I think it should be among the zapotes. I have left it with the name that some Indians gave it.
(PUTIAN.) Leaves alternate, half lanceolate, entire and smooth. Flowers axillary, in a kind of umbel. Calyx very small, inferior, bell-shaped, entire. Corolla very long, with six linear petals. Stamens six, the length of the corolla, fixed between the calyx and the receptacle. Filaments very short, compressed. Anthers very long, linear. Ovary like a flat pyramid with many sides. Style thick and long, like the stamens. Stigma thick, pointed. Fruit... = A tree that grows as large as a man's body. I do not know of any use made of it. Flowers in January. — I made this description when I was still new to these matters.
ALLIUM. Corolla in six parts, and extended. Spathe with many flowers. Umbel clustered, and with a small sheath inside the flower. Palao. transl. of the practical part of Lin. vol. 3. 5.
Allium tricoccum. Garlic of three little husks. Root with scales. Leaves flat, growing from a single stalk. Flowers in a single-leafed spathe, with many small florets arranged in a nearly flat umbel, placed on a stout stem, and with some other confused angle. Own peduncle very long. Calyx none. Corolla open (white), deeply cleft into six lanceolate parts. Stamens six, shorter than the corolla, and united below by a common membrane. Filaments broad below. Anthers regular. Ovary of three lobes, seated within the corolla. Style the length of the stamens. Stigma simple. Capsule of three angles, and three little husks, and in each one, one compressed seed. = A very well-known plant, used in place of leeks in the Philippines. It is native, as it grows spontaneously in Leite; but that of Manila is originally from China. The smell of the leaves is not strong; but that of the root is, spreading widely, forming a broad, continuous, and compact body, from which grow countless little stalks that have scales at the bottom. The flowers are white. It is close to the species tricocum. Flowers in July. *T., Cuchai, and in Leite Ganda. Lin. Syst. veg. 544.
MUSA. Corolla superior, of two petals; one erect with five teeth, the other short and concave, serving as a nectary. Filaments six: of which either one or five are perfect. The ovary

168
aborts in many species. Berry inferior, long, with three angles, and many seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 523. 567.
Musa paradisiaca. Banana of paradise.—The description of this species given by Linnaeus is the following. Spadice nutante, floribus abortientibus persistentibus. Although I have examined many flowers of various species of Plantains, I have never seen that only the sixth filament bears an anther while the five others lack them: for the contrary regularly occurs. Nevertheless, I place under this species the following, which I consider to be varieties of the said Paradisiaca. On the Islands up to 57 varieties are counted, all of which bear the generic name of Saguing, in addition to their own names. The Spaniards call them Plántanos, and also Plátanos; although the first name does not seem very apt. The Portuguese call them bananas. Others call them fig-tree of Adam: because they believe that having eaten its fruit, it caused our common ruin. They say that he clothed himself with its leaves, and for that reason they call them the breeches or underpants of Adam, though they are quite unsuitable for the purpose. The spadix in all plantains is inclined toward the ground; but the berries turn back upward, with their tips facing the sky. This precious plant was known and cultivated in Spain long before the discovery of America, as is evident from the work of Abu-zacharia, which speaks of it and calls it Musa, a name preserved by Linnaeus: it is probable that the Arabs brought it from the East Indies. See the additions to volume 2 of the Agricultura de Herrera.
* Plantains with a thick rind on the fruit at maturity.
Musa paradisiaca compressa. Compressed banana of paradise. Stem cylindrical, formed by the petioles of the leaves, which serve one another as sheaths: and in this all other plantains agree. Leaves elliptical, elongated, very large. All flowers hermaphroditic, arranged on a common receptacle, furnished with large, single-ranked, ovate, imbricate scales that elongate considerably as the flowers open. Each scale covers about twelve small flowers. Corolla of two petals: the upper one with the blade cleft into five parts: three of these end in small hoods; the other two, shorter, without hoods, arise from the interior and from the divisions of the first three. Lower petal, without a pit on the outside. Stamens: five perfect, and a rudiment of a sixth. Anthers very long and covered with abundant pollen. Style a little longer than the stamens. Stigma thick, compressed, with ridges. Berry usually a little more than three inches long and one inch thick, with three angles, though very often it has up to five, formed by the mutual pressure of the berries. Each cluster has

169
at times, though rarely, more than four hundred berries, crowned
until maturity with the flowers. = This banana called in some
parts of the Islands Bisco, rises to a height of nine
or twelve feet, depending on the terrain, and not counting the leaves, which
are sometimes eight or nine feet long, and two feet wide.
Its fruit is among the most esteemed; and rightly so, because it is
said to be very wholesome; and both this and the other species
are narcotic; but if they are not fully ripe, they are flatulent,
especially those with thick skin. The Spaniards call it Obispo,
surely a distortion of the name mentioned above. Its flesh appears
somewhat fibrous, or full of stringy threads; but the flavor is a
little sour, and inferior in this respect to that of many other species,
which there is no reason not to consider equally wholesome: the
flowers have an unpleasant smell, as do those of the other bananas.
The use made of the leaves for wrapping is well known. The veins
and leaf stalks serve for tying. The skins of the berries, dried
and burned, yield an ash prized by women who dye with Bancudo, or Niño.
The trunk of this species, as well as those of the others, contains
a great deal of water: the natives cut it near the root, which is
semi-globular and larger than a man's head, and hollow out a cavity
or pit, which quickly fills with water; after a day it turns sour,
and into it they put the tinder they collect from the Cavon: with
this treatment it becomes very well suited to catching fire at the
slightest strike of flint against stone.
The seeds of the berries almost never come to maturity; but
now and then isolated seeds are found, well formed and perfect.
To ensure that all of them reached perfection, I believe it would be
necessary to carefully remove all the new small shoots that spring
from the main root, and not only the shoots that have grown, but
all the buds found at the root, ready to sprout. I have heard from
the natives that any banana plant from which the leaves are frequently
removed will produce small fruit, and that in such cases some seeds
can be seen. The shape of those found to be perfect is
very flat and circular, with a stalk at one surface and a
navel on the opposite side. The same shape is generally found in
all the seeds of the other banana species that I have found in isolation.
To obtain very large bananas, most of the berries are removed
from the bunch. It is also worth knowing that to make a plant
bear fruit sooner, it is advisable to plant the root stalk upside down
or mouth down: but little progress is actually gained by this.
From the trunk of this banana, very fine cloths are made in the
Visayas, like those of abaca, and by the same methods. Some
are accustomed to rub the dried leaves of bananas on the ta-

170
boards of house floors to give them a shine; but they become so slippery that it is sometimes dangerous to walk on them. *T., Saba, Bisco, Obispo.— There are various varieties of this species. Here I speak of the most common one in Batangas, in which I have seen the sterile filament. In the Visayas there is one with small fruit; and in Parañaque, another with large fruit which they call Saba Iloco.

Musa paradisiaca ternatensis. Musa of the paradise of Ternate. Flowers: each scale covers about twenty small hermaphroditic florets. The lower petal, ending in a cavity on the outer side; the upper one, as in the variety compresa. Stamens numbering five, without a rudiment of the sixth. Fruit with three very prominent angles, and sometimes four or five, crowned with the flower, which persists until the fruit ripens. = This species reaches the same height as the previous one. Although in appearance one cannot be distinguished from the other, the natives can tell them apart at a glance by the color of the leaves. The fruit is more than five inches long and is among the most flavorful when allowed to ripen on the plant, which is rarely achieved: because the native hastens to convert it quickly into money, even if this means accelerating its ripening by immersing it in sea water, or by hanging the bunch inside a pit covered with leaves, or by placing it uncut in a sack of straw or leaves, or by other forceful means. The seeds rarely come to full development; but the occasional one is found at maturity. * Ternate, Gloria.

Musa paradisiaca lacatan. Musa of the paradise Lacatan. Flowers. Each scale covers fourteen small hermaphroditic florets. Corolla. The upper lip with five teeth; the three alternating ones larger. The lower one bulging, ending in two notches and a small horn, and a row of small pits; the alternating ones on the inside, and the others on the outside. Stamens five, without a rudiment of the sixth, and rarely six perfect ones. Stigma manifestly cleft in two parts: one subdivided into two lobes, and the other into three or four. Fruit with a blunt tip, and with angles as in the other preceding species, but which nearly disappear at maturity, crowned with the flower, which persists until the fruit ripens. = This species is native to Pampanga, and about forty years ago it was unknown in Manila. An Augustinian friar caused it to be propagated throughout the Province of Bulacan, and today it is already very common. The fruit comes to be as large as the one called Gloria; but its flesh is denser, firmer, fragrant, and in the opinion of many, holds primacy over the other species. Indeed it seems to combine in itself the flavor and aroma of the so-called Bungulan, with the firmness and wholesomeness of the Ternate. * T., Lacatan.

171
Musa paradisiaca pumila. Small Paradise Banana. The fruit is like the Bungulan, which I will describe later; but not as tasty: the stalk is very small, so that the clusters reach the ground. The Indians call it Tampohin, or the irritable one, because if its leaves are cut, it dies. * T., Tampohin.
Musa paradisiaca suaveolens. Sweet-scented Paradise Banana. Fruit. It is longer than the Lacatan. The skin is always green, like that of the Tampohin; but unlike that one, it does not have small yellowish spots at maturity, like the bungulan. The angles are not as prominent as in the other species; indeed they almost disappear at perfect ripeness, as generally happens with all bananas. The flesh has a very delicate smell and flavor, and this banana would be the most prized were it not for the property attributed to it — I do not know whether with good reason — of being extremely cold in nature. * T., Bungulan.
Musa paradisiaca magna. Large Paradise Banana. Fruit with three or more angles, which disappear at maturity. This banana produces a cluster sparsely populated with fruits; but in compensation they are very large in length, sometimes more than a foot, and in thickness like a wrist. This fruit when cooked has a flavor resembling that of apples, and for that reason is highly esteemed. Cloth is also made from its stalk, like that of abacá; but it is not as good. * T., Tondoc.
Musa paradisiaca violacea. Purple Paradise Banana. The fruit is nearly round, as thick as a wrist, and as long as a good Ternate banana. It is similar in flavor to that one, and I do not believe it is inferior to it. It is a banana recently introduced in Manila, and I do not know where it has come from.
Musa paradisiaca subrubea. Half-red Paradise Banana. The fruit is the size of the Ternate, with angles, somewhat reddish, and in flavor resembles it a little; but when cooked its flavor is very similar to the Tonduc. It is an uncommon banana. The Indians living near Manila do not know what to call it, and simply say it is a banana from the Coast.
Musa paradisiaca glaberrima. Very Smooth Paradise Banana. The fruit is as long as the Saba, slender, with angles, of a light purple color, and very smooth: it is not very tasty. * T., Galamay Señora, Dinuguan.
Musa paradisiaca maxima. Very Large Paradise Banana. Berry very large, long and thick, with firm flesh; but not very tasty. I do not know if it is from the Islands. * T., Batavia, Matavia, Songai Anuang.
Musa paradisiaca longa. Long Paradise Banana. Berry tapering at the end, long and not very thick. Its flavor is good; but not among the best. * T., Quinauayan.
Musa paradisiaca tombak. Tombac Paradise Banana. The

172
The fruit is of a regular size. The flesh is the color of tombac, tending toward red; but it is not among the most flavorful.
* T., Tinumbaga, Goyoran.

Musa paradisiaca ulnaris. Paradise banana of one braza. = This banana is known only to the black inhabitants of the mountains of Balanga, who have occasionally brought its fruit to the nearby towns. Those who have seen and eaten it say that it is as thick as a calf of the leg, and that it can reach up to one braza in length, which is a monstrous size. It has no seeds; it is eaten cooked, and its flavor is similar to the Tunduc. I consider this account to be reliable; but not what the black inhabitants say, namely, that the bunch produces only one fruit: I think it more likely that the others simply fail to develop fully.

Musa trogloditarum. Banana of the troglodytes. Flowers: each scale of the spathe covers about twenty small florets. Cor. as in the variety Ternatensis. Stamens and Anthers as in the variety compressa. Berry similar to the ternate, and full of round seeds, very flattened, and with a navel. = This very common banana, which grows wild in some forests, produces all perfect seeds, from which it takes its name. The fruit, which is of regular size, is used to make vinegar, and can also be eaten, as it is also tasty. A buffalo kept for several months on the trunk of this banana plant without any other food lost all its teeth; this being so even though it was very young, which is quite remarkable. The water collected at the base of the cut trunk has a great reputation for curing contraction of the virile member. * T., Botohan, Botoan.

Musa trogloditarum errans. Wandering banana of the troglodytes. Each scale covers about twenty small florets. Cor. the upper lip with five laciniae, the two alternating ones smaller; the lower one much shorter, with small teeth barely noticeable at the tip, and without a hollow on the outer part of the base; there is likewise no rudiment of a sixth filament. Berry with three to five ribs, full of perfect seeds. = This rare banana grows wild in the forests, and its height and form are like those of the other varieties. The spadix is nearly one braza long, and the scales of the spathe are green, not colored. The fruits are not much larger than the middle finger, and cannot be eaten even when ripe, as they are bitter. They are full of black seeds when mature, and with a single bunch this banana could easily be spread throughout an entire province; and it might be worth doing so, because its fibers have seemed to me stronger than those of the Abacá, with which it has much in common: and perhaps that plant gave rise to this one, now cultivated and bearing edible fruit. The one I am discussing here inhabits the mountains of Tala. * T., Saguing Machin, Saguing na ligao.

173
Musa trogloditarum textoria. Musa of the loom-using troglodytes. Cor. the lower lip, almost without notches. Stamens five, without rudiment of the sixth. Fruit with three ribs, and many perfect seeds.= This banana called Abacá, I consider a variety of the previous one: it is one of the most useful, and is cultivated with care in the Province of Camarines, and in other places. At first glance it does not differ from the others. The fruit is edible, and very small; for the ones I have seen barely exceeded two inches in length. The seeds reach full maturity. The use made of this banana is immense. From it are made ropes, cables, and fabrics of extreme fineness.
For this purpose the trunk is cut at the base and at the top, when it is close to bearing fruit, removing the leaves. The petioles are also removed one by one, and a lengthwise incision is made on the inner side in the middle with a knife, in order to remove the bark that covers them on the inside. Once the petiole has been stripped of its inner bark, strips two fingers wide are made, which are placed one by one beneath the blade of a knife fixed to a long cane that acts as a spring, whose longer end is secured in the ground.
The strip of abacá having been placed beneath the knife with its outer bark facing upward, it is pulled forcefully from one end, which is done one or two times, and the fibers then appear clearly; but with this method half of the abacá is wasted. They still have to be passed through a kind of saw that serves the function of a comb, like those used in Europe for linen: this second operation I have not seen performed; but I have seen the other.
