There the fibers are arranged in order; but some are finer than others, and for that reason the women take care to separate them into various grades, before weaving: this they carry out with great skill, even in the dark.
If the abacá is to be used for making cloth, they first form it into a tight ball, like the head of a large child, which is thrown into the mortar in which rice is pounded, and there it is struck many times with the wooden pestle. This operation makes the abacá very flexible and less prone to breaking.
Once this is done, one has only to tie one thread to another at the ends, which is regularly done by the women and girls. The weaving is done as with cotton; but if the abacá is too fine, the women go inside a pavilion to weave it, because the wind easily breaks the threads.
When the cloths are finished, they are soaked for a day and a night in water with a little shell lime. They are then washed and stretched.
30

174
Although abacá is quite strong, it is much inferior to flax and hemp, both in this regard and in its luster and feel.
Abacá grows very well in the Province of Batangas, and in other places; but it is not as good as that of Camarines; and the latter appears to be inferior also to that of Panai and Marinduque, though there are differing opinions on this. I consider it very probable, however, that these others are distinct from that of Camarines: for the fruit of this one is bitter and not eaten, while that of Batangas is eaten.
The water that collects in a hole made at the foot of a cut trunk is said to be good for contraction of the virile member, a singular ailment that is not uncommon in the Visayan Provinces, and that is regularly accompanied by contraction of the tongue.
The Englishman Dampier, as one reads in the History of the Abbot Prevost, was mistaken when he said that abacá was known only in Mindanao.
Abacá is easily dyed blue and red. To dye it blue, the leaves of a shrub or climbing plant, called Payanguit and Aringuit in Camarines, have been used since ancient times; according to the learned account that the curious and diligent observer Fr. José de Mata, a Franciscan friar, has presented to the Economic Society of Manila, he is the one who has made this plant known in our times to the Europeans of the Philippines. The leaves of this shrub yield a very abundant blue color. See Marsdenia.
To dye abacá red, I have heard that in Camarines the bark of the root of the Morinda is boiled with a little lime or alum until the desired color is achieved, and then the dyeing is carried out. But it is better to dye it in the manner used with cotton thread, that is, with lye and sesame oil. * T., Abacá.— These last two plantains have been placed here so as to bring together all those with thick bark.
Musa trogloditarun dolioliformis. The Troglodyte Musa of jar-like shape. The stalk is slender at the base, much thicker higher up, and then tapering again as in other plantains, with similar leaves and flowers. Five stamens. Berry with angles and seeds, large, hard, and similar in appearance to the other species. — It is a very singular plantain that has been brought to me whole from Tanauan, and about which the learned and industrious Mr. Azaola, who has assisted me so greatly with his knowledge in the formation of this work, had already given me an account. This plantain is known in La Laguna and in Tanauan: and its most notable feature is that the trunk, a little above the ground, swells to the size of a jar, larger than the body—

175
human-like, from which I took the name of the species, and afterwards
it thins out like the other plantains, which it resembles in its
leaves, flowers, clusters, and berries. The seeds, however, are
much larger, and the natives use them to make very ugly rosaries.
In the said Province they call this plantain the Virgin's plantain.
* Plantains with thin fruit skin at maturity.
Musa paradisiaca glauca. Gray-colored Paradise Banana.
The fruit is small, with a very thin skin of a gray color,
oval in shape, and without angles: sometimes two inches long,
or even a little more, cylindrical, and very
blunt at both ends. Its flesh is bittersweet, delicate, and
flavorful. * T., Bingticohol, Tinalong.
Musa paradisiaca cinerea. Ashen Paradise Banana.
The fruit has thin skin, without notable angles, and whit-
ish, and is the size of the ternate: its flesh is delicate, and
somewhat ashen in color. Nevertheless its flavor is not superior
to other plantains and it is a pity that for its sake the natives have almost aban-
doned the other species which are much better:
its berries are the only ones whose skin splits and bursts. Some
years ago a French clergyman named Mr. Letondal brought it from India to Manila.
In it I have found perfect seeds on quite a few occasions. I have also seen twin fruits, wrapped
in a single skin, with two flowers contributing to their formation,
as I have said happens with the climbing Coffee plant. * Letondal.
CRINUM. Corolla superior, divided into six parts, and regularly
funnel-shaped: the three alternating laciniae, with
hooks or barbs. Germen covered at the base by the corolla.
Stamens distant, fixed at the throat. Lin. Sist. veg. 524. 537.
Pers. Sin. pl. 352.
Crinum asiaticum. Asian Crinum. Root globose, with scales.
Leaves keeled. Flowers on a compressed stem, in
a spathe of two small leaves and some dry threads, which contain four
small flowers. Corolla funnel-shaped with a long tube,
roughly triangular, and with six horizontal, lance-
olate laciniae; the three alternate ones, with hooks. Stamens six, shorter
than the corolla. Anthers long. Stigma with three points. Inferior
ovary, with three chambers, each containing one seed. = A plant
unknown to the natives, with white flowers. I saw it in Manda-
loyon and it blooms in July. Lin. ibid. 537.
I have seen in Manila another species with purple flowers. The
flower stem compressed; the spathe with many flowers, and
the rest as in the preceding species. Inferior fruit, with three
solitary seeds: each one in its own chamber.
Crinum giganteum. Very tall Crinum. Root solid. Leaves
linear, undulate, pointed, tongue-shaped. Flowers in
great number, on a somewhat compressed scape, and in es-

176
foot of two broad leaflets, containing many small flowers: each one with a short little stalk and at the base a long bract. Cor. (Cal. according to Jus.) superior, in six channeled parts and curled downward: the three alternate ones, with hooks at the tip: the tube of the corolla, longer than the limb. Stam. equal in height, fixed at the throat of the tube and curled downward. Stigma with three angles. Capsule oval, fleshy, with three chambers and very large solitary seeds: almost always one aborts. = This plant barely has a stem, and its root is solid and without husks: made into powder it is taken internally, and it is an antidote to poison, as the writers of this Country affirm. With a husk of the lower stem, closest to the root, which is white, the tuna fishermen prepare their hooks in place of bait; and in this way, adding some small white chicken feathers, they catch not only tuna, but also hake and other fish. The leaves are as tall as a man: the corollas white, and seven or more inches long. In each spathe there are more than thirty small flowers: the stamens and styles are purple. In the Tagalog vocabulary we are assured that this plant is very good for curing herpes: it is not said in what way it is used for this; but I suspect it would be by rubbing the affected area with a piece of a leaf, because this is the method I have observed the Indians use for the treatment of this disease. The thin skin, or white undershirt, of the lower part of the stem, serves the Indians during carnival time to make fun of others, since they make small tubes of this skin: they tie them at both ends full of water, and throw them at someone's face or head, so that they break. The learned Fr. Clain supposes it to be a Scilla, and it is indeed one, also called by the same name, Bacong; but it is not the one I am discussing. The Scilla is rare in this Country, and only some curious person cultivates it: I have seen it only once. What is said about the bacong in the work of Tissot, translated by me into Tagalog, asserting that it is a species of Hypoxis, must be corrected; as must the placing of it in the genus Hæmanthus in the first edition of this Flora: for it is not that either. *T., Bacong. Pers. ibid. 352.
PANCRATIUM. Cor. superior with six petals. Nectary split into twelve parts, and terminating with the stamens. Capsule nearly round, with three angles, three chambers, and three valves. Lin. Sis. veg. 523. Palau, trad. de la p. prát. de Lin. t. 3. 46.
Pancratium illiricum. Illyrian Pancratium. Root globose with husks. Stem very short, formed by the leaves that emerge joined together at first. Leaves shaped like a tongue, thinning from the middle upward. Flowers in a spathe of two leaflets, very numerous, gathered on a two-edged stalk. Cal. none. Cor. (Cal. according to Jus.) superior, as in the genus. Petals flat and lanceolate, and twice

177
longer than the nectary, with a hook or small horn on the inner and outer edge of each alternate petal. (These hooks are also seen in the following species.) Nectary funnel-shaped, with many folds and irregular points on the limb. Stamens run attached to the nectary, and are nearly as long as the petals. Anthers very long, lying over the filaments. Style longer than the stamens. Stigma three-sided. Fruit as in the genus. = The Indians use the root of this plant for wounds. Its leaves are about a yard long. The nectary is entirely white. Flowers in June. *T., Tagalhi. Lin. ibid. 537. It may perhaps be the species Declinatum of Lin. ibid. 536?

Pancratium maritimum. Sea Pancratium. Leaves sword-shaped. Spathe with many flowers. Nectary without folds or other teeth, except for the six angles where the stamens are attached. = This plant, which some Indians in Batangas call Cebollas del Monte (Mountain Onions), although the same name is also given to another plant, is not common, and I do not know that any use is made of it; but I have seen it planted in flowerpots.

Pancratium Amboinense. Pancratium of Amboina. Leaves somewhat heart-shaped and circular, with many veins. Petioles very long. Flowers in a spathe of many lanceolate leaflets, turned downward, containing many small florets. The scape is nearly cylindrical. Nectary much shorter than the corolla, with twelve sharpened teeth. Stamens shorter than the corolla and longer than the nectary. = This plant is well known and grows on sandy seashores. The Indians use the root, in a quantity equal to half a broad bean, or in powder at a weight of one drachm, as a very mild purgative and as an emetic. Flowers in April. *T., Catongal. V., Abur, Panabor, Catangal, Talaonor, Tonuar, Dausum.

Pancratium Zeylanicum. Pancratium of Ceylon. Root globose with tunics. Leaves sword-shaped, smooth, and soft. Flowers on a two-edged stalk, in a single-leaved spathe that splits along one of its planes and contains only one small floret. Corolla superior, of six lanceolate petals, turned outward. Nectary with folds and twelve teeth. Stamens longer than the nectary, attached at the intervals between its teeth. Stigma with three angles. Capsule three-angled, with three cells each containing many seeds. = This plant, whose leaves are about a hand-span long and whose flowers are not fragrant, is known to the Indians, who plant it in their gardens. The nectary is white like the corolla. Flowers in April. *T., Catongal, Rosas de Persia, Lunas.

(SIRAYOYO.) Root. Leaves... Flowers in a very large racemose panicle: the partial peduncles with a bract of about one span

178
and sword-shaped, or like an arundinaceous plant. Each of the three small proper pieces, arranged in an umbel and with about four rounded, white, and very thin scales at the base. Cor. (or Cal. of Jus.) of six linear leaflets with very thin edges in the manner of petals. Stamens six, fixed near the base of the corolla, flat, broad, and white below, and higher up still broader and flesh-colored, terminating in a point. Anthers white and folded from top to bottom on both sides. Ovary oblong, barely with a small stalk, with three angles. Style the length of the anthers. Stigma thick and with lobes. Fruit with three? chambers, and in each one one? seed. = A plant sent to me from Cebu. The panicle is three feet long; it is very branching and with countless small flowers, which will have about two lines in length and half a line in thickness. In Boljoon they regard the root as a kind of garlic, and apply it to burst abscesses. They call it there Sirayoyo.
AMARYLLIS. Cor. of six petals, bell-shaped. Stigma in three parts. Lin. Sist. veg. 538.
Amaryllis atamasco. Atamasco Amaryllis. Bulbous root, with tunics. Leaves lanceolate, tongue-shaped, and smooth. Flowers in a spathe of two pointed bracts, containing two flowers, and sometimes three, on a two-edged stalk. Cor. (Cal. according to Jus.) large, bell-shaped, deeply cleft into six lanceolate parts, and with striations at the base. Nect. six glands, hairy, fixed toward the base of the corolla and behind the stamens. Stamens six, the length of the corolla, of equal height, fixed toward their base, arched, rising together, inclining to one side and with the tips pointing upward. Ovary below the flower, with three angles, and widening toward the top. Style longer than the stamens, and arched like them. Stigma with three teeth. Capsule triangular, with three chambers, and in each one many seeds. = This plant, about three feet tall, has beautiful, large, and flesh-colored flowers. The bulbs have no notable spicy flavor. Flowers in February. * T., Bacong, Talicoran. Lin. ibid. 539.— Could this be that species, or rather the formosissima?
PONTEDERIA. Cor. monopetalous, two-lipped, and with six lobes. Stamens six: three at the apex, and the others in the tube of the corolla. Capsule of three chambers. Lin. ibid. 533.
Pontederia vaginalis. Vaginal Pontederia. No stem. Leaves arrow-shaped, with the two lobes slightly divergent, entire, and smooth. Petioles very long, appearing to have four angles. Flowers in a corymb, inclined downward, in great numbers, covered with a common single-leaved sheath, which opens on one side and which emerges from the same petiole, swollen toward the end, and which splits open; forming as it were a

179
a type of spathe. Cal. none. Cor. (Cal. according to Jus.) arched, deeply split into six oval parts, the upper ones barely longer. Stam. six, shorter than the corolla, and fixed between it and the ovary. Filam. flat below: the alternate ones longer, and the one bearing the distinct anther has a small appendage at the upper part. Ant. long: one much larger, and of a distinct color, placed upon the forked filament. Ovary oval, with three angles, seated within the flower. Style short. Stigma simple. Cagilla oval, with three angles, three chambers, and many small seeds.= A well-known plant, which grows in freshwater pools. Its root and leaves are caustic, and cause redness of the skin, and sometimes a very useful eruption. The flowers are a color between green and blue. The roots, crushed with coconut oil and applied to cancers, heal them wonderfully, so they say. The leaves placed in hot water, and applied to the chest, back, and kidneys of one suffering from asthma, bring great relief. This must be repeated every three months. Flowers in Aug. * T., Calaboa. Lin. ibid. 534.
ALOE. Cor. tubular, with six laciniae, with an open mouth, and nectariferous base. Stam. inserted on the receptacle. Upper cagilla with three chambers. Lin. ibid. 562.
Aloe humilis. Low Aloe. No stem. Leaves rise immediately from the root, crowded together, and joined at the base, upright, shaped somewhat like a tongue, very fleshy, tapering toward the tip, and with stiff points along the edges. Flowers drooping, in a raceme, on a cylindrical, simple, and sometimes branched scape; with some distant scale, and each small flower has one at its base. Peduncle very short and proper. Cor. (Cal. according to Jus.) cylindrical, somewhat curved, split to the middle into six parts: the three outer ones pointed, and overlapping the inner ones, which are obtuse at the apex, and of a different color. Stam. six, fixed close to the nectariferous base of the ovary, and as long as the corolla. Ant. straight. Ovary cylindrical, with six grooves. Style at maturity longer than the corolla, and with three grooves. Stigma obtuse, and with a frayed edge. Cagilla egg-shaped, with three valves, three chambers, and about two seeds in each, furnished with three spongy wings.= This plant is well known, as curious persons often cultivate it: I have seen it in light green color and in purple: the flowers are between red and yellow on the outside, and pale yellow within. It is reputed to be a variety of the perfoliate Aloe. The flower stalk is about three feet long. The length of its leaves, which are thick and very juicy, is two palms. From these plants is extracted a very bitter juice, commonly called aloes, which according to some learned Authors, is more or

180
less pure, according to the procedures used to obtain it. The one that results from the simple juice, which drips from wounded leaves and is thickened in the sun or over a gentle fire, is the best, and is called Socotra aloes. If the leaves, which no longer yield juice, are cut into pieces and boiled in a little water, a less pure aloes is obtained, called hepatic aloes. An even coarser variety is also obtained, called equine or horse aloes, by boiling the residues of the hepatic aloes a second time. Notwithstanding the above, other Authors maintain that the aforementioned types of juices are extracted from different varieties of aloe. These juices are very bitter, purgative, and form the basis of many heroic medicines. They are useful in cases of obstruction, hypochondria, and jaundice, in ulcers and caries; they kill roundworms, as well as the worms that breed in the sores of horses, by dropping a few drops of the juice on them. Aloe is harmful to pregnant women and to those who suffer from convulsions and hemorrhoids. According to the doctrine of the estimable and learned Author of the Flora of the Antilles, whom I draw upon many times in this book, it may be inferred that if the booksellers of the Philippines were to mix the juice of the aloe with the glue, we would have books free from the plague of insects that devour them. This information is of great interest to scholars. Cots would also be freed from bedbugs by rubbing them occasionally with the leaves. The Indians use aloe juice for bruises and falls. They also mix a piece of a leaf with gogo and wash their heads with it to prevent, according to them, hair loss: which is confirmed by a local writer, adding (surely by way of exaggeration) that it will make hair grow back even on a bald man. I do not know whether the plant is native, though I am much inclined to think it is. * T., Sabila. V., Dilang boaya. Lin. ibid.
AGAVE. Cor. superior, upright with five laciniae. Filaments longer than the corolla, straight. Lin. ibid. 524. 563.
American Agave. Agave americana. No trunk. Leaves with a row of hooks that point upward along the edges. Flowers on a stout, knotted, branching scape, in compound racemes, umbellate. Cal. none. Cor. (Cal. according to Jus.) superior, of six petals, straight, linear, keeled. Stamens six. Filaments shorter than the corolla, fixed at the base of the petals. Anthers very long. Ovary oval, with channels. Style shorter than the petals. Stigma with three angles. Capsule with three compartments and many seeds. = A well-known plant: the Indians use it in medicine. The leaves are not as large as those of America. The flower stalk is two fathoms tall and grows with great speed. It is likely that it came from that country. From its leaves ropes are made, and at another time (I do not know if still today) they were woven

181
in Visayas very fine fabrics, which were called nipis. The same leaves, crushed and applied to cancerous sores, are said to cure them. Flowers in July. * Magui. Lin. ibid. 563.

POLYANTHES. Corolla funnel-shaped, curved, regular. Filaments fixed at its throat, and the ovary at its base. Lin. ibid. 559.

Polyanthes tuberosa. Tuberous Polianthes. Root globose, fleshy, with small lateral roots. Leaves nearly flat, sword-shaped. Flowers on a long cylindrical scape, arranged alternately in pairs, sessile with an ovate, pointed bract at the base of each pair, and at the base of each flower another very small one. Corolla (Calyx, according to Jussieu) funnel-shaped, curved, with the limb divided into six lanceolate, equal lobes. Stamens six, fixed at the throat of the corolla. Filaments very short. Anthers linear, longer than the filaments. Ovary oblong, at the base of the corolla. Style shorter than the stamens. Stigmas three, somewhat thick, pressed together, and at maturity oval and divergent. Seed capsule oval, with three angles, three chambers, and many seeds in each.= This plant, which I have seen in Manila, has no stem: from the main root sprout other small rootlets, from which grow many other densely packed shoots. In Manila this plant is called azucena. The fragrance is pleasant and is perceived more strongly at night. Linnaeus says in his treatise Viribus plantarum that its scent causes hysterical women to faint as if dead. Flowers in May. * Azucena. Lin. ibid.

GETHILLIS. Corolla superior, divided into six parts. Calyx none. Berry that emerges from the roots, club-shaped, with one chamber. Lin. ibid. 524. 564.

Gethillis acaulis. Stemless Gethillis. Roots central, thick, and fleshy. No stem. Leaves in a tuft, grass-like, sword-shaped. Flowers emerge solitarily from the root. Calyx none, but with some leaf-like scales. Corolla superior, very long, with a slender, solid tube (and thus in reality not truly a tube) with a closed throat, where the stamens and style are fixed in the middle: the limb with six lobes: the three outer ones oval, tipped with bristles, and some also on the back: the three inner ones oval, of deeper color, covered by the other three, and with some bristles on the back. If the three outer pieces are taken as the calyx, then the lobes of the corolla would number three. Stamens six. Filaments short. Anthers arrow-shaped. Style one, very short, at the tip of the tube. Stigma thick, with three angles. Seed capsule at the base of the flower, covered with some scales, not opening, pointed, with three angles, two chambers, and in each two seeds, striated, half heart-shaped, and
31

182
with one tooth at the upper end. = A plant that I have seen in Malinta, growing close to the ground. Were it not for the flower, which is yellow and more than an inch long, it would be impossible to distinguish it from the grasses. The fruit will be three or four lines long and two wide, and does not appear to be edible; but the roots are, and are sometimes as thick as a finger. Flowers in Oct. New species.

TACCA. Calyx superior, in six parts. The six filaments of the stamens, broad at the base, rise up forming hoods, and are fixed in the middle of the lobes of the calyx. Anthers six, with two chambers, hidden inside the hoods. Dry berry with three chambers and many seeds. Jussieu, Gén. pl. 56.

Tacca palmata. Palmate Tacca. Root bulbous, globose, solid, or without scales. Leaves palmate, with five lanceolate lobes. Petioles very long. Flowers on a very long, rounded, and striated stalk, in a simple umbel, with many small flowers, with rather long pedicels: there are no long threads between them, as in other species. Universal involucre of four broad lanceolate bracts. Partial involucre none. Calyx superior. (Corolla according to Linn.) bell-shaped, with the limb divided into six laciniae; the three alternate ones ovate; the other three, narrow toward the middle. Stamens six. Filaments broad, fixed in the middle of the laciniae. Anthers hidden in small hoods formed by the filaments. Ovary inferior, with three angles. Style one, with three edges. Stigmas three, very broad, and turned downward. Berry globose, soft, with five channels, one chamber, and many globose seeds. = A plant of two or three palms in height: the Indians chew and swallow the scrapings of its roots, which are bitter, for stomach complaints. I saw it in Malinta. The corollas are violet-colored, and the berries red. Flowers in Jul. * C., Corazon de Angel. V., Magsaloro. New species.

This genus also very probably belongs to the genus Leontice of Linnaeus. But the descriptions of the genera Tacca and Leontice of Linnaeus do not agree very well with what I have given for this plant; though Jussieu's does. I have seen another species with a much longer stalk, the fruit with six ribs at the six angles and many seeds wrapped in a pulp.

Tacca pinnatifida. Pinnatifid Tacca. Root fleshy, half-round or oval, compressed. Stem erect, striated, dividing into three parts, which subdivide two or three times. Leaflets alternate, runoff. Flowers on a long stalk, terminated by an involucre of eight bracts; the two outer ones bifid or trifid, containing about forty small flowers in an umbel, with pedicels somewhat long, mixed with an equal number of long threads of one palm in length. Calyx in six parts,

183
The filaments of the six stamens are shaped like concave hoods, fixed at the middle of the calyx parts, with two small ears at the base, and at the tip of each one an anther with three ridges is attached. Inferior ovary. Style thick, triangular, and winged. Stigma broad, with six lobes. Berry globose with six ribs, three partitions that disappear at maturity, three chambers, and in each chamber many oval seeds, beautifully furrowed and wrapped in a pulp. = A plant the height of a man, with a stem about an inch thick. It is very common in Ilocos, and even more so in Zambales, where I saw it for the first time, in an inlet called Tambobon. The roots are the size of one or two fists, irregular, though generally somewhat rounded or oval, and slightly flattened: their color and flesh are identical to those of Chinese potatoes. They are grated against a rough stone in water, where the flour that falls is washed, and once dry it is extremely white, and sells well in Manila. A very good starch is made from it; and mixed with sugar, it is eaten and has a pleasant flavor. It is also sprinkled on places where children tend to get chafing, and on erysipelas, to soothe the burning irritation. It is an annual plant, and propagates easily. I brought some roots from Zambales to Manila, and from these sent a few to Batangas, and they have flowered and fruited. The stem grows covered with a spathe. The Ilocos people call this plant Panarien, and the flour is known in Manila by the name gagao. The calyces of the flowers are green, and the six little hollows of the anthers are white: the long threads hanging from the flower make a pleasing sight. I have not noticed these in the other species. Sometimes more than one stem grows from a single root. I have also observed that the roots do not die even if left out of the ground for four or more months, provided they are watered from time to time. Those that I planted produced only one shoot each, attached by a thread to the first ones: and so the propagation of the plant must be done by seeds. It should be noted that the flour of the gagao, mixed with wheat flour in a small quantity (about one fifth part more or less) makes the bread very white and gives it a pleasant flavor, as those who have eaten it have assured me. Flowers in May.
* I., Panarien. Pers. Syn. pl. 382 — It should by no means be considered a species of Maranta.
DRACAENA. Corolla straight, in six parts. Filaments somewhat thicker in the middle. Berry superior, with three chambers, and in each one a seed. Lin. Syst. Veg. 559.
Dracaena terminalis. Terminal Dracaena. Trunk erect. Leaves closely overlapping at the ends of the branches, broadly lanceolate, with a thin membrane along the edges.

184
Long petioles, with two wings by which they sheath the stem. Flowers in compound racemes. Calyx? small, with three leaflets and six laciniae. Stamens fixed to the parts of the limb. Anthers incumbent. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma in three parts. Fruit superior. = This shrub grows upright to a height of two fathoms. The roots, according to Persoon, are good against diarrhea. Its leaves are flesh-colored underneath and green on top. The natives plant it for the beauty of its leaves. The flowers give off no notable scent. Flowers in January. * T. Varas hari, Varas ni Jesé, Toncod Obispo. Lin. ibid.
CAPURA. Calyx tubular (corolla according to Lin.) with six laciniae, the alternating outer ones narrower. Corolla none. Stamens inserted within a tube. Stigma one. Berry? Jus. Gen. pl. 437.
Capura purpurata. Purple Capura. Winged leaves. Leaflets blunt-lanceolate, entire and smooth. Common petiole with two orbicular stipules at the base. Flowers in an umbellate panicle. Calyx inferior, split nearly to the base into six ovate, concave, colored parts. Corolla none. In the center there is a hairy ring on which the germ rests. Stamens six, shorter than the calyx and fixed to the base of the ring. Filaments very short. Anthers thick. Germ ovate, compressed. Style none. Stigmas two laminae. Berry drupaceous, ovate, compressed, with two seeds. = A small tree of three or four varas in height. The natives barely know it. Its flowers are of a dark flesh color. Flowers in December. — Could this be the species of Lin. Sist. veg. 575?
CALAMUS. Calyx of six pieces. Corolla none. Berry very dry with one seed and with imbricated scales pointing backward. Lin. Sist. veg. 570.
Calamus mollis. Soft Rattan. The stem climbs by throwing itself over neighboring trees. Leaves sword-shaped, and they emerge from the nodes of the stem. They can barely be distinguished from the leaves of other species. Flowers in panicles composed of distichous spikes. Calyx in six parts: the three outer ones very small; the inner ones larger. Stamens six, fixed to the inner parts of the calyx and shorter than them. Filaments flat and pointed. Anthers almost arrow-shaped. Germ globose, seated within the flower. Style none. Stigmas three, somewhat thick, awl-shaped and straight. Berry globose with a separable covering formed of green, imbricated scales pointing backward, and each scale with a fold. The seed is single, of a horny substance, and covered with juicy flesh. = This plant, common in all the forests of the Islands and known to the natives, spreads very extensively, sometimes reaching twenty or thirty fathoms, like the other species. This rattan is softer and more supple than others,

185
and for this reason it is suited to certain uses. In the Tagalog vocabulary, it is said to be poisonous: and indeed the fruit is not edible. Flowers in September. *T., Dit-an.— The Spaniards call this and other species of Calamus bejuco. New species.

Calamus usitatus. Common Rattan. The trunk leans upon neighboring trees. Leaves sometimes opposite, sometimes alternate and winged, in pairs or in threes, not wrapping around the trunk but only at the nodes. Leaflets lanceolate, with three veins; and on them, on the upper surface and along the edges, there is a row of spines. Petioles spiny, sheathing the stem for a great length. Flowers in a compound panicle, with distichous spikes. Calyx persistent, of six pieces, the three outer ones larger. Berry globose, with a single uniform seed, very hard, covered with pulp, and the covering of the berry thin, composed of colored scales whose tips point downward. = This plant, about an inch thick, is well known to the natives: it climbs up into the trees and sometimes extends to a distance of twenty fathoms. Since it is covered entirely with spines, as are all other rattans, the natives arm themselves with a stick and, cutting the rattan at its base, beat it with the stick to strip the spiny petioles from the leaves, which is easily done; and the stem of the rattan is left extremely clean and well suited for tying and for the many other uses to which the natives put it every day, which are endless. They do the same with the other species. The rattan, although of extraordinary toughness, withstands exposure to the elements less well than cane. The fruit is eaten and is even sold in Manila; it is sweet and astringent. The stem is also included in the list of plants used without success to fix the colors of dyes prepared with sapang. Flowers in June. *T. Yantoc, Oayi. Species: nuexa.

Calamus maximus. Very Large Rattan. Leaves nearly opposite, winged. Leaflets lanceolate, with three prominent veins, and on each of the two lateral veins a row of stiff hairs on the upper surface, and on the lower surface a single row of the same. Common petioles sheathe the stem and are very full of spines. Flowers in compound panicles of spikes, with the florets distichous and very closely packed: each spike has at its base an involucre shaped like a funnel. Each floret likewise has at its base a scale of the same shape. Calyx deeply six-parted, the three outer parts somewhat shorter than the others. Stamens six, longer than the calyx. Anthers incumbent, slender, and curved. Ovary with a small stalk. Stigmas three, bent downward. A single oblong seed, with four indistinct angles, and in all other respects like the preceding species. = This very common and well-known rattan extends to thirty or fifty fathoms; its thickness, not counting the base, is more than two

186
inches, and sometimes as thick as a wrist. When cut, it yields drinking water in abundance, which is considered medicinal. Its tenacity, like that of the other rattans, is astonishing. Its bark, made into very fine strips dyed in various colors, is used to make hats and other delicate works. The stem stripped of its spines, roasted over fire and then boiled, is eaten as a salad with oil and vinegar, and is very tasty; although a little bitter, the raw fruit is also eaten and is not disagreeable. I doubt whether this species is hermaphroditic or monoecious, though I lean toward the latter. The seed has a substance like horn, as do those of the other species. * T., Palasan. P., Labni. V., Parasan, Calapi. C., Labnit, Calapi. New species.
Calamus gracilis. Slender Rattan. Leaves sometimes opposite, sometimes alternate, winged in pairs, and also simple. Long, lanceolate leaflets, with a single midrib, with spines on the edges and also on the midrib, on the upper surface. = It is a very common and well-known rattan, for from it are made the staffs of the ministers of justice. The thick sap that drips from the cut stem is said to be very good for curing mouth sores in children. The fruit is slightly larger than a pea. * T., Talola. New species. — This same rattan with edible fruit appears to be what they call in Manila Balinguai, but incorrectly.
There are other species of rattan, among them one called limoran, with a large, edible fruit, and another on the Island of Negros with black spots, which is used for walking sticks. But I have neither heard nor seen that the fruit of any of them is covered with a resinous bark which, when crumbled and melted by fire, yields globules that constitute the finest dragon's blood used in apothecaries, as Rumphius and Kaempfer, eyewitnesses, assert. Speaking of the soft Calamus, I noted that its seed was hard and horn-like; and such are all those of the other species: they vary in shape, for some are half-round, others appear to have four angles, and that of the limoran, mentioned above, is oval, somewhat compressed, with prominences, surrounded from top to bottom by a groove, a small navel on one face, and also extremely hard.
In the mountains of Angat there also grows another species of rattan that grows upright and does not climb over trees: its height is one braza, as the natives have assured me, for I have only seen it cut. The nodes are very close together and it has a flesh-colored appearance: they call it there Curag.
There are furthermore on the Islands more than thirty species or varieties of rattan, which those with the means to do so will be able to describe.

187

HEXANDRIA.

DIGINIA.

BAMBUS. The spikes contain five flowers and have three bracts. Cal. none. Cor. bivalve, the lower valve swollen: the inner one fringed. Nectary of two pieces. One seed covered by the corolla. Lin. Sist. veg. 579.

Bambus monogyna. Single-pistil Bambus. Leaves sword-shaped, with stiff and short hairs on both surfaces, and small hooks along the edges. Petioles hairy. Flowers in distichous, dense spikelets containing many small florets, each glume covering one. Cor. of two very small petals. Stamens six. Anthers very long. Style one. Stigmas two. Fruit.= This cane rises to a height of 30, 40 or more feet. It emerges already arched, and not as straight as the other species, and so the native calls it Quiling, meaning inclined. Its thickness is like an arm. The bark is tough, and thus it has little hollow space. The natives, always inclined toward difficult remedies, boil wine with the scrapings of this cane inside the hollow of a piece of the same cane, and give it to drink to women who have recently given birth, in certain cases. They call this medicine, which they consider marvelous, alac sa quiling, that is: wine of the quiling. Flowers in Aug. * T., Cauayang quiling. A new species?

Bambus diffusa. Spreading Bambus. Trunk that regularly lies along the ground. Leaves sword-shaped, hairy underneath, with edges set with small spines. Flowers as in the monogina species. Stamens six. Stigmas three, hairy. Fruit a single seed (as large as a chickpea), globose, covered with a membrane, marked with four lines.= This cane, called Bocaui in Bulacan, is well known to all the natives, and very common at the edges of forests, where it spreads extensively. It rarely rises straight up from the ground, but rather emerges already leaning to one side, or lying down and spreading along the ground. The natives make much use of this cane for building the fences of their plantations and for countless other purposes. The regular thickness of this cane is more than one inch. In some of the hollow sections I have seen on several occasions a crust about a line thick, and even as thick as a little finger, of a very white, crumbly substance, sometimes hard, odorless and somewhat tasteless, which native healers use in the manner of Tabashir for certain illnesses. The shoots of this cane, when they are no more than a hand's breadth in height, the

188
they are also used to consume the clouding of the cornea of the eyes. For this purpose they are cut at the base and at the tip, and the two outer layers are stripped away. A little rock sugar is placed in the remaining core, and the whole thing is set out in the open air in a small bowl. Then, with the water found in the morning in the core of the shoot, the clouded spots are moistened with a small feather. * T., Osiu, Bocavi. New species.

Bambus textoria. Weavers' Bamboo. Straight trunk. Leaves sword-shaped, smooth on the upper surface and somewhat rough below and along the edges. = This cane does not grow as tall as the other species; its maximum height is about six varas. Its diameter is about an inch and a half. It is beautiful, very straight and clean, and is much used in looms. It is very common in the forests, but not in all of them. *T., Calbang. New species.

Bambus arundo. Reed Bamboo. Branches with sharp, stiff, and pointed buds. Leaves narrow, sword-shaped, smooth beneath, somewhat rough above, and with barely noticeable small hooks along the edges. Petioles with very few hairs. Stamens six. Ovary with a cluster of hairs at the base. Style long. Stigma either branched or split halfway into two parts. = This cane, which sometimes measures eight or more inches in diameter, is the most widely used for all kinds of work, and is among the tallest. It would take a very long time to describe the countless uses and applications of this and of other canes: for from them alone are made very sharp weapons, houses, bridges, scaffolding, very strong ropes, and everything one could want. They also serve as jugs and pots; for when this cane is used for that purpose, a small hole is made in it to pour in water and rice, and when laid on its side over the fire, the grain comes out well cooked, tasty, and fragrant. Inside a house and sheltered from rain, it is incorruptible; buried in the earth and even in mud, it lasts for some and even many years. In summertime, the leaves serve as fodder for horses and cattle; but the water from the cane infusion is fatal to pigs that drink it. The inner film of the cane, carefully extracted, can be used in place of paper. Inside this cane, there is sometimes found a small stony concretion called Tabaxir, a remarkable medicine used by superstitious natives. The small young shoots of the cane are eaten in salad. I have seen female flowers on the same plant. The pointed buds are two at the base of the branches, and resemble thorns; but I take them to be buds that have not yet unfolded. I do not know whether this cane yields potable and medicinal water like the following species. *T., Cauayang totoo. Lin. Sist. veg. 579.

Bambus mitis. Spineless Bamboo. Leaves sword-shaped, with short stiff hairs on both surfaces, and small hooks

189
very small on the edges. Petioles hairy along their entire length.= This cane is among the tallest. At the nodes, those pointed buds that sting as in the true cane are not observed. Some say that this species is the same as the Monogyna. By cutting a thick branch the size of a finger, clear water is collected at night in abundance, which has a good flavor, and when drunk is assured to be excellent for consumptives: and I believe there is no other basis for this than the natives seeing the resemblance that the consumptive has with the cane in its dry and wasted state. T., *Taiuanac.
Bambus lima. Bambus lima. Leaves lanceolate-like, broad, with rough and short hair on both surfaces, and small hooks, barely noticeable on the edges. Petioles hairy at the tip, and smooth on the rest.= This cane only reaches a height of twelve or fifteen feet. It is like the middle finger, or at most an inch thick. The distance between node and node is great. The bark, although it appears smooth, is so rough and hard that bronze is filed very well with it; and I have noted that it does not dull afterward. *T., Anos. New species.— I have not been able to see the flowers of the Anos and Calban.
Bambus levis. Bambus liviana. Leaves sword-shaped; the last ones of the large branches broad, with soft down underneath, with short stiff hair on top, and very small hooks on the edges, and an upper midrib. Petioles hairy along their entire length.= This cane is among the tallest. It is more fragile than the ordinary one, which stings. The native calls it entera (whole): because the hollow is very large. I saw the dry flowers in June: perhaps it will flower in February. *T., Cauayang boo. New species?
Bambus lumampao. Bambus lumampao. Trunk straight without spines. Flowers in a compound, interrupted spike, forming groups of small flowers, some round, some elongated. In each group there are more than fifty small flowers. The valves are not fringed. Stamens six. Style one. Stigmas two, very short.= It is a beautiful cane, very well known, which grows naturally in the forests, and reaches a height of six to eight varas. They take it to sell in Manila, and its thickness is like the wrist. Bronze can also be filed with it. *T., Lumampao, Bocaui. New species?
ORYZA. Cal. A bivalve glume with one flower. Cor. of two nearly equal valves, joined to the seed. Lin. Syst. Veg. 578— Rice grows in water, and in high and dry lands: I will speak first of Water rice.

* Water rice.

Oryza sativa binambang. Binambang rice. Leaves sword-shaped, with short hairs, especially on the upper surface-
32

190
rior. Flowers in panicle. Calyx very small, and as in the genus. Corolla: the valves of the glume, covered with short hairs. The larger one with two ribs running lengthwise, and ending in a small white horn. The smaller valve has at the base a small scale, split in the middle into two parts, and at the apex a small horn smaller than that of the other valve. Stamens six. Filaments very long. Stigmas two, divergent and hairy. Seed closely covered by the glume of the corolla. = This variety, like all the others, grows to a height of about four feet more or less. It grows in water, and flowers in December. * T., Binambang.

Oryza sativa lamuyo. Lamuyo Rice. Calyx white. Corolla: the valves are hairy between rib and rib, brownish in color; but not particularly notable. In other respects like the preceding variety. = This variety is the one most widely cultivated, and the one that in Batangas regularly forms the sustenance of those who live on the seashore. * T., Lamuyo.

Oryza sativa glutinosa. Glutinous Rice. Calyx red at maturity. Corolla: the valves hairy, purplish toward the base and at the apex, and with the small horns not very notable. = This rice is called malagcquit or sticky because it does in fact display that property after cooking. Various kinds of dishes are made with it, which the natives consider delicious; but which are in reality indigestible, especially if coconut milk is added, as is commonly done. It is also used to whitewash walls, by mixing this kind of rice with plaster; and it is worth noting that this coating is very firm, even when exposed to rain. * T., Malagcquit.

Oryza aristata. Awned Rice. The outer glume ends in an awn of more than one inch in length. = It is a common species of rice in Ilocos, and grows in water, although in Batangas it grows in dry-land fields, where they call it bontot cabayo (horse's tail). The Ilocos variety has a plump grain and is therefore sought after; although it is not among the most flavorful to eat, as it has a certain roughness.

* Dry-land varieties.

Oryza sativa præcox. Early Rice. Leaves sword-shaped, with hairs and other features as in the other varieties of water rice. Calyx as in the genus. Corolla: the valves of the glume smooth, each ending in a very short small horn. = This variety of rice grows in highland fields, and not in standing water like the others I have discussed before. The natives call it dumali, meaning early, because it is harvested at three months. The seed is a little broader and shorter than that of the following variety. Despite the fact that this rice

191
it matures very quickly, the Indians never plant much of it, and the reason is that because it is early, insects and birds destroy a great deal of it. * T., Dumali.
Oryza sativa quinanda. Quinanda Rice. Leaves sword-shaped, smooth. Calyx as in the genus. Corolla as in the dumali variety. = This variety is the most esteemed, and the one most generally sown in great abundance in Batangas. The reason the natives give for this preference is that, besides the flavor of the rice, the grain after cooking swells more than that of other varieties: it therefore requires a little more water than others to cook. It is sown in May and harvested in October. * T., Quinanda.
Oryza sativa pilosa. Hairy Rice. Leaves as in the Praecox variety. Calyx as in the genus. Corolla: the valves of the glume are covered with very conspicuous hairs and end in two very short little horns. = This dry-land variety of rice is not among the most esteemed, but the Indians grow it because they say it is not easily attacked by the diseases to which rice is generally susceptible. * T., Bolohan.
Oryza sativa rubra. Red Rice. Leaves sword-shaped, smooth on both surfaces, with short hairs on the edges. Calyx and the short little horns of the glume are red, unlike the previous varieties in which they are whitish. The valves have some hairs, but not very conspicuous ones. = This dry-land variety of rice, when cooked in water, is notably sticky in the mouth, from which it takes its name. The Indians are accustomed to planting a little of it on the borders of the seedbeds, to use it in the same way described for water Malagcquit. This species of rice, given to horses suffering from worms, is said to kill them. For this purpose the rice is soaked in its husk with a little water and honey. * T., Malagcquit.
Oryza sativa violacea. Purple Rice. Leaves sword-shaped, with short hairs on both surfaces and on the edges. Calyx and the little horns of the glume are purple in color. The valves are hairy. = This variety of rice, which also grows in highland areas, is highly esteemed for its flavor. * T., Tangi.
It would be a very tedious task to list all the species or varieties of rice, both wet and dry; for they are very numerous, and in general the Indian distinguishes them by the shape of the grain. I will now briefly describe the method observed by the natives of the Province of Batangas in the cultivation of rice.
Cultivation of wet rice. The land where wet rice is sown is laid out in squares or plots, so that the rainwater, or water from ponds or reservoirs, may be-

192
have it there. When the soil is well saturated with water, which usually happens in Batangas around the end of June, the natives prepare a small area where they form their seedbed. By August, when the rains are heaviest and the paddies fill with water, they plow the flooded fields with buffaloes, pull up the rice they sowed in the seedbed, and cutting off part of the roots and half the length of the stalks, they plant them in the ground by making small holes with a finger and placing in each one a small handful, which will yield about five or more feet. In the Provinces of Tondo and Bulacan, it is the miserable women who carry out this tiresome task, while their cruel husbands rest comfortably.
When the rice is ripe, which usually occurs in December or after the new year, they reap it with sickles or with small knives, cutting the ears one by one. This is work for men, women, and boys. The reapers are given the fifth, or the fourth, and sometimes the third part of the rice they harvest as payment for their labor; and once this is done, the owner carries the remaining ears to his house, where he piles them up until, after a few months or sooner, they separate the grain from the straw by trampling it with bare feet, for which the men and women who perform this operation are paid a fifth part. From the account I have just given, the imperfection of rice harvest practices is immediately apparent. Piling up the rice before sunning and drying it causes the grain to overheat, turn dark, and acquire a bad smell and taste. Nevertheless, this is the common practice among the natives, and they excuse themselves by saying that harvest time is rainy and they cannot dry it; but they could place it, as is done elsewhere, in large piles out in the open air with the ears facing inward.
The harvesting of rice ear by ear, which Europeans would scarcely believe, is an even more outlandish custom, and it would be very good if the Government were to prohibit it on account of the very serious drawbacks it brings with it. In the year 1823, at least a third of the rice crop was left standing in the fields, because there was no one to reap it, and those who agreed to do it demanded a third of the crop and that the owner carry it to their own homes. At times it was necessary to give them half, so as not to lose everything. Moreover, the fields that are not very lush and do not have thick, well-filled rice are also refused by reapers, because they spend more time and harvest less. On top of all this, they must be fed. So everything amounts to losses for the poor farmer. This mob of reapers is generally made up of the most idle and vagabond people of the Provin-

193
ces, who at that time abandon their homes and towns to devote themselves to this trade.
Cultivation of Upland Rice, or Dry-field Rice. The rice sown in upland areas requires much more labor than that of flooded lands; but this is unavoidable, since the latter are not very extensive. The soil must be plowed three or four times, and the clods broken up with a kind of harrow; and once the rice has sprouted, until it stands nearly two spans tall, it must be weeded at least twice, because in this country, if one is negligent even for a short while, the ground is immediately overrun with all manner of weeds that choke the rice paddies. Sowing time, in which the rice is broadcast like wheat in Europe, falls in May, or earlier if it rains; and the harvest is usually finished by November.
The operations of harvesting and collecting dry-field rice are the same as those of the flooded fields; it should be noted, however, that dry-field rice is very rarely reaped with sickles, whereas the other kind is reaped with sickles more frequently. The reason the natives give is that cutting with sickles causes much grain to fall to the ground, which does not happen, they say, when it is gathered ear by ear; because the grains in upland rice do not cling to the stalk as firmly as those of flooded-field rice. I have no difficulty believing this; but it would also be troublesome, if the crop were to be reaped with sickles, to move the bundles many times or disturb them unnecessarily, and it would be better to thresh them in small heaps. And if so much grain is wasted by reaping with sickles, how much more must be lost in the north of Ilocos, where I have seen with great dismay the bare bundles of rice loaded onto horses, cows, and buffalo to be carried from one town to another? The instrument with which they cut the rice ear by ear is of such a strange design that I believe few Europeans could manage it properly, even if it were placed directly in their hands. It is a narrow blade of steel, whose cutting edge forms a segment of a circle, and on the opposite side or back it has the shape of the leaves that botanists call lunulate. The angle found on the back opposite the edge is fitted into a small stick, which ends up forming a right angle with the blade. Gripping the stick, the cutting edge protrudes precisely on the outside, between the ring finger and the middle finger; and thus, taking an ear of grain with the index finger, the hand is pushed against that same ear so that the blade cuts it. This unusual instrument is called yatap.
Cultivation of Rice on Newly Opened Dry Lands. On ordinary dry lands, the rice harvest will be about thirty to one, according to what I have been able to learn from the natives; although others have told me that yields of as many as cin-

194
counted as one. In flooded lands the harvest comes to the same. But in dryland fields, which are transformed from forests into cultivated plots, the harvest is astonishing; because through the continuous shedding of leaves from the trees that covered them, they have come to acquire a thick layer of black earth, through which the rice extends its roots with great ease, so that from one measure called a chupa, one caban of rice is harvested, and in this the accounts of the natives agree. One chupa is 1/200 part of a caban. Let us suppose there is exaggeration in what has been said, and that not 200 but only 100 are gathered per one; it is still plain to see, in this case, with what diligence the natives ought to obtain lands of this kind, even if it required some labor. From what I have said, it is already apparent that a well-fertilized land would always yield harvests equal to those described. In few places can fertilizers be obtained with the ease that they can in the Philippines. Vegetation in trees and plants is extremely rapid, and if each farmer were to have a pit a few feet deep, in which he piled every kind of leaves and plants, with a couple of inches of soil on top, until they rotted in the sun and rain, and then transferred this compost to his field, one would harvest in the Islands a double quantity of rice compared to what is gathered today. The natives call newly opened fields bacal or bacalan, and sowing is done by dropping four or five grains of rice into small holes that the sower makes in the earth with his finger.
Upland rice does not need much water. The natives never irrigate it, and I have seen years in which it grows very vigorously with very scarce rainfall. It seems to me, from what I have observed, that provided it rains regularly every 15 days, a good harvest will be obtained. In Spain not even this would be necessary, because the heat of the sun not being as intense there, the soil would take much longer to dry out after a rain; and thus (as I believe) dryland rice could be grown there with the same ease as in the Philippines. The most difficult thing is choosing the most suitable time for sowing.
The dangers and diseases to which rice is exposed are very numerous. Sometimes it is lost from being too lush, other times from lack of water, and still other times from an excess of it. Locusts in these Islands rarely fail to appear in one year: if not in one Province, then in another. There are also countless other insects that destroy this plant. Among these, one that is quite harmful is the one the Tagalog natives call atangya; and in Spain in some towns of Casti-

195
the old one, which I recall they call parpaja. The one from these Islands is of worse appearance than that one; and to exterminate it, the Indians light small bonfires at night in the corners of the sown fields. The insect flies toward the fire, and in this way a prodigious number are killed.

The use of husked rice (generally called palay) in fevers instead of barley is well known, and produces very good effects, as it is very cooling. The lye made from burned rice straw, the Indians say, is excellent for removing dandruff from the head. Some have also devised (and let this pass as a digression) a rather strange method of shaving, without the need of a barber or razors, using only a few grains of palay. They take two grains of these — or perhaps just one — between the tips of the thumb and index finger of the right hand, and grasping some beard hairs between them, they press the tips together, and the grains then act as a pair of tweezers and pull the hairs out. This operation cannot be very pleasant; but some do it this way and end up quite clean: and as a reward they practice it at great leisure, even at night while lying on their backs. When these extraordinary little tweezers become blunted, they take two more grains and continue their shaving, something which no European could hardly endure. But leaving this aside, well-cooked rice applied warm has good effect on swollen testicles, when these arise, as often happens in this land, from a sudden chill. It is also applied to abscesses of women's breasts, and is preferable in this case, according to physicians, to a bread poultice: and if it is the glutinous rice called malagcquit, it has great virtue for softening the hardest tumors. Rice has finally, among the Indians, countless other uses, which I omit as already known.

HEXANDRIA.

TRIGINIA.

RUMEX. Calyx of three small leaves. Petals three, pressed together. One seed, with three faces inside the corolla. Lin. Syst. Veg. 584.

RUMEX MURICATUS. DOCK WITH SOFT SPINES. Root thick and irregular. Stem erect, striated, somewhat swollen at the joints, and not very branched. Leaves alternate, oblong, smooth, wavy and wrinkled: the new ones finely notched and edged, and on the lower surface with a horn-

196
awl-shaped base, attached near the tip of the midrib. Petioles clasping the stem at the base, equal, shorter than the leaves, and at the base bearing a very thin involucre that disappears at maturity. Flowers axillary and terminal, in racemes covered with a very thin membrane that disappears as the small flowers expand, these forming whorls. Peduncle proper, long. Calyx shaped like a bell, with three diverging, blunt lobes. Corolla (if not considered part of the Calyx, which is green, in which case it is divided into six parts) of three petals, alternating with the lobes of the calyx and attached to it, twice as long as it, oval, straight, with margins notched at the middle, and a short nerve on the back, marked with small dots. Both the calyx and the corolla are persistent. Filaments six, alternating with the petals and attached two by two at the base of the three calyx lobes, and of the same height. Anthers oval with two opposite furrows, through which they themselves divide in two. Ovary with three angles, seated within the flower. Styles three. Stigmas more than twelve on each style, forming a brush. One seed with a covering, enclosed within three slender angles inside the now large, triangular corolla, with notched margins, and also a short, thick nerve on the back of each division. = A plant cultivated without difficulty by some curious persons, and of whose origin I am ignorant. It puts out many stems, which can be transplanted. In Ilocos I have been assured that it grows spontaneously. I have had several specimens, the greatest height of which did not reach half a fathom. Its leaves with the petioles are one foot long: the root, which is very caustic, becomes larger than a fist, and is of a beautiful yellow color when fresh, which it loses when dry. The natives regard it as rhubarb; but they do not use it for anything. The anthers fall off very quickly, as soon as the corolla opens: the seeds germinate very easily. Flowers in August. — From the description given, which is exact, it can be seen that this plant perhaps ought to constitute a species distinct from those brought by Linnaeus.
FLAGELLARIA. Calyx of six pieces. Corolla none. Drupe like a berry with three chambers. Lin. Syst. Veg. 586.
Flagellaria indica. Indian Flagellaria. Stem round and prostrate. Leaves sheathing the stem, alternate, sessile, entire, smooth, sword-shaped, long-tapering, with three or four transverse folds, and the tip thicker and coiled upon itself in a spiral. Flowers in compound racemes. Calyx inferior of six pieces. Corolla none. Stamens.... ...Styles two or three, short. Drupe like a pea, slightly fleshy, with a hard nut and one seed. = A plant somewhat resembling a liana, but harder and tougher than it, and which serves equally-

197

thick enough to use for tying; it is as thick as a writing quill: the fruit is edible. It is a remarkable thing that the tips of the leaves are coiled with great symmetry and cannot be unrolled without tearing them. It is common in many places, and its true name is given below. * T., Balinguai.

HEXANDRIA.

HEXAGINIA.

ARISTOLOCHIA. Calyx: none. Corolla: monopetalous, tongue-shaped. Stamens: immediately adjacent to the germ. Inferior capsule, with six compartments. Lin. Syst. Veg. 590.

ARISTOLOCHIA INDICA. INDIAN ARISTOLOCHIA. Stem twining. Leaves heart-shaped, ovate, pointed, and smooth. Short petioles. Flowers in panicles. Calyx: none. Corolla globose at the base, with a cylindrical tube, widened at the tip and cut very obliquely. Anthers: six twin ones, fixed on a membrane that has six angles. Filaments: none. Styles six, very thick, enlarged at the base with a membrane that surrounds them all. Stigmas simple. Inferior capsule, with six ribs, six compartments, and many seeds, each surrounded by its own wing. = This plant climbs by coiling around everything it encounters. It is known by the name timbangan, which means balance or scale, because after the capsules have shed their seeds, they resemble small scales with their trays: although others use this same name for a species of asclepiad. It is also used in medicine. Flowers in November. * T., Timbangan, Malaubi. Lin. ibid. 591.

ARISTOLOCHIA SUBSAGITATA. NEARLY ARROW-SHAPED ARISTOLOCHIA. Stem round, twining, with striations, somewhat hairy. Leaves alternate, nearly arrow-shaped, pointed, with five veins, with finely notched margins, and barely hairy. Petioles as long as the leaves. Flowers axillary in panicles. Calyx, corolla, and the rest as in the previous species. Anthers: six twin ones. = This plant, which I have seen in Batangas and other places, grows very tall. The flowers have a purple spot at the tip of the lip. It is also known in Pasig by the name Malaubi, and the Indians greatly prize the root, which is sold publicly for stomach and intestinal complaints and for flatulent colic and indigestion. For this purpose, they have the sick person chew the bark of the root. The learned Father Clain says it is emetic; but I have observed that if it has this property, it is to a very mild degree. He is probably referring to another species that is bitter, and
33

198
which I have not seen. Flowers in Feb. * T., Timbangan, Timbangan timbangan, Malaubi. I., Taointaoin. New species?
In Pampanga I have seen a variety with leaves that are very elongated and arrow-shaped, with wavy edges: its length is about one palm-span: the decoction of the root is also drunk.
Aristolochia sericea. Silky Aristoloquia. Trunk straight. Leaves alternate, almost sessile, barely heart-shaped, egg-shaped, with three or five veins, entire, soft and silky. Flowers very small, axillary, in racemes. = Small trees about the height of a man, in Agoo. The fruit is smaller than a chickpea. New species.

OCTANDRIA.

MONOGINIA.

MIMUSOPS. Calyx of four pieces. Corolla of four petals. Nectary pointed, of sixteen pieces. Oval drupe with one or two seeds. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 416. Jus. Gen. pl. 152. Palau trad. de la p. pract. de Lin. t. 3. 319.
Mimusops talosan. Mimusops talosan. Leaves alternate, obliquely egg-shaped, with five veins, doubly serrated obtusely, hairy and soft. Petioles very short. Calyx inferior, tubular, fuzzy, with five teeth. Corolla of five petals (red) longer than the calyx, widened in the middle, with what appear to be lateral wings. Nectary a tube as long as the petals, with five white scales, very small (resembling lanceolate small petals) toward the tip, where there are ten short teeth, which are the filaments of as many stamens. Anthers before maturity shaped like a half-moon. Ovary oval, with a small stalk longer than the nectary. Styles two, very short. Stigmas simple. Drupe? (only one) oval, hairy, with one chamber and one seed? = Small trees that I have seen in Malinta, little known. I do not know whether the fruit, which is smaller than a pine nut, is a berry or a drupe, nor whether it has chambers. I believe it does not grow very large. Flowers in Sept. * T., Talosan. New species. It is the same as the Binectaria of Forsk.
The ten teeth of the nectary, and the five scales that it also has at the end of the tube, may be regarded as fifteen laciniae of the nectariferous tube: and although they are not truly separate pieces, the flower appears to bear a great resemblance to that of Mimusops, even though it lacks one piece: for the authors give it sixteen, and eight stamens. Nevertheless, it may perhaps be a new genus. The characteristics of this genus vary considerably among authors.

199
EUPHORIA. Cor. of five doubled petals, and on the inside, somewhat woolly at their center. Cal. divided halfway into five parts. Ovary twin. Stigmas two. Fruit double, globose, with tubercles, with one chamber, and a bony seed. (The Genus Litchi has today been incorporated with Euphoria.) Lin. Syst. Veg. 611.

Euphoria annularis. Euphoria with a ring. Leaves sub-opposite, winged without an odd leaflet. Leaflets in number of three pairs, more or less, lanceolate, entire, smooth and stiff. Flowers globose, in panicles. Cal. divided almost to the base, into four or five parts, concave. Cor. of four petals, ovate, much smaller than the calyx, woolly, placed regularly around the receptacle, and between the divisions of the calyx. Nect. a glandular ring, which encircles the base of the stamens. Stam. eight. Filam: longer than the calyx, woolly, separate, arranged regularly around the receptacle. Ant. thick. Ovary superior, somewhat bilobed. Style none. Stigma a small eminence on the ovary. Two pericarpels, and sometimes three, ovate, membranous, very compressed, joined at the middle, and in each one a single seed. = This tree, which must not be confused with the guijo, as it is called in Manila, is well known to the natives, for the extreme hardness of its wood. The one called guijo in Manila, which is used for carriage wheels, is a species of Diptero carpus. Fl. in Aug. * T., Guisian, Guisihan. New species? — The genera Euphoria Sapindo, Aporetica, Ornitrophe, and Schmidelia bear much resemblance to one another.

Euphoria litchi. Euphoria litchi. Leaves sub-opposite, winged without an odd leaflet. The leaflets approach a lanceolate shape, entire, and somewhat hairy underneath. Flowers in a panicle. Cal. divided almost to the base into five or six parts. Cor. of five ovate petals, very woolly. Stam. eight. Filam. woolly. Style none. Stigma in two parts. Nect. two very small glands at the base of the ovary. Fruit, three pericarpels, with scales or stalks, globose (one or both abort), containing a well-formed nut, with its covering surrounded by a fleshy aril. = This tree grows tall enough to become a second-order tree. Its wood is hard and very useful for various purposes. The natives, and even Europeans, enjoy the fruit, which in Manila is called Lechias, and by the natives Alpai, and to gather it they sometimes cut down the trees. The only edible part is the aril, which amounts to a little whitish flesh whose flavor somewhat resembles that of grapes. Fl. in March. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 611. It is the sinensis species of Lin. in the cited location.
I have seen other trees with six stamens. The nectary has

200
Five lobes. Three-lobed ovary. Style as long as the stamens. Two stigmas. * T., Alpai, Lechias, Alipai, Alupai. V., Boboa. The lechias from China have no nipples except when the fruit is small, as they fall off afterward: as I have observed in those brought from that country to Manila; but in the forests of the Islands, the same lechias from China grow without nipples at maturity.

Euphoria? Nephelium? Euforia? Nefelio? Leaves alternate, elongated-ovate, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers monoecious? * Males.... * Females axillary, solitary, with a very short and very thick peduncle, on which is placed an ovate pouch, bristling with nipples curved downward like hooks, hard at maturity.= I can say nothing more about this tree, which, according to some Indians who told me, grows as large as a man's body; although those I saw in the forests of Angat were smaller than a fist. Despite all my efforts, it was not possible for me to see its flowers. Its leaves are one span long. The husk is like a hen's egg. Those I have seen, which have been many, contained nothing inside, as the insects had devoured them. In only one was I able to discover a seed. This rare tree is called in Angat, malaanonan. It may belong to this genus, and be the species cited in Decand. prod. p. 1. 612?

Euphoria cubili. Euforia cubili. Leaves alternate or opposite, pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets about four or five pairs, lanceolate, entire, smooth and stiff. Common petioles swollen at the base. Proper petioles very short, channeled. Flowers terminal, in large, racemose panicles. Calyx inferior, hairy, and with five lobes. Corolla of five small, woolly petals, fixed upon as many glands or excrescences situated at the base of the calyx. Stamens five, around the base of the ovary. Filaments broad and curved inward. Anthers thick, projecting beyond the calyx. Ovary hairy, with two or three lobes. Styles two, very short. Stigmas simple. Three oval pericarps, covered with nipples, which when ripe split in two: two of them regularly abort, and each one contains a single well-formed seed, with a thin rind, with a fleshy aril at the base, and notched at the edges.= A very large tree, known in the forests of Angat and S. Mateo, from which good planks are obtained. The seeds are large like a walnut, with a purple-colored rind, thinner than that of a chestnut. They are not eaten raw because they cause dizziness; but cooked or toasted they are very tasty. The outer covering, inside which they are enclosed, is in two pieces when broken, and is covered on the outside with small nipple-like projections. This is all I can say about this extraor-

201
ordinary, whose flowers I managed to see after three years, through the diligence of Fr. Antonio Llanos, Augustinian, Parish Priest in Angat. Flowers in April, in the mountains of Tala and Angat, where it is called Cubili, and in Balanga, Lubilubi. New species.
Euphoria didyma. Twin Euphoria. Leaves opposite, winged without an odd leaflet. Leaflets in about three or four pairs, lanceolate, entire, stiff, and smooth. Terminal flowers, in panicles. Calyx bell-shaped, with four or five lobes. Around the germen there is a circle of glands. Stamens about eight. Germen of two divergent lobes (rarely three), rough. Style one, rather long. Stigmas two, twisted to the sides. Two fruits (rarely three), oval, compressed, and with scales. = Small trees, well known. Both this species and the others of this genus and of Sapindus, called Guisian or Guisihan, have heavy, very hard wood, very well suited to the uses for which the wood called guijo is used in Manila. I have not seen the fruit of this species advanced. Flowers in May. * T., Guisian, Guisihan, Tinaingui. It seems to be the same one I called anularis.
The famous bayoco wood so prized in Iloilo for its hardness, I believe is the one described here, or one of the Sapindus.
Sapindus. Calyx of four pieces. Corolla of four petals, scaly, glandular, or bearded on the inside. Stamens eight, with hairy filaments. Style one. Stigmas three. Three drupes in the form of joined, swollen berries, each with one seed. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 607.
Sapindus guisian. Guisian Sapindus. Leaves alternating or opposite, winged without an odd leaflet. Leaflets in groups of three or more pairs, wedge-shaped, and covered with short down. Terminal flowers in panicles. Calyx of five pieces; three opposite the two smaller ones. Corolla of four petals, rarely five, placed on one side only of the flower, and not in a circle: on the inner surface of each petal, there is a woolly gland. Stamens regularly seven or eight, placed on one side only of the corolla, joined together at the base into a single body. Nectary of four glands placed on the receptacle, in addition to the four mentioned above. Superior germen, with three angles, placed at the center of the stamens. Styles two or three, very small, straight: but with time they bend to the sides. Three drupes, sometimes two, egg-shaped, reversed: joined at the middle, and each containing one large seed. = A small tree, well known, of very hard and slightly fragrant wood. Some old writers have said that it is the Lentisk. Flowers in April. * T., Guisihan. V., Duca. New species. — Perhaps the Bayoco?
Sapindus edulis. Edible Sapindus. Leaves opposite, and sometimes alternate, winged without an odd leaflet. Leaflets nearly sessile, oval, hairy beneath, entire. Flowers in a compound raceme. Calyx.

202
of five pieces: the two opposite to the three, larger. Corolla of four petals, with a small-stalked and woolly gland in the middle of each one. Stamens eight, hairy, and fixed on the side opposite the petals. Style one, with a somewhat thick stigma. Three oval, somewhat fleshy, horizontal drupes. = Trees that grow in Marigondon, of which I have seen only a few branches: the fruit is half an inch long, and its flesh, which is purple, is eaten. New species.
KOELREUTERIA. Calyx of five pieces. Corolla of four petals, with as many scales at the base, cleft in two. Capsule with three chambers, inflated, and two seeds in each one. Pers. Syn. pl. 413.
Koelreuteria arborea. Koelreuteria tree. Leaves sometimes opposite, sometimes alternate, winged without a terminal leaflet, and in its place a bristle. Leaflets nearly sessile, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Flowers in a panicle. Calyx deeply four-parted, concave, and hairy at the extremities. Corolla of five petals, egg-shaped in reverse, and at the base of each one an appendage that divides into two parts: each of these subdivides again into two, globose and hairy. Stamens eight, to one side of the ovary. Filaments hairy. Ovary oval, sessile, and hollowed in the middle. Style none. Stigma pyramidal, with indistinct angles. Fruit. = A tree as thick as a human body: its timber is used in carpentry. Not very well known. New species. — The capsules in this species I have not seen, and I do not know whether they may be berries, as in the following.
Koelreuteria edulis. Edible Koelreuteria. Leaves opposite, winged without a terminal leaflet, in whose place there is a bristle. Leaflets about four pairs, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Petioles very short, with two large, round stipules fixed upon themselves. Flowers axillary, in compound racemes. Calyx the same color as the corolla, very deeply four-parted. Corolla of four petals with claws: and each one with a broad appendage at the base. Stamens eight, fixed between a small disk that lies below the ovary and the ovary itself. Filaments flat and velvety. Ovary oval, with a protuberance on top that serves as the stigma. Berry club-shaped, somewhat compressed, with a channel, and two seeds in a single chamber. = Trees of about eight varas in height, which I have seen in Pampanga and Pangasinan. The flowers resemble peas and are purple in color; as is the fruit, which is eaten and resembles a cherry. The bark of the tree smells bad. Flowers in December. * P., Talinouno. I., Dirig. — New species; but the fruit was certainly imperfect.
APORETICA. Calyx of four pieces, the two outer ones larger. Petals four: and as many inner scales, very small. Stamens eight. Anthers nearly round. Ovary didymous. Stigmas

203
two, divergent. Jus. Gen. pl. 247.— It is barely distinguishable from Schmidelia according to some Authors.
Aporetica gemella. Twin Aporetica. Leaves ternate. Leaflets approaching a lanceolate shape, pointed, and serrated. Axillary flowers in a panicle. Calyx split almost to the base into four parts: the two opposite ones larger. Corolla of four petals, on one side of the flower, with a gland or woolly scale at the base of each. Stamens eight: there are also four glands on the receptacle. Ovary of two lobes. Style one. Stigmas two, very small before maturity. Two drupes (and never three) united below.= This tree reaches a height of four or five varas. The flowers are small, and shaped like a lentil. When a small twig is twisted between the fingers, a rather pleasant odor is noticed. The natives do not regard it as Guisihan. Flowers in June. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 610.— There is another species with leaves that are sometimes ternate, sometimes quinate.
Aporetica penicellata. Brush Aporetica. Leaves ternate. Leaflets ovate, serrated, with small points at the serrations, and another at the apex, smooth, with a small tuft of wool in the axils of the veins. Flowers in umbellate racemes. Each small umbel with two or three small flowers. Calyx concave in four parts. Corolla of four woolly petals, with a tuft of wool at the apex, placed on one side of the flower. Nectary of four smooth glands at the base of the petals. Stamens eight, united in one body, and on the opposite side from the petals. Anthers regular. Ovary in the middle of the stamens. Style one. Stigmas two. Two small, smooth, globose drupes: one of them aborts many times.= A shrub that grows very little, and whose trunk is weak, seemingly in need of the support of other trees. The natives do not know it. When a small twig is twisted, a rather pleasant odor is perceived. It is necessary to search carefully for the ovary in the center of the stamens.
