Flowers in June.— It has been given the name above on account of the woolly tips of the petals. New species.
MELICOCCA. Calyx in four parts. Petals four, folded inside the calyx. Stigma half-shielded. Drupe leathery, half-round, with two or three seeds, or one by abortion. Lin. Sist. veg. 613. Jus. Gén. pl. 248.
Melicocca triptera. Three-winged Melicocca. Leaves alternate, winged without an odd leaflet, replaced by a small stylet. Leaflets about five pairs, almost sessile, lanceolate, wavy, entire and smooth. Terminal flowers, in racemose panicles: the rachis is not winged. Calyx in five rounded and hairy parts: two of them partly cover the other three. Corolla absent. A fleshy, hypogynous disk, with teeth at the edge, bearing eight hairy filaments with thick anthers, or fitted with a small stipe or beak at the apices. Ovary hairy. Style

204
thick, which is slow to emerge from the germ. Stigma simple and hard at maturity. Drupe globose, somewhat fleshy, with a small stalk, with three wings two lines wide, triangular, narrow and folded to one side, with a hard nut of three chambers and solitary seeds, without aril, fixed on the axis of the drupe. = A tree like a thigh, with whitish bark, which I have seen in Parañaque; and it is found mixed with the one called salub. It is not known; although there they called it Cahoi dalaga. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 615. Sect. Schleichera.

CUPANIA. Calyx of five pieces. Corolla of five hooded petals. Stamens eight. Style split in three parts. Upper capsule with three valves, three chambers, and in each one one or two seeds with aril, fixed on the partitions of the valves. Trees, which are sometimes found with male flowers. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 612.

CUPANIA SPINOSA. SPINY CUPANIA. Trunk erect, with spines. Leaves alternate, sometimes solitary, sometimes grouped in threes or fours, egg-shaped and reversed, finely serrated, somewhat fleshy and smooth. Petioles very short, with a spine on the inner side of the base. Flowers axillary, in panicles. Calyx free, flat, in five parts. Corolla much larger than the calyx, with five linear petals. Stamens five, alternating with the petals and shorter than them. Anthers pointed. Ovary globose, seated on the calyx. Style single, very short. Stigmas three. Capsule egg-shaped and reversed, crowned with the style, like a small cherry grown large, (crimson) with three ribs, three valves bearing the partitions, three chambers, and in each one two seeds, oval, girdled at the base with a fleshy, notched aril. = Very common small trees in Malinta, about three fathoms tall, with hard wood. The seeds are somewhat smaller than peas. The Indians there wrongly call it Malarayap, because of the leaves, which somewhat resemble those of the lemon. New species. — It agrees with Molinæa in having the partitions fixed to the valves.

MOLINÆA. Calyx in five parts. Petals five, with slightly hairy claws. Filaments hairy at the base. Style none. Capsule with three angles, three valves, three chambers, and as many seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 611.

MOLINÆA ARBOREA. TREE MOLINEA. Leaves opposite, pinnate without a terminal leaflet. Leaflets four pairs, or fewer, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers arise on the branches, in panicles. Calyx inferior, deeply divided into five lanceolate parts. Corolla of five petals, flat, rounded and hairy. Nectary globose with eight teeth. Stamens eight, placed at the apex and teeth of the nectary, and divergent. Filaments awl-shaped and hairy. Anthers regular. Ovary with

205
angles that the flower is slow to emerge from. Style none. Stigma a small hairy body. Capsule oval, truncated, with three or four sides, containing three or four chambers, and in each one an oval seed, girdled to the middle with a fleshy, granular aril. = A small tree common on the beaches of Batangas and Parañaque, which in the forests reaches three fathoms in height. The tips of the branches are notable for the fiery color of their leaves. The fruit is also red. Flowers in January. T., Salab. Lin. ibid.

MELICOPE. Calyx in four parts, inferior. Corolla of four petals. Nectary of four twin glands at the base of the ovary. Style of four angles. Four capsules with solitary seeds. Lin. ibid. 620. Pres. Sist. pl. 416.

Melicope conferta. Clustered Melicope. Leaves clustered, oval, entire, and with many pores. Petioles very short. Terminal flowers in a dichotomous panicle. Calyx inferior, very small, with four lobes. Corolla much longer than the calyx, with four linear petals, rolled downward at maturity, hairy on the inside toward the base, and with a hood at the tip. Stamens eight, the length of the petals, and rolled downward at maturity: the four alternate ones longer. Filaments broad and hairy on the inside to their midpoint. Anthers oval. Ovary conical, with four channels and surrounded at the base by a fleshy ring. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma somewhat thickened. Capsule? with four chambers and solitary seeds. = Small trees found in Angat, as thick as a calf of the leg. The leaves are more than four inches long. The pores of the leaves can only be seen clearly with a lens. I have not seen the ripe fruit. Flowers in June. New species. — By the form of the ovary, it cannot belong to the genus Clausena.

OSBECKIA. Calyx with four laciniae, separated by a scale of the calyx. Corolla of four petals. Anthers beak-shaped. Capsule of four chambers, surrounded by the truncated tube of the calyx. Lin. Sist. veg. 605.

Osbeckia sinensis. Chinese Osbeckia. Stem erect, without branches, with short hairs. Leaves opposite, half-clasping the stem, with three nerves, and lined with hair underneath. Flowers axillary and terminal, in groups of four to six small florets, sessile. Calyx cylindrical, with about six eyelash-like glandular hairs on the outer surface, and terminated with five laciniae, deciduous, and other similar glandular lashes. Corolla of four petals, broad, inversely egg-shaped, attached at the throat of the calyx. Stamens eight, inclined downward, attached at the base of the petals, and with anthers shaped like a bird's beak, terminated with a thread or awn, as if pierced at the tip. Ovary globose, seated within the calyx, and terminated with a

206
Small hairy crown. Style curved, longer than the stamens. Stigma simple. Capsule oval, with four chambers, and many seeds. = A plant very similar to the Melastomas, common in Tala, two palms tall, with purple flowers. Flowers in July. * In Angat, Changparang. Lin. ibid.
LAUSONIA. Calyx inferior, divided in four parts. Corolla of four petals. Stamens arranged in four pairs. Capsule of four chambers, and many seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 619.
Lausonia inermis. Lawsonia inermis. Trunk with scattered branches. Leaves opposite, broadly lanceolate, entire, smooth, and stiff; with the edges rolled downward. Petioles nearly absent. Flowers terminal, in racemose panicles, with opposite peduncles. Calyx inferior, bell-shaped, divided in four pointed parts, with a circular outgrowth or membrane on the inner surface: and between this and the calyx, the petals and stamens are fixed. Corolla of four petals, longer than the calyx, with wavy edges, fixed between the divisions of the calyx. Stamens eight, fixed in pairs on the segments of the calyx, alternating with the petals, and longer than them. Anthers kidney-shaped. Ovary at the base of the calyx, globose. Styles as long as the stamens. Stigma obtuse. Capsule globose, with four chambers, and many seeds shaped like an inverted pyramid. = Small trees of barely two fathoms in height, without spines; although sometimes the tips of the small branches have the appearance of them. They are native to the East Indies, and perhaps to this country itself. They also grow in Arabia and Egypt, and are cultivated in Europe. There they are called Alchena, Alcana, and Oriental Henna. The Turks use the root as a cosmetic: moreover, all parts of the tree contain a red coloring matter. The dried leaves, reduced to an impalpable powder, are used after moistening with a few drops of water, to paint the face, which is practiced particularly by women: this coloring does not come off, except when the skin renews itself; and they even claim that it is preserved in mummies, after many centuries. The flowers, according to the women of Manila, are fragrant; but their true scent is nothing more than that of yeast: the fruit is slightly larger than a pea: in Manila the tree is known by the name of Cinamomo, and takes root easily from a cutting. Flowers in July. Lin. ibid.
COMBRETUM. Calyx superior, bell-shaped, with four or five teeth. Corolla of four or five petals, inserted on the calyx. Stamens eight or ten, very long. Seed one, with four or five wings. Lin. ibid. 609.
Combretum laxum. Lax Combretum. Leaves opposite, oval, suddenly pointed at the apex, entire, and smooth. Petioles short. Flowers terminal, in racemose panicles, close-

207
tadas. The upper calyx, with scales or small plates, which make it fuzzy, with eight or ten teeth on the edge; the smaller alternating ones, and toward their middle with a membranous and hairy crown. Corolla of four or five petals, very small, fixed at the base of the small calyx teeth, that is: eight or ten fixed near the base of the teeth. Filaments very long and diverging. Anthers oval, split at the base. Ovary below the calyx, four-angled. Style long and somewhat thick. Stigmas four in the dried flowers. Fruit a long seed, with four large and slender wings. = They are small trees with drooping branches, somewhat thicker than a calf: and these are the ones that produce flowers. Their twisted branches give off a confusing smell of onion, and they rise to a height of two fathoms. The leaves have transparent pores, like the pitchers of Nepenthes. I have seen them in Batangas, on the Abra River of Ilocos, and in Malinta: and the most singular thing about them is the abundant, crystal-clear water that pours out when a thick branch is cut, which can be drunk. Who would believe that these little trees are hardly known to the natives? In the Abra of Ilocos they call them Malacadog, and in Malinta * T., Pamulaclaquin. Flowers in November. Lin. ibid. — It is a congener of the Cristaria of Sonnerat.
XYLOCARPUS. Calyx with four or five lobes, club-shaped, and half the size of the corolla. Petals four or five. Stamens eight or ten, fixed in an egg-shaped, swollen nectary. Stigma broad and furrowed. Drupe dry, globose, with a woody and fibrous rind on the inside, of four or five valves, containing eight or more unequal nuts, with a fragile nucleus. Decand. Prod. p. 1. 626 in the genus. Calapa. Lin. Sist. Veg. 611.
Xylocarpus granatum. Xylocarpus like the pomegranate. Leaves opposite, pinnate without a terminal leaflet. Leaflets in two pairs, wedge-shaped, entire, and smooth. Petiole proper very short. Calyx inferior, with four or five teeth. Corolla of four or five petals, concave, slightly notched at the tip. Nectary egg-shaped, terminating above in eight or nine notched teeth. Filaments none. Anthers according to the number of the nectary teeth and fixed in its divisions. Ovary very thick, globose. Stigma shield-shaped. Drupe globose, dry, very large, with four thin, soft partitions, four compartments, and in each one two or more seeds, very tightly packed together. Seeds of irregular shape due to mutual compression, convex on one side, concave on the others, angular, and with a smooth outer covering and fibrous within. = A common tree near the sea, in flooded terrain. It rises to a height of twenty or more feet. The wood is red-colored: and both it and its bark give an abundant red color—

208
dante, although with a yellowish tinge, in the water in which they are steeped as an infusion. Fishing nets and abacá fabrics are placed in this hot liquid, and the dye is very fast, though not very pleasing to the eye. The fruit resembles a very large orange; boiled in water, it produces a warm bath, very good for treating venereal complaints. The seeds have a slightly bitter flavor, very astringent, and when ground in water with a little copperas, they produce a fairly good black ink. In the Visayas, a hard salt in lumps is known, called Tap-on, which is used in food: it is made by burning the tabigui, the cegiceras, the avicennia, the rhizophoras, and other shoreline trees. While they burn, they are continuously sprinkled with seawater: and from the lye of the ashes, evaporated in pots, the said salt results. * T., Tabigui, Nigui, Calumpang sa lati. P., Migui. Lin. ibid. It is the Carapa of other Authors.
GNIDIA. Calyx funnel-shaped, with four lobes. Four petals, inserted in the calyx. One seed, almost berry-like. Lin. Sist. Veg. 633.
GNIDIA OPPOSITIFOLIA. GNIDIA WITH OPPOSITE LEAVES. Trunk erect. Leaves opposite, ovate, pointed, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in compound racemes. Own peduncle, short. Calyx inferior, funnel-shaped, with four teeth and the throat full of down. Corolla of four oval, small petals, which end below in long little claws, fixed near the edge of the calyx, between the alternating and taller stamens, of the eight of the flower. Stamens eight, fixed near the edge of the calyx: four higher than the others. Filaments three times longer than the calyx. Anthers ovate, incumbent. Pistil shorter than the stamens. Stigma simple. Fruit at the base of the calyx, superior, with one seed. = Small trees as thick as an arm, and the height of a man, which I saw in Angat. They have no name among the Indians. The fruit was not ripe. The corollas are white. Flowers in December. Lin. ibid.
MEMECYLON. Calyx superior, with a striated base, and a very entire margin. Corolla of one petal. Anthers inserted on one side of the apex of the filament. Berry crowned with a cylindrical calyx. Lin. ibid. 619.
MEMECYLON TINCTORIUM. DYE MEMECILON. Trunk erect, branched. Leaves opposite, pinnate without an odd leaflet, in whose place there is a small stylet. Leaflets ovate, fleshy, and smooth. Flowers axillary, in umbels. Calyx colored, superior, swollen, with four obtuse teeth, not very noticeable, and with more than six membranous rays at the base, running from the center to the circumference. Corolla of four broad lanceolate petals, fixed on the four teeth of the calyx. Stamens eight;

209
the four fixed ones on the edges of the calyx, alternating with the petals; the others fixed at their base. The filaments bend inward, with a node toward the middle. Anthers shaped like a half-moon. Style single. Stigma simple. Berry globose, with one or more glands at the tip, crowned by the calyx, with one chamber and one seed; sometimes there are two, three, or four chambers, with only one large one; and in each one seed. = A well-known tree: its flowers are blue, and the calyces are pale pink. It rises to a height of about twelve feet, and its wood is heavy and hard. With its leaves, or those of the following species, a somewhat sticky decoction is made, into which the Indians dip the leaves of the Buli, or of the Palm, with which they make their mats, and it serves as a mordant, to give them afterward a red or straw-colored dye. This same tree is what they call Cacha in India. See Morinda. Flowers at the beginning of August. * T., Colis. I., Candon. V., Saguinsin. Pers Syn. pl. t. 1. 411.

Memecylon lanceolatum. Lanceolate Memecylon. Trunk erect. Leaves opposite, winged without an odd one; in whose place there is a small stylet. Leaflets lanceolate, very entire, and smooth. Flowers in one or two umbels, axillary. Everything else as in the preceding species. = This tree rises to the same height as the previous one: its flowers are somewhat larger. The uses are the same. It flowers at the same time as the other. * T., Colis. I., Candong.— I have seen another tree much larger than the preceding ones, which had fruit. The leaves are opposite, lanceolate, narrow, wavy, entire, and smooth. Berry crowned by the calyx, with four chambers, and in each one two seeds. The flowers had already fallen.

** Diospyros. The flowers on some trees are hermaphrodite; on others male only. Calyx monosepálous with four lobes. Corolla swollen below, narrowing above, monopetalous and with four lobes. Style in four parts. Berry with four to eight seeds.

Diospyros embriopteris. Diospyros with a winged embryo. Leaves alternate, approaching a lanceolate shape, hairy beneath, with a notch; and in some with two glands at the base, and a small stylet at the apex, with two other rows of very small glands below, along the sides of the midrib. The new leaves are gray-colored and downy. Petioles very short. Flowers some solitary and axillary, others terminal in a spike. Calyx and Corolla as in the genus. Stamens much shorter than the corolla, four in number regularly, though sometimes five and even ten are seen. Anthers sessile, arrow-shaped, nearly as long as the filaments. Ovary very large and hairy. Styles four. Berry large

210
very hairy, with eight or more chambers, and in each one an oval seed, convex on the outside, and sharpened by compression from the others, very hard and horn-like, surrounded by filamentous flesh that adheres tenaciously to the pit. = This tree reaches a height of forty or more feet. Its wood is very hard, of a dark flesh-red color, which blackens with time, like ebony. The fruit has a pleasant smell (for some it does not) and is like quince. It is edible, though it is necessary to remove the hairs with which it is covered. * T., Talang, Mabolo. V., Amaga. P., Talang. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 2. 624. The species discolor of Pers. and this one, I believe, are the same. — The species known by the name of Malacapai has alternate, oval leaves, with some scattered glands, especially at the tip. Flowers axillary, either solitary, or two or three. Calyx with four lobes. Berry globose, with four chambers, and in each two bony seeds. = A small tree, with yellow wood, with some black spots. They say it repels bedbugs; but this is only verified when the wood is fresh. * T., Malacapai.
Diospyros biflora. Two-flowered Diospyros. Leaves alternate, somewhat lanceolate, with only two glands at the base on the underside, entire, smooth, and somewhat stiff. Petiole very short, and without glands. Flowers axillary, in pairs, masculine. Calyx bell-shaped, with three or four laciniae. Corolla fleshy, twice as long as the calyx, swollen in the middle and narrowed toward the top, forming a throat, with the limb divided into four parts rolled downward. Stamens fixed in the corolla, not reaching the height of its throat, numbering seventeen to thirty. Filaments very short, woolly. Anthers very long. Ovary hairy. Style very short. Stigma none. Fruit none. = This tree grows up to ten yards tall. Its flowers are very fragrant. Blooms in June. * T., Talang.
Diospyros lotus? Lotus Diospyros? Leaves alternate, lanceolate, with only two glands at the base, and barely downy below. Flowers axillary, sessile, in clusters of more than eight small flowers, all masculine. Calyx with four or five laciniae, with the edges rolled backward, and bordered at maturity. Corolla as in Diospyros biflora. Stamens more than fifteen, fixed at the base of the corolla. Pistil none. = This tree bears no fruit: but the one from hermaphrodite flowers does bear fruit, which is very poisonous, and is reputed to intoxicate fish: it even drives the caiman out of the water precipitously. Its flowers are very fragrant. Rubbing with its bark and leaves, cases of herpes or ringworm disappear: and it should be noted that the leaves of nearly all the species are more or less caustic.

211
* T., Canomoi, Canomai. — Could this species be the one from Pers. ibid. 624?

Diospyros kaki. Diospiros kaki. This is a tree known in Mahaihai of Laguna, which I have not seen myself; but I have seen the fruit, which has raised portions and resembles a small apple. Its flesh is tasty, yellowish, soft, and threaded with fine fibers. The most singular thing about the fruit is the skin, which is so thin it looks like a simple membrane. The Indians erroneously call it Pagatpat. I have not seen its seeds.

Diospyros nigra. Black Diospiros. Leaves alternate, lance-shaped, stiff, smooth, and with very tiny glands scattered on the underside. Flowers axillary, solitary. Peduncle very short. Calyx inferior, large, swollen, divided into five keeled parts turned backwards, or with the concave side facing outward, and its edges very wavy. Corolla shaped like a small jar, narrowing toward the top, fleshy, in five egg-shaped lobes placed one over the other at the edges, and folded back downward. Stamens from fourteen to twenty, unequal in height, shorter than the corolla, and fixed at their base: some set deeper than others. Filaments short. Anthers long, half arrow-shaped. Ovary conical. Style absent. Stigmas three or four, awl-shaped. Berry globose, with a leathery rind, dark-colored flesh, and many seeds. == This tree is native to the Islands, and grows to a height of eight or ten varas. Curious Indians also cultivate it, and call it Black Zapote. The fruit, whose flesh is dark, though edible, has no pleasing flavor. In its skin it resembles the fruit of the Kaki species. In the History of the Voyages of Abbé Prevost, vol. 22, p. 122, (Madrid edition) it states: that the fruit before ripening poisons fish. The leaves and especially the bark serve as caustics. Flowers in July. * T., Black Zapote.

Diospyros pilosanthera. Diospiros with hairy anthers. Leaves alternate, lance-shaped, entire, smooth, and stiff, with two or three pits resembling glands at the base, on the underside. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, sessile, six or more in number. Calyx with four or five large teeth, turned outward, and edged at maturity. Corolla longer than the calyx, covered with hair on the outside, the throat bare, and the limb with five lobes. Stamens five or six. Filaments short. Anthers with a row of hairs in the middle. Stigmas four. Berry with ten horny, semicircular seeds, thinned on both sides and convex on the outside. == Trees of hard wood and great beauty according to some. The fruit is edible and resembles a small guava. All trees of this genus have the wood

212
more or less hard, and similar to that of the Ebony, its relative,
called Luyon in Tagalog, whose flowers I have not seen. That of
Amaga in Leyte, they say, is excellent. The one called Camagon,
which some believe to be the same as the Malacapai, and the black
Zapote, also belong to the gen. Diospyros. * T., Bolongaeta. V.,
Dalondong, Amaga.
Here belongs without doubt the one called Alintatao, whose wood
usually has some black spots. There are entire forests of ebonies
on the Islands, which differ from one another in being more or
less black, and in the shape or color of the grain. They say that
large trees cannot be cut, because they give off a
poisonous vapor that kills. The very black ebony is called
in Tagalog, as I said above, Luyon, although they also give
this name to the brava palm: in Visayas Bantolinao, Barlis:
in Pampanga Coloyauang, Colohadia, Calohadiang. In Ilo-
cos, Balatinao.
(CUNALON.) Trunk straight, branching. Leaves alternate, broad,
lanceolate, with the edges folded downward, and the
apex obtuse, entire and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers
in small, racemose panicles. Cal. free, persistent, bell-shaped,
in four, rarely five rounded parts.
Cor. longer than the calyx, deeply cleft into four
pointed parts. Stam. eight fixed to the corolla, four at the
base, and the others in the middle of the laciniae. Filam. shorter
than the corolla, compressed. Ant. sessile, pointed. Ovary
globose, set within the flower. Styles two, linear, com-
pressed. Stigmas simple. Berry globose, juicy, with four
chambers, and in each one an oblong seed, convex on the
outside, and with a channel, angular within, very hard,
like horn, and covered with a thin aril. = A tree known
in Cebu. The leaves and the fruit, which turn very black
at maturity, are used in Cebu and in Leyte to dye
cotton and abaca cloth black, without any other addition.
For this purpose, the tender leaves and the fruit are boiled in water, or the
leaves alone, in which the cloth is immersed: it is dried, washed,
and dyed again up to six or eight times, to achieve the desired
color. I have endeavored to spread this precious tree to Ba-
tangas and Ilocos, and although the results have not been very successful,
some living specimens exist in various places: they take quite a long time to grow.
The color given by the new leaves (not the old ones) and the fruit
is good, lasting, does not stain, and has no notable odor. To obtain
the black color more quickly, the cloths are first dyed with indigo one or two
times; but this is not necessary. The wood is good
for planks. Flowers in Oct. * V. Cunalon.
There is another species in Visayas, and I have also seen it in An-
gat, with axillary, solitary flowers, and the calyx at maturity

213
turned downward. These trees must be closely related to the genus Diospyros, yet they are distinct from it by the insertion of the stamens, and they come very close to the genus Royena. One should not think that this tree alone is used to produce a perfect black dye. There are several others, among them the Obool, known in Leyte. The Tagalog Indians have very limited knowledge of their trees, and those who live near Manila understand them even less. The Visayans are more intelligent and make good use of the valuable things found in their forests.

CEDROTA. Calyx in six parts. Corolla none. Ovary encircled by a gland. Style short. Lin. Sist. veg. 629.
Cedrota guianensis. Cedrota of Guiana. Leaves opposite, broad, lanceolate, and smooth. Petioles short. Flowers axillary in small panicles. Calyx tubular, inferior, with six lobes. Corolla none. Stamens ten or eleven, fixed on the receptacle. Fruit four-angled, long, and with one seed. = A tree found in Cebu, whose size I do not know. The leaves are one span long. It is called there Tac-an.

NIOTA. Calyx inferior, with four or five lobes. Corolla very long, of four or five petals. Filaments with some glands at the base. Stamens eight or ten with a scale at the base. Style and stigma one. Four or five compressed legumes (sometimes one aborts), placed on a stipe, with solitary seeds. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 592.
Niota tetrapetala. Niota with four petals. Trunk somewhat forked, erect. Leaves alternate, half-winged, oval, pointed, entire, smooth, stiff, and veined. Petioles very short, without stipules. Flowers terminal in an umbel, with four to six small florets, each with a moderately long peduncle. Common peduncle very slender, very long, and hanging. Calyx the color of the corolla, inferior, very small, with four lobes. Corolla very long, of four petals, linear, straight. Stamens eight, fixed on the receptacle. Filaments as long as the petals, with one or two appendages or glandular prominences at the base. Anthers coiled in a spiral. Ovary with a small stalk and five lobes. Style one, as long as the stamens, and above the center of the five lobes of the ovary, which are the five future legumes. Stigma simple. Five woody legumes, short, joined at the center on a small stalk, crescent-shaped, swollen in the middle, with veins, and with a kidney-shaped seed, rough, and attached by a thread at the upper suture. = Small trees, well known throughout the Islands, and highly valued for the great use made of their wood; and of the root and bark, which have a very strong bitter taste and have been used with great success against cholera morbus. The root, the wood, and even the fruit are white and very light. The leaves

214
They are a palm's length long. Some make the soles of shoes from the tree's wood, and say it is very healthful. They are not common in all places. The description given here was made from some branches and flowers sent to me from Capis. The corollas are purple. Flowers in February. * T., P., C., Manungal. V., Manungal, Linatong anac, Linton gamai. Palagium, Palagarium, Ponoan, Mavindato, Darapot. Dec. ibid. — This is what I formerly called Manungala: it has now been placed by Endlicher in the genus Samadera.

Niota? globosa. Niota? globosa. Leaves alternate, broadly lanceolate, remotely serrate, leathery, and veined. Petioles short. Flowers axillary, solitary, with very long peduncles. One style. Stigma in two parts. One capsule, globose, woody, with the beginning of another on one side, and in the middle the style, with two sutures as in legumes, and one conforming seed, with a bony, mottled, spotted covering. = Trees of Angat, of which I have only seen some branches, and so I am ignorant of their bearing. The leaves are about five inches long. The fruit is like a hazelnut, and the woody covering is not as hard as that of the seed. This is quite bitter; the branches less so. New species.

BUGINVILLEA. Calyx inferior, tubular, narrowed toward its middle, and the limb almost entire. Stamens on a disk. Jus-Gen. pl. 91.

Buginvillea racemosa. Buginbillea racemosa. Leaves opposite, broad, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers terminal, in compound clusters, without a notable bract on the peduncles. Calyx tubular at the base, slightly swollen, narrowed toward the middle, and with five barely noticeable lobes on the limb. Corolla none. Stamens eight, fixed on a membrane placed on the receptacle, and as long as the tube of the calyx. Filaments: the ends of the membrane are flattened and nearly equal in height. Anthers oval. Ovary egg-shaped. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma very thick, and with lobes. Fruit a single seed. = A tree of the mountains of Angat, of which I have seen only one branch, on which there were no traces of thorns, and it bore no ripe fruit. The ovary was very small, and I saw in it only one seed. It seems to me, then, that it belongs to this genus. The leaves turn very black as they dry, and are half a foot long. It is not known to the natives. It is as thick as a human body, and its wood is extremely soft. New species.

DAPHNE. Calyx none. Corolla with four laciniae, which wither and enclose the stamens. Drupe of one seed. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1, 434.

Daphne fætida. Daphne foetida. Trunk with branches me-

215
forked at the middle. Leaves opposite, somewhat heart-shaped, ovate, very pointed, entire and smooth. Petioles very short, and above with a winged channel. Terminal flowers in a simple umbel. Involucre of the umbel, none. Calyx none, unless one wishes to call the corolla a calyx. Corolla tubular, fleshy, rough, greenish in color, and the limb with four laciniae. Stamens eight, fixed to the walls of the corolla, and placed in two series, that is: four at the throat, and the others alternating below. Filaments very short. Anthers arrow-shaped. Germ cylindrical, surrounded by two small scales, notched at the ends. Style none. Stigma globose. Berry superior, with one globose seed, with a leathery and thin rind. = These small trees, thinner than one's arm, rise to a height of nine feet. The Indians generally know it as Salago, although they sometimes confuse one thing for another. They are common on the seashores. Their bark is extremely tough, and I have seen that paper can easily be made from it. To do this, one need only soak it in water and take it out the following day, or after two days. It is returned to the water after drying, and is well trampled with the feet, then left to dry in the sun. This operation is continued for several days, until the material takes on the desired whiteness. Although I do not believe it necessary, based on my own experience, to grind it in mills; it will always be good to do so, in order to achieve a greater and more perfect separation. This paper has an ash-gray color, and I do not know whether it can be bleached further. The leaves are used with very satisfactory results as a purgative: and on this point, both in the number of leaves taken and in the manner of picking them, the Indians hold various superstitions. According to them, the leaves may only be taken in an odd number: and if they are picked pulling downward, the entire operation will work downward; and as an emetic, if they are picked pulling upward. Their powder is taken in a dose of twelve grains, or the fourth part of a drachm, in chocolate; or with bread crumbs, made into pills. The Indians of Tanauan believe that the mumps, a common ailment there, and in some other town of Batangas, is relieved by wrapping a strip of the bark of this small tree around the neck. Flowers in June. * T., Salagó, Malasampaga. Pers. ibid. 435.
Daphne indica. Indian Daphne. Leaves opposite, ovate, elongated, pointed, entire and smooth. Petioles very short, with a slightly winged channel. Terminal flowers in an umbel. Corolla yellow in color, funnel-shaped, arched, with four lanceolate laciniae. Stamens as in the other species. Anthers flesh-colored. Style short. Everything else as in the preceding species. = Small trees known in Bulacan, whose leaves serve as a purgative, as I mentioned before: the flowers are not unattractive, unlike those of the preceding salago. * T., Salago, Malasampaga differs little from the other species.

216
Daphne aquilaria. Eagle Daphne. Trunk erect, branching. Leaves opposite, oval, entire, smooth and somewhat fleshy, with the lateral veins barely visible. Petioles very short (white.) Flowers axillary, hermaphrodite, in panicles of very few small florets. Calyx: none. Corolla: yellow, tubular, with a large limb divided into four oval segments. Stamens eight (sometimes six and seven) fixed to the walls of the corolla tube, near the throat: the four alternate ones taller than the others. Filaments very short. Anthers rather long, oval. Ovary with a small stalk, oval, compressed, and at the base with two opposite scales, fleshy, and bifid at the apex. Style: none. Stigma very thick and shield-shaped. Drupe very small, oval, barely fleshy; the nut coriaceous and fragile, with one seed. = Small trees about as thick as a thigh, and of little height; but worthy of every regard. I have seen them on the beaches of Darigayos, and at the Port of Santiago, near Santa Maria in Ilocos. No one had any knowledge of such trees until, not many years ago, Father Barranco, a Dominican, a very learned man and devoted to the study of plants, saw them at the said location, and explained their uses and properties according to what he had seen practiced in Cochinchina. The heartwood of these trees is black, and regularly marked with white spots. Not all the trees have black heartwood; only those that have been injured by some strong wind or other mishap. Their chips when burned give off a very soft and aromatic smell, and at that point they release a resin that bubbles and prevents the chip from turning to ash. Their shavings are taken in water or wine, and are bitter and good for the stomach. In a word: they correspond almost entirely in properties to what is called Agallocha, Lignum Aloes, Eagle Wood, Calamba, and Calambok: for this reason I gave it the name of the species. Its leaves closely resemble those of the Camochile; but not in their arrangement. In Ilocos they told me it is called Arandon, and it has been used for purging combined with other things. It is impossible that it should be absent from other parts of the Islands. The bark is filamentous; the flowers small, and the fruit like a pea. The leaves are two inches long and one wide, and are dark green. The nut has the hardness of hemp seeds; but the fruit I saw was not fully ripe, and I know it grows larger. Flowers in June. I., Arandon. New species.
In the flowers of the tree I have described, there are no lobes alternating with the stamens, as in Aquileria, nor anything beyond what has been said. In Visayas there are other fragrant-wooded trees. These are the Atanangui, Cadot, Baliton, Bayaboa, Otsangui, and Tanoog. All of these ought to be examined by those who are able to do so, especially in Leyte.

217
DODONAEA. Calyx of four leaflets. (Calyx in four parts. Jus.) Corolla none. Capsule of three cells, inflated, with seeds in pairs. Lin. Syst. veg.
Dodonaea angustifolia. Narrow-leaved Dodonaea. Leaves sessile, alternate, lanceolate, smooth, with margins rolled downward. Flowers in racemose panicles. Calyx cleft almost to the base, in four or six parts, lanceolate and concave. Corolla none. Stamens opposite the calyx, from five to seven, most commonly six. Anthers with four furrows. Ovary superior, inversely egg-shaped, compressed. Style one, short and thick, marked with a line along its length. Stigmas two. Capsule membranous, compressed (sometimes with three angles), inflated, with a channel in the middle and a wing at the edge, notched at the apex, with two cells (sometimes three), each containing one or two small kidney-shaped seeds. = This small tree, which closely resembles the genus Ptelea, grows to a height of nine feet. It is common on seashores, and its leaves are narrow. The native people hardly know it; but they use its branches as stakes in betel plantations. * T., Calapinai. Lin. ibid.

OCTANDRIA.

DIGINIA.

SCHMIDELLIA. Calyx in four parts. Four petals bearded on the inside in the middle. Two fruits like berries, half-joined at the base, with solitary seeds. Decand. Prod. p. 610.
Schmidellia conferta. Clustered Schmidellia. Leaves simple and clustered, oval, slightly pointed at both ends, entire and smooth. Petioles short. Flowers axillary in half-spiked racemes. Calyx in five parts rolled downward. Corolla. Disk. Stamens... Ovaries two, oval, joined at the base. Styles two, very small, with simple stigmas. Two oval berries, joined at the base and afterward somewhat divergent, compressed, with solitary seeds covered by a fleshy aril up to one-third of their length. One of them regularly aborts. = Trees as thick as a thigh, of hard wood, found in Angat, and little known. The leaves are a palm's length, as are the racemes. The two berries are always in pairs, purple in color, opening lengthwise along the outer side, and joined up to their midpoint where the two very short styles are located. They are the size of almond seeds. I have observed the vestiges of the corolla, disk, and stamens.

218
Schmidellia triandra. Schmidelia with three stamens. Leaves opposite, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets numbering two pairs, lanceolate, doubly serrated, soft and hairy. Common petiole long. Proper petiole very short. Flowers axillary, in racemes. Calyx of four concave leaflets; the two opposite ones larger. Corolla of two? petals, wedge-shaped, with small claws. Nectary none. Stamens three. Filaments short. Germens two, superior, ovate. Style one. Stigmas two, divergent. Two drupes inversely ovate, joined at the base, with solitary globose seeds.= A tree taller than a man's body. I have not been certain of the number of petals, and it seems to me that although it varies in the number of stamens, it is Schmidelia, rather than Ornitrophe, as I once believed.

OCTANDRIA.

TRIGINIA.

CARDIOSPERMUM. Calyx of five leaflets. Petals four. Nectary of four unequal pieces. Three capsules joined to an axis and swollen. Seeds globose, solitary. Lin. Sys. veg. 642.
Cardiospermum halicacabum. Balloon vine. Stem trailing along the ground, angular and smooth. Leaves doubly ternate. Common and partial petioles with small wings on the edges, especially the middle one. Leaflets cleft, with lanceolate and winged incisions. All flowers hermaphrodite, lateral at the leaf axils, in a small panicle, placed at the end of a very long and angular common peduncle, with two tendrils at the base of the panicle. Proper peduncle short. Calyx persistent, inferior, half as small as the corolla, cleft into four rounded and concave parts. Corolla cleft almost to the base into six parts, ovate, unequal; and two of them overlapping two of the others. Nectary appears to be a seventh channeled petal, or part of the corolla, with the apex folded inward, the fold with two teeth, and at the base with two nearly globose glands. Stamens to one side of the flower, eight in number, arising from a single point, as long as the corolla, and fixed at the base of the germen, which they conceal in the middle. Filaments close together, straight, flat and somewhat hairy. Anthers oval, versatile. Germen globose, with three angles. Style almost none. Stigmas three, straight. Three inflated capsules, united to each other by means of a membrane. Seeds in each capsule, one globose, lam-

219
pineapple, with a small stalk, and fitted at the base with a blade or white membrane, heart-shaped.= This plant spreads along the ground. I have seen it in the gardens of Pasig, and in other places. The seeds are like a pea; and from the blade at the base, the plant takes its botanical name. The Indians use it as a poultice for headache. A decoction of the root, when drunk, is useful in catarrh of the bladder. Flowers in December. * T., Bangcolon. Lin. ibid.
POLYGONUM. Calyx: none. Corolla: in five parts, unless it be called a calyx. One angular seed, enclosed within the corolla, naked in very many species. Lin. Sys. veg. 637. Jus. Gén. pl. 82.
Polygonum stoloniferum? Polygonum with stolons? Stem spreading, without branches, round and knotted. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, fringed with eyelash-like hairs. Petioles sheathing the stem, forming a very slender tube, with long hairs at the joint. Flowers in a spiked panicle, with a long, dense spike. Each small flower with a short stalk, enclosed in a small, one-leaved, conical involucre, reverse-facing and fringed. Calyx: none. Corolla: in five ovate and nearly entire parts. Stamens: eight. Filaments: nearly none, above the ovary; but they pass through it on the inside, until they attach to the receptacle. Anthers: between oval and round, pressed against what appears to be the ovary. Ovary globose, inside the calyx and attached to it. Styles three, short. Stigmas globose. The husk inside the calyx is full of powder and contains no seed.= This spreading plant grows in Pasig at the place called Uaua. It grows tall in places where it touches the ground, and the root is black, with bends, and very juicy. The husk is entirely full of powder of a purple color; and the anthers are flesh-colored. The stamens and styles pass through the covering of what appears to be the ovary; but inside it I have not been able to find any seed, only a purple powder. All of this is the work of insects. Flowers in February. * T., Subsuban. P., Canubsuban.
Polygonum bellardi? Polygonum of Bellard? Stem erect, with many nodes, and a very hairy sheath between node and node. Leaves clasping the stem at the base, lanceolate, and also hairy. Petioles very short. Flowers lenticular, in somewhat dense and conical spikes. Each small flower with a very short peduncle, fitted into a conical involucre that is reverse-facing and hairy. Calyx: in five parts, ovate and entire. Corolla: none. Stamens: seven, fixed at the middle of the corolla, and barely longer than it. Anthers angular. Ovary seated within the flower, oval, compressed. Styles two. Stigmas somewhat thick, with lobes. One seed enclosed in the calyx, ovate, compressed, and with a lustrous coat.= This plant, barely known to the local people, inhabits Taguiig, and other places, on the banks

220
of the rivers. It grows to the height of a man. The flowers are white, and the interior of the stem of the plant is purple. In general, all species of knotweed (polygonum) are highly medicinal, and are used for kidney stones, difficulty urinating, and dropsy. As for the plants described, I doubt whether they are the cited species. Flowers in March. * T., Subsuban. P., Canucsuban.

OCTANDRIA.

TETRAGINIA.

BRYOPHYLLUM. Calyx inflated, with four lobes. Corolla hypogynous, four-sided below, and with four pointed lobes at the apex. Stamens eight. Four glands at the base of the ovary. Dec. Prod. p. 3. 395. According to other authors: Cotyledon.
Bryophyllum germinans. THE GERMINATING BRYOPHYLLUM. Leaves opposite, oval, notched, fleshy. Flowers in racemose panicles. Calyx very long, inflated, cylindrical, with four straight teeth. Corolla longer than the calyx, narrow toward the base, cylindrical, and with four pointed lobes. Stamens eight, shorter than the corolla. Anthers straight, shaped like an arrowhead. Ovary divided into four parts. Styles as long as the stamens. Stigmas awl-shaped. Nectary: four glands at the base of the ovary. Four capsules, each with one chamber containing many oblong seeds. = This plant is common in many places. The flowering stem rises to the height of a vara, though the plant itself does not reach as tall. The whole plant is very fleshy and full of juice; the flowers are yellow. Some indigenous people call it Angelico, and others Catacataca, and it is considered an evergreen perennial. Years ago it was eagerly sought by the indigenous people, and because of what they observed in it, they called it Catacataca, meaning something wonderful. A leaf pulled off and left anywhere — even indoors on a table — will, after a few days, sprout new shoots at the angles of its notched edges. I myself have seen and verified this. Decandolle has already written of this phenomenon. Crushed and applied to the soles of the feet, it is believed to be good for stopping any flow of blood. * T., Angelico, Catacataca. A species whose name I have taken from what was said above.
Bryophyllum serratum. THE SERRATED BRYOPHYLLUM. Leaves sessile, opposite, oval, doubly serrated, fleshy. Flowers in an umbel. Calyx very short, very deeply cleft into four parts. Corolla narrows toward its middle. In all other respects like the preceding species. A new species.

221
Bryophyllum triangulare. Triangular Bryophyllum. Leaves sessile, opposite, very fleshy, lanceolate, and three-angled in the shape of a bayonet, very entire. Calyx as in the previous species. Corolla very long, with four angles, and the limb with four laciniae. Stamens eight: four of them taller than the others. Ovary with four lobes. Stigmas globose. Nectary: four glands at the base of the ovary. Species new.

ENNEANDRIA.

MONOGINIA.

SALGADA. Calyx superior, in six parts, with an equal number of glands at the divisions, and three more glands at the base. Stamens six, opposite the parts of the calyx, and three others at the base surrounding the ovary. Anthers with two alveoli and two small lateral bodies: the three inner ones facing those on the outside. Style and Stigma oval, with one seed. Genus new.
Salgada lauriflora. Salgada with laurel flowers. Trunk straight. Leaves nearly sessile, alternate, lanceolate, entire, smooth above, and somewhat hairy below. Flowers in a panicle. Calyx superior (as in Bucida) in six oval, hairy parts, with one gland in each division. Corolla none. Stamens nine: six fixed in the middle of the calyx parts and opposite them. Filaments very short. Anthers each with two alveoli and other small lateral bodies beside the alveoli, which appear to be the true anthers. In addition, there are three others at the base of the calyx, surrounding the ovary with their alveoli and small bodies in the manner of anthers, as in the other six; but facing outward. Between these three stamens alternate three glands. Ovary inferior, cylindrical. Style one, longer than the stamens. Stigma capitate. Glans oval, rounded, pointed, with a leathery bark and one seed. = A tree smaller than a thigh in girth, found in Angat: the leaves measure three to six inches in length. The alveoli and glands closely resemble those of the Laurels; but the fruit is inferior, the size of an acorn, and somewhat fragrant. The description is exact. The small flowers are smaller than peas. It is closely related to the family of the Homalineae; but the fruit is one-seeded. It is not known, and since it appears to me to be a new genus, I have dedicated it to Señor Salgado, a very industrious person eager for the advancement of the country, as he demonstrated in Calauan by planting many thousands of cinnamon trees brought from Mindanao.
LAURUS. Calyx none, unless what is so called is considered as
36

222
corolla. Cor. in four or six parts. Nect. three glands, each terminated by two bristles, which encircle the germ. The inner filaments have glands. Berry superior, hollow, corky, with one seed. Flowers in general hermaphrodite; but male flowers also occur on some trees alone. Stam. from nine to fourteen. Lin. Syst. veg. 649.

Laurus culilaban. Culilaban Laurel. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, with three nerves, which unite a little above the base and fade out before reaching the apex, very entire and smooth. Flowers in small clusters of umbellate panicles. Common peduncles very long. Proper to the small flower, long. Cal. none. Cor. in six parts, ovate and hairy. Stam. nine: six of them projecting further out than the rest. Anthers on the six outer ones, four on each, the two lower ones set into the alveoli or niches of an oval lamina that terminates the filament, all facing inward in pairs: the anthers of the other three filaments are two on each one, also fixed on a small terminal lamina, and face outward. Nect. six glands with a small stalk.== This tree reaches a height of fifteen or twenty feet. It is common in all forests and quite well known, since Indian healers use its bark for poultices, which has the smell of camphor. Its leaves also give off a very pleasant scent, though inferior to that of the Laurel of Spain. Flowers in March. * T., Calingag, Macalingag. V. Calingag, Calinga Man. P., Calingad. I., Candaroma. Lin. ibid.— Compare with the genus Ocotea. The Laurus Culilaban that I have seen on Mount Arayat is hardly distinguishable from the one I have described. It is as follows.
Leaves opposite, broad, lanceolate, with three nerves that unite very near the base, entire and smooth. Flowers terminal in loose panicles: the last small stalks dichotomous. Cor. in six ovate parts. Stam. nine. Filaments: the six fixed on the receptacle, spatula-shaped: and at the tip, on the inner face, each has four attached anthers: further inward there are three other thick filaments with a small stalk, similar to the others, each with four anthers facing outward. Moreover, between the filaments whose anthers face outward there are eight glands, nearly globose, with a short stalk, three between each pair: on one of them there are only two. Germ conical, seated within the flower. Style the length of the stamens. Stigmas with three angles. Fruit.. = A tree of the second order, which grows in Angat and on Mount Arayat. Its bark is thick, with a mild smell and taste like cinnamon, without the camphor scent detectable in other species. Flowers in January. * P., Calingag.
Laurus hexandra. Six-stamened Laurel. Leaves me-

223
opposite, lanceolate, smooth, and stiff. Petioles very short. Flowers in umbellate panicles: each small flower with a very tiny scale at the base. Calyx (according to Jussieu) fleshy, funnel-shaped, with six concave divisions; the three alternating ones larger. Corolla none. Stamens six, opposite the lobes of the calyx and attached at its base. Filaments almost none. Anthers with a tuft of wool at the base, composed of two irregular pieces that face each other and are fitted into small niches. Sometimes some are of one piece. Ovary globose with angles, sessile on the flower. Style very short. Stigma thick, shield-shaped, with points. Fruit..... = This is a well-known tree of the second rank. The wood is whitish and somewhat soft. It is excellent according to some natives, and widely used for boats, because they hold up for many years in water. Its flowers smell like jasmine. Flowers in August. *T., Malabonga. Pers. Sin. pl. 449.— The anthers number twelve and face each other. This hexandrous species belongs to the genus Ajovea of Linnaeus.

Laurus cassia. Laurel casia. Leaves opposite, narrow, lanceolate, entire, very pointed, stiff, lustrous, and smooth, with three veins that almost converge at the base and fade near the apex: nearly a palm in length and two fingers in width. = These are trees of eight or more varas in height; and in Balanga they are used as posts for houses. The smell and taste of the bark is very aromatic, mild, and similar to that of Cinnamon: it ought at least to be as good as the kind that comes from China. *T., Samilin. Lin. ibid.

Laurus martinicensis. Laurel of Martinique. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Flowers in a panicle. Calyx none. Corolla funnel-shaped, indistinct, with six deep divisions. Stamens twelve, attached to the corolla in two series; six perfect ones higher up, and three more below also perfect, which alternate with three sterile ones. Filaments of the perfect stamens somewhat long, and in the sterile ones very short. Anthers of the upper perfect stamens, two paired on each one, facing the center of the flower, fixed in two alveoli of an egg-shaped blade: those of the lower ones in the same manner, but facing the opposite side. Anthers of the sterile stamens large, producing no pollen. (Could they be glands?) Nectaries six glands, or scales, semicircular, with a short stalk, placed between the two series of stamens. Ovary conical, inside the corolla. Style enclosed within a sheath. Stigma somewhat thick, shield-shaped with points. = This tree is of the second rank. The wood is white. Some natives call this tree Dinglas; but it is not this one, but rather a very different species. Others, with more justification, call it Malabonga. Flowers in December. Lin. ibid. 650.

224
Laurus lanosa. Woolly Laurel. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Flowers terminal on a kind of spike, on which the small flowers are gathered in small groups. Partial involucre, a single concave bract, funnel-shaped. Calyx none. Corolla very deeply cleft into six parts, ovate and woolly. Stamens nine, fixed at the base of the corolla, alternating two with one. Filaments shorter than the corolla. Anthers nearly arrow-shaped, those of the paired stamens facing one another. Nectary of nine glands with a small stalk, thick and paired, somewhat arrow-shaped, fixed between the stamens and the ovary. Ovary conical, placed within the flower. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma split halfway into two parts. Fruit...= This tree reaches the thickness of the human body. Its wood is used in the construction of houses. The pistil has no sheath. Fl. in January. * T., V., Batobato. New species?
Compare the description of the preceding tree with this one, and it will be seen that they are similar: because in the former there are twelve stamens and six glands, making 18 parts, and in this one, nine stamens and the same number of glands, also making 18 parts. The flowers in both were not fully developed, and so no exact judgment can be formed. It cannot belong to the genus Ocotea, since each filament does not have four anthers.
Laurus serrata. Serrated Laurel. Leaves alternate, ovate-oblong, obtusely serrated, smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in groups. Peduncles long. Corolla inferior, cleft almost to the base into five obtuse parts. Stamens eight, sometimes six, as long as the corolla, alternating with the same number of cylindrical woolly bodies terminated by three bristles. Ovary small and elongated, angular. Style none. Stigma globose. = It is a small tree that grows to a height of five or six varas. The natives hardly know it. Fl. in August. * T., Inignin. It is neither the lucida nor the umbellata species of Linnaeus, ibid. 651.
Laurus persea. Persea Laurel. Branches compressed at the tip. Leaves alternate, between oval and obovate, membranous, tomentose beneath, with alternate veins. Petioles very short. Flowers in racemes, with the small flowers gathered in clusters: the tip of their own small stalks very thick at maturity. Corolla (according to Linnaeus) in six parts: the three alternating ones outer and smaller. Stamens nine: the six outermost, and the other three thicker; long, and surrounding the ovary. Anthers at the ends of the thickened filaments, oval-shaped and set into small niches: four in each of the six outer ones, facing toward the center of the flower; in the three inner ones, sometimes two, sometimes four anthers facing those of the others. In addition there are nine glands, six in the form of appendages

225
at the base of the inner filaments: the other three between the outer filaments. Ovoid germen. Two styles. Pointed stigmas. Berry very fleshy, elongated in the shape of a club, with some ridges on the bark, and one egg-shaped seed. = The tree that produced the flowers described above exists in Sta. Ana near Manila, and came from America. Its leaves are a hand-span long. The fruit that I saw was like a medium-sized mango, and the seed like a hen's egg. Its skin is shiny and dark green in color, like that of an unripe walnut. It has already borne fruit in other years, and is very tasty eaten with salt. In New Spain they call it ahuacate or abogado. Flowers in March.

Laurus cinnamomum. Cinnamon Laurel. Leaves half-opposite, egg-shaped, elongated, with three veins somewhat distant from the base, fading toward the tip, entire, smooth, and stiff. Flowers at the ends of the branches, in umbel-like clusters. Calyx none. Corolla of six petals, lance-shaped and hairy. Stamens nine, shorter than the corolla. The six filaments are regular, with anthers and without glands: these are further out, facing the three irregular ones, which are closer to the germen. The three irregular ones also have anthers, and each one additionally has two glands on the sides. There are still three more glands that also resemble anthers, arrow-shaped. Fertile anthers, four: two on top of the other two, fixed in each of the nine perfect filaments on a kind of lamina: the anthers, then, are in total twenty-four, and the glands nine. Germen globose. Stigma thick, irregular, somewhat square. Berry oval, sunk halfway into the calyx, with one seed. = It is a small tree that I have seen in a garden in Pasig and in other places. Its flowers, leaves, and bark have the smell of cinnamon. I believe it is simply a variety of the species Cinnamomum, and that both this individual and others found in various places descended from those planted in Calauan by Mr. Salgado.

All the species of Laurus found in the Islands have been examined, and yet we do not find that any notable benefit has been drawn from them. At another time, samples of a cinnamon gathered in the forests of Butuan were taken to Spain. A Dutchman had made some plantations of it there. Mr. Salgado, more than thirty years ago, planted many cinnamon trees in Calauan, which he brought from Mindanao. As I have heard, very many of them were lost after his death. The cinnamon is a little more pungent than that of Ceylon, but has the same smell and flavor. That of the province of Caraga, in Mindanao, is equal to Ceylon cinnamon and not pungent, according to Father Delgado. I believe that the cinnamon of Arayat, and perhaps that of Balanga, must be very good. Note that the cinnamon from young branches,

226
or three years old, is the most delicate. The exposure and cultivation of the tree contribute to its greater or lesser quality. The barks are dried in the sun and curl up on their own. No tests have yet been made on the roots of these trees, which yield very fragrant and medicinal oils, and the celebrated camphor. Likewise the timbers of many of the cited species have not been tested, and perhaps they would be very valuable for furniture, on account of the pleasant smell they would give off: the sawdust of some, spread over cots, is said to repel bedbugs. The Samilin of Balanga and the Calingag, so common in all the forests, called for curious observers to devote themselves to investigating their properties. Indian healers use them in medicine. Doctor Bodard asserts that cinnamon is perhaps one of the exotic drugs most beneficial to man. It wonderfully restores vital forces, strengthens the stomach, dispels flatulence, and cures diarrheas caused by weakness. It is used to mask the repugnant taste of some medicines. In habitual diarrheas, doctors advise chewing cinnamon in the morning and swallowing the saliva. One drachm of cinnamon in powder, according to another sage, mixed with one ounce of quinine, is excellent, especially in periodic fevers caused by scurvy, or scrofula. Flowers in January. * T., Cinnamon.
CASSYTA. Cor. calyx-like, cleft in six parts. Nect. with three truncated glands that encircle the germen. Filaments interior, with glands. Drupe superior, with one seed, without a valve, and covered by the calyx which forms a berry. Linn. Sist. Veg. 653.
Cassyta filiformis. Thread-like Cassyta. Stem parasitic, without leaves, cylindrical, smooth, twining by its extremities around neighboring trees. Flowers in a spike, globose, very small, with six scales at the base of each, five on one side and the sixth on the opposite. Calyx cleft almost to the base, in three concave and stiff parts: unless these be called bracts as with Jussieu. Cor. (calyx according to Juss.) of six petals, smaller than the calyx, enclosed within it, connivent, and fixed to the calyx itself. Stamens three only. Filaments thick, with two glands at the side of each one. Anthers eighteen (or nine double, divergent after shedding the pollen): twelve, or six double, inserted in niches found at the extremities of the petals, two in each; the remaining six, or three double, placed in niches seen at the apices of the three thick filaments, on the outer side. Nect. three small glands surrounding the germen. Germen above the calyx. Style none. Stigma short, either bifid or three-sided. Drupe globose,

227
formed by the same corolla, which grows large and fleshy. = This plant, whose sap is sticky, spreads widely over the small trees on whose trunks it grows: it sometimes covers them so completely that from a distance they appear wrapped in a blanket. Its stem is like wire, and the ripe fruit, which at most will be two lines in diameter, is slightly fragrant. I have seen this plant in Bauang, and in other places near the sea. The natives barely know it. Its appearance is that of Cuscuta: its stamens those of Laurel: its fruit, that of Basella. * T., Malabohoc. Lin.ibid.— Lin.'s Cassytha is placed by Decand. in the new genus Rhipsalis Prod. p. 3. 476.
CASSUVIUM. Calyx in five parts. Five petals, turned downward. Anthers nine, with the tenth filament castrated. Nut kidney-shaped, placed upon a fleshy and large receptacle. Lin. Syst. Veg. 652. V. Anacardium.
Kidney-shaped Cassuvium. Kidney-shaped Cassuvio. Leaves wedge-shaped, stiff and smooth. Terminal flowers, in racemose panicles. Calyx as in the genus, inferior. Corolla of five petals, linear, pointed and turned downward. Stamens eight to eleven, fused at the base, forming a tube surrounding the future nut. Filaments unequal: one much longer than the rest, all bearing anthers. Ovary heart-shaped. Style very long in some trees, and very short in others. Fruit: the receptacle of the flower grows to the size of a small apple, and in the shape of a top, rising above the calyx, which remains quite distant, and at the tip a slightly compressed nut, of perfect kidney shape, with a smooth outer rind and inner surface full of small pits that exude a shining liquid, enclosing a single seed. = This tree, which some call the Western Anacardio, grows to a height of at most three fathoms, and produces a gum whose properties I am unaware of. Who knows whether it could be used in varnishes? It is known by the name Casóy, and also by that of Maluco, which must not be confused with another of the same name, which is a species of Cordia whose leaves are eaten. The corollas are marked with red streaks. The fruit is sold and is edible; that is, the fleshy receptacle, whose color, smell and flavor resemble those of an apple, although it is somewhat caustic, and much more so the nut that sits on top: for placing a small piece of it on the skin raises a blister, and sores even open in this way. Nevertheless, the natives roast it in embers and afterward eat the kernel found inside, which prepared in this manner is quite tasty, and can even be mixed with cacao to make chocolate. It blooms in February. * T. Casóy. I. Bollogo. Jus. Gen. pl. 368.
I have given this tree the name that Rumfio gave it, and

228
Jussieu retained it, omitting the Anacardium of Linnaeus, on the assumption that the Semecarpo is also called anacardio. I must note here that in the Flora described by Mr. Choumeton, of which I possess a portion, the western Anacardo appears with the notes indicated by Linnaeus; but the illustration does not correspond to it, for it is that of the Semicarpo, in which the nut is heart-shaped, and the flower has five stamens and three styles. In the Anacardo, ten or more stamens are found, monadelphous: the nut is of a fairly perfect kidney shape, and the flowers are much larger than in the semecarpo. In the latter, as I already noted in its place, the nut sits immediately upon the calyx, whose peduncle, as Jussieu very rightly observes, is thick and edible; but in the Cassuvium, the receptacle, which is much larger than the peduncle of the Semecarpo, elongates above the calyx, and the nut is not seated upon the calyx but upon the receptacle. These two trees bear great resemblance in appearance and in their fruit.

DECANDRIA.

MONOGINIA.

LANSIUM. Calyx in five parts. Petals five. A tube like a vinegar-cruet, with an entire margin, containing the anthers within. Stigmas with five rays. Corticate berry with one or five compartments and as many seeds with a pulpy covering. Sprengel. Sist. veg. Lin.

Lansium domesticum. Domestic Lancio. Leaves alternate, pinnate without a terminal leaflet. Leaflets lanceolate, wavy, stiff, entire, and glabrous. Petioles very short. Flowers in a raceme, with three scales at the base of each flower, the middle one largest. Calyx in four or five rounded parts, overlapping one another. Corolla slightly longer than the calyx, of five rounded, concave petals overlapping one another. Nectary globose, with eight or ten small teeth. Filaments: none. Anthers regular, somewhat elongated. Ovary superior, conical. Style stout, striate. Stigma stout, depressed, barely divided into two parts, each with small teeth. Berry oval, covered with a white, tough membrane: the flesh divided into five segments, each still covered by its own membrane (like oranges), and in each one an oval, compressed seed: some abort. — This tree is native to the Islands; it grows very well in the province of La Laguna, and in other parts. It reaches a height of twelve feet, and in other places

229
places much more. The fruit of the cultivated lanzon is nonetheless flavorful: its rind gives off a sticky milk, and the seeds are green and bitter; but they are not at all poisonous as some believe. It is known to everyone in the Islands; but I do not know whether the word lanzones or lansones is foreign or native: they resemble lasona, which is the onion; and indeed the lansones are in certain respects similar to that root. Its size is like that of a small walnut. Flowers in June. * T., Lansone. V. Bulahan, Boocan, Boboa.

In the mountains of Balanga, and in other places, wild lanzones are found, with fruit of an harsh flavor. Leaves opposite, pinnate without a terminal leaflet. Leaflets about three pairs, broad, lanceolate, entire, nearly smooth, and with the midrib often drawn to one side. Petioles nearly absent. — The leaves are three to four inches long.

SOPHORA. Calyx with five teeth, gibbous above. Corolla butterfly-shaped, with wings the length of the standard. Pod knotted, without wings, and with many seeds. Lin. Sist. Veg. 664. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 95.

Sophora tomentosa. Hairy Sophora. Trunk covered with large prominent dots. Leaves opposite, pinnate with a terminal leaflet. Leaflets numbering seven to nine or more pairs, oval, smooth, entirely covered with down, white, and with the margins rolled under. Terminal flowers in racemes. Calyx widened above, with five very small teeth; three below and two above. Corolla butterfly-shaped, with five petals: the upper one or vexillum much larger, with a notch at the tip; the remaining four equal and oblong. Stamens ten, all separate. Pistil as long as the stamens, directed upward. Pod knotted, or like rosary beads. Seeds round, tapering at both ends, with a long scar. = This small tree with yellow flowers reaches a height of nine feet. The seeds are very bitter and purgative, and although Father Delgado advises those suffering from tertian fever to take three of them, the learned Father Clain affirms that just two seeds alone make an intolerable purge. The Indians use them greatly to give to those suffering from stomach complaints. They also acquired great renown at another time for treating cholera morbus, as I will mention later. The leaves are about an inch long and are silvery in color. The pods are about half a foot long. These small trees are common on seashores. Flowers in January. * T., V., Tambalisa, Cabaicabai, Yabag, Cauai, Mantala, Tambalaguisai, Guison, Sandalitan, Pangalangan, Baraumaran, Olaomag, Rocnohan, Bangil. Lin. ibid.

Sophora heptaphylla. Seven-leaflet Sophora. Leaves
37

230
winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets about seven pairs, approaching an oval shape, with a small notch at the apex, smooth. Fruit jointed, as in the previous species, somewhat fuzzy. = Small trees like those of the other species, with yellow flowers. In the Spanish translation of Linnaeus, it is said that the root and seeds are excellent for cholera, pleurisy, colic, and dysuria. But it must be observed that, according to the learned Father Clain, and as I have already noted, the seeds purge with great force. This species is not as common as the other; but both have become famous, and not long ago were used in some places with benefit in cholera morbus. I think they are only effective when the attack is not violent. For this illness, some have used with very happy results an infusion of one drachm of the seed of St. Ignatius and two drachms of the Manungal wood, all in scrapings, in a bottle of strong spirits, giving the patient half a cup, or a full cup, or a spoonful of this liquor in tea several times. * T., Tambalisa, Cabaicabai. Lin. ibid.
ORMOSIA. Calyx two-lipped. Stigmas, two: the lower one curved. Legume compressed, woody; about two seeds. Spr. Syst. veg. t. 2. 281.
Ormosia calavensis. Ormosia of Calauan. Branches straight, with rust-colored spots. Leaves winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets, three or four pairs, ovate, pointed. Partial petiole, short, thickened at the base, without stipules. Calyx two-lipped: the upper lip bifid; the lower, trifid, with rust-colored tomentum. Corolla butterfly-shaped. Standard rounded, barely notched, and with a gland near the claw. Wings slightly smaller than the standard. Keel of two petals, equal to the wings, and both these and the keel purple in color, as is the standard along its margin; but in the center, yellowish-green. Stamens perigynous, ten, free, smooth: four equal in height, and the remaining three somewhat shorter than the other three. Anthers seated on the tips of the filaments, bilocular, round. Ovary somewhat ovate. Style curved, as long as the three filaments. Legume woody, as wide as it is long, about one inch, compressed, of two valves, with one, two, or three seeds, round, oblong, coral-colored, with a scar at one end. = Trees of fifteen fathoms in height, seen in Calauan by Mr. D. Iñigo Gonzalez y Azaola, from whom the description given comes.
BAUHINIA. Calyx with five lobes, which falls off when the other parts of the flower are present. Petals spreading, oblong with claws: the upper one more distant: all inserted in the calyx, with the pericarp a legume. Lin. Syst. veg. 666.
Bauhinia tomentosa. Bauhinia tomentosa. Leaves alternate, half shield-shaped, somewhat heart-shaped, orbicular, with the apex di-

231
divided into two large lobes, with a style in the middle, smooth on top and somewhat hairy below, with veins that meet at the base where two large flat glands can be seen. Short petioles. Cymose flowers. Long proper peduncle. Calyx inferior, funnel-shaped, in four or five parts, and as long as the corolla. Corolla of five petals. Stamens ten: the five alternating ones longer. Stigma thick, shield-shaped, with two lobes. Pod with a small stalk, linear, with many seeds separated from each other by cottony partitions. = This tree reaches a height of twenty feet. Its leaves have an acidic flavor, quite pleasant, and the poor Indians use them as vinegar in their food. The fruit is one foot long. Its flowers should be examined before they open. Flowers in November. * T., Alibanban, V., liuas, Alibanban, Balibanban, Marulinao, Diis, Ahihiro, Alambihor, Alibihil. P., Alibanban. Lin. ibid.
Bauhinia binnata. Bauhinia with paired leaves. Leaves opposite, two per branch, and at the junction there is a style. Leaflets somewhat egg-shaped in reverse, entire and smooth. No proper petiole. = This small tree, which I have seen in the town of Bauang, in a place called Mainaga, reaches a height of nine feet: its leaves do not have the pleasant acidic flavor of those described before. The leaflets resemble the wings of a butterfly, and the two could almost be taken for one. It was bearing fruit in October. * T., Alibanban. New species.
Bauhinia purpurea. ? Bauhinia purpurea? Leaves alternate, somewhat heart-shaped, orbicular, with two large lobes, and a style in the middle, and two flat glands at the base where all the veins meet. Flowers in a racemose panicle. Proper peduncle hollow and closed at the top. Calyx in five deep, lanceolate parts, colored at the edges. Corolla of five lanceolate petals, with small claws, fixed to the covering of the hollow peduncle of the calyx. Stamens ten: three fertile, and the remaining seven partly sterile and partly castrated. Anthers elongated. Stigma somewhat shield-shaped. Pod.... = It is a tree of six or seven varas in height. I have seen it in a garden in Pasig. The leaves are barely distinguishable from those of the Alibanban; but they are not acidic. Flowers in October. * Alibanban. — I doubt whether this is the species; but it comes very close. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 515.
Bauhinia grandiflora. Bauhinia with large flowers. Leaves alternate, heart-shaped, pointed, without glands, fuzzy below, and with veins meeting at the base. Short petioles. Terminal flowers, in clusters. Proper peduncle, colored, very long, hollow and closed at the top. Calyx fleshy, colored, split into five equal lanceolate parts. Corolla not butterfly-shaped, longer than the calyx, of five equal, large, lanceolate, upright petals, overlapping one another by

232
the shores, and fixed with the stamens and pistil, in the covering of the hollow part of the peduncle. Stamens ten, unequal in height. Filaments awl-shaped. Anthers long. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma obtuse. Legume with a small stalk, lanceolate, with many seeds, separated by isthmuses. = This tree resembles the body of a man: from its wounded bark, an astringent gum flows. Its leaves do not have the flavor of those of the Alibanban. The flowers are extremely beautiful, white, more than half a palm in length, and very fragrant. The wood, which is white, is used by the Indians in the construction of their houses, and serves for gunstock cases. The calyx is cinnamon-colored, and not white like the corolla. The tree is known in the province of Batangas, and is found near the beaches. Flowers in August. * T., Bonga in Batangas; but in other places, the same name is given to a different tree, of the genus Rhizophora. — A new species, and not the grandiflora of Dec. Prod. t. 2. 513. But it seems to me it should form a new genus, and cannot be the genus Amaria of the same Author ibid. 519, to which it somewhat approaches among all the leguminosae. Perhaps a species of Schotia.?
Bauhinia scandens. Climbing Bauhinia. Leaves alternate, heart-shaped, round, with two pointed lobes, not diverging at the tip, and about eleven nerves that unite at the base, where there is a kind of indistinct gland. Petioles short, with simple tendrils in the axils. Terminal flowers in a corymb, with their own peduncles, very long. Calyx of five oval leaflets, turned downward. Corolla erect, of five irregular petals, with claws: the four nearly equal in height, oval; the fifth very small and lanceolate. Stamens three only; all fertile. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma shield-shaped. Legume woody, very compressed, one foot long and three fingers wide, with many seeds. = A shrub, as thick as a thigh, that climbs neighboring trees. The leaves have barely any acid taste; but it is slightly perceptible, and they are about five inches long. The flowers are at times straw-colored, at times flesh-colored, and at first glance are confused with those of the Poinciana: the bark is extremely tough, and the wild Indians make from it the strings of their bows, for their arrows. I have seen these shrubs in the mountains of Batangas, and in those of S. Mateo. Flowers in July. * T., Banot. Lin. ibid.
POINCIANA. Calyx in five parts. Petals five, of which the uppermost is the largest. Stamens long, all fertile. Legume oblong, with many seeds. Lin. Sist. Veg. 671.
Poinciana pulcherrima. Very Beautiful Poinciana. Trunk studded with large, paired spines. Leaves doubly pinnate without a terminal leaflet, with three stipules at each pair of leaflets,

233
three others at the base of the partial petioles, and at the base of the large common petioles, two others fringed with lashes. Leaflets smooth, numbering five to eight pairs, either inversely ovate or elliptical, with a small point at the tip. Terminal flowers in a corymb. Individual peduncles very long. Calyx divided almost to the base into five concave parts: four on one side, and the other on the opposite side. Corolla of five petals with small claws: one very small and upright; the other four very large, with very wavy margins. Stamens ten, woolly, and pressed together at their lower part. Filaments erect, very long. Anthers drooping. Pistil as long as the stamens. Stigma somewhat concave. Pod compressed, with seven or more seeds fixed at the upper suture and separated from one another by fleshy partitions. = These small trees, common everywhere, rise to a height of three or four varas. They have a beautiful appearance, owing to the abundance, size, and beauty of their flowers, which are between yellow and red. Boys eat the seeds raw. I have seen no other use made of this tree. When the ripe fruit is boiled in water and a little copperas is added, a middling ink is obtained, though much inferior to that of Mimosa farneciana. The bark and root yield a faint purple color. The pods will be about three inches long. The author of the Flora of the Antilles attributes very valuable properties to this small tree. The flowers, in the quantity of a small handful, steeped in four pounds of boiling water and left to infuse for half an hour, make a reliable febrifuge, and more excellent than quinine, because of its pleasant taste; giving the patient several cups at intervals, two hours before the onset of fever. Sugar must be added to the water, and it must be kept hot. These flowers in strong doses cause abortion. Flowers in nearly all months. * T., Flores, Rosas Caballero Lin. ibid.
REICHARDIA. Calyx half bell-shaped, with small notches, formed by five elongately united pieces. Petals somewhat butterfly-like, six to ten, unequal. Stamens ten, joined toward the middle by means of beards. Style one. Stigma widened. Pod in the manner of a Samara, terminated by an oblong wing. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 484.
