REICHARDIA PENTAPETALA. FIVE-PETALED REICHARDIA. Leaves opposite, twice pinnate without an odd leaflet. Common petioles full of paired thorns below the partial petioles, which number about nine or ten pairs, without thorns. Leaflets about seven pairs, linear, half an inch long. Flowers in a racemose panicle. Lower calyx very small, in five pointed parts. Corolla not butterfly-shaped, of five oblong petals, fixed at the divisions of the calyx, alternating with its parts and longer than them. Stamens ten, more or less, fixed at the base of the co-

234
rola, with hairy filaments and twin anthers. Four germens, hairy: three of them abort. One style in each germen with the stigma, slightly split and widened. Legume, like a samara, knife-shaped, with the edge folded along the margins on the lower part, where it conceals a lens-shaped seed, and afterward elongated, with a long membranous extension whose tip curves backward. = Very rare small trees, which I have seen in Agoo and in Tagudin in Ilocos. Their height is two or three varas, and the branches are drooping. The leaves, as well as the legumes, are a pleasant green color, and the latter are about two inches long: the seed is a single one, found at the base, with the legume rising from the middle of the seed and its margins coiling to one side. Afterward the legume consists of nothing more than a very thin wing: so that the fruit could almost be taken for a samara. In those towns they call it, without knowing why, palo santo. Flowers in October. New species.

CAESALPINIA. Calyx with five lobes, of which the lower one is larger than the rest. Five petals; the lower one more beautiful than the others. Legume rhomboidal in shape. Seeds of the same shape. Lin. Syst. veg. 655. 672.

Caesalpinia sappan. Cesalpinia sapang. Trunk studded with spines. Leaves twice-pinnate, without a terminal leaflet. Leaflets approaching a linear shape, with unequal sides and a notch at the apex. Flowers in racemes. Calyx boat-shaped, with five lobes turned downward. Corolla fixed in the calyx, of five petals: four nearly equal, the upper one broader, shorter, and with small red spots. Stamens very unequal in height, fixed in the calyx and closely bunched below. Filaments woolly at the base. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma thick and compressed, appearing split into two plates. Legume woody, saber-like, truncated at the apex and narrowing toward the base, with three or four seeds and a spongy partition between each one. Seeds oblong, with a leathery coat, and slightly mottled. = A very common tree in the Philippines, which reaches a height of twelve or fifteen feet. Everyone knows it, as a great trade is carried on with it in Manila, where it is brought from the provinces; the Spaniards call it Sapang, or Sibucao, as the Indians do. The Visayans in some areas use the wood in place of iron to make nails with which they fasten their boats, because they say the wood is incorruptible. The decoction of the wood in water, which is blood-colored, is given to drink to those who have suffered a fall or a blow, because popular opinion attributes to it a special virtue for dissolving clotted blood; and Father Mercado says it is good to drink it regularly, because it purges bad humors through the urine. The use

235
that the wood is used for red dye is well known. Fl. in Sept.
* T., Sapang, Sibucao.
Caesalpinia ignota. Unknown Caesalpinia. Leaves twice-pinnate without an odd leaflet. Leaflets about seventeen pairs, somewhat linear, truncated at the base with a bristle-tip, and notched at the apex. Partial petioles about nine pairs. Calyx like that of the Sappang. Corolla: the painted petal smaller than the others. Stamens ten, very woolly at the base. Pod shaped like a saber, with the tip elongated, sharpened, and curved upward. = Small trees found in various places: the flowers are yellow, and almost entirely similar to those of the Sapang: the pod differs greatly: the leaflets do not reach half an inch in length: I do not know whether the trunk has thorns, or whether the wood serves for dyeing. It has no name among the Indians. Fl. in Sept. — Perhaps the species Mimosoides of Dec. Prod. p. 2. 482?
MEZONEURUM. Calyx of five pieces joined at the base, the lower one arched. Corolla of five petals with claws, the upper one smaller. Stamens ten, hairy below. Pod leaf-like, flat, oblong-ovate, that does not open, with one chamber and many seeds: the upper suture widened into a wing. Decand. Prod. p. 2. 484.
Mezoneurum procumbens. Trailing Mezoneurum. Trunk lying on the ground and studded with spines. Leaves twice-pinnate without an odd leaflet, in whose place there is a small spine. Leaflets linear, with a notch at the apex where there is a small spine. Calyx elongated in the shape of a boat, with five lobes: one very long and concave, enclosing the stamens and pistil. Corolla: the largest petal opposite the concave segment of the calyx, shaped like a jaw, or like half a collar ring: the other four small. Stamens and other features as in the Sappan species. Pod very compressed, with many seeds, and adorned with a wing that runs the entire length of the upper suture. = This woody plant spreads and propagates widely. It is easy to recognize by the tips of the branches and the flower clusters, which have a very beautiful crimson color. The tender shoots are eaten cooked in salads, and the decoction of its leaves relieves asthmatics. Fl. in Feb. * T., Sagnit, Sapnit, Cabitcabag. P., Sapnit. V., Tugabang, Ugabang. New species.
CASSIA. Calyx of five leaflets. Petals five, unequal. Anthers: the three upper ones sterile; the three lower ones beak-shaped. Pod divided by partitions. Lin. Syst. veg. 655. 667.
• Cassia tora. Cassa tora. Central root with lateral rootlets, blackish. Stem round. Leaves opposite, pinnate without an odd leaflet, replaced by a gland. Leaflets three pairs, reverse egg-shaped, with a bristle-tip at the apex, somewhat hairy, and between each pair a short gland. Common petioles swol-

236
two, without a gland at the base, and with two awl-shaped stipules on it. Flowers axillary and terminal. Calyx of five unequal parts. Corolla of five unequal petals, ending in small claws. Stamens ten. Anthers: seven with a beak, and two of these larger; the remaining three sterile. Pistil longer than the stamens, arched. Stigma thick. Legume with many long, semi-cylindrical seeds, with barely notable angles, arranged lengthwise in a line one after another, and cut obliquely at the ends. = This plant is common everywhere and grows to a height of two feet. The fruit is half a foot long. The root has a somewhat sharp taste. I have not seen the natives make use of it, though many know it; and in the town of Macati, the juice of a handful of the tender plants is used as a purgative, with the addition of warm water. A spoonful of the green seeds of this species, or perhaps of the longisiliqua variety, eaten according to Father Juan Delgado, purges gently. It agrees, though not entirely, with the species that Linnaeus calls Tora. * T., Manimanihan Catandang aso, Mongomongohan. Lin. ibid. 668.

Cassia occidentalis. Western Cassia. Central root, with lateral rootlets. Stem erect and branching. Leaves opposite, pinnate without a terminal leaflet, replaced by a bristle. Leaflets in five or six pairs: the lower ones smaller, ovate, oblong, with hairy margins and lower surface. Common petiole swollen at the base, with a gland and two stipules. Legume compressed, linear, with many heart-shaped compressed seeds, separated by thin partitions. = This plant produces yellow flowers and grows to a height of three feet. The legume is three inches long. Children eat the raw seeds when they are tender. * T., Tighiman, Balatongaso. Lin. ibid. 669.

Cassia sulcata. Grooved Cassia. Central root, blackish, with lateral rootlets. Stem branching and channeled on the upper part. Leaves opposite, pinnate without a terminal leaflet, replaced by a gland. Leaflets: the lower ones smaller, in four, five or six pairs, between ovate and lanceolate, soft and woolly on both surfaces. Common petiole with three channels, swollen, with a gland and two bearded stipules at the base. Legume quadrangular, with many long, somewhat angular seeds, arranged in a row lengthwise, and separated by thin partitions. = This plant grows to a height of six or more feet. I have not seen the natives make use of it. The fruit is more than one foot long. It is called Tighiman by some, though this name is also given by others to the previous species. It is found everywhere along roadsides. Flowers in October. * T., Tighiman. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 498.

237

Cassia fistula. Casia fistula. Leaves opposite, pinnate without terminal leaflet. Leaflets: the lower ones smaller, numbering five pairs, ovate, tapering at the tips, smooth and somewhat stiff. Common petiole swollen at the base and without a gland. Flowers in corymbose racemes. Stamens as in the species Tora; and additionally the three longest ones have a small lentil-shaped prominence in their middle. Pod cylindrical, pointed, woody, very long, with many circular seeds surrounded by pulp and separated by partitions. = The cañafistula grows into a tree as thick as a human body. Its flowers are large, very beautiful, white and flesh-colored. The pulp of the fruit is used in inflammatory fevers, in rheumatic and gouty pains, as a purgative, in doses of two ounces, or somewhat less. It is also given with good effect to pregnant women and to children, though in small quantities. The tender young shoots are eaten in salad and act as a very good purgative. The wood is very hard and dark, and is sometimes sold as ebony. The bark is excellent for tanning hides. Flowers in March. * T., Cañafistula. V., Lombayong, Ibabao, Balayong. P., Cañafistula. Lin. ibid. 669.— It belongs to the genus Cathartocarpus of Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 459.

Cassia alata. Winged Casia. Stem erect, branching. Leaves opposite, pinnate without terminal leaflet, replaced by a thick stylet. Leaflets numbering ten to thirteen pairs, approaching a linear shape (the lower ones smaller), smooth, somewhat rough, with a stylet at the apex. Common petiole swollen, with two horizontal stipules at the base. Pod long, with two wings or membranes on both sides, and with many seeds that approach the shape of a cross with blunt ends. = This plant sometimes reaches a height of nine feet and becomes a small tree as thick as a calf. Besides the various names by which it is known, the natives also call it Gamot sa buni, which means remedy against herpes. They use it to treat this disease by rubbing the affected areas with the leaves, and even when dry the leaves heal well and with complete certainty. But if the cases are long-standing, it will be advisable to purge, to bathe, and above all to consult a physician. Flowers in May. * T., Sonting, Acapulco, Gamot sa buni, Catanda. V., Sunting, Casitas. P., Pacayomcom Castila. Lin. Sist. veg. 670.

Cassia mimosoides. Mimosa-like Casia. Stem half prostrate on the ground. Leaves pinnate without terminal leaflet, replaced by a stylet. Leaflets about twenty-five pairs, sessile, oblong, fringed with hairs, tipped with a small point, and with a gland at the base of the first pair. Common petiole with two membranous, pointed stipules. Flowers axillary, solitary. Calyx and Corolla as in the other species. Stamens ten: one very short, horn-shaped and without an anther; the other nine fertile, and with
38

238
anthers endowed with two holes at the apex; the alternate ones longer, and two of them of a different color. Ovary curved and the stigma half truncated. Pod linear, compressed, with many seeds separated by partitions. = A very small plant, which I have seen in Malinta: it is woody, and resembles the mimosas in its leaflets. It barely rises a hand's breadth, and does not spread much either. The holes of the anthers are very notable, and resemble two lips. Two of them are purple in color, and the others straw-colored, like the corolla. The leaflets are no more than one line in length, the common petiole one inch, and the same for the pod. Fl. in Oct. Lin. ibid. 671.
GE-JUA. Leaves alternate. Calyx inferior, monophyllous, bell-shaped, cut somewhat obliquely, with five teeth; two on the lower side, and three on the other. Corolla of five petals: the upper one larger. Stamens ten, separate. Filaments unequal in height. Anthers regular. Ovary linear, thick, hairy. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma obtuse. Pod apparently. = These flowers, which the Chinese bring to Manila, are used to dye cotton straw-yellow, and for that reason the dyers buy them. For the incomplete description above, I have relied on the same flowers that are sold in the shop; and what has been said is what I have been able to gather from them, with considerable effort. I believe this plant must not be absent from the Philippines, if one searches for it. The flowers are straw-colored. The Dyers of Tondo know it by the name of Ge-jua.
MORINGA. Calyx deeply divided into five parts. Corolla of five sessile petals: four below, and the other directed upward. Stamens ten (some sterile or with smaller anthers), short and unequal. Pod long, three-sided, three valves, and seeds with three wings. Jussieu. Gén. pl. 348.
Moringa oleifera. Oil-producing Moringa. Trunk terminating in three or more branches arranged in an umbel. Leaves thrice pinnate, ending in twice pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets oval, very entire, and smooth. Calyx the color of the corolla, in five linear, concave parts, almost as long as the corolla, and bent downward. Corolla somewhat butterfly-shaped, of five petals. The upper one inclined forward, covering the stamens; the two lateral ones with rounded edges. The two lower ones shorter than the rest, and folded back like the lateral ones, downward. Stamens nine or ten, drawn together at the base, but separating easily. The five filaments bearing anthers increase successively in height, alternating with those that lack them. Style awl-shaped and curved downward. Pod long, cylindrical, pointed, fleshy, with three very deep channels, through which it

239
it splits into three parts, with three channeled valves, in which the globose seeds are fixed, wrapped in a fleshy aril that has three wings. = This tree, whose flowers are white, rises to a height of about three or four fathoms. It is known to all the Indians, who eat its leaves and fruit boiled in water, when the fruit is tender. The tenderest young shoots are eaten cooked by nursing women when they lack milk, and the desired effect is achieved. The white parrots called Cockatoos, and by the Indians Calangai, eagerly seek the fruit of this tree. Its root is considered very medicinal and serves for mustard plasters. From its seeds an odorless oil is extracted that does not go rancid; however, it is caustic and also purges violently. The marks of smallpox are sometimes removed by anointing them with it. The root boiled in plenty of water is considered an antiscorbutic; that of the coconut is more harmless and easy to obtain. Rumphius considers it most useful, taken in moderation as a drink, for sailors. It is also said to be very good for other diseases, and even for some considered incurable, such as leprosy. The Indians say that lightning never strikes the Malungay. It is the Hyperanthera of Lamarck, and the Guilandina Moringa of Linnaeus. Flowering in November and in other months. * T., Malungay, Camalungai, Calungai. V., P., Malungai, Calungai, Dool, Malungit. It is the species Pterygosperma of De Candolle, Prod. p. 2. 478.
GUILANDINA. Calyx of one piece in the form of a saucer: (in five parts, Dec.) Petals inserted at the neck of the calyx, nearly equal. Legume rhomboidal; with one compartment. Bony seeds. Lin. Syst. Veg. 572.
Guilandina bonducela. Guilandina bonducela. Trunk prostrate on the ground and bristling with spines. Leaves twice pinnate without an odd leaflet, in whose place there is a spine. Leaflets numbering ten or fourteen pairs, ovate, elongated, with a spine at the tip. Common petioles with spines, and with four stipules in the form of small leaflets at the base. Flowers in a raceme. Calyx in five parts, turned downward. Corolla fixed in the calyx, of five petals: the four nearly equal; the upper one broader and shorter, and marked with some crimson dots. Stamens ten. Filaments very unequal in height, fixed in the calyx, very close together, and woolly at the base. Pistil very short. Stigma thick. Legume rhomboidal before maturity, full of spines, and containing two half-globose seeds whose skin is leathery, hard, very tough, and mottled. = This plant, whose fruit is called Calambibit, spreads widely over the ground. The seeds, which serve children for their games, are much used by the Indians in medicine, giving their scrapings to drink, but in very small quantities, in wine or water, for diseases of the belly. They also appear on the list of remedies

240
believed to be suitable for facilitating childbirth. With the roots of this plant, beads are made for rosaries; but it has happened that they have raised persistent, poor-quality blisters on the necks of those who have used them, as I have seen myself. Flowers in December. * T., Bayag cambing, Calambibit. V., Dalugdug. Lin. ibid. 673.

Guilandina nuga. Mock Guilandina. Trunk prostrate and dotted with hooks. Leaves twice-pinnate without an odd leaflet, in whose place there is a small spine. Leaflets in sets of three pairs, egg-shaped, elongated, and at the tip with an almost invisible spine, very entire, smooth, and stiff. Calyx and the rest as in the previous species. Stigma thick, compressed, as if split into two plates. Pod oval, compressed, smooth, with one large seed. = This plant spreads widely through the forests, clinging obstinately and easily to clothing with its spines, which is the origin of its botanical name. It is not put to any use. Flowers in February. * T. Camit cabag, Cabit cabag. Lin. ibid.

PETALOMA. Calyx shaped like a jar, with five teeth and two scales at the base. Five petals, inserted in the calyx and between its teeth. Stamens on the rim of the calyx. Berry crowned, with one up to four seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 678. Jus. Gen. pl. 320.

Petaloma alba. White Petaloma. Fleshy leaves, crowded at the ends of the branches, approaching the shape of a wedge, notched at the edges and at the tip. Flowers in a spike. Calyx adherent, long, swollen in the middle, curved, compressed, with five teeth on the rim and two other lateral teeth arising toward the middle of the belly. Corolla of five petals, fixed to the edges of the calyx. Stamens ten, fixed to the calyx, and sometimes eight or nine: five alternating, somewhat shorter than the others. Style arising toward one side of the fruit, and as long as the stamens. Stigma pointed. Drupe small, not very fleshy, conical and inverted, swollen in the middle, with a very hard, fibrous stone and a similar seed. = A tree that grows three or four fathoms tall, and is well known to the natives. It is quite common on some seashores, and is called Culasi; by incision it yields a kind of balsam which, mixed with oil, is good for herpes and mange when rubbed on with it. I do not know whether the one I am speaking of produces this. Its wood is nonetheless hard, and the natives use it for building their houses. The flowers are white. Flowers in May. * T., Culasi. New species. — The fibrous bark of the fruit adheres entirely to the stone. It belongs to the genus Muriria of Linnaeus and Jussieu.

Petaloma occinea. Crimson Petaloma.

241
Leaves opposite, fleshy, clustered at the ends of the branches, wedge-shaped, notched at the margins and apex. Stamens eight or nine, of unequal height, and not uniform, as in the previous species. = This tree grows as large as the previous one. The flowers are flesh-colored, of a very vivid color. * T., Culasi. New species.
MELIA. Calyx with five teeth. Petals five. Nectary cylindrical, bearing the anthers at its mouth. Drupe with a nut of five seeds, in five chambers. Lin. Syst. Veg. 680.
Melia composita. Compound Melia. Leaves opposite, twice pinnate with an odd leaflet, ending in simply pinnate. Leaflets lanceolate, pointed, slightly notched, very wavy, and smooth. Flowers in a panicle, in small umbels. Calyx deeply five-parted. Corolla of five linear petals, rolled downward. Nectary a cylindrical tube (not attached to the corolla) with ten teeth at the rim, where the same number of anthers are fixed, nearly without filaments. Stigma five-parted. Drupe oval, dotted with small points that disappear at maturity, with a very hard nut, five-angled, five-chambered, with one egg-shaped seed in each.= This tree grows to the thickness of a man's body, and the natives call it malungayin because its leaves bear some resemblance in their arrangement to those of the Moringa. Its bark has a very nauseating smell. The wood, which is soft, is used in building houses. The fruit, which is straw-colored and resembles a small olive when ripe, is also fragrant; but slightly bitter, and is not eaten. It is very common in Bauang at a place called munting tubig, and I have not seen it in many other places. The fruit of the Melia Azedarach, of which this is a congener, contains a solid oil that serves for paint; and the flesh of the drupe is also used to make candles. The seeds are used for rosaries. No experiment has been made with the melia I am discussing: although I applied the flesh of the fruit to a flame, and saw that it did not burn. Flowers in March. * T., Malongain. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 622. — In Spain they commonly call the Melia azedarach cinamomo, but today in Manila that name is given to a species of Lausonia.
Melia iloilo. Iloilo Melia. Leaves opposite, pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets twelve pairs, linear, toothed, and wavy, with the margins rolled downward, somewhat pointed (white beneath) and smooth on both surfaces. Petioles very short. Flowers very small, in spiked panicles. Calyx inferior, in five rounded parts. Corolla of five linear petals, thick, and three times longer than the calyx. There is also a cylindrical tube with five inconspicuous teeth. Stamens five, as tall as the tube and fixed at its base. Anthers medium

242
arrow-shaped. Germ sessile, inside the flower. Style very short, thick. Stigma as if split into two parts. Fruit.... = Tree of the second order, common in Arayat. Flowers in January. * P., Iloilo. — By analogy I have placed this tree here, although it differs in the number of anthers.

SANDORICUM. Calyx with five teeth. Five linear petals. Nectary with ten teeth, where the anthers are located. Drupe spherical, with five nuts having two valves at the base, and one seed. Lin. ibid. 680.

Sandoricum indicum. Indian Sandoricum. Leaves ternate. Leaflets half-ovate, obtuse, stiff, entire, and hairy: the middle one somewhat elliptical. Flowers in panicles. Stalk proper, very short. Calyx small, cylindrical, with five obtuse teeth. Corolla much longer than the calyx, with five greenish, linear petals, turned downward. Nectary a cylindrical tube, attached nearly to the middle of the corolla, with ten teeth at the edge, where an equal number of sessile anthers are fixed. Style somewhat longer than the stamens. Stigma erect in five parts. Fruit as in the genus. = This well-known tree grows to twelve yards tall or more. The rind of the fruit is very sour and is not eaten, but from it a very good sweet preserve is made, as everyone knows. The five nuts found inside are surrounded by a whitish, spongy flesh, difficult to separate, and this is what is sucked and nothing more. The wood, especially when very dry, has a most pleasant scent, like that of juniper, and the same when burned. Flowers in April. * T., Santol. Lin. ibid.

BOSWELLIA. Calyx with five teeth. Five petals, inverted, oblong, and very open. A cup-shaped disk, notched, surrounding the base of the ovary, which bears ten stamens. Style one. Stigma with three grooves? in a head. Capsule with three sides, three valves, and three compartments, with solitary seeds surrounded by a broad membranous wing. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 76.

Boswellia? integra. Entire Boswellia. Leaves alternate, pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets lanceolate, wavy, entire, smooth, with very prominent veins below. Petioles very short, somewhat swollen at the base. Flowers axillary, in panicles of few small florets. Calyx free, small, with five teeth. Corolla.... Fruit. A fleshy capsule, which opens at the top, club-shaped, with two or four slightly notable channels (sometimes three), with three or four compartments, and in each one a seed surrounded by a fleshy aril, attached to the central axis of the capsule. = A large, little-known tree: its wood tends toward red. The fruit resembles a cherry, purple in color; and when wounded it exudes a resin like a very fragrant balsam.

243
It is common in the mountains of S. Mateo, and in other places. It had fruit in June. It is not the Calamansanai, although an Indian affirmed it to be so. *T., Polayagan.
Boswellia? obliqua. Boswellia? oblique. Leaves opposite, winged, without? an odd one. Leaflets numbering about seven pairs, obliquely egg-shaped, elongated, entire, fleshy and smooth. Flowers in racemes. Cal.... Cor.... Stam.... Pistil.... Superior capsule, shaped like a club, with three obtuse angles, three chambers, and in each two seeds, one above the other, surrounded by an aril, and fixed on the central axis of the capsule.= A large tree, known to the Indians, with hard wood. The fruit is crimson, and somewhat larger than a cherry, and gives off a fragrant resin similar to that of the preceding. It flowers in March. *T., Pandapanda.— I suspect that these two trees belong to this genus, or perhaps to the genus Trichilia. See also the genus Philagonia of Dec. Prod. p. 2. 90.
TURRAEA. Calyx with five teeth. Petals five. Nectary cylindrical, bearing the anthers on its rim. Fruit of five capsules, each containing two seeds. Lin. Sist. veg. 679.
Turraea virens. Turrea very green. Leaves regularly opposite, nearly sessile, obliquely egg-shaped, oblong, pointed, entire and smooth. Flowers terminal, in a compound raceme. Common peduncle very long. Individual peduncle very short. Calyx very small, in five parts. Corolla much longer than the calyx, cylindrical, split to the middle into five linear parts. Nectary a cylindrical tube, somewhat shorter than the corolla, and attached to it up to the middle, with ten teeth on the rim, where ten anthers are fixed. Style one, somewhat longer than the stamens, enclosed in a tube or sheath of its own, which girds it to near half its height. Stigma thick and depressed. Capsule globose, somewhat hairy, depressed, with five angles and five small chambers, each containing two seeds one above the other. Although it appears to be one, in reality there are two, joined by a spongy isthmus in the middle: some abort.= An excellent tree, very common in the province of Batangas, and in other places, but not far from the sea. It rises to a height of ten or fifteen varas, and does not usually put out branches except at the very top. It is one of the most precious and useful trees we have in the Islands. Its bark, which has a nauseating smell, when sun-dried, ground, and passed through a fine cloth, is a very reliable emetic and specific remedy for putrid fevers, without our needing the much-praised Ipecacuanha or Bejuquillo. I myself have been witness many times to its marvelous efficacy. The taste of the bark is slightly bitter. The dose for an adult man is half a real or three-quarters of a columnar real, given to drink in a little warm water; and not con-

244
it tends to give more, because it is a very energetic emetic: even the bark of the tree, the healers say, should not be taken close to the ground, but at a height of one fathom. Father Ignacio de Mercado speaks very highly of this tree, and with good reason. Its seeds are crimson. The leaves are pale green.
The effect of the bark of this tree, if finely ground, is to expel bilious matter by vomiting, and it does not usually work through the bowels. But if the bark is only coarsely ground, it also tends to purge downward at the same time. The fruit falls from the tree in November. * P., Iguin, Aguiu, Talictan. V., Ananangtang, Mananangtang, Bacugan, Macasili, Bingliu, Palnhambobocag, Bolongtambal. P., Malabangao. I., Basiloag. Lin. ibid.
Turraea octandra. Turrea with eight stamens. Leaves sometimes opposite, sometimes alternate, obliquely lanceolate, ovate, entire, and smooth. Flowers in umbellate panicles. Calyx in four parts. Corolla in four parts, turned downward. The nectary tube with eight notched lobes, and as many anthers. The style enclosed in a sheath up to its midpoint. Fruit.... = A tree known to the natives, which grows larger than a man's body, and which must not be confused with the Himbabao. Its wood is hard and used in carpentry. The bark has a nauseating smell and will probably possess the same properties as the Iguio. Flowers in August. * T., Himamao. New species.
DOMBEYA. Calyx lobed, divided into five parts. Petals five. Filaments fifteen or twenty, fertile, and five sterile, on a proper tube. Five capsules joined together, with one chamber and many seeds. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 498.
Dombeya biserrata. Dombeya twice-serrate. Leaves alternate, oblique, somewhat heart-shaped, elongated, pointed, with four veins (one more on one side), doubly serrate, soft, and hairy. Petioles very short. Flowers terminal, in small racemes. Calyx with two awl-shaped bracts at the base, free, cylindrical, curved, woolly, with five teeth: three on one side and the two longest on the opposite side. Corolla tubular, somewhat longer than the calyx, in five deep divisions: the two upper ones larger, spatula-shaped, and the three lower ones narrower. Stamens ten at the tip of a cylindrical tube, split into ten parts, which are the filaments of the stamens, nearly as long as the corolla. Anthers attached at the inner side of the filaments. Additionally, there are five small leaves, or laminae (white), fixed on the staminal tube toward the tip, some taller than others, and these are the sterile stamens. Ovary oval, seated within the flower. Style longer than the stamens. Stigma apparently with incisions. Fruit

245
conical, very bristly with soft hairs, composed of five long, sharp-pointed pods, simply pressed together, which separate at maturity, each with one chamber and many half-rhomboidal seeds. = It is a small tree that I have seen in Malinta and in other places, whose fruit is more than two inches long. The anthers are white. It has affinity with the Melhania. Flowers in July. * I., Baquinbaquit. V., T., Dangling aso, Bontot usa. New species.
TRIBULUS. Calyx in five parts. Five petals, open. No style. Five pods, united, gibbous, spiny, and with two or three seeds, with transverse chambers. Lin. Sist. veg. 683. Jus. Gen. pl. 296.
Tribulus lanuginosus? Woolly Tribulus? Stem cylindrical, creeping. Leaves opposite, winged without an odd leaflet, rarely with one. Leaflets, numbering six or seven pairs, unequal, almost sessile, linear, hairy and with three veins. Common petioles, with two awl-shaped stipules at the base. Rachis very short. Flowers axillary, solitary. Peduncles long. Calyx cleft almost to the base, in five awl-shaped, hairy parts. Corolla of five petals, twice as long as the calyx, inversely egg-shaped and oblong. Stamens ten. Filaments short. Anthers long, like the filaments, and almost arrow-shaped. Ovary seated within the flower, somewhat conical and very hairy. Stigma thick, with five ridges. Five bony pods, gathered in the shape of a globe, each with four sharp points, the two longest; with three chambers, and in each one a seed. = This plant, which I have seen between Parañaque and Las Piñas, and at Punta de Santiago, is a creeper. The flowers are yellow and about an inch long. It is known in Spain by the name of abrojos (caltrop). According to botanical authors, the seeds are astringent and useful in nosebleeds, dysentery, and other flows of blood. It is good as a gargle, for ulcers and inflammations of the gums, mouth, and throat. The one from Punta Santiago has only two spines on the underside. Flowers in January. — It does not agree very well with the lanuginosus species.
OCHNA. Calyx of five pieces. Corolla of five or ten petals. Anthers half-sessile. Berries from five to ten, inserted on a thick, round, and fleshy receptacle; each with one chamber and one seed. Lin. Sist. veg. 682. Dec. Prod. 1. 735.
Ochma fascicularis. Fascicled Ochma. Leaves alternate, almost sessile, between oval and lanceolate, entire, smooth, and veined. Stipules deciduous. Terminal flowers in fascicled racemes, with very long peduncles. Calyx inferior with six or more lobes: but at maturity in as many parts. Corolla of six or more petals, equal to the calyx. Stamens.
39

246
number up to twenty-four, fixed on a thick and elevated receptacle. Anthers long, linear. Ovaries six or more, still sessile on the receptacle. Style single, with a simple and somewhat thick stigma. Six or more oval, compressed drupes, not very fleshy, with a thin and bony covering, four cells, and solitary seeds. = Small trees about as thick as an arm, found in Angat, and unknown to the natives. Their leaves reach up to about three inches in length. The drupes are somewhat larger than lentils, with purple flesh. In this species the drupes have four chambers and as many seeds. Flowers in June. T., Aniatan. New species. — There is another species in the Visayas with serrated leaves, very smooth, and without veins. They call it Bansilai.

QUASSIA. Five separate capsules, of two valves, and a single seed, fixed on the fleshy receptacle. Calyx of five pieces. Five petals. Nectary of five pieces. Lin. Syst. veg. 682.

Quassia tricarpa. Three-fruited Quassia. Leaves either opposite or alternate, smoothly winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets lanceolate, entire, smooth, and with two woody glands at the base, on the lower side. Terminal flowers, in very large panicles, all hermaphroditic. Calyx the same color as the corolla, of four or five unequal, concave, and somewhat fringed leaflets. Corolla smaller than the calyx, of five unequal, concave petals, hairy at the base and edges. Nectary a somewhat concave disk, with lobes at the edges, placed below the stamens. Stamens eight, fixed between the base of the ovary and the nectary, and shorter than the corolla. Filaments thick, compressed, and hairy at the base. Anthers regular. Ovary seated on the nectary, conical with three angles. Style very short. Stigma somewhat thick, appearing lobed. Three dry, globose capsules, with the style in the middle, joined and compressed (one or two generally abort), seated within the flower, with a leathery and fragile covering, and one seed in each. = Small trees that grow to at most the thickness of a thigh, and only the large ones bear flowers. I have been told that fish are intoxicated by the leaves and can be caught by hand. I should note that the natives, on account of the resemblance of the seeds, also give the name Tiquis tiquis to a species of Canna. The said tree is common at the entrances to forests. Its flowers are seen in October or November, and not in other months. In the province of Balanga it is known by the names Catiquis and Sansanli, and there the decoction of its roots, which is bitter, is used in place of quinine. Some celebrated physicians use it with happy success against gout. The one I am speaking of is a variety of Quassia amara.

247
Even if the tree has only three capsules instead of five, it undoubtedly belongs to the genus Quassia. Perhaps other trees will be found with five; but even among the three, two often abort, leaving only their rudiments, as I have seen in a Quassia from Ilocos. Barrelier's plate of the Coccos Indorum agrees with this tree. The properties of Quassia amara are well known. Both its bark and its roots in cold infusion are excellent against malignant fevers, because they are a powerful antiseptic. Cups or vessels are also made from its wood, in which wine or water is poured, and within a few minutes it turns bitter and serves for weak stomachs. *T., Tiquistiquis, Catiquis, Sausanli. I.: Cusiben. P., Malapalitpit.
Quassia simaruba. Quasia simaruba. Pinnate leaves without a terminal leaflet: the common petiole is not winged. Leaflets about three pairs, nearly sessile, opposite, and sometimes barely alternate, lanceolate, wavy, with the margins rolled downward, entire, smooth, and leathery. Axillary flowers in compound racemes, with very long common peduncles. Calyx in five parts. Corolla.... Stamens.... Style one. Stigma appears to be cleft in three parts. Three oval, leathery, compressed capsules, joined to the middle and separated above, which split open inwardly, each containing one seed. = Trees almost unknown to the natives, which I have seen in Angat, about five fathoms tall and as thick as a thigh. The leaves are about four inches long. When the capsules open, the style divides into three: and the fruits are likewise constantly three. In the fruit one notices a kind of transparent, somewhat yellowish resin. It closely resembles the Simaruba species, and is surely a variety of it. It is therefore probable that it shares its properties. The bark of the root of the Simaruba is esteemed and used as a stomachic and very useful in dysentery and diarrhea; if taken after evacuation: otherwise it will be harmful, and thus it is necessary to act on the advice of a physician. It had fruit in February.
ENTADA. Polygamous flowers. Five distinct petals. Stamens from ten to twenty-five, with glandular anthers at the apex. Legume compressed, articulated, the valves separating at maturity, leaving the sutures, and with solitary seeds. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 424.
Entada pursaetha. Entada purseta. Twining trunk, with the ends of the branches striated. Opposite leaves, doubly pinnate, without a terminal leaflet, in whose place there is a small bristle. Leaflets about five pairs, elliptical, with a notch at the apex, very entire, smooth. Common petiole with two stipules at the base, rolled downward, and at the end a bifid tendril. Flowers in a spike. Calyx obliquely truncated, with five teeth.

248
Corolla of five oval petals, much larger than the calyx. Stamens ten to thirteen. Filaments longer than the corolla. Anthers with one or two globose, white glands, with a small stalk at the tip. Ovary cylindrical. Style short. Stigma somewhat widened at the tip. Pod woody, very large, with deep notches along the edges, with many chambers, and many very large, circular, compressed seeds, with a bony covering that lacks the circular line running parallel to the contour or edge, as in the Mimosas.= This shrub thickens until it becomes like a thigh; it is twining, and climbs to a height of six fathoms. All the Indians know it well, because of the great use made of every part of its trunk, which is soft, fibrous, and spongy. After being beaten with a stick, it is used in place of soap to wash the body, but not clothing; and the Indians use it in the bath to cleanse sweat and remove dandruff from the head. This is achieved through the lather that the trunk produces in water when rubbed with the hands. From experiments conducted with this shrub, I have come to be persuaded that it is a species of marvelous natural soap, and that for certain uses, especially for removing sticky perspiration from the body, it holds great advantages even over European soap. It is also a purgative, used by the Indians. It is common in all the forests: the fruit is among the strangest and most monstrous, for it is four to six feet long, or more, and four fingers wide. By placing the dried gogo in the bottom of the tinaguelas where Cacao is usually stored, and covering the Cacao with the same, the Indians assure us that worms do not destroy it. I have also heard that drinking the soapy water of the Gogo gives much relief to those suffering from asthma, and has even radically cured some. Smoking a large cigar made from it is likewise beneficial in this illness. Flowers in May. *T. Gogo, Bayogo. V. P. Balogo. Gohong bacay. Dec. ibid. 425.— In the Flora of the Antilles, vol. 3, p. 226, it is the Mimosa scandens of Linnaeus; and at another time I myself considered it a species of Adenanthera. Many mimosas have a saponaceous bark. The flowers of the gogo have been examined carefully, and the description above is exact.
TRICHILIA. Calyx as if with four or five teeth. Petals four or five. Nectary cylindrical, bearing on its eight or ten teeth just as many anthers: sometimes the filaments are separate. Capsule trilocular, trivalvate, with berry-like seeds: sometimes with two chambers and valves, and in each chamber one or two seeds with an aril. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 622.
TRICHILIA TRIPETALA. TRICHILIA WITH THREE PETALS. Leaves opposite, pinnate. Leaflets lanceolate, entire, nearly smooth, with many glands scattered toward the tip, on the pa-

249
lower page. Flowers axillary, in very long clusters. Calyx very small, divided almost to the base into five parts. Corolla much larger than the calyx, with three concave petals. Nectary smaller than the corolla, with three angles, and divided into six or seven deep, blunt parts. Stamens six or seven, fixed at the base of the nectary. Filaments almost none. Anthers thick, like small arrows. Ovary superior, very small. Style almost none. Stigma thick, conical, with three lobes. Capsule globose, with two chambers, each containing one seed: sometimes one aborts. = This well-known tree is of the third rank. Its wood, which is reddish in color and fairly hard, is used by the Indians in their houses; but it is not good, as woodworm gets into it, and it does not hold up well when exposed to rain. Flowers in July. * T, Salaquing pula. V. Agac-ac. New species.

Trichilia pentandra. Five-stamened Trichilia. Leaves opposite, winged. Leaflets ovate, oblong, entire, and smooth. Flowers in panicles. Calyx very small, with five teeth. Corolla much longer than the calyx, with five linear petals. Nectary cylindrical, somewhat shorter than the corolla, with five teeth. Flowers terminal, in compound clusters. Stamens five. Filaments none. Anthers somewhat long, fixed at the tip of the nectary. Ovary superior, globose. Style as long as the nectary. Stigma globose. Capsule the size of a cherry, globose, with a corky interior substance, with two chambers, each containing one seed. = Tree like the previous one. * T, Salaqui. V. Agapañga. New species.

Botanists have combined the genera Portesia and Trichilia into one.

Trichilia volubilis? Climbing Trichilia. Trunk climbing. Leaves partly opposite, winged, with an odd leaflet. Leaflets about eight pairs, the last ones larger and notched at the base, ovate, oblong, entire, membranaceous, smooth on top, and on the underside with white down, and the midvein with small grooves. Petioles very short without glands. Flowers axillary in long, spike-like panicles. Calyx inferior, with five rounded lobes. Corolla.... Style one. Stigma.... Capsule somewhat like a berry? oval, with three chambers and solitary seeds. = A climbing, whitish shrub, which grows as thick as a calf and even more so. It climbs the tallest trees. The leaves are more than a palm in length; on top they are a purplish green color, and below they are whitish with a light down. The flower panicles are a foot long. This shrub is celebrated for its bark, which is used for washing and is better than ordinary gogo, whose entire trunk is pounded with a stick for that purpose: whereas with the plant I am speaking of now, only the bark is used. The fruits that I saw were not ripe, and were like chickpeas pe-

250
ones: they had three chambers and in each one a seed. In some, a short style was seen, and no stigmas, which I suppose had fallen off along with the styles of others. Their flowers should be sought in Dec. or Jan. *T. Gogong toco, Cubatili, Gogong bisaya.— I still think that this gogo de Visaya is not a trichilia, but rather a species of mimosa, and perhaps one of those I have described in this work.

Trichilia rimosa. Trichilia with crevices. * Trees that I have never seen with fruit, and whose flowers are hermaphroditic. Alternate leaves, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets many pairs, lanceolate, covered with small whitish points, wavy, with many crevices on the midvein underneath, and on the common petiole. Flowers in panicles, with opposite and horizontal branches, and with crevices on the peduncles. Calyx very small, in five parts. Corolla the color of the calyx, with five petals. Nectary hemispherical, with notches on the edge. Stamens six or eight, corresponding to the divisions of the nectary. Filaments united with the nectary on the inside; only the anthers protrude. Ovary superior, globose. Style and Stigma none. Fruit none. There is a variety with smooth leaves.

All these flowers (which closely resemble those of the Mangifera) fall off, and I have never seen them open, nor the anthers, despite their being large; they shed a fine dust. Perhaps (though I have not seen it) as maturity approaches, the corolla, nectary, and stamens fall away, and the fruit of the following description appears. * Trees that bear fruit with female and hermaphroditic flowers. Leaves opposite, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets lanceolate, wavy, with crevices on the midvein, and a common petiole. Calyx very small, in five parts. Corolla and Stamens none. Ovary superior, globose. Style very short. Stigma somewhat thick. Dry berry, small, club-shaped, somewhat compressed, with a groove and two chambers formed by a complete partition, each containing one large seed, oval, flat on one side, convex on the other, surrounded by an aril of floury substance. The berry is the size of a cherry, cinnamon-colored, and the surface slightly rough.

These trees also have flowers that lack a stigma, like those described above, but they do possess stamens and a nectary, as do the others. = Small trees known in Batangas, which the natives confuse with the one described under the genus Prockia; they reach a height of three fathoms. Their wood is soft, white, and clean, and is used for various purposes. It should be noted, however, that there is a distinct variety or species, of very hard and tough wood, known in Batangas by the name of Bayanti. This wood is in many ways superior to the so-called Guijo. Only birds eat the fruit. Flowers in May. * T. Busilac. New species.

251

SCHOTIA. Calyx divided to the middle into five equal parts, colored, inferior, and smaller than the corolla. Five petals, equally placed upon the tube of the calyx. Legume with a small stalk. Lin. Syst. veg. 673.

Schotia? speciosa. BEAUTIFUL SCHOCIA. Leaves opposite, pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets in two pairs: the last ones much larger, wedge-shaped, with a notch at the apex, very entire, smooth, and stiff. Axillary flowers. Calyx the same color as the corolla, with five leaflets. Corolla of five petals, smaller and narrower than the calyx leaflets. Stamens ten. Style shorter than the stamens. Stigma simple. Legume.... = This tree, known in the province of Batangas, is of the second rank. Its wood is used, although it is not very hard, for certain purposes. The calyxes and corollas are white. * T. Balitbitan according to some; but I believe the true name belongs to the genus Sideroxylon. — It is very doubtful whether it belongs to this genus.

LIMONIA. Calyx divided into three, up to five lobes. Petals from three to five. Filaments from six to ten. Berry with three compartments. Seeds solitary, wrapped in a kind of pulp. Lin. Syst. veg. 684.

Limonia laureola. LIMONIA LAUREOLA. Branches somewhat forked. Leaves without stipules, nearly sessile, sometimes scattered, sometimes whorled, lanceolate, keeled, notched, smooth, and with a narrow membrane along the edges. Terminal flowers in racemose panicles. Calyx very small, in five concave parts. Corolla much longer than the calyx, with linear petals. Five stamens fixed near the base of the ovary. No disk. Filaments shorter than the corolla. Anthers oval in shape. Ovary oval, seated upon the flower. Style very short at maturity. Stigma rounded. Berry globose, prolonged at the base with a small stalk, of two valves, rarely three, which bear a short partition, and along which, toward the base, are fixed some thirteen or fourteen seeds, kidney-shaped, compressed, lightly wrapped in a pulp. = Trees without spines found in Angat, with white and soft wood. They are as thick as the human body, and three or four fathoms tall. Their leaves are about four inches long, one inch wide, and without pores like those of orange trees. They have a strong and pleasant smell, as does the fruit, which is yellow at maturity and the size of a chickpea. The seeds are also yellow. They are very well known to the natives. The decoction of their leaves is widely used to bathe women who have recently given birth. * T. Mamalis. Dec. Prod. p. l. 536.

Limonia corymbosa. LIMONIA DE CORIMBOS. Trunk with spines, sometimes arranged in pairs. Leaves scattered, lanceolate, with a notch at the apex, doubly serrated

252
very finely, and full of small pores on both surfaces. Flowers terminal, in corymbs. Calyx with four or six teeth. Corolla of five linear petals, somewhat thick, and sprinkled with pores. Stamens ten: the five alternating ones longer. Stigma thick, depressed. Fruit. = This tree rises to a height of eight yards or more, and planks are cut from its wood. The leaves have such a strong smell, though pleasant, that smelling them frequently seems to hurt the nose. * T. Malarayap. New species.
Limonia monophylla. Single-leaved Limonia. Trunk with solitary spines. Leaves linear, with a large notch at the apex, and finely serrated. Fruit three or four lines in diameter, with slightly raised dots, and with one or two seeds. = The juice of the fruit is very sticky. It is a small tree of three or four feet in height, and I have seen it on the island called Maricaban. Flowers in July. * T. Dayap na monti.
Limonia trifoliata. Three-leaved Limonia. Leaves small, ternate. Leaflets half lanceolate, the middle one larger; the lateral ones half elliptic, finely notched, and with a notch at the apex. Common petiole short, with two spines at the base. Petiolule very short. Flowers axillary, solitary. Calyx with three teeth. Corolla of three petals. Stigma thick, with lobes. Pome very small, globose, with four chambers, and one seed in each. = These small trees, known in Manila and found everywhere, rise to more than the height of a man. The fruit is four or six lines in diameter, and sweets are made from it. Its juice is very sticky and serves to paste paper. * T. Limoncitos. Lin. Syst. veg. 684.
FERONIA. Calyx flat, in five parts. Petals five, oblong. Filaments broad at the base, hairy, inserted on a raised hypogynous disk. Berry with a hard rind, many chambers and many seeds in each, wrapped in a spongy flesh. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 538.
Feronia ternata. Ternate-leaved Feronia. Trunk with large solitary spines. Leaves alternate, ternate. Leaflets lanceolate, notched, and smooth: the middle one larger. Calyx with five teeth. Corolla of five petals, thick and linear, much longer than the calyx. Stamens ten. Ovary cylindrical. Style and Stigma thick. Pome oblong, more than three inches long and more than two inches thick, with ridges and irregular channels on the surface, with about ten chambers, and some seeds in each, egg-shaped, compressed, ending in a tuft resembling wool. = A tree of eight to ten yards, not very thick. It is used for the pillars of houses. The fruit is aromatic and the juice sour. It resembles the citron, and serves as glue. I saw it on Mount Arayat. Flowers in December. * T. Malacabuyao. P. T. Tabog. New species.

253
COOKIA. Calyx with five lobes. Petals five, keeled. Stamens ten, separate. Ovary with a small stalk. Style one. Stigma capitate. Berry small, with tiny dots, five chambers, and solitary seeds. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 537.
Cookia wampi. Cookia wampi. Leaves alternate, winged. Leaflets petiolate, obliquely lanceolate, slightly serrate, and somewhat stiff. Flowers in a compound raceme. Calyx fleshy, inferior, with five teeth. Corolla of five petals, keeled and stiff. Stamens nine, ten, or eleven, fixed on the receptacle. Filaments very short. Anthers thick, paired. Ovary seated at the flower, oval, with five grooves, hairy, and with small stalks. Style almost none. Stigma very thick, with five dark lobes. Berry with small dots on the rind, pulpy, oval in shape, with four or five chambers, and in each one an egg-shaped seed covered with a simple membrane. =This tree, with straight branches, which I have seen at the parish house of Pasig, is related to Limonia, and is uncommon: it grows to a height of about five varas. Neither the leaves nor the fruit have a notable scent. Its origin is from China. The fruit, which is about the size of a cherry, is eaten and is sweet-sour. The seeds are green. Flowers in November. *T., Huampit.— Perhaps the spec. punctata of Dec. ibid.?
Cookia anisodora. Cookia that smells of anise. Trunk without spines. Leaves sometimes opposite, sometimes alternate, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets obliquely lanceolate, serrate with a notch at the apex, and with transparent pores or dots. Proper petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in a panicle. Calyx very small, split almost to the base into five parts. Corolla much larger than the calyx, of five lanceolate petals. Stamens ten, somewhat shorter than the corolla: the five alternate ones longer, and all fixed between the base of the petals and the ovary. Filaments with an angle or bend toward the base. Anthers with a glandular point toward the tip, on the back. Ovary with a small stalk, placed inside the calyx, with angles. Stigma shield-shaped. Berry globose, with small dots on the rind, with five chambers, and in each one a seed: some abort. = It is a well-known tree, which grows to a height of two or three brazas. They are found in the mountains of S. Mateo, in Mariveles, and in many other places. The fruit is the size of a pea. From its leaves, which have the same smell and flavor as anise, the Indians use them to give flavor to sweets and for other things. It bears a great resemblance to those placed in the genus Bergera. *T., Maisipaisi, Calomata, Camanguianis. New species.
BERGERA. Calyx very small, in five parts and persistent. Petals five, spreading. Stamens ten: the alternate ones, shorter—
40

254
tops. Stigma shaped like a spinning top, with crosswise grooves. Berry half-globose, with two seeds. Jus. Gen. pl. 260.
Bergera compressa. Compressed Bergera. Alternate leaves, obliquely egg-shaped, indistinctly notched twice, and full of pores barely visible on both surfaces. Axillary flowers, in a kind of umbellate panicle. Calyx small, with five blunt teeth. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, with five thick petals and pores. Stamens from eight to eleven: the alternate ones longer. Germ conical. Style very short. Stigma shield-shaped. Berry very small, egg-shaped, compressed, with one seed. = This tree with simple leaves, and which I have not observed to have thorns, is well known, and grows to the thickness of a man's body. The fruit is three lines long, aromatic, and seems somewhat caustic, as it irritates the tongue. The natives use it in medicine. Flowers in August. *T., Piris. New species.
Bergera ternata. Ternate Bergera. Opposite, ternate leaves. Leaflets lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Own petioles very short. Fruit very small, with the smell of lemon, with one cell and two seeds. It is common in Tala. *T., Malamolauin.
There is yet another species, with compound, ternate leaves. The fruit is small, with one smooth seed. = They are small trees found in Tala. The fruit is fragrant, like the other.
Bergera koenigii. Koenig's Bergera. Alternate leaves, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets obliquely egg-shaped, elongated, pointed, narrower on one side, very soft, hairy, and somewhat saw-toothed, with down in the serrations. Flowers in umbellate panicles. Calyx inferior, very small, with four lobes. Corolla green like the calyx, with five oval and concave petals. Stamens ten. Filaments very short. Germ nearly cylindrical. Style very short. Stigma thick, shield-shaped. Berry oval, pointed, with one seed. It seems there may be more cells. = Trees of about two fathoms, found in Malinta. The leaves viewed under a lens show transparent dots. The fruit closely resembles that of the Piris; but it has no fragrance, nor do the leaves either. Flowers in October and December. Prod. p. 1. 537.
The genera Limonia, Bergera, Cookia, and Murraya closely resemble one another. The fruit of those I have placed under the genus Bergera is very small; and that of the ternate species is a cagilla, not a berry.
QUISQUALIS. Corolla of five petals, placed upon a filiform calyx whose border is divided into five laciniae. Dry drupe, with five angles. Palau trad. de Lin. ibid. t. 3. 577.
Quisqualis spinosa. Spiny Quisqualis. Trunk set with long, opposite spines. Leaves in a star pattern, three by three,

255
Ovate, oblong, pointed, entire and smooth. Very short petioles. Axillary flowers in a spike. Calyx very long, almost cylindrical, with five teeth. Corolla of five petals, fixed between the teeth of the calyx. Stamens ten, fixed in the tube of the calyx, shorter than the corolla, arranged in two series: the five upper ones taller. Style as long as the stamens; adhering almost its entire length to the wall of the calyx tube, from which it separates near the stigma. Stigma somewhat thick. Upper glans ovate; with five very prominent angles, sharpened at the bark, and with one large seed, pointed at one end. = This shrub grows at most to a height of two or three varas; but always leaning upon trees. The flowers are white, mottled with red. The Indians know it on account of its fruit, which children eat; but it is not good, as it causes hiccups. Nevertheless, it is considered with good reason an excellent specific against worms, giving a child of three years three fruits, a child of four years four, and for adults the dose is increased; but it is best to begin with a small quantity, especially if it is to be taken on an empty stomach. A Franciscan friar, very skilled in medicine, cured an Indian who had a very swollen abdomen, with two fruits ground up and mixed with honey and two ounces of water; and having taken it on an empty stomach, he expelled a tapeworm seventy-eight feet long. With another equal repeated dose, the patient expelled another forty-four feet long. This occurred in the year 1658 in the town of Los Baños, as related by Father Mercado. The Indians call this plant niogniogan, but in it there is nothing that resembles the coconut, although the fruit is somewhat similar in flavor. Flowers in May. *T., Niogniogan, Tagarao V., Tangolon. P., Babevabe. I., Tartarao. New species.
MURRAYA. Calyx in five parts. Corolla bell-shaped, with five petals. Nectary encircling the ovary. Berry with a thin rind, and one or two seeds. Jus. Gen. pl. 261.
Murraya exotica. Exotic Murraya. Trunk without spines. Leaves alternate, ternate. Leaflets narrow, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Axillary flowers in racemose panicles, with very short proper peduncles. Calyx very small, with five small leaves. Corolla fixed on the receptacle, of five petals, erect, concave, semi-rounded, and terminated with three teeth. Stamens ten, fixed on the receptacle, and outside the nectary, as long as the corolla. Filaments very thick. Anthers oval, with three channels, and terminated with a beak. Ovary globose, upon a nectary also globose, set within the flower. Style and Stigma very thick, with small translucent dots. Berry globose, with a very thin covering, with five barely noticeable lines, two chambers, and solitary globose seeds: one of them usually

256
abort.= A small tree of three varas in height, which I have seen in a garden in Pasig, and which I believe is native to China. The leaves are four inches long. The fruit is eaten and is somewhat tasty. The color is like that of the sour cherry, and the seeds are somewhat green. There they call it by the name (Chinese, it appears) guinguen. Flowers in Nov. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 537.

MURRAYA ODORATA. FRAGRANT MURRAYA. Leaves opposite, pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets in two pairs, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Common petiole, compressed above. Terminal flowers in a racemose panicle, with compressed peduncles. Calyx inferior, in five or six parts. Corolla of five or six petals. Stamens ten to twelve, united to the middle in a cylindrical body, and shorter than the petals. Anthers oval. Ovary globose, encircled by a ring. Style short and thick. Stigma large and globose. Fruit...= A tree two or three fathoms tall and thick as a thigh, found in the forests of Angat, and not well known. I have not observed whether it has thorns. The smell of the leaves resembles that of the lemon. Flowers in Feb. New species.

MURRAYA LOBATA. LOBED MURRAYA. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, entire, smooth and stiff. Petioles very short. Axillary flowers, in racemose clusters. Berry with three lobes at maturity, globose, depressed, with one or two globose seeds.= Small trees that I have seen in Mandaloyon: the fruit is not very different from the Guinguen, and its flavor is not disagreeable; although it irritates the tongue a little. The smell of the leaves, which are not winged, is somewhat aromatic. Flowers in May. New species.

ICICA. Calyx with four or five teeth. Petals four or five, inserted on a disk. Stamens eight or ten, inserted on the same. Ovary surrounded by a disk. Style very short. Stigma in a head, with four grooves. Fruit coriaceous, enclosing four or five small stones with a single seed. Jus. Gén. pl. 370. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 77.

ICICA ABILO. ICICA ABILO. Leaves opposite, pinnate without an odd leaflet; but most often with an odd one. Leaflets about twelve pairs, between ovate and linear, pointed, obtusely serrated, soft and hairy: the last pairs smaller, and without stipules; the others with two rounded stipules at each pair, one at each leaflet. Common petioles imbricated at the ends of the branches. Proper petioles very short. Flowers below the common petioles, in umbellate panicles. Calyx with five teeth. Corolla of five linear petals, fixed between the divisions of the calyx, and double its length. A wide disk in the middle of the flower. Stamens ten, somewhat shorter than the petals, with hairy filaments: five fixed to the calyx and the others to the petals toward the base. Ovary superior, globose and hairy. Style

257
the length of the stamens. Stigma globose, with five lobes. Berry somewhat irregular in shape, wrinkled, thicker in the middle, and tapering toward the ends, with channels running from top to bottom according to the number of cells, and with one to five small bones bearing prominences, and a small hole in the scar, by which they are fixed in the berry; and in each one, one or two seeds. = This tree, which I once took for Guayaco, is known in Bauang by the name of ábilo, and is considered first-rate. It produces much resin, and more so in hot weather; and it is very fragrant. The fruit does not open, and is like a chickpea; when dry, it is smaller and black: the flavor is harsh and slightly aromatic. The Indians use its wood, which is hard, for various purposes, and also give a decoction of its root to drink to those suffering from consumption. The leaves are sometimes found without an odd one at the tip (lacking one at the end, or with one of the last pair oblique) and they much resemble those of Averrhoa; but they are softer. The flowers that I have seen several times were dry; but well preserved. In them the disk is observed, but not very clearly. Flowers in February. *T., Ábilo in the Province of Batangas. New species. — Spr. unites the Icica with the Amyris.

JUSSIEUA. Calyx in four or five parts. Petals four or five. Capsule with four or five chambers, column-shaped, inferior, which splits along the angles. Seeds numerous, small. Lin. Syst. veg. 686.

Jussieua erecta. Upright Jussieua. Stem erect, square, winged. Leaves alternate, decurrent, lanceolate, almost entire, and smooth. Flowers axillary, sessile, solitary. Calyx adherent, with four lanceolate lobes, slightly longer than the corolla. Corolla of four lanceolate petals, fixed between the divisions of the calyx. Stamens eight: the four alternating ones shorter. Filaments the length of the corolla. Anthers oval. Ovary very long, cylindrical, below the calyx. Style the length of the stamens. Stigma club-shaped, compressed, and lobed. Capsule very long, nearly without angles; crowned with the parts of the calyx, with four chambers, and in each one a row of many small, elongated, angular seeds. = This plant is common, but barely known to the Indians; it grows in cultivated fields and on the banks of rivers: it is distinguished from Oenothera in that in the latter the calyx is not persistent. Its flavor is somewhat pungent, and its height is one foot. When the capsule is broken, four nerves are visible on the covering. In the Spanish Translation of Linnaeus, a species similar to this one (or perhaps the same) is said to cure cutaneous blemishes. Flowers in January and March. *T., Malapaco, Balacbac?

Jussieua fluviatilis. River Jussieua. Stem rounded, smooth-

258
pine, which sends out roots at the nodes. Leaves oval, barely remotely serrated and smooth. Petioles short, with two stipules. Flowers solitary, with long peduncles. Calyx with five lacinae. Corolla of five petals, egg-shaped and reversed. Receptacle with five angles, formed by ten glandular lines. Stigma in a small head, with five lobes. Long capsule, with five chambers.= An aquatic plant, about one third of a vara tall, which I have seen in Sta. Rita de la Pampanga. The leaves are two inches long, and the corollas are white. From the joints of the stem grow roots that are very white and spongy, which grow as long as three or more inches and at first sight resemble worms. *T., Cangcong dapo. Dec. prod. p. 3. 54.
MELASTOMA. Corolla of four or five petals, placed above the calyx. Anthers turned outward, with an opening at the tips. Berry of two to five chambers, with many seeds, and covered by the calyx. Calyx bell-shaped, with four or five lacinae. Lin. Syst. veg. 658. 687.
Melastoma malabatrica. Melastoma of Malabar. Branches opposite, covered with hairs. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, egg-shaped, with five veins, entire and covered with short, very rough hair. Petioles very short. Terminal flowers in panicles, with opposite peduncles. Calyx bell-shaped, with ten awl-like teeth; the five alternate ones barely noticeable. Corolla of five petals with small claws, fixed toward the edges of the calyx. Stamens ten. Filaments curved in various directions; the five alternate ones fixed at the base of the petals, and of a different color from the others; these latter have a gland toward the middle. Anthers long, and beak-shaped, with a small hole at the tip. Ovary conical, seated within the flower. Style longer than the stamens. Stigma somewhat thick, concave at the top. Berry? enclosed within the calyx, with many chambers and many seeds shaped like small snails.= A small tree found in Cebu, of which I have seen one branch. The fruit was not yet mature. Father Delgado says (he would have heard it from the Indians) that by rubbing one's hands with the bark of this small tree, one can handle all kinds of snakes without risk. *V. Buyong. Lin. ibid. 689.
Melastoma dodecandra. Melastoma dodecandra. Leaves opposite, lanceolate (whitish) woolly beneath, fringed, with five veins. Flowers in a panicle. Calyx hairy, bell-shaped, in six parts, and a support of two small concave leaflets at the base, in the manner of a second calyx. Corolla salver-shaped, of six oval petals, very wide, (flesh-colored) fixed in the calyx. Stamens twelve: six purple, and the other six opposite, yellow: all exserted and curved. Stigma somewhat thick. Capsule enclosed within the calyx, globose, with many

259
small seeds. = Beautiful little trees, two or three fathoms tall, which I have seen in Passi, Lambunao, and in the forests of Iloilo bordering Capis. Their flowers make a pleasant sight. Flowering in March and December. Prod. p. 3. 146. It appears to be the species tamonea of Linnaeus. ibid.
Melastoma obvoluta. Enveloped Melastoma. Opposite branches, with hairy tips. Opposite leaves, with three veins, and very rough, with short hairs. Very short petioles. Terminal flowers, in panicles. Stamens ten. Filaments, the alternating ones shorter and of a different color. Anthers with two hanging appendages at the base, and the five alternating ones with two simple small glands. = Small trees known in Angat. The leaves are barely more than one inch long, and very rough. The petals and five stamens are purple; the other five are pale yellow. The people of Angat call these little trees by the presumptuous name of granates (pomegranates), a name which, along with many others, has been borrowed from the Spanish language. It is close to this species of Dec. Prod. p. 3. 146.
CLETHRA. Calyx in five parts. Corolla in five parts, or nearly five petals, broad at the base. Stigma cleft in three parts. Superior capsule, with three valves, three chambers and many seeds.
Clethra alnifolia. Clethra with alder leaves. Alternate leaves, lanceolate, serrated from the middle upward, and with white tomentum beneath. Short petioles. Terminal flowers in spiked racemes. Each small flower with a bract at the base. Inferior calyx, in five very deep parts, keeled and pointed. Corolla of five petals, widened toward the top, and twice as long as the calyx. Stamens ten. Filaments somewhat shorter than the corolla, and broad below. Anthers straight, shaped like a half moon, with two lobes at the tip, and a small hole in each. Ovary three-sided and hairy. One style, with a thick stigma. Capsule with three angles, three chambers and in each one many small seeds. = Trees of the forests of Angat, about one fathom thick, and seven or eight fathoms tall. The leaves are silvery in color below, and smooth above: their length about four inches, and one inch wide. The racemes are one span long. The mountain natives call them Malaclac.
EPERUA. Calyx in four parts. Petal, one, fixed to the calyx, wrapped at the sides at the base. Filaments very long, of which nine are joined below. Ovary with a small stalk. Leathery legume, sickle-shaped: with one chamber, two valves, and three or four seeds. Lin. Syst. veg. 672.
Eperua decandra. Ten-stamened Eperua. Opposite leaves, winged without an odd leaflet. Leaflets egg-shaped, smooth. Own petioles, very short, swollen. Flowers in panicles. Peduncles

260
their own, long. Calyx tube-shaped, divided into four large parts, rolled downward. Corolla on one side of the calyx, consisting of one petal widened at the top and with a small claw at the bottom. Stamens ten, fixed to the calyx and woolly on the lower part: three very long, bearing anthers; the other seven alternating, very short and without anthers. Pistil longer than the stamens. Ovary with a small stalk. Stigma thick, compressed. Legume. = A first-order tree, handsome, and well known for its highly prized timber, which is pale in color and not red like the Balayon, with which the natives ordinarily confuse it: with age, it acquires a blackness somewhat resembling that of the walnut of Europe. Its hardness, weight, and other properties are as in the following species. * T., Ipil, Taal. New species.

Eperua rhomboidea. Rhombus-shaped Eperua. Leaves opposite, pinnate without an odd leaflet. Leaflets five or six pairs, egg-shaped, smooth. Calyx of four leaflets, with very bare small teeth on the edge; the two opposite ones smaller. Corolla hairy on the lower part, placed on one side of the calyx, consisting of one or two small petals with small claws. Stamens fixed to the calyx, from eight to twelve. Filaments some very short and sterile. Anthers sometimes three, on certain filaments. Pistil from one to three, as long as the stamens. Legume single, short and wide, woody, somewhat rhombus-shaped, containing from two to seven large seeds, girdled by a fleshy, yellow aril up to their midpoint on both sides, somewhat compressed, oval, with a leathery, black and smooth covering. = This tree becomes first-rate timber. The legume is usually single; and although there are sometimes more than one pistil, the others abort. The wood has a pleasant reddish color, hard and heavy; but after many years it becomes entirely black: it is said that by wetting it from time to time with sea water, the color does not fade. It is one of the most prized in the Philippines for tables, chairs, and other things; and when freshly worked, it gives off a pleasant smell, distinct from that of the Narra. Exposed to the elements, it does not rot, but it does if buried in the ground. The ant called anay, even when it passes over it, does not penetrate it or damage it at all; but it destroys it if it is buried. The seeds of the Balayon, ground up and placed in water, serve as glue because of the starch they contain. The Indian card players, who for the most part are poor and cannot afford to buy many decks of cards, when the edges of the cards come apart, split a balayon seed, moisten it in water, and rub the cards with it to stick them back together. Young Indian women have one of the said seeds set in silver and wear it hung around their neck, to protect themselves (they say) from evil wind. * T., Balayon, Tíndalo. New species.

261
See the genus Afcelia of Persoon, where these trees perhaps belong, along with the genera Pariboa and Vonapa of Jussieu. The stamens are separate: at least at another time, when I wrote this, I did not notice them being joined. Also to be noted is the variable number of stamens, anthers, and pistils.

ANDROMEDA. Calyx inferior, in five parts. Corolla more or less ovate, with five lacinia. Capsule with five chambers, and few seeds. Lin. Syst. veg. 695.

Andromeda japonica. Japanese Andromeda. Trunk straight, somewhat rough. Leaves sometimes opposite, sometimes alternate, obliquely ovate, elongated, half-serrate, smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers terminal, in umbellate panicles. Calyx very small, with five teeth. Corolla with five lacinia. Stamens ten, shorter than the corolla, and fixed at its base: the five alternating ones longer. Anthers large, appearing to have four chambers. Ovary inside the flower, with a small stalk. Style somewhat elongated. Stigma funnel-shaped. Capsule oblong, with three barely notable angles, with two or three chambers, each containing one seed. = Small trees that I have seen in Baliuag. The wood has a slight fragrance, and toothpicks are made from it. Sometimes the chambers appear to be four, each containing one seed. The corollas are green. Flowers in December. *T., Tulibas.

CRUDIA. Calyx with four lacinia, and two bracts at the base. Corolla none. Stamens eight or ten, somewhat widened at the base. Ovary hairy, with a stipe. Style thread-like. Pod leathery, thick, rounded, with one or two seeds. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 1. 462. Decand. Prod. p. 2. 519.

Crudya spicata. Spiked Crudia. Leaves alternate, pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets from six to thirteen on each side, widely spaced, ovate, pointed, with very small veins, leathery, entire, smooth above, and barely tomentose below. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary in spikes, small, clustered, each scale bearing a small flower. Calyx inferior, with five deep lacinia, and furnished at the base with two small hairy bracts, like the scales of the spike. Corolla none. Stamens ten, fixed at the base of the calyx, somewhat wide at the base, with round and compressed anthers. Ovary hairy. Style very short. Pod not winged, fleshy, crescent-shaped, very compressed, somewhat rough, with two very small seeds and often only one at maturity, without an aril, separated by a septum, and attached at the upper suture. = A tree larger than a man's body, which I have seen in Parañaque, Mandaloyon, and other places. The leaflets are up to thirteen (some unequal) counting those on both sides, and are about three inches long: the small spikes

262
two lines: the little flowers half a line at most, and they are compressed. The pods are barely an inch; their surface appears covered with scales of a somewhat shiny gray color, and for that reason they call the tree malatumbaga, or tumbaga. The one they call by this name in Angat, which I have placed in the genus Myrtus, is not the true malatumbaga. Its wood is tough, dark purple in color, and difficult to saw when very dry. The heartwood in old trees is black and very hard, and has no particular smell, even when burned. The wood is used for planks and for the teeth of mills used to husk rice, which they call guilingan. Flowers in November. *T., Malatumbaga, Hintotoor. Decand. ibid.—I cannot affirm whether these flowers are fertile: I have not seen any open, although there were ripe pods on the same branch.

CASEARIA. Calyx regularly in five parts. Corolla none; but there is a membrane in the manner of a petal, attached inside the calyx, which carries in the tube from twelve to thirty stamens, monadelphous at the base: the alternate ones fertile, and the others sterile, often woolly or fringed. Cagilla leathery, with one chamber and three or five valves, and many seeds fixed on the pulpy parts of the valves. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 50.

Casearia fuliginosa. Sooty Casearia. Alternate leaves, egg-shaped, elongated, barely serrated, smooth and somewhat spotted with black. Petioles very short, without stipules. Small axillary flowers, in clusters. Calyx shaped like a jar, in five rounded parts. Corolla none. Stamens ten, fixed on the same calyx, in a small crown: the five alternate ones shorter. Filaments hairy at the base. Anthers somewhat triangular. In addition there are five small hairy bodies, like castrated filaments, alternating with the longer stamens. Ovary free, globose. Style one. Stigma globose. Cagilla oval (like a cherry) with about eight angles that disappear at maturity, with three fleshy valves, and many bony, angular seeds, surrounded by a scarlet aril and fixed to the valves.— Small trees of three yards. The leaves are seven fingers long, and appear as if spotted with soot. The Indians have no name for them. The fruit when ripe is yellow. In Malinta. Flowers in March.— It belongs to the genus that others call Anavinga.

I have seen another tree with male flowers only. Alternate leaves, egg-shaped, lanceolate, very bluntly serrated, thick and smooth, without dots. Petioles very short. Axillary flowers in a small bundle of more than twelve little flowers, with long small stalks. Calyx in four deep, linear parts, rounded at the tip and hairy. Corolla none. A crown attached to the calyx with lobes. Stamens from ten to fourteen, fixed at the base

263
on the outside of the crown, not on the inside, nor at the tips, all
fertile and occasionally one castrated alone is seen. Anthers split
at the base where they are attached. Germen, style and
stigma none. = Small trees like the previous ones, found in
Parañaque. The leaves are not spotted with soot. Flowers in
August.
SAMIDA. Calyx colored, with five laciniae. Corolla none.
Nectary conical, truncated, with ten to eighteen teeth.
Capsule of four valves, one chamber, and many seeds
enclosed in a pulp. Lin. Sist. veg. 699.
Samyda pubescens. Samyda with hair. Leaves alternate, obli-
quely oblong, serrated, pointed, soft, and hairy
