beneath, and above almost smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers
axillary, in a kind of umbel of about five small flowers. Pe-
duncle of its own, somewhat long. Calyx inferior, persistent, bell-
shaped, in five ovate parts. Corolla none, but a disk,
in the manner of a cup, attached to the calyx, very hairy, with about
fifteen teeth on the edge. Stamens fifteen, fixed at the inci-
sions of the disk. Filaments short. Anthers sessile, pointed. Germen
globose, hairy, seated within the flower. Style very short.
Stigma globose. Capsule globose (like a hazelnut) appearing
to have four ribs, with one chamber and many seeds
(like those of the fig) fixed to the walls of the berry, oval,
and adorned with an aril of four threads, which grow from
its base. = Trees almost unknown to the natives, of about six
or seven rods in height, which I have seen in Sta. Ana in Pam-
panga. In Baliuag and Angat they are well known. The wood is
slightly fragrant, and toothpicks are made from it. They call it in
those towns Tulibas. Lin. ibid. 700.
Samyda trivalvis. Samida with three valves. Leaves alter-
nate, ovate, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Flowers axillary,
sessile, three or four in number. Calyx as in the previous
species; and the disk, with six lobes, hairy at the tips; and
between each one of them two short and fertile stamens. Berry
oval, red in color, with three grooves and three fleshy valves, and
the seeds fixed in them in two rows: the aril very thin,
and with some threads on the edge. = Small trees unknown to the
natives, found in Angat: the leaves are one span long. New species.
DAIS. Calyx an involucre of four small leaves. Corolla with four
or five laciniae, and a berry of one seed. Lin. Sist. veg. 686.
Dais laurifolia. Dais with laurel leaf. Leaves opposite,
lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Flo-
wers axillary, gathered on a common peduncle, long, and
with an involucre of more than eight lanceolate and compact
small leaves, within which there are found more than twenty small flowers se-

264
stiles. Cal. none. Cor. long, funnel-shaped, with four laciniae, rolled back downward. Stam. ten, fixed to the tube of the corolla, some lower down, and all longer than it. Ant. regular. Ovary conical, seated within the flower, with two broad glands at the base. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma in a small head. Berry superior, egg-shaped, pointed, with one seed, whose bark is leathery and fibrous. = Small trees of two fathoms in height. Their leaves are a palm's length: the flowers are white. The bark gives off an unpleasant odor, and would be excellent for making paper or other things. It is very tough. It agrees with the Paserina, and in various respects resembles the Daphne. Lin. ibid.
** TERMINALIA. Male flowers, mixed on the same stalk with the hermaphrodites. Cal. in five parts. Cor. none. Drupe in the hermaphrodite flowers, inferior, boat-shaped. Lin. Sist. veg. 701.
Terminalia mauritiana. Terminalia of Mauritius. Trunk with horizontal and star-shaped branches. Leaves clustered, notched at the base, sometimes inversely ovate, sometimes oval, indented, smooth, with two protuberances like glands at the base. Petiole very short, somewhat swollen and compressed. Flowers axillary, in clusters, with a scale at the base of each individual peduncle: some hermaphrodite, and others lacking a pistil. * Male flowers. Cal. hairy on the inside, with five laciniae. Cor. none. Stam. ten, fixed to the calyx: the five alternate ones longer. Pist. none. * Hermaphrodites, otherwise the same as the male flowers. Pist. as long as the stamens. Drupe fleshy, inferior, oval, with the edges rolled upward, with a very hard and fibrous stone, and a long, pointed seed. = This tree is used for binding timber and is well known. It grows to a height of seven or eight varas. Its leaves, when mature, are purple, and in former times the natives used to dye their cotton garments with them in this color (though a dirty one). In other places they dye cloth black by boiling the bark of the tree, soaking the cloth in it, then adding a decoction of guava bark, and finally leaving it to soak for a few days in mud, by which it takes on a black color, though not a very good one: this is how the women dye their skirts in Davin on the Island of Negros. In Agóo they add the bark of the mangrove, called Bacáo, to the dye. Monkeys are very fond of this fruit, but they eat only the bark when it is green, since they cannot break the stone, which is very hard. The seed has the same flavor as the almond, and an oil equal to that of the almond can be extracted from it, and with the same properties. With the juice of the tender leaves and the oil of its almonds, an ointment is made against leprosy and other skin conditions; in Manila they have been planted along the promenades

265
Many of these trees are found in public places: for by reason of the horizontal spread of their branches, and the breadth of their leaves, they are well suited to provide shade. The true name of this tree is Talisai, and no other. * T., Talisai. V., Talisai, Banilac, Nato, Hitam. P., Calisai. I., Lugo, Pandan.— This species, called Mauritiana, or of the Isle of Mauritius, according to Dec. Prod. p. 3. 11., produces a resin similar to Benzoc, or Benzoin. The one described above yields no resin; but in Malinta I have seen trees that do produce it, though it is odorless.

Terminalia edulis. Edible Terminalia. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, entire and nearly smooth. * Male flowers. Calyx placed on a fleshy, depressed globe, cleft nearly to the base into five parts, and filled with hairs on the inside. Corolla none. Stamens longer than the calyx. * Hermaphrodite flowers. Calyx placed over the ovary, cleft into five parts, and filled with hairs on the inside. Corolla none. Stamens longer than the calyx. * Hermaphrodite flowers. Calyx placed over the ovary, cleft into five parts, and hairy on the outside. Stamens ten. Filaments much longer than the calyx. Ovary inferior, lanceolate, compressed, crowned by the calyx. Drupe fleshy, oblong, somewhat compressed, with the edges slightly turned upward, rounded at maturity, with a hard, striate, fibrous nut containing one seed. = This tree, well known to the natives, grows to the second rank. Its bark is used to give cotton a dull, dirty, dark dye. The fruit is eaten when it is already black. The flesh is pinkish and somewhat tasty. Flowers in March. * T., Calumpit. New species.

Bucida. Calyx with five teeth, superior. Corolla none. Berry with one seed.

Bucida comintana. Bucida of Comintan. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, entire and smooth. Petioles short. Flowers terminal, in spiked panicles, semi-distichous. Calyx superior, colored, bell-shaped, hairy on the inside, and with five spreading teeth. Corolla none. Stamens ten, longer than the calyx, with rounded anthers. Ovary cylindrical, with an awl-shaped support at the base. Style curved, and longer than the stamens, with a simple stigma. Berry small? globose, with one seed, and crowned by the calyx. = Second-rank trees, known in the Province of Batangas by the other name Comintan, especially in S. José. The wood is soft, and the leaves are about three inches long. The fruit is like a pea; but since it was immature, I cannot say how large it will grow. The entire calyx crowns the fruit, and not the teeth alone, as happens when it is adherent. The natives tell me that this is the true diglas: I do not know whether they may be mistaken.

266
I have given it the name of the Province where it lives. Flowers in May. * T., Dinglas?
** GIMBERNATIA. Polygamous flowers. Calyx with five clefts. Corolla none. Stamens ten. * In the hermaphrodites. One style. Fruit of one seed, and winged. Flora Peruana. Prod. 138.
Gimbernatia calamansanai. Gimbernacia calamansanai.
Leaves crowded at the ends of the branches, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Petioles short. Hermaphrodite flowers, axillary, in spikes. Calyx adherent, small, deciduous, bell-shaped, one-leafed, woolly inside and out, with five rolled laciniae. Corolla none. Stamens ten: the five alternate ones fixed in the middle of the laciniae, and the others at the divisions. Filaments straight, and longer than the calyx. Anthers two-celled, and open lengthwise. Ovary one, as if four-sided. One style, longer than the stamens. Stigma simple and awl-shaped. Fruit resembling a globose nut, somewhat compressed, with three or more ribs and two wings not entirely opposite, on the belly, running from top to bottom, and with one hard, woody seed joined closely to the thin membrane of the nut. Sometimes the fruit lacks ribs. = Famous trees of thirty or more varas in height, known in the forests of Calauan by the name given below, according to what Mr. Azaola has told me, from whom comes the description of the flowers, formed from one he was able to find open, and who also sent me the fruit, which is more than one inch wide (including the two wings) and half an inch tall; but other fruits of the calamansanai from Angat reach up to two and a half inches: the leaves, more than two inches. The wood of the tree is somewhat fragrant, and very beautiful boards for house floors are cut from it. In Calauan they call it Calamansanai, and thus those that I had previously placed in the Flora under this name are distinct. The tree described above is, without doubt, a species of the genus Gimbernatia of the Flora Peruana, or of the Chuncoa of Jussieu; but the dry nut of the tree above is slightly smaller than a hazelnut (that of Angat, larger), and thus larger than that of the cited flora: nor are the leaves oblong: therefore I have given it the name of the Country.

DECANDRIA.
TRIGINIA.

TRISTELLATEIA. Calyx with five laciniae. Petals half-round. One style, or three points. Three fruits crowned with six appendages. Dec. Prod. p. 1. 583.

267
Tristellateia malintana. Tristellateia of Malinta. Trunk rough, with prominent points, climbing by means of tendrils over neighboring trees. Leaves opposite, egg-shaped, pointed, with veins not very prominent, entire and smooth, somewhat fleshy, with two small, blunt glands at the base. Petioles short, and with two awl-shaped glands at the base. Flowers terminal, in racemes. The proper peduncle has near the base a node with two awl-shaped bracts, and at the base there is another longer one. Calyx erect, persistent, in five awl-shaped parts without glands, alternating with the petals. Corolla of five petals, heart-shaped, with a fold along the middle, narrowing suddenly toward the lower part, forming long claw-like extensions. Stamens ten, fixed to the receptacle: the five alternate ones longer. Anthers almost as long as the filaments. Ovary globose, with three angles, and on each one a small pit. Styles at the center of the ovary, one or two, and sometimes three, longer than the stamens. Stigmas simple. Three capsules joined at the back, flattened on the outer part, and with about eight teeth on the edge, flat (except one which is set edgewise) and each with one chamber and one seed. The three capsules separate at maturity, and each carries with it the said crown of teeth. == This shrub, common in Malinta and other places, has an unpleasant smell; it climbs upward, as noted above, over nearby trees. The native people use it for tying, and I have not seen it put to any other use. The flowers are yellow, and the filaments of the stamens are purple. Flowers in May.— These shrubs differ greatly from Hiraea and other genera in the rings of teeth that crown the capsules; and so Decandolle formed this new genus from them. It does not have four star-shaped leaves below, as that author states. Sometimes there are no tendrils.
TRIOPTERIS. Calyx in five parts, with two glands on the outside at the base. (Decand.) The petals resemble the six wings of the ovary. Capsules three or four winged, each with one seed. Lin. ibid.
Triopteris jamaicensis. Triopteris of Jamaica. Leaves opposite: the lower ones oval; the upper ones lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, in lax racemes. Proper peduncle, long. Calyx deeply divided into five linear parts, rounded at the tips, and with one gland at the base on the outside. Corolla absent. Stamens ten, fixed below the ovary on a proper membrane. Filaments longer than the calyx. Ovary seated within the flower, shaped like an inverted cone. Styles long, two or three: (there are trees with only one, even when there is more than one capsule.) Stigmas somewhat thick. Three capsules united (one or two

268
they usually abort) in the shape of a top, and they separate at maturity: each one with three membranous wings, ovate on the reverse side, colored, long, and extended: the upper one longer and straight; and the two lower ones smaller and roughly horizontal, and between these a rudiment of a fourth wing, with one chamber and one seed in each capsule. = Trees like a thigh in size, of hard wood: the branches are half drooping. They are found in Malinta, and also inhabit the Island of Cebu. * V., Comimpol. Flowers in May. Lin. ibid. — Those of Malinta have no more than one curved style, although the capsules are two or three.
   Triopteris poliandra. Triopteris with many stamens.
Leaves half opposite, somewhat heart-shaped, broad, ovate, entire, and smooth. Petioles short. Flowers axillary, in racemes. Calyx inferior, with three or four lobes, bell-shaped. Corolla of four petals, much larger than the calyx, oval, and with a sinus at the apex. Stamens many in number, fixed on a proper ring that surrounds the ovary, and shorter than the corolla. Ovary seated within the flower, with three angles, and sometimes of irregular shape. Style one, very short. Stigma simple. Capsule conical, or half pyramidal, depressed, with three valves, three chambers, one seed in each, and two long horizontal and oval wings on each valve; sometimes these wings are four. = Small trees that I have seen in Angat and Malinta. Flowers in July. * T., Pacpac balang. New species.
   * * AILANTHUS. Flowers polygamous. Calyx very small, with five teeth. Petals five, wrapped at the base. * Hermaphrodite flowers. Stamens two or three. * Female flowers. Ovaries three or five, curved. Capsules three, up to five, compressed, membranous, tongue-shaped, swollen in the middle, and with one seed. Lin. Syst. veg. 726.
   Ailanthus pongelion. Ailantho pongelion. * Trees with male flowers. Leaves opposite, winged without a terminal leaflet, in whose place there is a small style. Leaflets half ovate, obliquely, entire, with three or more distant glands, distributed and placed in a row on both margins. Petioles proper, very short. Calyx bell-shaped, with two laciniae, and on each of these, three small teeth. Corolla the same color as the calyx, of five or six petals. Stamens ten or eleven, fixed on the receptacle. Pistil: the receptacle has the rudiment of five fruits. Styles and stigmas none. * Trees with hermaphrodite flowers.... Five samaras very long, joined at one point, which look like so many legumes, that do not split, very compressed, whose apparent upper suture does not continue beyond the middle, and in each one, a compressed, circular seed fixed on said upper suture. = This tree that the Indians are accustomed to know as a cure-

269
ders (although by the name below, they also call other distinct trees) it rises until it becomes a second-order tree. Its bark is granular and bitter, and is therefore used in medicine in small quantities. Because of the peculiarity of its fruit, it is easy to guard against the error of the Indians. They call this tree macaisa, from isa or one, because the seed that each wing contains is unique. Fl. in Mar. * T., Macaisa, Balocas! Lin. ibid.— It is the malabaricus species of Dec. Prod. p. 2. 89.
If this tree is the Balocas, says Clain, its root purges at a weight of four reales, or half a peso. It is very close to the glandular species, which is called in Spain Tree of Heaven, and Varnish of Japan.

DECANDRIA.

PENTAGINIA.

CYRTOCARPA. Calyx in five parts. Five petals, longer than the calyx. Stamens ten. One large disk, with ten notches. One pistil, according to Bonpl. Stigma in four parts. Drupe with five tubercles beyond the middle, with a hard small stone. Dec. Prod. p. 2. 91.
Cyrtocarpa quinquestila. Cyrtocarpa with five styles. Leaves opposite, pinnate with an odd leaflet. Leaflets egg-shaped, oblong, pointed, entire, and smooth. Flowers very small in panicles, and sometimes emerging from the trunk. Lower calyx very small, in five rounded parts. Corolla three times longer than the calyx, with five lanceolate petals. Stamens ten, very short, fixed on the receptacle, and united at the base by a membrane, with notches at the edge. Five pistils, arranged in a star pattern, and horizontal. Five styles. Five fleshy, oval drupes (four of them abort.) The nucleus is compressed, half kidney-shaped, between woody and leathery, full of raised veins, and contains one regular seed. = A tree known to all the Indians, which grows to second order. The color of the wood is dark red: it is widely used in houses, and good planks are obtained from it; but the anai ant destroys them greatly. In some parts of the Islands it is prized, because they claim that insect does not damage it there. The ripe fruit is whitish and edible. Fl. in Mar. * T., Amoguis. — It seems to me that this tree fits better in this genus than in others of the terebinth family.
CNESTIS. Calyx in five parts. Five petals. Hairy ovaries. Five leguminous, leathery pods, with mor- hair
42

270
smooth inside and out, with two valves and one seed. Lin. Sist. veg. 729.
Cnestis trifolia. Cnestis with three leaflets. Twining trunk. Leaves in threes. Leaflets lanceolate, very slender, and smooth. Common petiole very long, swollen at the base: proper petiole short. Flowers emerge on the branches, in small panicles. Calyx in five parts. Corolla of five linear petals, twice as long as the calyx. Stamens ten: the five alternating ones longer. Ovaries apparently united, but separating easily. Style five. Stigmas somewhat thick. Five small pods like little legumes, with one seed each. = This shrub, which sometimes grows as thick as a thigh, is climbing and rises high: its wood is full of pores; it has a pleasant smell and the infusion is flesh-colored. The natives hold this wood in great esteem, and given the effects that will have been noted, it will have deserved that they call it, as they indeed do, santo (holy). Its principal use is to administer it as a sudorific to women who have recently given birth. It is considered equivalent to sarsaparilla. * T. Camagsa taquilis. Palo santo. Guicos guicos. V. P. Hanmababao, Ungali na mapula, Magtabig, Mavindato. In the Philippines they call Palo santo the one described above. In other places they give this name to Guayaco and in others, as in Guadalupe, to Omphalobium pictum, whose decoction they give to women after delivery. Pers. Syn. pl. 510.
Cnestis poliphilla. Cnestis with many leaflets. Trunk lying on the ground. Leaves opposite, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets nine or more pairs in number, linear, pointed, hairy. Common petiole swollen at the base. Flowers in racemes. Stamens, the five alternating ones shorter than the others. Ovaries five, separated from one another. Five pods like legumes, fleshy, without hairs, and splitting lengthwise: some abort. Seeds solitary with an aril. = I have not seen the natives make any use of this plant. They call it ibaibaan, a diminutive of Iba, because it does indeed resemble it at first glance in its leaves; but it more closely resembles the Calamias. Flowers in March. * T. Ibaiban. Decand. Prod. p. 2. 87.
Cnestis corniculata. Cnestis with little horns. Leaves alternate; winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets egg-shaped, elongated, soft and hairy. Five cylindrical pods like legumes, fleshy, curved with the tip pointing downward, covered with hairs inside, and at the base a seed with an aril; some pods abort. = A shrub known in Tagudin, from where Father Juan Sorella sent me a branch. The fruits are fleshy, curved, and red in color. The seeds are black, the size of a small bean: they are eaten and are tasty; but very purgative. They call it in that town Sal-laday. Dec. ibid.

271
Cnestis glabra. Smooth Cnestis. Leaves opposite, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets numbering nine or more pairs; egg-shaped, very pointed, very entire, smooth, and somewhat stiff. In other respects, it is not distinguished from the preceding species. Decand. ibid.
OMPHALOBIUM. Calyx in five parts, persistent. Petals five. Stamens ten, monadelphous or half-polyadelphous at the base. Styles five. Pods from one to five, resembling legumes, with two valves that open, narrowed at the base, or with a small stalk. Seeds regularly solitary, rarely two, fixed at the lower part of the suture, and with an aril. Decand. Prod. p. 2. 85.
Omphalobium pictum. Painted Omphalobium. Trunk straight. Leaves alternate, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets numbering six or seven pairs, egg-shaped, elongated, pointed, entire, smooth, and somewhat sticky. Flowers in a panicle. Calyx the color of the corolla, persistent, in five parts. Corolla of five petals, linear, spotted with flesh-colored marks. Stamens ten, fixed on a common membrane that surrounds the ovary: the five alternate ones are longer. Anthers half-triangular. Ovaries five, barely joined below. Styles as long as the stamens. Stigmas slightly cleft in two parts. One pod, like a legume (the other four abort), egg-shaped with a point, without hairs inside, opening lengthwise, with one oval seed fixed at the base of the pod and entirely covered with a fleshy aril. = Small trees of about two or three varas, which I have seen in various places. Flowers in October. — All the species cited above have pods that are more or less swollen, of a flesh color, and which are already obtuse and obliquely truncated, or somewhat pointed. The seeds have a disagreeable odor. New species?
SPERGULA. Pod with one chamber, six valves (five according to Jussieu), and many seeds. Calyx in five parts. Corolla of five entire petals. Stamens five or ten. Decand. Prod. p. 1. 394.
Spergula serrata. Serrated Spergula. Stem straight, cylindrical. Leaves sessile, opposite, clasping the stem, lanceolate, serrated, with small dots on the surfaces, and with two stipules at the base. Flowers axillary, solitary? Peduncles very long. Calyx inferior, in five lanceolate parts. Corolla of five lanceolate, obtuse, and entire petals. Stamens ten (sometimes five or six), somewhat shorter than the corolla. Ovary seated within the flower, egg-shaped, with five channels. Style none. Stigmas five, globose before maturity. Pod with five channels and five valves, one chamber, and very many seeds, somewhat elongated, fixed on a column that has five channels. = This plant, which I have seen in Pasig, in fields already dry after rice has been planted, barely reaches the height of one palmo, and is not known to the Indians. It has much mucilage,

272
and it is neither caustic nor bitter. The ordinary number of stamens is ten; but I have seen flowers with five and six. Flower described in En. New species.

OXALIS. Calyx of five pieces. Petals joined below by their little claws, at which they terminate. Capsule with five chambers and five angles, along which it splits. Lin. Syst. veg. 784.

Oxalis acetosella. Wood Sorrel. Stem creeping, spreading, and smooth. Leaves horizontal, ternate, with a very long common petiole. Leaflets sessile, inversely heart-shaped, and hairy along the edges. Flowers axillary and terminal, up to three in number, on a very long common peduncle, which is likewise of the same length. Calyx as in the genus. Corolla of five petals, terminating in small claws. Stamens ten, monadelphous at the base: the five shorter ones bearing a gland on the outside of the base. Ovary long with striations. Styles five, short. Stigmas half-globose. Capsule pyramidal, with five angles and five chambers, each containing many oval seeds wrapped in an aril, from which they spring loose elastically. = This plant, which barely reaches a foot in height, grows on walls as well as on the ground, and has an agreeable acid taste; from it an essential salt is extracted that removes iron stains and ink stains from clothing. In Spain it is called Aleluya. When the capsules are ripe, the slightest touch sends the seeds flying to a distance of two feet. Its flowers open at nine in the morning and close at one in the afternoon. *T. Taingan daga. Susocoyoli. V. Darasig. P., Malabalugbug daguis, Ayo, Cungi, Yayo. Lin. ibid. 734.

BIOPHYTUM. Calyx of five pieces. Petals five. Stamens ten, free. Styles five, split at the apex. Capsule egg-shaped and globose, appearing to have five sides. Decand. Prod. p. 1. 689.

Biophytum sensitivum. Sensitive Biophytum. Stem erect, knotted, and without branches. Leaves winged without an odd leaflet, in whose place there is a small stylet. Leaflets approaching a linear shape, with a small stylet at the apex, numbering eleven to thirteen pairs, with two stipules at each pair. Common petioles long, swollen at the base, arranged in a whorl around and at the end of the stem. Flowers sessile in a whorl at the ends of very long peduncles that rise from the center of the petioles. Calyx of five pieces. Corolla of five petals forming a tube, terminating in small claws, rounded and slightly notched at the top. Stamens ten, free. A small gland on the outer base of each short stamen. Styles five. Capsule egg-shaped, with five angles and many seeds. = This plant grows at most to the height of a hand's span. When touched by hand, it immediately closes its little leaves downward: which is why the natives call it the shameful plant, or the one that feels. The local healers say that by placing it—

273
placed under the head of the sick person, it induces sleep: this virtue, if it has it, they surely infer from the fact that the plant appears to sleep by closing its leaves. How many very certain virtues of plants might have been discovered by means of such omens? Father Clain, in his little treatise on the plants of the Philippines, calls it Cassia vomitoria, but I have not heard that it is used to cause vomiting. Its flowers should be observed in the morning. It is common in many places. Flowers in September. *T, Macahiya, Damonghiya. 1 Mahihiin. Decand. ibid. 690. — Some other pair of stamens is found slightly fused at the base.

SPONDIAS. Calyx with five teeth. Corolla of five petals. Drupe with a nut of five chambers. Linnaeus Syst. veg. 729.

Spondias dulcis. Sweet Spondias. Trunk with twisted and disordered branches. Alternate leaves, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets numbering four to nine pairs, approaching a lanceolate shape, serrated and smooth. Flowers in clusters. Own peduncle long. Calyx small, with five obtuse teeth. Corolla much longer than the calyx, of five fleshy petals. Stamens ten: the five alternating ones longer. Filaments thick, awl-shaped. Ovary very thick, with channels. Styles almost none. Stigmas globose. Drupe oval, fleshy, with four furrows that do not meet at the bottom, with a large and very hard nut, endowed with four or more ribs, and as many chambers, each containing one seed. = This tree, known to everyone, with its very disordered branches, rises to a height of four or five varas. It is as thick as a human body, and bears fruit before its leaves. The shape of the fruit is what has caused it to be called Sirihuelas; a word that can easily be seen to be a simple corruption of Ciruelas (plums), which it resembles. The fruit, then, has pale yellow flesh and purple skin. It is eaten and is not unpleasant, although it is noted to be astringent, and it is useful in dysentery; but the nut is reputed to be poisonous. The wood is hard, and the tree takes root easily, even from a stake. At the beginning of January, I put into the ground a branch as thick as an arm, and by the end of the month it already had flowers and fruit. On these trees I have grafted, by budding, small branches of mango, and they remained alive for more than a month: afterwards they died; it may be that they could be made to succeed with careful attention. *T, Sirihuelas. Lin. ibid.

AVERRHOA. Calyx of five leaflets. Five petals, inclined outward. Fruit with five angles, oblong, and with five chambers. Lin. Syst. veg. 728.

Averrhoa bilimbi. Averrhoa bilimbi. Leaves winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets numbering twelve pairs, egg-shaped, linear, pointed, soft, and hairy. Flowers on the trunk and branches. Stamens ten: the five alternating ones longer. Pistils divergent.

274
Stigmas thick. Pome oblong, blunt at the tip, with five large angles. = This tree is usually nine or twelve feet tall. Its leaves are somewhat sensitive and fold downward when touched. The fruit is valued by the natives, both for its pleasant acidity and for making sweets. Although Linnaeus applies the name Bilimbi to this species, in the Philippines that name is used for the following one. According to the learned Author of the Flora of the Antilles, a most useful syrup is made from the fruits of these trees for inflammatory diseases, and it is a pity it is not used in the Islands. Combined with a decoction of rice in its husk, they form an admirable remedy for those same diseases, and whenever one seeks to moderate the great activity of the blood and control bilious diarrheas and colic. *T, Calamias, Camias. V. Quilingiva. I. Pias. Lin. ibid.

Averrhoa carambola. Averroa carambola. Leaves winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets numbering three or four pairs, obliquely egg-shaped, pointed: the odd one approaches a lance shape. Flowers on the trunk, branches, and leaf axils. Pome oblong, with five very prominent angles. = Small trees like those of the previous species. With their fruits, which are acidic, a syrup is also made that is very useful in the diseases mentioned above. The leaves are sensitive and move downward when shaken with a little force, though not as much as those of the Camias. In a ceramic cup, grind the flowers of the Calamias, add water, and place the cup over a very gentle fire; a most beautiful purple color will be obtained, which will turn into a lovely violet if a little vinegar is added. The juice of the balimbin is said to be very effective for removing stains from clothing. Fl. in Jan. *T, Balimbin. Bilimbin Lin. ibid.

Averrhoa pentandra. Averroa with five stamens. Leaves sometimes opposite, sometimes alternate, winged with an odd leaflet. Leaflets numbering three or four pairs, obliquely egg-shaped, pointed, entire, and smooth. Petioles proper, very short. Flowers axillary, on the trunk and branches, in compound clusters. Calyx in five parts. Corolla twice as long as the calyx, bell-shaped, in five rounded parts. Stamens ten: five alternate, short, and sterile. Ovary seated within the flower, oval with five angles. Styles five, close together. Stigmas somewhat thick. Capsule with five chambers. = Small trees with crimson flowers; in Malinta I have not seen the ripe fruit. Fl. in Oct. — The corolla is monopetalous, but perhaps in time the petals separate. New species.

POUPARTIA. Calyx very small, with five lobes. Corolla of five petals. Receptacle notched. Styles close together. Nut with five chambers. Lin. Syst. veg. 728.

Poupartia pinnata. Pouparcia alada. Leaves semi-opposite,

275
winged with an odd one. Leaflets in number of seven or more pairs, obliquely egg-shaped, elongated, very entire, and smooth. Flowers in a panicle. Calyx inferior, split almost to the base into five parts. Corolla longer than the calyx, of five linear petals. Stamens ten, as long as the corolla, equal in height, fixed below the edges of the nectary, and united along their entire length to the petals. Nectary a flat, many-sided plate. Pistils five? pressed together at the top and separated below, of which four regularly abort. Drupe oval, appearing to have three rounded angles, with a not very hard nut, of three angles, three or four chambers, and solitary seeds. This tree is not well known, and is considered of the first rank. I have seen it in Bauang, Batangas. The wood is soft and not very durable. The natives use it to make small boats or canoes. The nut of the Drupe, although bony, can be cut easily with a knife, and some of its seeds do not fully develop; but one can see the vestiges of the chambers, narrowed by those of the perfect seeds, which naturally should have been five. The fruit is the size of a West Indian cherry, and I doubt whether it is edible. The tree produces no resin. The leaves are about two inches long. Flowers in March and August. — Although I have said that the pistils are five, this is because they appeared so to me when I wrote that many years ago; but perhaps they are thick styles, and the genus one, still hidden in the base of the calyx. New species!

DODECANDRIA.
MONOGINIA.

BRUGUIERA. Calyx with ten or twelve linear lobes. Petals ten or twelve, with two folds, bifid at the tip. Stamens twenty or twenty-two, fixed in pairs to the petals. Capsule of one chamber and one seed, arising from the calyx. Seeds girdled at the base with a fleshy, angular, club-shaped perisperm.

BRUGUIERA NEMOROSA. FOREST BRUGUIERA. Leaves opposite, oval, obtuse, with the edges rolled downward, entire and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary in compound, short racemes. Calyx adherent, globose, with eight or nine lobes. Corolla of eight or nine petals, as long as the calyx, egg-shaped, broad, truncated at the tip, which ends in three lobes, fixed by their little claws in the divisions of the calyx. Stamens sixteen or eighteen, as long as the calyx, some fixed in the middle of its lobes and the others in its divi-

276
Anthers small. Style as long as the stamens, and surrounded at the base by a glandular disk or crown of many lobes. Stigma shield-shaped, with five star-like lobes. Drupe slightly fleshy, globose, larger than a pea, crowned with the teeth of the calyx, the nut thin and fragile, with two seeds separated by a partition, and a single granular fleshy mass shaped like a half-moon that covers both of them. = Trees as thick as a thigh, three or four fathoms tall, which I have seen in the Pangisihan of Angat. The leaves are two or three inches long, and the flowers are like peas; the fruit is twice as large. They are not well known. The description by Boitard fits them better than those of the various authors cited by Decandolle in various places in part 3 of his work. It does not appear to be Rhizophora gymnorihza of Linnaeus either.

RHIZOPHORA. Calyx inferior, with four teeth. Petals four, or more. One very long seed, fleshy at the base, turned upside down. Lin. Syst. veg. 746.

Rhizophora gymnorhiza. Rhizophora with the exposed root. Roots emerge from the trunk of the tree, forming arches until they enter the ground, so that the trunk sometimes does not touch it at all. At times roots emerge from the extremities of the tree, directing themselves toward the ground until they reach it, where they take hold. Trunk rough, moderately covered with opposite branches. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, somewhat obtuse, smooth. Petioles short, compressed. Flowers terminal, in a kind of umbel. Calyx shaped like an inverted cone, with ribs and eight pointed teeth. Corolla of eight small petals, fixed between the divisions of the calyx, keeled, split to the middle into two lobes, with hairy edges and tips. Stamens sixteen, two per petal and fixed to them. Anthers small in this species. Style shorter than the corolla, awl-shaped. Stigma in three parts. Fruit a long seed shaped like a club, covered at the base by the receptacle, which becomes large. Below the fruit, or in the receptacle, there are four or six hidden glands. = This tree, called by some foreigners Paletuvier, and known to all the natives, is very common on the beaches. Its fruit is about three inches long. It grows to a height of nine or ten varas. The fruits hang pendulously, and when they fall into the mud they immediately embed themselves there, ready to put out roots. Its bark, called cascalote, is flesh-colored, astringent, and of great use. Fishermen steep it in water in a boat and immerse their cotton nets in it; the nets come out dyed a dark flesh-color like blood, which makes the thread very slippery and impenetrable to water. This operation, which they practice frequently, makes their nets last for many years. Other plants also serve the same purpose, and

277
among them the seed bananas, steeping them in the infusion. The blue dyers likewise prepare their skeins of cotton by steeping them in an infusion of this bark. I have tried to find out whether they do this for the fastness of the color, or to save dye; but I have been unable to arrive at a clear conclusion. I lean toward the latter: for they claim that by immersing the thread in bacao or bacauan, it very quickly takes on the deep blue color desired. Some also use the same infusion for dyeing fabrics the purple shade they call sarampuli, which is made with indigo, perfected by means of this bark. Washerwomen make great use of the charcoal of the Bacao for ironing clothes. The branches of the tree are also used as stakes to fence plantations, being quite durable for that purpose; they are likewise used as anchors for boats. In the trunk of the tree, one sometimes notices certain holes that show a kind of sweating, which serves as a sign to the natives that inside there lodges a worm sometimes a foot long, resembling a gut, which they call tambilog; they extract it by splitting the wood, and eat it alive as it is, adding at most a little lemon juice; and they consider it a delicious food.
* T., Bacao, Bacauan. I., Oongon. Lin. ibid. 747.—There is another species with regular roots and with a corolla of eight keeled petals, rounded and cleft in two at the tip, terminating in seven bristles or hairs, and one more in the cleft.= The cooked fruit is edible. In Cavite they call the tree Biuas.

Rhizophora polyandra. Many-stamened Rhizophora.
Leaves clustered at the ends of the branches, opposite, very entire, and smooth. Petioles half as long as the leaf, cylindrical. Flowers axillary, solitary. Calyx fleshy, very large, with eleven to thirteen long, awl-shaped teeth. Corolla: the number of petals corresponds to that of the calyx teeth, and their shape as in the preceding species. Stamens in double the number of the calyx teeth, that is, twenty-two, twenty-four, or twenty-six: two per petal. Anthers long. Stigma in three parts. Fruit as in the preceding species, but larger.= The properties are the same.
* T., Bacao, Bacauan.—This may be the species Sexangula of Dec. Prod. p. 3. 32.

Rhizophora candel. Candel Rhizophora.
Leaves opposite, wedge-shaped, with a small notch at the apex, very entire, smooth. Petiole half as long as the leaf, cylindrical. Flowers axillary, regularly in groups of two or three, and rarely more, placed on a short common peduncle. Calyx small, with four or five straight teeth, set upon three scales. Corolla of five petals, somewhat notched at
43

278
above, and with the tips laciniate. Nect. one zone, or rim, that surrounds the germ. Stam. ten. Filam. very short. Style thick. Stigmas three. Fruit a single seed shaped like a club, very long, with small angles, and whose base is enclosed within the receptacle, which becomes long and rough.= The properties are the same as in the other species. *T., Ligasan, Tigasan, Bacao. V., Pototan. Lin. ibid. 747.
Rhizophora mangle. Rizofora mangle. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, very entire, dotted with small points underneath, and terminating in a rather long deciduous tip. Petiole short with a channel. Flowers in pairs, on a common peduncle. Cal. as in the genus. Cor. of four narrow petals. Nect. none. Stam. twelve. Filam. none. Anthers very large, angular. Style none. Stigmas two prominent points. Fruit the same as in the previous species (candel) but larger and without striations.= Trees similar in every way to those of the species gymnorhiza, noting that in these everything expressed there is verified even more perfectly. I also suspect that the bark would be suitable for tanning hides. The natives use the fruits of this tree to make a kind of fairly good glue: for this purpose they boil them in water, and after grinding them in a mortar, they spread this paste over the bamboo partitions of houses, or between the teeth of the cane mills used to grind rice, and it adheres very well. To become well acquainted with the flowers, it is necessary to examine those that are about to open. The petals have a small red spot at the tip. Fl. in Feb. *T., Bacao, Bacauan. Lin. ibid.
Rhizophora longissima. Rizofora very long. Leaves opposite, wedge-shaped, very entire, smooth, and fleshy. Petioles short, cylindrical. Flowers in an umbel, five in number. Common peduncle, with a single-leaved involucre of five teeth at the base. Cal. double: the outer one with two teeth, long and fleshy. Cor. of five petals. Stam. ten. Style almost as long as the stamens. Fruit as in the previous species, but much longer and larger, dotted with raised points that make it rough.= This tree grows as large as those of the other species. Its wood is hard, like ebony, solid, incorruptible, and reddish. The fruit is sometimes two and a half feet long. The bark of the tree yields a red dye, with which silk and abaca have been colored in former times, producing a very fine color. It can also serve for painting; but the principal use that the native makes of the bark is to add it to the liquor drawn from coconuts and other palm species, which they call tuba, to give it strength. It would also be excellent for tanning hides, especially deer hide. *T., Tangal. V., Tongog. New species.

279
Rhizophora plicata. Rhizophora with folds. Leaves opposite, lanceolate, entire, smooth, with one very conspicuous fold, and rarely two, parallel to the midrib. Petiole short, channeled above. Flowers solitary. Corolla with petals split to the base, hairy along the margins, and with a single long hair rising from the back of each one. In all other respects, as was said of Rhizophora polyandra, of which it may perhaps be a simple variety. *T., Bacao, Bacauan.
HALESIA. Corolla with four laciniae. Calyx with four teeth, superior. Drupe dry, inflated, with four seeds, and as many winged angles. Lin. Syst. veg. 749.
Halesia? Ternata. Halesia? ternate. Trunk striate. Leaves alternate, ternate. Common petiole long. Leaflets broad, ovate, entire and smooth. Flowers axillary, in a sort of raceme. Cal. Cor. Stam. Pist.... Drupe with a dry nut, with four wings arranged in a cross: the two opposite ones ovate, very large, extending horizontally, with small veins running toward the apex; the other two much smaller, and sometimes like simple projecting, pointed angles. The seed nucleus thin, bony, compressed, with four angles: the two opposite ones most notable; the seed with four sides: the two opposite ones more acute: at times it appears that there is a chamber for another.= A vine that climbs over trees. Each large wing is one inch long, and equally wide at the base. The dry seed smells of balsam. I saw it in Angat, and it is not known. Flowers in September. A new species?— Although I have not seen the flowers, I am persuaded that it belongs to this genus. Nevertheless, it is necessary to examine them carefully.
CRATÆVA. Corolla of four petals, directed to one side. Calyx with four laciniae, inferior. Berry with a small stalk, with two chambers, and many seeds in a pulp. Lin. ibid. Jus. Gén. pl. 244.
Cratæva religiosa. Crateva religiosa. Trunk erect, without thorns. Leaves scattered, ternate, all equal. Common petiole long. Leaflets broad, lanceolate, and smooth. Flowers in a corymb. Calyx of four small leaves, distant from each other, broad, lanceolate, of the color of the corolla, alternating with its petals, and fixed on the edge of a flat fleshy body. Corolla of four petals (the two smaller ones) ovate, inserted in the said fleshy body, four times longer than the calyx, and with long claws: all directed a little to one side. Stamens more than twenty, as long as the petals, and fixed in the elevated center of the receptacle. Filaments purple. Anthers oval. Ovary on a stipe as long as the stamens. Style none. Stigma thick. Berry globose, with one chamber, and many bony seeds, submerged confusedly in a

280
pulp. = A small tree of about five to seven varas in height, without thorns, and with very beautiful flowers, which I have seen near Santa Cruz in Ilocos, and it is also found in Imos. The petals are between white and pale yellow; and the stamens, purple. The thickness of the trunk is like that of a thigh: the petals are one inch long. It is known to the natives. Flowers in January. * I., Balai namoc. Lin. ibid.

Crataeva octandra. Crataeva with eight stamens. Trunk without thorns or hooks. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, very entire, smooth, and with a stiff little point at the apex. Petioles very short. Axillary flowers in umbellate racemes. Calyx inferior, in four oval, deep, concave, and tomentose on the outside divisions, fixed on a fleshy torus. Corolla green in color, with four oval petals, somewhat longer than the calyx, fixed on the said torus from below. Stamens eight. Filaments longer than the corolla and disordered, fixed at the central point of the flower, and united at the base. Anthers oval. Ovary globose, placed on a long stipe. Style none. Stigma round. Berry oval, with one chamber and many seeds. = A weak shrub, two brazas in height, and with two disordered branches. I have seen it in Ilocos, in the town of Piddig. The torus or fleshy body, where the calyx and corolla are fixed, resembles that of the previous species. It is not known to the natives. — By its eight stamens, it agrees with the genus Sodada; but in the plant described above those are monadelphous.

Vatica. Calyx with five laciniae. Corolla of five petals. Anthers fifteen, sessile, with four chambers. Fruit . . . Lin. Syst. veg. 748.

Vatica sinensis. Chinese Vatica. Leaves alternate, entire, smooth and stiff. Petioles very short. Axillary flowers in panicles. Calyx in five pointed and deep divisions: the two longer ones. Corolla of five petals, four times longer than the calyx, linear, fixed between the ovary and the base of the calyx, and alternate with its parts. Stamens fifteen, shorter than the calyx, fixed on the receptacle, and as if resting the base of the ovary upon them. Filaments very short and broad, in the manner of small pointed scales: the five solitary ones, alternating with five others that are double, one placed over the other. Anthers terminating in a stipe, flat, with two double wings; or if one prefers, four; two of them opposite the others. Ovary free, half-globose, seated upon the flower, depressed, with five lobes. Style short, and perforated along its length. Stigma depressed, with three or more lobes. Drupe with three, four, or five seeds. = A tree larger than the body of a man, eight or more brazas in height. It is common in the mountains of San Mateo, and can barely be distinguished from the following species except in its anthers. The corollas and the wings of the anthers are white. Flowers in May. Lin. ibid.

Vatica apteranthera. Vatica without wings on the anthers.
Leaves alternate, between ovate and lanceolate, entire, smooth and rather stiff. Petioles very short. Flowers in a panicle. Calyx, Corolla and Stamens as in the species sinensis. Anthers as if divided crosswise, and without wings. Drupe globose, with a thin nut, having three compartments and as many seeds. Everything else as in the other species. = It is a tree taller and more stout than the preceding one, which the Indians of Angat erroneously claim to be the true mangachapoi, from which very beautiful planks are obtained, and whose fruit, they say, is eaten roasted in the embers. The parts of the calyx are unequal: for two of them are longer. The anthers are singular, and as described above. The drupe, which is not fleshy, exudes a very transparent and nearly odorless resin before ripening. Flowers in May. * In Angat, Mangachapoi; but this belongs to the genus Dipterocarpus. New species.
Azaola. Calyx narrowed toward the middle and cleft into four parts. Corolla with nine to eleven laciniae, the alternating ones on the inside. Anthers with an awn. Pome oblong with about six seeds, whose covering is coriaceous and provided with a long scar: four of them abort. New genus.
Azaola betis. Azaola betis. Leaves crowded at the ends of the branches, lanceolate, broader beyond the middle, wavy, and stiff. Petioles very short, without stipules. Flowers terminal, in a dense raceme. Peduncle proper, long. Calyx inferior, somewhat shorter than the corolla, monofilous, swollen at the base and narrowed toward the middle, and afterwards cleft into four long, linear parts. Corolla the same color as the calyx, fixed on the receptacle, monopetalous, with a short tube, divided into ten lanceolate, straight laciniae; the five alternating ones inside the others. Stamens ten to twenty, fixed in the throat of the corolla. Filaments nearly absent. Anthers long, terminated by an awn. Ovary globose, seated within the calyx. Style very long and deciduous. Stigma as if lobed. Pome oblong, pointed, with about six seeds, also oblong, covered with a fragile membranous bark, which has one projecting or raised side, adorned with a long scar: four of them abort. = A second-order tree, with hard, incorruptible, reddish, very bitter wood and yellow bark. The fruit is two inches long and looks like a plum; the flowers are sparse, and the seeds contain much oil. When the trunk is wounded it exudes a milky sap, which applied to the abdomen expels intestinal worms; the corollas are green like the calyx. The Indians use the wood and bark in medicine and in the construction of their houses. Some grind the wood into powder and use it like tobacco, as it causes sneezing. It is common in Pampanga and other parts, and is excellent for the keels of

282
vessels. The laciniae of the corolla number nine to eleven. — Could this be the same tree that in Pangasinan they call Bacayao? It is close to the genus Bassia. As it seems to me a new genus, in testimony of my gratitude, I have dedicated the tree to Mr. D. Iñigo Gonzalez y Azaola, who has greatly assisted me with his knowledge and some very useful books for the composition of this work. Flowers in February. *T., P., Betis. — It differs from Achras dissecta and from the variety Baluta of Pers. Syn. pl. 236. t. 1.

PALAQUIUM. Calyx in six parts: the three inner ones. Corolla very long, in five or six parts. Stamens united two by two, or three by three. Pome oval, crowned with the hardened style, with six compartments, and solitary seeds. New genus.

Palaquium lanceolatum. Lance-leaved Palaquio. Leaves alternate, lanceolate, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Flowers solitary? Calyx inferior, persistent, in six parts, fleshy, egg-shaped: the three inner ones within the others. Corolla three or four times longer than the calyx, monopetalous, with an open throat, in five or six deep, narrow, pointed parts, very much recurved downward. Stamens numbering about eighteen or nineteen, or fewer, fixed at the throat of the corolla, longer than it, and opposite its parts. Filaments flat, united at the base, two by two, or three by three. Anthers long and twisted. Style longer than the stamens. Stigma simple. Pome oval, crowned with the hardened style, with six compartments, each containing one seed: some regularly abort. = A first-order tree, known in Batangas and in other areas, though under various names. Its wood is quite hard and is used in the construction of houses. The fruit is larger than a hazelnut; but I do not know whether it grows larger, since I have never seen it ripe. The flowers were dried. Flowers in March. *T., Bagalangit.

The flowers resemble, in their calyx, those of Achras Zapote. This tree, I am persuaded, is a new genus, and should be placed among the zapotes of Jussieu, although it does not match any of those that the Author lists there. It is very similar to the following one.

Palaquium latifolium. Broad-leaved Palaquio. Leaves crowded at the tips of the branches, obtuse, lanceolate, entire, smooth above and somewhat hairy below. Petioles very short, somewhat angular. Flowers axillary, solitary. Peduncle long. Calyx free, split almost to the base, in six oval parts: the three inner ones more rounded and with membranous margins. Corolla. Stamens. Pistil... Pome oblong, pointed, somewhat curved, crowned with the long and hard style, with one or two oval, pointed seeds, with a leathery, thin covering, convex on the outside, and on the inside somewhat ex-

283
hollowed and flat: but it is evident that there are chambers for others. = A large, beautiful tree, worthy of being transplanted to Gardens. It is known in S. Mateo and Tala. It exudes a milky sap, and its leaves are about one foot long and some four inches wide, with a light, soft, tawny-colored down on the underside. In the calyx it cannot be distinguished from the Achras zapote. The fruit is like a small plum, edible and somewhat tasty: the outer bark is smooth and of a pale green color. The seed, though smaller, closely resembles that of the Achras lucuma, which in Manila they call maméi. Flowers in February. *T., Palac palac.
These trees are very similar to the Duclitan and Balitbitan, which I have placed in the genus Sideroxylon.
Palaquium oloiferum. Oil-bearing Palaquio. Leaves lanceolate, broader from the middle upward, with tawny-colored down. Terminal flowers, with a short stalk. Oval pome, like a small hen's egg, with a gray skin, two or more chambers, and solitary seeds, oblong, pointed, with a long scar, and the covering between membranous and bony. = Large trees, known in Tagudin, and nearly identical to the palacpalac. From their seeds the native people of that town extract a very clean, fragrant oil, which they use in cooking and for lighting: for this purpose they gather and store the seeds. I., Daracan.
TRIUMFETTA. Corolla of five petals. Calyx of five pieces, or none. Capsule with four chambers, and bristling with stiff hairs. Lin. Syst. veg. 750.
Triumfetta semitriloba. Three-lobed Triumfetta. Stem erect. Leaves scattered: the lower ones semi-trilobed, unevenly serrated, soft, and downy: the upper ones ovate and pointed: the uppermost, nearly lanceolate. Petioles shorter than the leaves. Flowers axillary and terminal. Calyx deciduous, of five leaflets, linear, colored, and terminating above in a hood. Corolla of five petals, with small claws, somewhat shorter than the calyx, and rounded at the top. Stamens ten, sometimes twelve, separated from one another, shorter than the corolla, and surrounded by a small membrane. Style as long as the stamens. Stigmas in two parts, bent to the sides. Upper capsule small, globose, bristling with soft spines directed upward, with four chambers and one seed in each. = This plant reaches the height of a fathom or more. The native commonly confuses it with the Urena, which is used as mallow, employing the root in enemas; but I have not heard that any harmful accident has resulted from this. It resembles the Urena in every respect except in the flower. The bark is also very tough, like that of the Urena. When a decoction of the root is drunk in doses of one ounce,

284
it is useful in ulcers of the intestines. Its flowers should be examined in the afternoon, as they are then open. By the flower and the membrane that encircles the stamens, it closely resembles Corchorus. Flowers in October. *T., Colotan bilog. Lin. ibid.
LITSÆA. Involucre of five or six pieces, very small, containing four to twelve small florets. Corolla nearly absent. Stamens ten to eighteen. Filaments inferior, glandular at the base. Berry (Drupa?) with one seed. Flowers clustered, axillary: sometimes dioecious. Pers. Syn. pl. t. 2. 4.
LITSÆA LUZONICA. LITSEA OF LUZON. Leaves opposite, egg-shaped, oblong, entire, and smooth. Petioles very short. Terminal flowers in a panicle, with opposite peduncles: each one bearing six lanceolate, large, colored bracts; three on each side: and containing united about seven small florets. Calyx proper to the floret, persistent, funnel-shaped, narrowed toward the middle, shorter than the corolla, with five or six rounded teeth, and hairy inside. Corolla funnel-shaped, with the limb divided into six rounded parts, with a hairy and open throat. Stamens eleven or twelve, fixed at the throat. Filaments longer than the corolla. Anthers oval, two-chambered. Ovary superior, oval, sessile. Style single, as long as the stamens. Stigmas two, shield-shaped and bordered. Glans with one seed. = Small trees barely known, about three varas tall, that lean over their neighbors, which I saw in Arayat. The bracts are whitish, and the corollas are violet-colored. The seeds are like peas. I have not seen the ripe fruit. Flowers in January. * P., Balibai. New species.
PORTULACA. Corolla of five petals. Calyx bifid, inferior. Capsule with one chamber, which splits horizontally; sometimes with three valves. Lin. Syst. veg. 751.
PORTULACA OLERACEA. GARDEN PURSLANE. Stem prostrate on the ground, with branches spreading in a star pattern. Leaves fleshy, wedge-shaped, with bare axils. Flowers sessile, terminal on the small branches. Calyx with two large, deciduous teeth. Corolla of four or five petals, with a notch at the top. Stamens nine to fourteen. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma in four or six parts. Capsule that splits horizontally, with many very small, heart-shaped seeds. = This plant is well known to everyone, and is eaten cooked. It spreads so widely that it takes infinite effort to eradicate it. The stamens move with ease when touched with a needle or other object. Its yellowish flowers open at half past eight in the morning and close at ten. The syrup of purslane has at times cured the spitting of blood, even in chronic cases, as I have witnessed with amazement. The juice of the leaves is good, according to some authors, for removing cloudiness from the cornea of the

285
eyes. This plant, as well as the following one, in certain soils is purple in color. *T. Olasiman, Colasiman. C. Ausiman. Lin. ibid.
Portulaca meridiana. Meridian Purslane. Stem spreading, full of nodes covered with hairs. Leaves imbricate, very small, fleshy, elliptical, somewhat concave below and convex above. Flowers terminal, sessile. Calyx with four lobes, and hairy on the inside. Corolla of four petals, slightly notched at the top. There are also two small leaflets, or opposite membranes, shorter than the corolla, placed between it and the calyx, which serve as support for the corolla. Stamens seven or eight. Stigma in two or four parts. Fruit as in the preceding species.= This plant, very well known, spreads so extensively across the cultivated fields that it is very difficult to eradicate. Its pale yellow flowers open at noon and close at two o'clock. At other times they open at one in the afternoon; it also serves to treat spitting of blood, as does the preceding. * T., Sayican, but this name is also given to a species of euphorbia. Lin. ibid. 752.
Portulaca axiliflora. Axillary-flowered Purslane. Stem prostrate on the ground, with branches arranged like stars. Leaves sheathing the stem, opposite (one smaller than the other), between oval and round, barely notched, smooth. Petioles with two stipules at the base and two small teeth toward the middle. Flowers axillary, solitary, sessile. Calyx in two pointed parts. Corolla longer than the calyx, with five oval petals bearing small claws. Stamens about fifteen, somewhat shorter than the corolla. Style as long as the stamens. Stigma simple. Capsule shaped like an inverted pyramid, with many seeds, splitting horizontally.= This plant, well known in the vicinity of Manila, is eaten. At first glance it can be confused with a species of Boerhaavia. The leaves have a red border on their edge. Fl. in En. * T., Toston. Pers. Sin. pl. t. 2. 6.
PEMPHIS. Calyx shaped like a top, with twelve teeth: the alternating ones smaller. Petals six. Stamens twelve: the alternating ones shorter. Capsule semi-spherical, one-chambered, with many seeds, splitting circularly toward the base. Jus. Gen. pl. 331.
Pemphis setosa. Bristly Pemphis. Leaves opposite, approaching a lanceolate shape, entire, very fleshy, and hairy. Petioles very short. Flowers axillary, solitary. Calyx bell-shaped, striate, with twelve small teeth: the six alternating ones longer. Corolla of six petals, attached to the six shorter teeth of the calyx. Stamens twelve, attached to the walls of the calyx: the six alternating ones longer. Ovary superior, globose. Stigma thick, depressed, from which many long fine threads emerge. Capsule superior, splitting circularly, with many irregularly shaped seeds.= These trees-

286
trees, which grow only on the rocks of the seashores,
are very small, reaching at most six feet in
height. The leaves are one inch long, and the wood is
very hard. The natives do not know it. The resemblance is great
to the eye, between the flowers of this tree and those of the Banaba.
Flowers in April. — Linnaeus places it among the Lythrums. The name
of the species, which appears to be new, has been taken from the threads
of the stigma.

DODECANDRIA.

TRIGINIA.

EUPHORBIA. Calyx one-leafed, swollen. Corolla of four or
five petals, seated in the calyx. Capsule of three pods,
with solitary seeds. Lin Syst. veg. 759.
Euphorbia parannaquensis. Euphorbia of Parañaque.
Stem erect, somewhat branched. Leaves opposite, linear, ser-
rated, with smooth spiny serrations. Petioles very short.
Flowers in an umbel, which divides into two parts, and subdivides
again afterward. = A plant one foot tall, in Parañaque.
New Sp.
Euphorbia hirta. Rough-haired Euphorbia. Stem erect,
cylindrical, and hairy. Leaves opposite, between obliquely
ovate and rhombus-shaped, serrated and hairy. Petioles
very short, with two awl-shaped stipules at the base. Flowers in
a hemispherical umbel, split into five parts, and each one
subdivides again two more times. Universal involucre of three awl-shaped
leaflets: the middle one larger. Calyx bell-shaped,
in five laciniate parts. Corolla of five petals, fixed in the
parts of the calyx, fleshy, orbicular, and at the base with an
appendage also orbicular, concave, and of a different color from
the petals. Stamens eight, fixed at the base of the calyx. Filaments
some longer than others. Anthers two on each filament. In addition
there are four filaments without anthers, also fixed in the ca-
lyx. Ovary with a stalk longer than the flower, bent
downward. Styles three, bifid. Stigmas simple. Three capsules
united, hairy, with three angles, and in each one a
globose seed. = This precious plant, which exudes milk, is very common
everywhere. It grows in good soil to the height of two
feet, and is used in medicine. It is applied to venomous
bites, like piper parvifolium. Crushed and applied
as well, it is celebrated for its virtue in stopping the blood of
wounds, as if by miracle. Everyone who is a lover of their fellow
human beings ought to take the greatest interest in knowing it: I myself have seen

287
the prodigious effects it produces, stopping the bleeding of wounds. Sometimes it is enough to apply it just once. * T., Batobatonis, Sayican, Gatasgatas, Golandrina. V., Gatasgatas, Buyayava, Tavava, Bovi. P., Malismalis, Sisiohan, Bolobotones, Magatas. Others call it golondrina. Lin. ibid. 762.

Euphorbia dulcis? Sweet Euphorbia? Leaves opposite, obliquely egg-shaped, oblong, smooth. Petioles very short. Axillary flowers in an umbel, which divides into two parts, with a solitary small flower in the middle; and then subdivides further several times. = It is a common plant on the seashores, greenish-white in color: its height is about two feet, and it puts out branches. I doubt whether this is the species. It is very heavily infested with light red cochineal insects. Lin. ibid. 764.

Euphorbia tiraculli. Tiraculli Euphorbia. Trunk erect. Branches cylindrical, joined one to another, with very small leaves at the tips. Flowers in an umbel. Calyx remote from the fruit, with five rounded, fleshy little leaflets. Corolla has no more than five groups of woolly hairs in the divisions of the calyx. Stamens easily deciduous, five in number, in the divisions of the calyx, with anthers either doubled or irregular. Everything else as in the genus. = Small trees about the thickness of a thigh, and three or four varas tall. They are common in Parañaque and in some other places, where they are known by the name Consuelda. Writers both from outside and within the country say it is admirable for joining broken bones. The basis of this discovery was probably the observation of how the branches fuse together. Anyone wishing to try it should be careful: its sap is so caustic that it raises blisters immediately, and even buffaloes fear it; for this reason they use it to make fences. * T., Catuit, Consuelda. Lin. ibid. 760.

Euphorbia pentagona. Five-sided Euphorbia. Trunk erect, jointed, five-sided, with two rows of paired spines at the angles. Leaves spatula-shaped, somewhat pointed and fleshy. Calyx bell-shaped, with five lobes having two angles at the tip and four scales below, the two outermost being the most distant. Corolla with many imbricated petals, spatula-shaped, with frayed tips. Stamens arranged in groups. Styles three. Stigmas somewhat thickened. Capsule three-celled, on a small stalk. = This plant reaches the height of a man. The natives use it to stupefy fish. In some places, especially in Ilocos, they make excellent fences with it for gardens. It is highly effective for treating corns and earaches; and some even say it cures deafness. For this purpose a leaf is roasted in the embers, and the warm juice is applied to the corn or dropped into the ear. * T., P., N., sorosoro, Sorog sorog, Bait, Lengua de perro. I., Carambuaya. New Spanish species?

288

DODECANDRIA.

PENTAGINIA.

GLINUS. Cal. of five leaflets. Cor. none. Nect. five bristles, split in two parts. Capsule with five angles, five chambers, five valves, and many seeds. Lin. Syst. veg. 768.

Glinus lotoides. Glinus resembling lotus. Stem half-forked, and nearly entirely prostrate, hairy. Lateral branches, articulated. Leaves sometimes lateral and opposite, sometimes star-like, between orbicular and elliptical, tomentose. Petioles short. Axillary flowers, two or more in number. Peduncles very short. Cal. inferior of five uncolored leaflets, concave and hairy: the two inner ones keeled and with their edges folded inward. Cor. none (according to Lin.) Nect. (Cor. according to Jus.) Five filaments, split in two parts. Stamens nine, ten, or eleven, fixed at the base of the calyx, and as long as it. Filaments flat, wide at the base. Anthers thick. Ovary with a small stalk, inside the calyx, conical, and with grooves. Styles five, short and somewhat stout. Stigmas simple. Capsule with five angles and five chambers: and in each one many seeds arranged in two rows. Seeds kidney-shaped, each attached to a spongy aril, with a long thread at the scar. = It is a common plant in the fields where rice is sown, yet hardly known. To become well acquainted with these flowers, one must examine the smallest ones, which are not yet very far advanced. Fl. in Jan. * T. Lobio. Lin ibid.

ICOSANDRIA.

MONOGINIA.

CACTUS. Cal. monophyllous, superior, imbricated. Cor. of many petals. Berry with one chamber and many seeds. Lin. Syst. veg. 770. 784.

Cactus opuntia. Prickly pear cactus. Trunk articulated, with thick, proliferous, obovate joints, or spatula-shaped, with clusters of stiff bristles, of which one or two are longer. Cal. very large, nearly cylindrical, superior, with fleshy, conical scales, and with clusters of hairs

289
stiff at the base. Cor. of many petals, terminating in small claws: the outer ones, smaller, broad, and terminating above with a point; the inner ones, larger, and broader, with a large sinus and a point at the apex. Stam. many, fixed in the calyx. Filam. much shorter than the corolla. Anth. elongated. Germen below the calyx. Style the length of the stamens. Stigmas more than six, awl-shaped. Berry oblong, with one chamber and many seeds.= I have seen this little tree in various gardens, and I believe it is from America. In Pasig it is called dilang baca, or tongue of the cow, and in Bauang espátula or spoon, on account of the shape of the leaves. It grows little more than a fathom tall. The calyx is marked with channels that form a network of scales, as in the Anonas. With the ash of this plant (which I suppose will be lye) and the fruit of the Aroma, they say a very good ink is obtained. The bruised leaves make a lather; and the Indians say that rubbing it on the head makes the hair grow or multiply. I have heard that in Spain an Augustinian friar cured kidney stones by having patients take in broth, or another liquor, the powders of the leaves of this plant, toasted in a new pot sealed with mud. Flowers in March. * T., Sandocsandoc, Dilang baca. Lin. ibid.

Cactus pitahaya. Cacto pitahaya. Stem erect, articulated, with segments of three compressed angles, and the edges remotely serrated, with three or four small spines in bundles at the serrations. Flowers solitary. Cal. monophyllous, tubular, much widened above, with many fleshy scales, imbricated and joined to one another at the base: the lower ones very short and rounded; the uppermost ones numbering more than twenty, very long, lanceolate, and some of the inner ones nearly the color of the corolla. Cor. bell-shaped, of about twenty nearly equal petals: one within another, the length of the calyx, and fixed toward their middle. Stam. innumerable, shorter than the corolla, some fixed at the base of the petals and others on the rest of the calyx tube, almost down to its base. Filam. forming a spiraling bell. Anth. oblong, very slender, with slightly wavy margins. Germen inferior. Style thick, hollow, and the length of the corolla. Stigma shield-shaped and divided into about twenty-eight thick awl-shaped parts. Berry lobed, with one chamber and innumerable seeds.= A most singular plant on account of its monstrous flowers, for the great size they reach, which I have seen in Manila. Their length is more than a foot, from the lower calyx scales; and their width above, a palm-breadth. The narrowest part, corresponding to the tube, is more than an inch. The highest scales of the calyx are grayish in color and about a hand's breadth
